x: Summer holidays in Europe are over and chartering activity has returned, with September laycans in the U.S. largely covered now and the gaze raising to October. Surplus vessels remain but as enquiries begin to build, there has been renewed interest for periods covering winter. Rate expectations are a significant discounts to average traded levels for modern vessels for this time of year, and reflect the growing sense that weak shipping fundamentals will override high LNG pricing and trading opportunities. Whether the Winter bid continues to improve remains to be seen, but a bridging of the wide bid/offer spread suggests a softer view of winter and that portfolios continue to edge to the long side heading into a Q4 where Qatari supply is still stranded and DES markets East and West keep putting off demand until it really hits. The Pacific has now corrected with challenging supply/demand balance, and unfortunately for owners the market has come off rather than the Atlantic market picking up. The few multi-month fixtures reported suggest that several players see this as the bottom of the market – so perhaps rates can only strengthen from here?

n: LNG Market Report
x: Spot activity remains broadly muted although the list of developing requirements has begun to build in both basins, giving some much needed encouragement to. High LNG prices prove a double-edged sword in a market predominantly controlled by subletters; whilst some prefer to hold back, the cost of idling and boil-off for others is of greater concern than negligible rates of hire and this has been a factor in rates falling so fast on the back of weak sentiment and high competition. The supply and demand fundamentals have reached a particularly soft level in recent weeks thanks to fewer cargoes, shorter distances and substantial fleet growth being felt in the Atlantic, where the majority of modern vessels have been positioned. The resistance shown in the East is proving to be more of a lag than a snag and rates look set to fall further unless more demand emerges for September laycans. There remains a real possibility that availability becomes constricted by tonnage warming up, with insufficient opportunities East of Suez and unattractive econs further West.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The complete collapse in the Atlantic freight market continues, with owners and subletters having to battle not only against a considerable number of competing vessel but also against sharp FOB economics. The fall in headline rates is stark and is highly unusual outside of the shoulder months, but reflects a dynamic often seen in the LNG spot market: when rates begin to move one way or the other, they can accelerate so rapidly as subletters see the same market signals. There are signs that some players will prefer to hold on to tonnage rather than sublet in this market, although this is likely to support a modest floor rather than materially raise rates at this stage. The Pacific is still considerably higher, although it is somewhat illiquid and deals have been concluded at surprisingly high rates given the number of available vessels (mainly due to cargo-specific restrictions). Looking a little further forward, there is more tonnage emerging in September and with less motivation to ballast back West this may apply some downward pressure. If the spread does close, will it be led by an Atlantic revival or a softening Pacific?

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The Atlantic spot market remains muted, with a small number of requirements seeing a considerable number of open vessels. Rates have cooled considerably and with the ongoing lack of liquidity, what bids there are suggest the trend will continue downwards for a while yet. However, where the West is quiet, the market East of Suez has gained momentum and seen a steady stream of firm requirements and subsequent fixtures to keep owners and subletters busy. This activity has helped whittle down the availability list and softened the decline, although it has not been enough to see rates reverse their recent fall. Charterers’ cargo-specific preferences are often dictating the vessel fixed rather than price tag, so average rates remain relatively firm across the tonnage classes versus the drops seen in the Atlantic. The growing delta between the basins is significant enough that owners with ships redelivering in the East, or who had plans to ballast West, may now opt to stay put and trade in the more active Pacific spot market.  The multimonth market continues to point the way through winter, and that way looks to be relatively flat. High LNG prices and low European storage may not come to Owners’ rescue in the coming months, as the bearish fundamentals are finally winning through.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Atlantic rates have come under considerable pressure, with a growing availability list chasing relatively few requirements and competing not just against each other but also against aggressive FOB structures. The impact on spot rates has been dramatic, to the extent that the Pacific basin now commands a premium for the first time this year. The market East of Suez has also had to contend with excess tonnage, but so far rates have been supported by the premiums charterers are prepared to pay for larger, more modern vessels. There is more likely to be further downward pressure in both basins, as Atlantic sublets try to accommodate their own backstops dates while Pacific vessels are at risk of warming up; unless more cargoes emerge to fill the gap between now and the early-September requirements, the list of ships requiring cool-down threatens to grow substantially. There have also been several multi-month fixtures, spanning periods through this winter out to the end of next year, at rates that suggest a muted winter season. There has been some discussion as to whether the winter freight market will be buoyed by higher LNG prices and thus attractive LNG trading dynamics or weighed down by soft fundamentals; the signs today suggest the latter trends may dictate the coming months.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: A lack of requirements to work and a sensitive arbitrage has continued to pressure Atlantic rates, and with abundant tonnage there is likely to be strong competition among owners for the emerging fresh cargoes. Rates have been bound within a fairly narrow range for several months, but it is likely the next round of fixtures will align closer with the bid than the offer. Conversely, in the East recent requirements have been covered at steady levels that suggest a balanced or even slight undersupplied spot market, aided by owners opting to relocate vessels West to take advantage of premium rates. However, there remains high competition for smaller cargoes among the TFDE fleet, with owners showing sharp numbers to attract Charterers' attention.    The Middle East situation remains tense and seemingly at a stalemate, and LNG prices have been edging higher - trading strategies that account for a higher LNG price through winter will be gaining traction. The multimonth market has remained active with several tenders underway or recently concluded and levels are broadly flat or trending down, so reducing risk by forward fixing winter coverage at today’s softer rates is clearly attractive to certain charterers.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: High fixing activity has cleared the long list of active requirements seen over the past weeks in the Atlantic. As the market pauses for breath and the number of firm cargoes thins, headline rates have dipped slightly - while still maintaining a significant premium to the East. Availability has widened for mid/late-August laycans, but Charterers requiring worldwide redelivery flex will be constrained by Autumn backstops for most opening tonnage.  A slowdown in Pacific requirements and fixing activity has bolstered the TFDE availability lists in the East. Conversely, with 2-strokes being enticed West, securing larger tonnage for 2H August laycans proves more of a challenge. Competition for cargoes is putting downward pressure on TFDE rates, with 2-stroke owners also needing to sharpen to compete for smaller cargoes.  Delivered LNG price continues to rally, and this week saw the most expensive cargo per MMBtu since 2022, at USD 21.88. These levels are justifying charter rates at a significant premium to the levels otherwise expected in a market that is structurally oversupplied. With pricing unlikely to dip significantly as we head towards Northern Hemisphere winter, it will be a fascinating second half of the year.  Certain portfolio players continue to release tonnage on multi-month and 1-year bases, with fixing rates below current spot rates. This does signal bearish sentiment into next year, although it is not clear-cut yet how different trading strategies will play out in the coming months and thus whether there will be more demand building as LNG players shape up for winter.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The Atlantic market strengthened further during the week, with modern 2-stroke rates pushing towards the $100,000/day mark and TFDE tonnage from the East seen covering outstanding Atlantic requirements in the first half of August. Availability appears healthy but is typically tighter once flexibility between basins is required. A growing theme is the disconnect between spot freight rates and cargo economics, with the same flexibility sought by FOB buyers also attracting a premium on the cargo side.  The Pacific has seen one of its busiest weeks in recent memory with fixtures East of Suez touching double digits, although rates have so far remained relatively contained. Activity from West Africa has also picked up noticeably. While it is too early to determine whether this signals a repeat of the production growth that drove the market higher in Q4-25, it is a development worth monitoring.   Looking ahead, the balance of the year remains backwardated with multimonth interest increasingly price sensitive as availability builds and both owners and subletters seek coverage into 2027. For the traditionalists, the idea of Winter trading at a discount to Summer remains difficult to reconcile. With geopolitical uncertainty persisting, and in some regard increasing, there remains a credible case behind both sides of the bid-offer spread.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have put LNG directly in the firing line, but the freight market has held its nerve - spot rates remain broadly stable for now. Steady fixing since the start of the month has eroded the long availability lists of recent weeks and longer voyages driven by the open arbitrage has created some tightness in the early August window in the Atlantic. Rates for modern tonnage in the West are therefore increasing, albeit at a modest pace and still within the bounds we have seen in recent months. TFDEs in the East have seen some downward pressure, but rate levels for modern tonnage remains resilient, supported by firming DES prices and thinning availability. Current availability is concentrated on the prompt to mid-July, while demand on both sides of Suez sits early August onwards - leaving owners to absorb idle time to bridge the gap into their next employment. In contrast to recent weeks, a broad spread of firm requirements is being worked, keeping all participants busy. Charterers continue to pay up for worldwide redelivery flexibility, with the economics of sending Atlantic cargoes East still justifying the premium.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As many had feared, hopes for resumed safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz in the near future were once again dented as further attacks on commercial shipping were followed by retaliatory strikes on Iran over the weekend. The brief window of free transit enjoyed by LNG Carriers last week is back on hiatus and there was an immediate reaction in the LNG market, with pricing into Asia ticking higher and the arbitrage widening. It is clear now if it wasn’t before, that there will be no quick fixes and there remains a lot of risk heading into the second half of the year and through winter. For now though, despite continued uncertainty, the summertime lull in the spot market is apparent: availability lists are quite thin but there are also a relative lack of requirements, so there is a slight oversupply of tonnage putting downward pressure on 2-stroke and TFDE rates. This is more pronounced East of Suez than West where there is considerable premium, although Atlantic rates dipped below $90k/d for the first time in months off the back of a rush of QatarEnergy sublets. Looking further ahead, there has been little change for multimonth periods and rates have remained fairly flat through to 1Q 2027.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: After weeks’ of “will they, won’t they” in the Middle East, an agreement to try to work towards an agreement has finally emerged and will be heavily scrutinised as more details emerge. It does appear that some of the key pillars should lead to the resumption of merchant traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (without tolls or hinderance); however, the devil will be in the detail and the detail is sorely lacking at this stage. One of the Articles refers to a resumption of traffic within 30 days, although the same Article does note there are challenges including mines that could impact that timeline, and of course there will be operational matters to handle in production itself.   Nonetheless, this is a welcome development and markets have reacted accordingly. Prices are already lower and the inter-basin arbitrage has been squeezed. How this will shape the LNG shipping market in the weeks and months to come remains to be seen, but we may expect some temporary disruptions and tightening East of Suez as scheduling is reworked to accommodate the additional volume while further out. Further out into winter, the competition between Europe and Asia for US volume should ease and lead to lower peak pricing and also to a softer market than we could have seen, yet while we work through the uncertainties and until we see more concrete steps it is unlikely there will be major changes to shipping strategies.  Thus, the markets in all basins have remained broadly steady. There are a number of multimonth requirements being worked and these should provide interesting data points for winter tonnage, although as mentioned last week there is a divergence of views for winter trading split between those pricing in weak freight fundamental versus a strong trading environment and we may see these plans revisited across the board in the days ahead.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The persistent arbitrage to head East and a relative lack of available vessels should be squeezing the spot market, but the Atlantic looks to be holding steady at best or slightly softening. A clear-out of tonnage for prompt dates in the Pacific has resulted in some uplift for TFDE’s, despite pocket lengths on modern tonnage being priced aggressively. Higher LNG prices and a more volatile trading environment will present traders and portfolios with opportunities and this should lead to higher freight, which is certainly the case where any real flexibility is preserved for charterers, yet there is a natural counter to this with lost volume and weak shipping fundamentals. The interplay between these competing forces is driving the bid/offer spread at the moment, and many freight discussions are run in parallel with traders looking at FOB sales so there is a cap on spot rates. Interestingly, this dynamic is already leading to divergent strategies for winter. Most market participants see the same factors (less volume, more ships, higher LNG prices, buyers competing), but while some see the potentially strong trading dynamics as a basis for taking on additional tonnage others see the weak fundamentals as a reason to hold off - markets are always more active and much more interesting when there are such different views.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Rates continue to stay buoyant across the basins, as both Atlantic and Pacific markets enjoy increased liquidity over spot and term periods.  Several competing requirements in the East for 2H June have made availability among TFDEs appear tight for the first time in some weeks, which is reflected by gently increasing headline rates.  The Atlantic market looks increasingly tight for July, driven mainly by a sustained arbitrage pulling ships out of the intra-basin trade flows to which we have become accustomed.  These patterns show little sign of slowing down, as both developing and firm requirements for 1H July have already hit the market.  Layer on to the current market dynamics the continuing difficulties resolving the conflict in the Middle East, and the firmness we're seeing today looks set to persist for the foreseeable future.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: After many weeks of static rates in the West and a slow softening in the East, there is now clear momentum building in the spot market. A modest yet sustained arbitrage for cargoes heading out of the Atlantic into Asia has put a little more pressure on the fleet, and although there are not a vast number of requirements there are even fewer ships to meet them. The upwards pressure on rates is thus supply driven, and will remain sensitive to trade flows and the availability of sublets. Traders and schedulers are being kept busy by the continuing uncertainty in the Middle East, fuelled by repeated contradictory hype of an impending “deal” and an unusual ceasefire in name only. It is clear the LNG and LNG shipping markets will be impacted well into 2027, and after a brief pause there has been more activity in the multi-month space. Control of tonnage will be key to navigating what could be a strong winter, and we expect more appetite for charterers to take on tonnage for longer periods.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The Atlantic market had been showing early signs of a typical summer slowdown, driven in part by an overhang of prompt tonnage following the impact of production issues at Freeport. However, this softer sentiment has proven short lived, as  prompt requirements have emerged including additional production in West and North Africa. As a result, vessel availability has tightened at the front end. Overall rate levels remain firm. While isolated fixtures have been concluded at marginal discounts where availability has been more constrained, these appear to be exceptions rather than a broader trend. Charterers continue to demonstrate a willingness to pay a premium to secure operational flexibility, particularly for multi-voyage employment and/or redelivery into Asia. The prompt forward curve remains supported, although visibility further out is becoming increasingly limited. There is discernible interest in covering positions across the next two quarters; however, the absence of meaningful 12 month bidding suggests a degree of caution. This has, in effect, introduced a pronounced backwardation extending into 2027. Beyond the near term, the outlook remains highly uncertain. Much will depend on the evolution of geopolitical factors, including the ongoing and unresolved disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. In this context, further volatility cannot be ruled out. At the same time, the broader balance of global gas supply remains under scrutiny, particularly with several traditionally quiet buying regions expected to return to the market ahead of peak demand in the second half of the year.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Some significant LNG shipping developments in the Middle East over the past week, as both QELM and ADNOC vessels are reported to have transited the Strait of Hormuz on laden voyages. This marks the first LNG cargoes loaded within the Gulf to exit via the Strait of Hormuz since conflict began in late February. While this is not a signal that regular LNG transits are on the horizon, and the scope of the agreements (if any) between the counterparties and Iran are unknown, it gives some hope that Qatari and Abu Dhabi volumes are not beyond reach.   In the East, sparse May cargoes coupled with ample supply has led to hot competition across the tonnage classes for prompt requirements. Owners that are able to call Qalhat are somewhat insulated from the quieter SEA market, and continue to enjoy a steady stream of opportunities to load Omani volumes at premium freight rates. Requirements are emerging for June but currently these are stacked towards the second half of the month, giving owners the dilemma of fixing forward and absorbing idle time, or waiting and risking unemployed vessels. Requirements out of the US East Coast and especially West Africa have been able to entice tonnage to reposition from the East, offering attractive utilisation and a rate premium to Pacific cargoes. While Kitimat’s schedule remains uncertain, Barossa loadings are expected to be resume, which the market hopes will boost liquidity East of Suez.   The Atlantic market has proved very stubborn, with rates remaining tightly bound in the mid-$90k/d range when accounting for vessel specifications. The requirement list has been a little lumpy though, with relatively few cargoes in early June set against an extensive list from mid-June onwards. We may therefore see a little more variability as charterers face more or less competition for individual requirements, but the fundamentals and in particular the situation in the Middle East are showing no signs of change in the coming weeks.   Following the trend we have seen through the past few weeks, multi-month coverage through Q3/Q4 remains of interest but charterers have eased back on taking on tonnage. The bullish sentiment of the major portfolio players has trickled through the market and we do see some additional subletters hoping to lock-in utilisation, and this may explain the “wait and see” approach among charterers now.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The dormant spot market East of Suez has been somewhat roused this week by a number of requirements firming up for late May through mid-June. Qalhat liftings continues to feature heavily, with wide disparities in additional war risk premia playing a key role in assessment of candidates. Uncertainty on production across various load terminals in Australia as well as Canada continue to stall prompt transactions and stifle liquidity.  After a very quiet long weekend covering a number of public holidays, the West is now enjoying a far more active spot market, and is continuing to command a premium on freight rates for the May-June fixing window. This comes despite recent disruptions at Freeport LNG leading to several cancelled cargoes, and subsequent unexpected short-term length from scheduled lifters. Although open tonnage feels a little sparse, firm requirements have seen interest from 2-stroke owners but not with sufficient competition to force rates significantly lower, while a preference for worldwide redelivery optionality is supporting the price floor. Despite the Atlantic liquidity, players on both sides of the transaction will be keeping one eye on spot, and one eye on the quarter ahead …  A rush of activity from the portfolio players resulted in a flurry of term fixtures late last week, as charterers sought coverage into Q1 2027. Modern 2-strokes with worldwide redelivery are the vessels of choice, owing to charterers’ need for maximum geographical optionality as a hedge against a bullish LNG price outlook. A widening arbitrage and the highest levels of Inter-basin cargoes in over a year, coupled with low EU storage levels and injections down 20% on last year, is signalling strong East-West jostling for volumes and subsequent LNG price volatility. We’re now in a strange situation where forward 2-stroke availability is tightening while we experience fleet oversupply on the spot. Owners seem to be following the trend, opting to market their multimonth length rather than pure spot availability. Let’s see if other market participants take heed and look to bolster their fleets ahead of Q3.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
x: Saudi Aramco announced May CP at $750 for C3 and $800 for C4, a rollover from April, which lagged behind the recent spike in oil price, amid concerns over middle East supply disruptions.   Arbitrage strengthened this week with improved premium on CFR FAR EAST, with FEI/Lst spread widening to $376 for May and $308 for June. However terminal fee for Jun lifting US FOBs declined further against soaring freight and higher Panama transit costs. Mid Jun lifting 2/2 spot cargo was reported traded in low 20 cpg, while 4/0 was discussed at low teens only. U.S. propane/propylene inventories declined by 1.1 mmt barrels to 78.8 million barrels in the week ended 24th Apr, leaving stocks remained 67% higher year on year.   On Thursday window, a 23/0 parcel for 2h Jun delivery basis Chiba was changed hand at May FEI plus $8, equivalent to Jun FEI plus around $83. Outside window, a couple of 4/0 parcels for 2h Jun delivery basis Chiba were reported traded at May FEI plus $2-$3. Separately, a few lots of 4/0 parcels for 1h Jun delivery basis Ningbo were concluded at May FEI plus mid 40s reportedly. One SChina PDH procured a 2/0 lot for 1-20 Jun delivery, Australia stem, at Jun FEI plus $190 reportedly. Another EChina petchem player also tendered to buy similar cargo for Jun delivery into Ningbo. China PDH run rates reduced to 44% this week, marking a record low. This being said, several PDHs are expected to restart in late May/Jun, and have started inquiring on Jun feedstock.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: There is unmissable irony in the description of spot charter rates for modern tonnage as “healthy”, given the ongoing crisis in the LNG market where the world’s largest single supplier continues to be cut off from its global customer base. Despite the forcibly idle tonnage unable to reach home base in the Middle East, levels continue to show resistance around a similar range as long-term charter rates.   Whilst the worst of the conflict is hopefully behind us, what lies ahead remains wholly uncertain. However, amongst strong activity in the spot market, some consensus has also emerged for periods covering the balance of the year and into Q1-27. Portfolios are taking positions down the curve at rates largely in line with current Atlantic spot, supported by higher LNG prices and anticipation of competition between basins in the second half of the year.    We continue to see signs of weak underlying fundamentals in the spot market, with length beginning to build on TFDE’s in the East and new requirements often flushing out fresh 2-stroke availabilities for short spot employment in the Atlantic. However, the same cannot be said for term availabilities, where 2-strokes are beginning to thin out and TFDE’s under independent control are less forthcoming when asked to lock in prevailing spot levels for longer period. It remains to be seen which strategy will pay off but with summer looming and speculation that tonne-miles could take another boost in the third quarter, we are eager to see how this plays out.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
x: Another week of volatility as the US-Iran talks remains unclear and supply disruptions continues. A Korean importer bid in window for a May FOB 2/2 or 4/0 cargo ex Yanbu at $850 for C3 and C4 respectively. By the time of writing, May CP swap was assessed at $710 for C3 and $755 for C4, with the May/June CP spread at an $80 backwardation.  Terminal fees dropped sharply as arbs narrowed further with slackening far east demand. FEI/Lst declined to $300 for May and $255 for Jun by the time of writing. An early Jun lifting 2/2 cargo ex US was reportedly sold to an Indian player at low 30s cpg, and a similar ratio for later Jun loading heard in 20s range. However, a 4/0 parcel for 1h Jun lifting was done at 18 cpg only. U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 2.1 mmt barrels to 77.9 million barrels in the week ended 17th Apr, leaving stocks remained 71.5% higher year on year.   Activity in the Asian was muted earlier this week, as market participants monitored US–Iran talks before committing to June programs. Outside window, one 23/0 parcel for 2h May delivery basis Chiba was changed hand at May FEI plus around $70. Similar parcel for 2h Jun delivery was concluded at May FEI plus $7-8. Additionally, a couple of Jun arrival 46/0 parcels have been placed into Echina at May FEI plus high $30s reportedly, which equates to Jun FEI plus mid $80s based on latest swap. Chinese PDH run rate fell by 10% to 46% in two weeks, which subsequently led to significant reduction in propane demand. With flat prices and discussing premium easing, PDH margins have slightly improved. Hopefully, some plants might restart on schedule rather than extend maintenance.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The market appears to have entered a more stable, albeit still fragile phase. Volatility on commodity pricing has subsided somewhat, perhaps in protest in response to weeks of wild swings at the news and non-news dominating the public discourse around closure or opening of the Straits of Hormuz. Paper markets have grown increasingly resistant to new "news" with the reality already priced in on the physical.  In the Atlantic basin, activity remains subdued, with several participants describing the market as quiet and lacking liquidity. Despite this, underlying concerns around European storage and forward balances persist, providing some support to sentiment. Vessel availability is still sufficient, but increasingly fragmented, and there is a growing expectation that tonnage could tighten further toward end-May.   East of Suez, buyers remain largely absent with an eye on softer prices down the curve and prompt supply well covered.   Looking ahead, the key question remains whether late-May demand materialises and translates into fixing activity. For now, the market remains finely balanced, with limited downside but no clear catalyst for upside unless activity picks up.

x: Uncertainties over US-Iran talks, coupled with worsening supply disruptions after US blockade over SoH, continued to heighten market volatility. By the time of writing, May CP was traded at $680 for C3 and $720 for C4.    Arbs crashed this week as of declining landed price against soaring freight. The FEI/Lst swap narrowed to $326 for May and $269 for Jun, down by roughly $50 and $30 respectively week on week. Terminal fee declined to mid 20s cpg to low 30s cpg for Jun lifting propane, however one end May evenly split cargo was reported traded at high 30s cpg, reflecting the butane shortage. U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 301,000 barrels to 77.9 million barrels in the week ended 10th Apr, leaving stocks remained 75.6% higher year on year.   Window trades are relatively active this week, with 4 deals concluded for 23/0 parcels delivered in 2h May basis Chiba, at the price of May FEI plus $128/$130 or Balmo Apr (15-30) Apr FEI plus $11. Outside window, a number of tenders failed to conclude. FPCC procured one 46/0 for 2h May delivery into Mailiao via tender, which reported at May FEI plus around $130 for US stem. A Canada origin 46/0 for May delivery was reported sold into Schina at May FEI plus $190s. However, butane inquiries are difficult to cover with limited alternatives outside AG. Several tenders seeking evenly split or butane cargo for May/Jun delivery were reported cancelled due to a lack of offers.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Another week, another batch of very bizarre news and non-news to digest. While geopolitical risk continues to support LNG prices, the impact on LNG shipping has eased considerably from the immediate spike after the early attacks. This is perhaps not a surprise given the underlying fundamentals, but rates remain at multiples of their pre-war levels. In the Atlantic basin, prompt requirements remains relatively scarce, and there is sufficient tonnage to keep rates broadly flat. However, there is a sense that more demand exists just below the surface and while rates may not have shifted significantly, the balance of risk is turning to the upside. East of Suez has shown comparatively steadier activity including from the sole Middle East producer, Oman. The availability list is not being stretched at present though, and rates are drifting slightly downwards. Looking ahead, much will depend on how regional imports respond to current pricing dynamics, such as whether Asia will draw more volumes out of the Atlantic and when Europe will begin refilling storage. For now, the market remains finely balanced but with freight lagging broader fundamentals, any shift in activity could see rates react quickly.

x: Crude price experienced high volatility amid ongoing uncertainties over ceasefire and persistent supply disruptions due to Middle East tensions. By the time of writing, May CP was traded at $680 for C3 and C4 was assessed at $30 higher as of tight supply.  Following crude movement, FEI/Lst fluctuates throughout the week. By the time of writing, FEI/Lst swap was assessed at $378 for May and $298 for Jun. Terminal fee for May liftings tumbled from previous mid-40s cpg to low-30s cpg, reflecting weakening netbacks as CFR market softened against soaring freight. Meanwhile, U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 570,000 barrels to 77.6 million barrels in the week ended 3rd Apr, leaving stocks remained 71% higher year on year.  A 46/0 lot for 1h May delivery basis Chiba was reportedly traded at Apr FEI plus 30s. 23/0 parcel for 2h May delivery was bid at May FEI plus $125 in the window however yet to entice offers. Outside tender, a total of 250k propane cargos for end Apr/1h May delivery were reportedly placed into China, which deal level concluded at May FEI plus 130s for US stems and plus 170-180s for non-US stems, with majority procured for petchem feedstock use. Additionally, Korean importers have issued a couple of tenders seeking May/Jun delivered butane but few heard awarded.

x: After several weeks of attacks, counterattacks and increasingly heated threats, the world woke up on Wednesday perhaps relieved to have woken up at all. If the present path of de-escalation is maintained, the energy and freight markets should return to normality but it will be a slow process and the impact and outcome on LNG shipping dynamics remains uncertain. This is a big "if" and the details will matter enormously as the negotiations unfold. In the coming weeks, much will depend on the demand profiles across different regions, especially while the Middle East production facilities slowly ramp back up. In the Atlantic basin, a lack of prompt firm requirements is contributing to softer rate sentiment, particularly as vessel availability builds through April and into 1H May. With limited liquidity, the market remains reactive, with participants trying to capture arbitrage opportunities or awaiting the next batch of cargoes. Although there have been few opportunities, the East of Suez has seen comparatively stronger fixture activity over the holiday period. This has created a competitive environment, particularly for owners of TFDE tonnage. Combined with a growing list of open vessels, sentiment has softened and players will be tracking markets carefully for clues as to how the market will develop as the ceasefire ensures.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Just when we thought this market had run out of surprises, the world of LNG Shipping was flipped on it's head (again) this week when Qatar Energy opened the top drawer and pulled out a playbook from the past. In an innovative move that would make Nobu Su proud, the world's biggest LNG Charterer launched their Qatar Max Coal Carrier project this week, to tap into the skyrocketing black diamond demand from their largest Asian customers. Dubbed the "Coal-Max" for short, a source in Doha (who spoke on the condition of anonymity) described how this latest masterpiece was born out of a particularly intense brain-storming session on Monday. "Basically, the shipping team said 'we're 20 ships long', the short-term marketing team said 'all our customers are switching to coal', and I said: 'let's just open up the tanks and fill them with Newcastle's finest?' Carbon is carbon, hey"? The upgraded vessels should start delivering their newest fossil fuel in Q3 this year, although at the time of print, neither Qatar Energy nor any Class Society were returning our calls. Stay tuned for further updates....

x: Heightened uncertainty and price volatility have dampened activities in both physical and paper market. Terminal fee for May liftings has fell sharply to 30s cpg, vs last week’s 50s cpg. U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 478,000 barrels to 73 million barrels in the week ended 20th Mar, leaving stocks remained 69% higher year on year.   In the window, 23/0 parcel 1h May delivery was bid at Apr FEI plus $15, equates to around May FEI plus $107, while similar parcel for 2h May delivery was bid at May FEI plus $100. 4/0 parcel for 2h May delivery basis Ningbo was also bid at Apr FEI plus $15. Earlier this week, some 2/0 for 2h May delivery was reported traded at Apr FEI plus mid high teens. Outside window, Pertamina was reported to have procured a Australian 3/1 stem for Apr delivery. However, one NChina PDH player cancelled their propane buy tender for late Apr/1h May delivery as offers are higher than expected.    Separately, bids from Indian players softened this week, as one Iranian cargo was reported sold into India market at CP plus $200s after US issued Iran General License for permitting the trade. Traders focused on Iranian market are holding off from forward purchase as monitoring the prospects of a US-Iran ceasefire.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Recent weeks have seen the energy markets try to adapt in real-time to the chaotic situation in the Middle East, and while still nothing is resolved there is at least more stability in the prompt LNG and LNG shipping markets. The LNG shipping market has remained largely secondary to the commodity side, where swings have determined the direction of traffic although high rates have impacted the arbitrage form the US to Asia.  There have been several fixtures at levels unthinkable just four weeks ago but the apparent easing of tensions has seen a softening of sentiment across the board, with prompt vessels competing more aggressively for employment. It remains to be seen whether the market is resilient enough to maintain levels above long term breakeven; however, in the short term it does appear that elevated cargo prices are supporting healthier freight levels.   Looking further out in anticipation of an end to the conflict, the impact of the attacks on Ras Laffan are not yet fully understood but the most recent updates confirm a considerable loss in production for a number of years. The uncertainty in when or how the conflict will end, how will production be affected in the Middle East and the direction of tradeflows are causing headaches in pricing longer term charters, and although owners are there to lock in longer periods, the lack clarity is impeding activity in the multimonth space. Forward availabilities provide even larger and perhaps sharper headaches for charterers, who wrestle with the risk of remaining short versus locking in flexibility at a premium to their now-outdated forecasts.

x: Oil and gas prices surged amid escalating strikes on key energy infrastructure in the Middle East. At the time of writing, April CP was traded at $620 for C3, with the C3/C4 spread assessed at $5. FEI spiked up on heightened supply concerns after Targa declared force majeure, with delays reportedly ranging from 7 to 10 days. April FEI was traded at $1,010, with the April/May FEI spread at $160 latest. Following this, US-FAR EAST arbitrage widened significantly to over $500 for Apr and over $400 for May in extreme volatility. One late Apr lifting full propane cargo was reported being traded at 42 cpg.  U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 810,000 barrels to 72.5 million barrels in the week ended 13rd Mar, leaving stocks remained 67.2% higher year on year.  In window one 23/0 parcel for 1h May delivery basis Chiba was bid at Apr FEI plus $30, and similar parcel for 2h May bid at May FEI plus $130, while no offers seen. Several petchem players with term supply and spot supplement in existing inventory continue to maintain run, max out downstream yields, and captured front margins; while the others plan to carry out maintenance or take a wait-n-see approach before procuring spot in later Apr or May as downstream price yet to keep pace with the surge in feedstock costs.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Market volatility has eased this week, perhaps as the reality of a prolonged conflict in the Middle East has sunk in and the opposing bull and bear factors surrounding the curtailment of Middle East supply is now beginning to shape up. A lack of liquidity in the Atlantic spot market and mystery shrouding a handful of Qatari fleet fixtures towards the end of last week saw implied levels pare back considerably before finding some support in the low-mid $100kpd's. Fresh fixtures have been few and far between as elevated cargo and freight costs jostle for position, keeping bid/offer spreads wide. East of Suez, fixing activity has been higher, led by continued Omani flows and strong volumes from other regions producing excess cargoes. Whilst levels have trended lower overall, TFDE and 2-stroke rates remain healthy and there is even life for some steamers finding spot employment. Whether, or not, the reappearance of previously underutilised or idle tonnage and the arrival of newbuildings will outweigh tonne mile increases amidst trade flow disruptions, remains to be seen. However, uncertainty and volatility on high LNG prices leave no doubt as to the value of flexible modern tonnage in the short term.

x: Middle East tensions have intensified amid escalating attacks, causing extreme volatility in oil prices. At the time of writing, April CP was traded at $583 for C3 and $578 for C4. South and Southeast Asian buyers have prioritized LPG for residential consumption over the petrochemical sector, given limited spot availabilities on US butane cargoes. Some cargoes with butane grade were reportedly sold into India at Apr CP plus over $300 for prompt delivery. t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Volatility remains the key theme as conflict in the Middle East continues. The questions posed in last week’s report remain largely unanswered and the swings seen on crude pricing after fresh assaults on Gulf region assets over the weekend have added another layer of uncertainty for LNG trading. This, along with many vessels marketed for sublet, has led to a cautious mood with more bearish undertones. Nevertheless, after a softening from the initial reactive spike we saw last week, rates appear to have held with prompt availabilities commanding strong charter rates around $200kpd for 2-strokes and above $100k for TFDE’s in both basins. There is a sense of charterers holding off for now as they hope for more clarity for laycans further out in the fixing window, especially with the emergence of more sublets and potential competition; however, every day brings fresh turmoil and we are now facing the prospect of mines in the Straits of Hormuz and several vessels have been struck by projectiles in the region. So while the early days of the attack saw charterers typically scrambling to charter in, reshuffle or sell FOB, the more recent days have been shaped by caution due to the underlying length in the market and the increasing number of availabilities shown. Where the LNG and the LNG shipping markets go in the coming days is still uncertain.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: The Middle East conflict that erupted over weekend has disrupted oil and gas export flows through the Strait of Hormuz. No spot deals or market discussions have been heard amid the prevailing uncertainty on geopolitical tensions. Swap values continued to surge on supply concerns, and by the time of writing, Apr CP was traded at $591/mt for C3 and $590/mt for C4 respectively.  U.S.–Far East arbitrage widened sharply to around minus $270s for April, as supply disruptions in the Middle East pushed landed costs higher. Terminal fees for April liftings surged to around 27 cpg, with sellers targeting higher margins from the wider arbitrage amid softening freight on the US–Chiba route. U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 819,000 barrels to 73.4 million barrels in the week ended Feb. 27, although stocks remained 50.7% higher year on year. The build came as a surprise to the market, as most had expected a decline.  Both Mar and Apr FEI and cash premiums surged amid tightening supply. A 23/0 parcel for 1h Apr delivery basis Chiba was concluded in window at Apr FEI plus $105, and similar parcel for 2h Apr delivery was traded at Mar FEI plus high single digit. A 46/0 parcel for 2h Apr delivery basis Chiba was also reported traded at Mar FEI plus mid-teens.  Asian refiners and petchem plants are reportedly cutting rates or shutting units due to feedstock shortages. China’s PDH operating rate is expected to fall from the current 64% to around 54% in the next two weeks, facing rising feedstock costs amid supply tightness. The resulting demand loss could exceed 2mmt of propane per month, which might partly offset Middle East supply disruptions and easing some tightness. However, India and some Southeast Asian buyers are more severely impacted, with few alternative butanes available for prompt Mar delivery. Some US exports are expected to be diverted into these markets, though arrivals will likely be mid/2h Apr range.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG and LNG shipping markets are suffering seismic shocks in the wake of military actions in the Middle East. The geopolitical situation is very fluid and information is flowing fast and is not always subject to validation, but it is increasingly apparent that there is no quick resolution on the horizon and the disruptions we are seeing to the LNG trade are likely to persist for some time. How long will Middle Eastern production remain offline? How will Asia adapt to reduced supply? When will Europe seek to replenish low storage levels? How will US volume be distributed between importers? It is too early to answer these questions with much certainty, but these past days have shown charterers are willing to pay rates of 10 times the levels from last week to secure prompt tonnage, and there is interest for multi-month periods up to a year in the six figure range – unthinkable as we prepared our report last week. Underpinning the frantic trading, chartering and operational activity that is keeping us all very busy, we are grateful to the brave seafarers working in increasingly challenging situations across all sectors.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping markets East and West of Suez have been moving in different directions lately, and the trend has continued this past week with rates softening in Asia and the Middle East while firming in the Atlantic. In the East, there continues to be a steady flow of requirements but competition among owners and subletters is giving charterers the edge in negotiations especially for those that can work with smaller vessels. The basis for the rising market in the Atlantic is well understood, with off-takers working hard to mitigate weather-related disruptions and delays. The market has climbed considerably week-on-week, and with portfolios holding on to tonnage there are some windows showing no availability at all. While there is speculation over whether the spot market will correct as these disruptions unwind, the multimonth market for periods through summer suggests a higher floor than we saw in January.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The momentum reported last week has continued in both basins, albeit in fits and starts, with spot rates in the Atlantic basin now edging higher than in the Pacific and Middle East. The primary driver in what is still a fundamentally over-supplied Atlantic market has been scheduling disruptions, mainly linked to cold weather impacting cargo operations as well as storm and adverse sea conditions. The result is several mis-matches between cargo dates and vessel arrival times, which has added to the usual steady stream of requirements and pushed rates back above $30,000 per day. The tight spell is currently within the middle decade of March, but if disruptions continue and if more requirements emerge this is likely to spread through towards the end of March. The markets East of Suez are a little quieter as expected through the holidays, although recent fixing levels are struggling to hold steady due to a healthy availability list. Multimonth activity is also a little more muted this past week, although with the interest shown in recent candidate vessels this is surely just a pause.  And for those celebrating, we hope you have enjoyed the holidays!!!

n: LNG Market Report
x: After a highly successful LNG2026 in Doha, it is London’s turn to be in the spotlight with International Energy Week and it feels appropriate that the focus shifts to the Atlantic. After a rollercoaster winter that saw rates surge well into the six digits before crashing down below $10,000 per day just weeks later, the region is enjoying a bounce in charter rates for early March with levels around double what they were this time last week. Turbulent weather is still impacting schedules and is leading to a tightening availability list, and with several uncovered cargoes right in the fixing window there is more likelihood the renaissance will continue than it will stall. The Middle East and Pacific regions are holding steady and are still at a premium to the Atlantic, although it there is a fair chance the situation will be reversed within days if current momentum holds. All this will give owners some comfort, yet the landscape remains challenging and will not be helped by the number of sublets being show for multimonth periods. We wouldn’t unbuckle the seatbelts just yet.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market appears to have paused for breath after the highs and lows of winter volatility, with enough activity to keep owners and charterers busy but with rates across all three major regions broadly steady. The status quo is for very low rates in the Atlantic and there doesn’t seem to be much respite in the near future for owners or sub-letters seeking to capture value in their open positions; there may be some more opportunities as US producers get back on track after the recent weather-related disruptions, but competition among 2-stroke tonnage remains fierce. The markets East of Suez still command a premium for now despite some softening sentiment, and players will be watching the ongoing spot tenders with interest. If there is a light on the horizon for owners, it is the multimonth/multiyear market for which recent fixtures price in a strengthening market later in the year. For those visiting Doha for LNG 2026, we hope you all enjoy a successful trip among old friends, with particular credit to our Qatari hosts for once again providing a fabulously warm and friendly welcome!

x: Last week we wrote of plummeting rates in the Atlantic, and this week we write of… plummeting rates in the Atlantic. While it was clear then that momentum was only going one way, the brakes have barely been applied as levels fell rapidly through the teens and now into the single digits. There are several more requirements within the traditional fixing window, but there are few signs of a recovery at this stage and competition remains fierce for each cargo. Our report also suggested that a reverse arbitrage could see some Asian cargoes heading into Europe and this has occurred, but it will probably not be a feature of the market going forward. The Pacific and Middle East regions are still trading at considerably higher levels than the Atlantic, and East of Suez there are TFDE vessels fixing out at higher rates than modern 2-stroke vessels are achieving in the Atlantic. All of this presents a challenging environment for owners; however, several 1-3 year fixtures have been concluded at levels that suggest a stronger second half of the year and should give encouragement to those with redelivering tonnage.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: This week has seen a bit of an ebb after the deluge of spot fixtures seen last week, when the number of ships placed on subjects hit double digits in the Atlantic Basin alone. Despite that fixing frenzy, spot charter rates have plummeted further into levels many had not expected to see in January, but such is the unpredictability of the LNG shipping market that this is just a mirror image of the spike seen in Q4, which also caught many by surprise. Market fundamentals may not always tell the full story, but the oversupply of modern tonnage has been fuelled by European gas prices soaring and a prevailing sense that tonne mile demand will take a hit in the short term. Such is the price disparity that options to deliver cargoes originating East of Suez into Europe have been sought by a number of players looking to capture value in a game of increasingly fine margins. Whilst this may be great for those managing to achieve it, there is not likely to be a significant impact for the overall fleet balance and now, more than halfway through January, the steady churn of new buildings from the yards is picking up again which is weighing further on sentiment for short multimonth periods. And regarding newbuilds, two fresh orders have been placed this week and the early signs suggest this may be a strong year for the shipyards.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Looser market fundamentals are reasserting influence on the spot side this week, as despite a slightly gentler decline in rates than some had predicted the downward pressure is growing. There is still an impressive amount of volume being produced and at the time of writing, there remains a healthy handful of requirements to be worked in both basins; however, despite the fixing frenzy continuing any fresh requirements are matched with fresh availabilities. Rising tensions between Iran and the US, along with colder weather across Europe, have led to a narrower TTF/JKM spread and a firmly closed Arb for Atlantic cargoes to the East. Uncertainty on scheduling in Egypt and the ongoing risk of bad weather in the Atlantic remain potential disrupters, but portfolios are confident enough to show the length that had all but disappeared through parts of Q4. Discussions for longer period remain active, with the soft front months blurring into concerns of a repeat of last winter on both owners and charterers minds. The busier streak in the newbuilding space continues with multiple orders being finalised, whilst several owners are leaning towards more speculative plays in anticipation of large-scale projects applying further upward pressure on prices.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Barely a week into 2026 and we have already seen some fairly drastic shifts. The unpredictable nature of geopolitics right now is raising all manner of questions, but even if we just focus on our more genteel LNG shipping market we will still have plenty to think about. Starting in the Atlantic, there has been a growing sense of a falling market with several vessels opening but very few new requirements. Charterers have generally been comfortable holding out in the circumstances, and some have been rewarded by securing much softer rates; however, the see-saw may already be tipping the other way with a number of fresh enquiries emerging and a much more balanced market, at least on paper. The Pacific basin has been a little more predictable, with downward pressure leading to a steady decline in fixing levels albeit from a lower base than in the Atlantic. The Middle East remains a more active region than has traditionally been seen, but with the build up of tonnage the premium for ballasting across is also coming under pressure. The question for many in these past weeks has been how the market will react to a weaker environment into Q1, and although it’s fair to say that things are cooling there is still some fight left in this market. The shipyards have also been very busy in closing out 2025, and we will provide a full summary in our next Quarterly Update – watch this space!

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we put down A Christmas Carol for another year, we can pick up another Dickens novel to see in the New Year. 2025 initially appeared to be a year of lows for LNG shipping, until a late surge in Q4 served as a timely reminder of the market’s capacity for sharp swings. The uptick, driven primarily by additional LNG supply, suggests there may be more opportunities ahead, though the path forward will be far from smooth. A 50% orderbook-to-fleet ratio highlights the growing pains of rapid expansion, while uncertainty over a potential medium-term LNG glut adds further complexity. In this multidirectional, technologically tiered, and fast-evolving market, volatility remains the only constant. So whether a charterer enjoying low rates but stung by this winter spike or an owner suffering the soft market but locking in historically high numbers of fixtures, 2025 really did see the best of times and the worst of times, and we all look forward to 2026 with Great Expectations.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: In our first Weekly Report of 2025, we brazenly asserted that “we can be sure that 2025 will be just as interesting as was 2024”. In what turned out to be our most accurate forecast to date, this year has indeed had it all. As we head into Christmas Day, however, it isn’t armed conflicts or trade wars that that are exerting the most influence on our market, rather it’s the reminder that shipping is a derived demand, and when there’s more LNG to be shipped, there’s more LNG carriers needed to ship it. Like most of the market, we were caught out by the dramatic jump in Atlantic exports in Q4, and the resultant strain on LNG shipping fleets which took us into the six-figure winter fixing mode. Whilst these rates had been par for the course in many previous years, they weren’t meant to appear this year, and the fact that the market still hasn’t properly corrected underlines the structural nature of this winter’s rate rise. This root cause has significant ramifications for 2026, with many charterers carrying recent reminders that being short shipping in LNG can be costly. So, whilst most owners won’t get to unwrap a clean term TCP tomorrow morning, those with available 2-strokes coming up on their books will be feeling considerably more Christmas cheer than they would have only two months ago.  There’s no shortage of festivities at the yards either, with Hudong-Zhonghua securing a hat-trick of Newbuilds for a producer’s fleet renewal needs, whilst Samsung have reportedly bagged a brace on the back of more long-term tender business. Merry Christmas, everyone!

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we race closer to the end of the year, the rush to cover requirements for the first half of January is starting to slow down and there is a corresponding softening in rates. The flagging momentum may suggest the winter spike is over, but there is still some shape to the curve and considerable volatility, particularly for earlier laycans in the Atlantic for which rates remain very much in the six-figures. Further out into the second half of January and into February, fixing levels are lower but is this due to a general market easing or have charterers fixed well-ahead, before the upcoming holidays? Regardless, the feeling remains that we will see a gradual decline in rates rather than an abrupt fall. Longer periods remain in limbo as independent owners and subletters seek to capture the recent strength while charterers hold off for the excitement to fade, but it is likely that levels will settle a little higher for multi-month and multi-year charters next year than they were through much of this year.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The festive season is in full swing in London, but that hasn’t led to a slowdown in the markets with fresh cargo sales and shipping requirements emerging almost daily. There has definitely been more for owners to celebrate in recent months and there is a little more optimism than there was for next year, but sentiment in the spot market has been more measured this week. Finding tonnage for prompt laycans is still challenging, but further out there are more ships emerging and some players are seemingly more open to subletting. Many of the key drivers for the current market strength remain in place including high production levels and FOB sales, so perhaps we are seeing the results of the fleet being worked harder. Despite this, rates in the Atlantic remain solidly in the six figures for laycans within December and although there is a steady softening into the new year, there have been very few fixtures concluded to give benchmarks for the second half of January. In contrast, the Pacific has been remarkably quiet on the prompt and rates have been moving sideways, with only distant requirements for second half January being considered. However, the Middle East continues to be a very hot market with tonnage being pulled into the region and Owners also considering ballasting to West Africa to lock in rates at the Atlantic premium.  On the newbuilding front, activity remains strong, with several deals in progress.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: December has started in a slightly softer mood in the Atlantic, as the recent flurry of relatively prompt fixtures has relaxed into requirements a little further out into January and thus towards some lower rates. Interestingly, the decline in levels hasn’t been as rapid or as sharp as some may have expected. Seasonal spikes have historically lasted little more than four weeks so whilst it’s natural to expect a downturn before too long, the recent rise has not come on the back of a cold snap or a regional demand swing. The main driver has been increased production and this is not likely to reverse anytime soon, instead the market will be seeing the benefits of sharper optimisations and the delivery of more newbuildings to help rebalance the picture. As the Atlantic eases a little, the Pacific remains a little quiet with very few requirements or fixtures and rates holding firm. Instead, we look to the Middle East again as the region has returned to the foreground with a number of spot requirements and FOB cargo sales, and therefore firming rates. If it feels a little quiet just look left or right or give it a day or two, it’s still a very busy market out there.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The spot market gains seen in recent weeks continue with significant increases across all basins, although trying to report any of these regions under a single headline rate may give a false impression of a smooth and steady rise. The reality has been a much more volatile climb that may surge one day then soften the next, and although this has appeared mildly chaotic at times we do now see an overarching curve through winter. In the Atlantic, the lack of 2-stroke tonnage has led to some very tight periods in which majors are allowing ships to be pried from their portfolios…at a premium. When there has been competition among owners and sub-letters, this has merely acted as a fluttering brake rather than an abrupt cliff edge. And yet, as we look ahead to the end of December and beyond, rates are clearly easing from the mid-December highs but do remain at elevated levels and this suggests a soft landing into 2026. The Pacific basin has also seen more activity and at higher levels, but with considerably less volatility than in the West. This may be because ST and TFDE vessels offer more of a relief valve when 2-strokes disappear (something we address in our recent LinkedIn post), but there is also much more opportunity to optimise shorter voyages. Amidst these two major basins, the Middle East has again asserted itself as a strong demand source and has been a focal point with a spate of new requirements and fixing levels that are attractive enough to pull ships in from Asia.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Spot charter rates in the Atlantic continued their ascent on an even steeper trajectory through the end of last week as a small number of prompt requirements were met with scant supply. Those able to release tonnage were able to capture large increments to last done, breaking the six-digit mark and by a considerable distance in at least one case. This has only added to the uncertainty around forward pricing, where better availabilities for end Dec look fairly evenly matched with requirements at the end of the fixing window. Owners in the Pacific have also notched up a few new highs for the year as firm availabilities have remained relatively tight, although charterers with more forward dates are beginning to pause and question whether the recent run has legs, given a healthy number of expected redeliveries. On the newbuilding front, Hyundai Samho, announced they signed a $507 million contract with a North American company, scheduled for delivery in the 2H 2028.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The spot market remains firm in the West, with rates hitting year-to-date records and the idea of a six-figure fixture may no longer be a wild fantasy. There are requirements emerging including some relatively prompt loadings out of West Africa and US Gulf cargoes within the second half of December, giving some rate support at the end of the current fixing window. Additional volumes marketed by producers are struggling a bit to find homes in the absence of suitable modern tonnage, and much of the underlying ship length remains tied up on longer laden legs with portfolios yet to turn towards chartering out to capture the trading value.    However, amidst all the bullish market talk there are clear reasons for caution; although the prompt market remains tight there are vessels redelivering in December and more availability is emerging, and we cannot expect the weather to help this year with mild conditions forecast in importing regions both East and West. There remains a large discount in the Pacific where rates for both 2-strokes and TFDE lag well behind the Atlantic, while the premium for 2-strokes over TFDEs is also widening, despite fewer requirements calling for larger ships East of Suez. The question of how long this firmer market lasts has to yet be answered, but for now it seems clear that the answer has been deferred at least another week.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The bubbling momentum in the spot markets for loadings through the end of November and early December has continued through this week, despite some uncertainty following news of some lost cargoes out of the US Gulf; however, the resulting prompt length does not really come into play for later laycans in the Atlantic and so rates have continued to firm. With many of these requirements now covered, focus shifts a little further back and we enter into speculative territory: how many of the FOB sales will take in tonnage? How many of the optimisations will play out? How many fresh firm requirements will hit the market? In short, owners and charterers are assessing how long will the current freight imbalance last and when the market will start to soften. The firming market in the East is trailing that in the West, and the dynamic quite different. Named positions are few and far between but equally, open requirements remain scarce.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The market through most of the year has remained quite flat and weekly reports had a sense of déjà vu; yet a glance back to our last report shows that a week can also be a very long time in LNG, and that a month ago can feel like ancient history. Rates across the three major regions have all moved higher, with Atlantic rates perhaps even entering “surging” territory, having more than doubled in recent weeks. One trigger for this tightening can be linked to delays discharging into Egypt and the knock-on impact on scheduling, but this was maybe only a starting gun for a winter upturn that many had thought would never come. There are now signs of an improving cargo market in Asia that is enticing for portfolios and traders, and ships are being pulled back from availability lists. East of Suez, there are very few 2-strokes available and TFDEs are now supporting the market at higher rates. It is often the case that a long freight market is only skin deep, and scratching the surface can quickly reveal a more complicated picture; that appears to be the case here. The opposite can happen too though, if the cargo market softens then recent gains can disappear even quicker. How long this upturn lasts is already a big topic of discussion.   There have been no new orders or project FIDs this week, but the announcement that Totalenergies have lifted the Force Majeure on Mozambique LNG was a very welcome step. There will be more challenges ahead but we wish the project well as they target first production by the end of the decade.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The tighter market conditions in the Atlantic persists still driven by uncertainties on discharge schedules, and 1H November is now effectively sold out. Bids have continued to improve to meet the offer and interestingly, sentiment remains strong enough to support a number of more forward fixtures at prevailing levels, including some rumoured for longer period closing out the remainder of the year. The pressing question for both Owners and Charterers now is whether these levels are maintained through year-end of whether the market eases again; for now, we're likely faced with a wait and see approach for liftings further out.  East of Suez, charter rates have also been lifted on the back of this shift, helped too by improved fundamentals with more supply online from Australia and a steadier flow of Canada volumes. Lots of opportunities for owners to assess although it remains to be seen if there will be sufficient to keep all available TFDE's moving.

x: We have seen less liquidity in the Atlantic spot market this week with several requirements sitting in the window for longer than usual in 2025. Ongoing strikes in Europe and deferrals in Egypt continue to create uncertainty in discharge schedules and subsequent vessel availabilities, resulting in limited firm candidates showing for outstanding first decade November cargoes. Whilst charterers’ expectations have increased week on week leading to a couple of fixtures, the gap between bid and offer remains wide, with owners’ ideas firming amid a thin availability list. However, fundamental vessel oversupply and weak sentiment is casting a shadow over hopes of a winterish bump into November, as portfolios still see value in keeping their fleet utilised in the low $20s RT. Meanwhile, market participants are evaluating the potential implications of recent geopolitical developments and their possible impact on LNG shipping. No newbuilding orders have been reported this week, with prices remaining stable.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: A relatively muted week on spot in the Atlantic as a gap between bids and offers has emerged for 1H November loadings, with most owners not in a rush to lock in vessels for what might be their final rotation before the year’s end. The potential for seasonal demand spikes and for further geopolitical disruptions to European gas supplies during the winter, such as the TTF uptick following the Qatari disruptions this week (later confirmed to have no effect on LNG shipping), may explain some of the hesitation ahead of December TTF/JKM pricing next week; however, the fundamentals are still winning out and longer periods are priced largely flat through to Q1 and even beyond well into 2026. There has been an uptick in activity in the Pacific this week with a number of vessels on subs for prompt employment, and although levels remain higher than in the Atlantic they are under downward pressure.   Long-term sentiment is underpinned by a good number of structural requirements from fleet renewal and the huge wave of supply coming towards the end of the decade, including further progress on pre-FID projects. However, the immediate outlook is hampering discussions for multiyear periods starting in the next 6-12 months.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The steady flow of requirements in the Atlantic appears to have absorbed much of the modern tonnage willing or able to show flexibility off October dates, with the remaining time- or price-sensitive availabilities held back for now. The most recent fixing levels suggest a floor may have been reached and also interest in multimonth requirements imply some charterers are now ready to snap up tonnage for winter, but the year has taught us not to get ahead of ourselves… either way, an immediate rebound in rates is unlikely given the overall supply imbalance. Requirements further out are yet to garner much interest at the lower end of the rate range of recent weeks, but we shall see how the market shapes up as we approach the fixing window. The Pacific continues to lag somewhat with lower liquidity, as challenges for owners remaining cold seem more likely to curb oversupply as opposed to a resurgence of requirements.   There is still a lot of interest in the medium- and long-term space, with some interesting pricing signs for existing and newbuild tonnage emerging for the remainder of the decade.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Spot charter rates have continued their decline this week despite a few more requirements emerging, mainly due to the oversupply of modern tonnage particularly in the Atlantic Basin. A handful of players had suggested a possible floor on freight at which traders would see more value in arbitrage opportunities to go East rather than subletting; however, with FOB bids pricing in-house tonnage very low, spot shipping is having to compete ever more aggressively and the result is yet more downward pressure. The Pacific Basin remains awash with idle tonnage and fresh multimonth enquiries from the Middle East saw competitive offers across vessel sizes and types. The prospect of a firming winter now seems very remote, with both FFAs and offer for physical tonnage holding fairly flat through until early 2026.  Whilst the long-term views coming from Gastech this year were wholly positive and have been bolstered by fresh reports of FIDs for new U.S. projects this week, reconciling the soft market of today and the likely conditions through the interim period remains challenging. There are a handful of requirements for periods bridging that stark contrast in sentiment. However, the gap between bid and offer for structural availabilities is likely to remain wide for the time being.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: We’re normally strapping ourselves in for spot rates’ annual trip to the moon at this time each year, but it appears as though the shuttle has been grounded in 2025. With an endless stream of uncovered cargos to be shipped, the hope for Owners is that vessel supply starts to dry-up as portfolios horde their tonnage as an insurance policy against any weather driven (or geopolitically driven) spikes. Unfortunately for those who are long tonnage, this has not happened. To focus on the positives, the spot market is working exactly the way it’s meant to - and this is great news for the handful of Charterers who are not also Owners. For everyone else (which is actually everyone else…) who is reliant upon a winter premium to balance the books in 2025, there’s just way too much vessel supply on offer to make this a plausible outcome for now. Of course, this is the cyclical nature of LNG shipping and whilst we need to brace for a couple of years of low spot rates, as mentioned in last week’s circular, the long-term outlook for the industry is very bullish. Reviews from Gastech have highlighted the sheer number of portfolios looking for long-term tonnage and this means that there’s more than enough work to keep Owners and Charterers busy for now. And whilst it might only be jam tomorrow for Owners, it at least provides some line of sight to better times ahead for all of us.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: With the party makers and Gastech shakers currently plying their trade throughout Milan, the market can be forgiven for its somewhat lacklustre performance in the first half of this week. Of course, seasonally a lull is expected at this time of year, and one assumes that this annual gathering of LNG protagonists is timed accordingly to combat depressing rate levels with some industrywide bonhomie. Rejuvenated and reseated at their desks next week, the hope is that the powers that be will ensure that trading volumes recover in time to provide Owners with the Christmas present they so justly deserve. This might sound like wishful thinking from a shipbroker who is wading through the market doldrums, but with Corpus Christi, LNG Canada and Barossa all set to push additional volumes onto the water in Q4, all that’s needed is a prolonged cold snap to flip the current market sentiment on its head. It’s also worth noting that spot shipping is just the very visible tip of the market in which we all operate and as observant readers of Tradewinds will have noted, vessel recycling, LNG bunkering and long-term tendering activities are all continuing apace. In short, whilst those of us operating in the short-term chartering market might be agitating for increased levels of activity, when the LNG shipping market is considered as a whole, we’ve probably all never been busier. Enjoy the rest of your week!

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Spot charter rates have come under pressure this week with vessel oversupply in both basins leading to fixtures concluded at close to $30,000 pd on modern tonnage. Additional requirements are naturally being shown as charterers look to dip into the weaker sentiment for Atlantic loadings throughout October. Extended periods are still valued at some premium whilst the spot fluctuates within a relatively tight range. Independent owners’ share of the short-term market is likely to continue growing through the balance year with an increase in redeliveries from term charters, as the gap between bid and offer for periods covering 2026/27 remains too wide in most cases. That said, there are a handful of structural requirements coming forward which may lead to more manageable levels for owners in that one-to-two-year space, though competition remains strong. On the longer-term side, fleet replacement and a healthy year for new FID’s continue to fuel discussions for long term coverage following the massive increases in LNG supply set to come online later in the decade.
