n: LNG Market Report
x: Activity levels in the Atlantic spot market have been somewhat lacklustre of late, though a slower August can certainly be forgiven in a year when the number of spot fixtures to date already totals close to 300. The resulting sentiment in the West has been a little mixed, with laycans moving out beyond marketed availabilities. Prompter enquiries for end September continue to emerge, though corresponding availabilities are largely untested with many requirements optimisation-led or linked to cargo purchases. All in all, this makes for a rather sideways trajectory for charter rates, as supported by the levels reported for an interbasin fixture for October implying minimal upside priced through the balance of Q4.  Rates have begun to soften in the Pacific despite a small number of fixtures. Tonnage continues to build up on TFDE’s and whilst new volumes are expected online in the next couple of months, current conditions are challenging with additional length brought about by maintenance at one Australian export terminal and limited activity out of the Middle East. New volumes from Barossa expected online in the next couple of months and further LNG Canada ramp up are needed to bring more balance.

Aside from those few deals, very little is occurring as holidays, vacations, and events have many regular market participants away from their desks. t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The ebb and flow of a soft summer market continues across all basins. In the Atlantic, after the record-breaking July followed by a much quieter August, the market is now beginning to pick up again although rates remain stubbornly range-bound. The Pacific basin had taken up a bit of the slack offered by the Atlantic but without coming close to matching the hectic pace of fixing in the West, while the Middle East has also been a little quiet of late following the surge of activity earlier in the summer that emphasised how important the region has become. For periods a little longer, the bid (and to an extent, the offer) suggests a fairly flat winter and one in which charterers will likely feel comfortable with a little more spot exposure… so we may be in for a busy winter.  After a quiet few months at the shipyards, this week felt like a bonanza with six orders reported by Samsung on behalf of two owners, for delivery between November 2027 and September 2028. The specifications remain under wraps for now so direct comparisons to previous orders are a little unclear, but all the indications are that pricing resists downward pressure despite relative inactivity this year.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Spot activity has eased off slightly over the past week, as could be expected after breakneck speed with which requirements were covered during July. Atlantic fixtures have continued to trickle through with little direction or movement on charter rates and whilst availabilities look patchier further forward, charterers are in no hurry expecting redeliveries to repopulate position lists in due course. The Pacific has remained quiet, and rates have come under further pressure with a single spot fixture for early September seeing plenty of offers.   Whilst we may have finally reached holiday mode on the spot, the long-awaited summer lull has not killed longer term discussions. Preparations are being made for some structural shorts next year, against growing availability profile from independent owners looking to take short term coverage before anticipated tightening later in the decade. Fresh newbuilding orders remain muted year-to-date though yards are comfortable with large orderbooks and a healthy pipeline of prospective requirements from the LNG space and other segments alike.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: US The US Gulf Coast FOB market is generally thin, with many abstaining in recent days/weeks due to tariff-related uncertainty.  As the arbs and netbacks have ebbed/flowed, a generally wide range is being seen in terms of the terminal fee pricing structure.  Where buy-side interest is in the mid/upper 4cpg range, sell side ideas are at/near 6cpg – and very little is being done in the middle.  The EIA data report this week showed a disappointing 1.2mmbbl increase in propane stocks as of 1st August which brought overall stock levels to 84.70mmbbls – or just over 96% of last year’s level.   It is thought that while production levels are at near record levels, exports were also seen to have improved (thanks in part to Energy Transfer’s newly installed “flex” capacity) which thus allowed for only a modest build.   Based on historical build averages (but barring any unforeseen events) stock levels are on course to reach some 97mmbbls by the end of Oct.

t: LNG Market Report

x: A continuation of last week’s themes as spot activity in the Atlantic remains high, with the fixing window stretching out to mid-September, although there has been a notable lack of movement on charter rates as underlying length amongst portfolios continues to absorb the bulk of requirements. On paper the market would appear tight with more enquires than there are marketed vessels, but with the fixing window stretched much further out it is likely that ships redelivering from charter or shaken out of schedules will emerge and competition should keep rates in check. The situation is somewhat reversed in the Pacific since there are more vessels available and few requirements to be worked, so the end result is the same. The term market continues to draw in resources with ongoing requirements for multi-year periods, and although pricing suggests a fairly flat winter this year the curve does trend upwards thereafter.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: US The US Gulf Coast LPG market is practically stagnated, since a large number of market participants are either taking holiday or – up to now – leery of the outcome of the tariff situation. By now it is known that the existing tariffs will remain in place for another 90 days, but basis the arb and current netbacks (both of which are rather poor), not much is expected.  The EIA, meanwhile, reported a modest and less-than-expected build of 1.2mmbbls for the week ending 25 July, and primary propane stocks stand at 83.50mmbbls – 96% of last year.  The market had largely been anticipating a build of some 2.5-3.0mmbbls based on strong production but somewhat limited exports.  Production was strong (2.822mmbbls/day against an all-time high of 2.897mmbbls/day) but exports over the week declined to 1.629mmbbls/day (against a YTD 2025 average of 1.839mmbbls/day.  Terminal fees presently range rather widely, with buy-side interest in the mid/upper 4cts/gal, but sellers (those who have shown themselves, anyway) are coming from 6cts/gal, and as a result very little is known to have been accomplished.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Another bumper week for spot fixtures worldwide, with the focus shifting back towards the Atlantic. Apart from a few discounted deals on outstanding prompt positions, charter rates for intra-Atlantic spot voyages have held steady in the mid $30s. The crowded requirement list for end-August should imply a firming market, but depending how each individual requirement matches with some tight restrictions on vessel availabilities there are still some trades being discussed at lower rates. That said, the pricing of worldwide flexibility and even longer periods through October/November remains flat in the low-mid $40s and we are entering what is typically the seasonal uplift. The gap for modern 2-stroke coverage through Q4 and into Q1 still requires some bridging, although this may be challenging considering a growing consensus that spot will remain accessible and range-bound through the Winter months, thanks to ample vessel supply on paper.   It's been another good week for the U.S. Energy sector and LNG producers, following Trump's deal with the EU, which has also seen the announcement of successful FID by Venture Global on their CP2 project. Whilst this creates additional demand for long-term shipping, current sentiment sees very limited new orders on the Newbuilding side as the market grapples with a large orderbook and stagnated demand growth in the immediate years.

x: US: The freight market has adeptly captured the widened US/Asia arb and simultaneously managed to retain much of its strength, even in the face of its narrowing.  This has kept US spot FOB terminal fees in the 5.00-5.00cpg range for August, though trade has been thin. While the Sep market has yet to fully develop, asking-levels at present are mildly higher and in the 6cpg range.   The EIA yesterday released its propane inventory findings and its data surprised the market with a half-million barrel decline for an overall US stock level of 82.30mmbbls – still within striking distance of the 100mmbbl mark at the end of Oct, but nonetheless revealing the strength of the US export market. Where the highest export month is pegged at 2.335mmbbls/day, the EIA reported that last week’s outbound volumes totaled 2.095mmbbls/day.  Conversely, production levels have not reacted to waning crude prices and at 2.871mmbbls/day is just off the high-water mark of 2.897mmbbls/day.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Whilst spot requirements in both basins continue to provide a steady flow of chartering activity, there has been little change in market direction or sentiment and rates have continued their slow drift down. There is surplus supply in the Atlantic and with most cargoes pointing to Europe and no arbitrage opening up, there are few signs of material changes as we approach the start of the shoulder months. Perhaps it is too early to call whether this persists through the Northern Hemisphere Winter, although September laycans being discussed at only very slight premiums to August suggests the seasonal uptick is at the very least a little late in coming this year. The premium we have seen for requirements East of Suez remains in place but is under pressure. Multi-year requirements continue to be worked and rumours abound with regards fixed laycans, periods and rates; as details emerge, new benchmarks will guide players for the years ahead.  On the newbuilding front, we may soon be able to point to the first “US-built” LNGC in a very long time: Hanwha Philly Shipyard secured an order from their parent company, although it remains to be seen how this will work in practise – the bulk of the construction will be in Korea and then finished in the US. Many questions remain, but it is certainly an interesting development.

Where a +2.5mmbbl increase was forecast, the EIA reported a 4.40mmbbl build for an overall stock level of 82.80mmbbls.  That, in turn, puts the US in position to potentially reach over 100mmbbls at end-Oct, but the startup of Energy Transfer’s expanded marine terminal capacity will likely have an impact on the outcome.  Meanwhile, the August market remains at between the 5.00-6.00cpg terminal fee level, depending on timing and ratio, etc.  The declining MB market, though, has allowed the arb to improve but whether terminal fees will rise or the freight market will capture that differential is presently in limbo.  The freight market has been quick and nimble and largely able to have remained on top of the changes in the market, but some FOB sellers have begun to (proverbially) draw a line in the sand and are offering at no less than 6cpg.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The spot market has continued to drift lower, confounding any thoughts of revival off the back of a number of Atlantic requirements towards the end of August. The relatively high level of activity across all basins has applied a brake to more significant downward pressure on rates; nonetheless, fixing levels across the key benchmarks of 2-strokes West of Suez and TFDEs East of Suez are down week on week. The Pacific premium is unusual this time of year, and is a sign of a challenging trading environment that hasn’t really seen much of an arbitrage pulling ships out of the Atlantic for some time. Those hoping for a recovery won’t be seeing many encouraging signs, other than increased energy demand due to above average temperatures, so for now “utilisation” remains the name of the game. If there is a silver lining for owners, it is the growing interest in multimonth/multiyear tonnage. Rate expectations will be muted, but securing business through this weaker market will hold some appeal.  On the cargo side, Venture Global will supply 2 MTPA of LNG from its Calcasieu Pass 2 project to Eni over 20 years. This deal marks Eni’s first long-term LNG contract from the U.S. On the Newbuilding front, there were no reported conventional LNGC orders over the last week and prices remain stable.

x: The EIA this week reported yet another propane inventory build which has overall US stocks resting at 78.40mmbbls, which is effectively on par with last year’s stock level, but more importantly, well beyond the 5yr average for the 27th week of the year.   It was only a few months ago when serious doubts were expressed as to whether 2025 inventories would rise to sufficient levels.    However, if historical averages are employed to calculate the balance of the inventory build season (which concludes 31 Oct) for 2025, stocks should then be at 99mmbbls – well above the 5yr average of 92.3mmbbls.  However, it is believed that operations have now begun at Energy Transfer’s Nederland terminal which should elevate export volumes, thus impacting overall propane inventory levels.  As for the Gulf Coast terminal fee market, where July is largely concluded, the August market is pretty well pegged at between 5-6cpg, depending on timing, ratio, etc.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: After a slightly quieter spell in the spot markets both East and West of Suez, rates have been softening and there has been a sense that the turnover of requirements was easing. That seems to have been a little premature, with a few early August requirements in the Pacific basin and a handful of fresh enquiries in the Atlantic basin for the second half of August. Given there is prompt tonnage but perhaps less availability further out, this has echoes of the tight patches that have emerged throughout this year; during these periods, the competition for prompt business drove down levels but further out rates rebounded, as especially as ships were gradually fixed out. We shall see whether this trend repeats itself in the coming weeks, but for now the East premium remains in place. In contrast, the term market hasn’t shown much sign of slowing down; while liquidity is naturally lower for longer periods, there have been several fixtures of one or two years reported and several enquiries remain ongoing. On the Newbuilding front, there we no reported conventional LNGC orders over the last week and prices remain stable. However, Samsung Heavy Industries has reportedly secured a contract for a 3.5mtpa FLNG production unit at $637m for Eni’s Coral Norte project offshore Mozambique, with the unit expected to be operational by 2028.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Congratulations to all those involved in the LNG Canada project as the newly commissioned export terminal shipped Canada's first LNG export cargo this week. A significant milestone for the LNG market as new volume directly enters the Pacific region free of Panama Canal risk or diversion to Europe. Whilst the ramp up this year will not be enough to absorb excess supply on the shipping side, it brings a new dynamic to the market in the East.   Most of the past week's chartering activity has also taken place East of Suez with a pair of Middle East fixtures levelling out what had become a hotspot for activity amidst rising geopolitical tensions. Rates have pulled back slightly, and competition remains for outstanding requirements in the Pacific, nonetheless at healthier levels than observed year to date. The Atlantic has been more muted with the lack of activity and a growing availability for prompter tonnage to load end July into 1H August leaving rates to drift downward. There are additional requirements further forward in both basins with some premiums expected for interbasin trade.    There has been an increasing interest in term tonnage in recent weeks, and several ships are now on subjects and a couple more requirements remain uncovered for now. The fundamentals remain unchanged although rates appear to be edging higher, so we are braced for interesting times ahead.

But considering all of the other factors currently competing with one another the market remains essentially flat. The larger-than-expected inventory build brought the overall total stock level at 72.60mmbbls, or 99% of last year’s 2H Jun level, and puts the U.S. inventories in a position to reach well in to the high 90mmbbl level by the end of Oct – the conclusion of the traditional ‘build’ season.   Meanwhile, the spot FOB terminal fee market continues to compete with freight and has been held largely to either side of the 5cpg level.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Welcome news of a ceasefire in the latest Middle East conflict this week has helped to settle concerns over LNG supply leading to a softening of Asian LNG prices. However, the situation appears far from stable and continues to highlight the speed with which sentiment can change in LNG shipping. A strong premium remains for charters loading from the region though plenty of owners are seeing this as business worth pursuing, which may lead to slightly softer levels achieved for the latest round of enquiry vs. prompter requirements last week.    Whilst there appears to be ample supply on paper, with all eyes on the Middle East, Pacific rates have firmed as offers are less forthcoming. Meantime, the Atlantic has been comparatively quiet thus far this week with Arb closed, further availabilities firming up and charterers with spot exposure holding off as the geopolitical situation shows signs of easing.    Nonetheless the term market remains abuzz with activity for periods covering 1-3 years with reports of a couple of the ongoing requirements closing this week. Further deadlines loom and sentiment is strong for 2-stroke tonnage providing coverage through next year.   On the LNG supply side, Cheniere announced it had taken FID on the final phase of its Corpus Christi phase 3 expansion which will see the producer’s volumes reach around 70mt by time of completion. Orders for newbuildings remain fairly muted this year but firmer sentiment on the prompt may encourage firmer discussions in that space.

x: US With the recent geopolitically oriented and tension-based gains seen in crude oil, which have brought WTI to its highest levels since January, propane itself has been quick to move in lock-step and has also now risen to its highest point since the first part of the year.  Where that had allowed the relationship between MB c3 and WTI to reach as much as 56%, by now the differential has relaxed to a more palatable 45% in recent trading days.  The EIA this week released its propane inventory data which showed a generally agreeable 1.5mmbbl build to an overall total of 67.50mmbbls as of 13 Jun.  Production levels in the US remain at high levels (2.880mmbbls/day) while export volumes were off just a bit at 1.911mmbbls/day.  This is believed to be due to recent weather-related issues which impacted the electrical systems at a couple of the terminals and caused single-digit days delays which are now being addressed.  Based on 5-yr averages, Week 25 should see a build of ~1.6mmbbls, though the longer-term outlook over the summer build season rests in the hands of production rates and export volumes, some of which could be impacted by the weather.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market is rarely immune from the influence of geopolitical events, though with Middle East tensions boiling over into further direct conflict, the risk posed by the potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting more than 20% of global LNG supply, brings a degree of uncertainty rarely seen in the industry. The reality of weak supply/demand fundamentals has kept rates subdued for the year to date, but sentiment has continued to firm this week with security of supply on the shipping side paramount in case of significant disruption to trade flows. On an operational level, owners face increased AWRP and greater vigilance when transiting high risk areas, and some additional logistical measures to limit time within the region, but it is business as usual for now for loadings out of the Middle East. Further international involvement would of course bring additional complexity to an already fragile situation.   Chartering activity remains robust with numerous fresh spot requirements being worked in all three major hubs, East, Middle East and West, and there remains a premium for vessels West of Suez. The end of July is looking a little tighter on paper, and combined with the backdrop in the Middle East sentiment is firming. Whilst charterers have been comfortable with spot exposure through the year thus far, there is now more incentivise to lock in tonnage for multimonth period against the backdrop of firming rates on the prompt and further forward

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: A rush of activity late last week saw the number of Atlantic spot fixtures reach double digits through the preceding seven days. Although many of these requirements were for intra-basin voyages with the usual cap on tonne-mile demand, there may be an outsized impact on the market due to some tonne-time affects; the Egypt and Jordan cargo sales drove much of the shipping demand and there are sometimes delays and uncertainty around discharge slots into the FSRUs. A large Argentina tender has the same effect of prompting lifters to seek additional tonnage in the Atlantic Basin, and flexibility around discharge dates remains key.   Despite the large volume of activity for July laycans in the Atlantic, we see spot charter levels fairly flat week-on-week and rates have settled only slightly higher than what was seen at the beginning of this quarter. Whether this small upward trajectory will continue throughout the summer remains to be seen, especially with limited signs of life in the arbitrage trades East, but there are several enquiries for near-term multi-month charters which should provide further support in the coming months.   The bid-offer remains wide on longer term periods, but there are now a number of open enquiries across a range of charter lengths so it will be interesting to see how rates converge.   Away from the day-to-day activities on the LNG shipping market, there are some promising noises from the US around a softening in tone regarding US-built LNGCs lifting US volume. This is an entirely practical and pragmatic development that many have expected, so although it may not be a surprise it is nonetheless a welcome step in removing uncertainty for projects, Owners and Charterers alike.

x: US Despite a robust (but generally anticipated) propane inventory build reported by the EIA this week, the Mont Belvieu propane market defied gravity yet again and closed up by over a penny on the day.  The 4.1mmbbl increase brought overall propane stocks in the US to 66mmbbls, or more than 94% of the same time last year, which is why the market saw the increase as a potential avenue toward a wider arb.   This was not to be the case, however, and even as of this writring the arb from the East remains in the high $-140s/mt.  Furthermore, with freight inching slightly higher with each of the next fixtures, the netback has been subdued. At present there are bids in the low 4cpg range, but inasmuch as the last done was vastly nearer to 5cp – sellers are standing their ground as terminal fees continue to hover just above cargo cancellation levels.

Calculated netbacks as of this writing are in the 6cpg range, though trade is thin as the number of offers vastly exceeds willing buyers.  That, combined with an undercurrent of strength in the near-term freight market may be keeping a lid on things, though. The EIA this week revealed a surprisingly large propane inventory build – one that was much needed, as it has been hoped that a wider arb could help activity levels improve.  As of 30th May stock levels increased by 6.8mmbbls to an overall total of 61.90mmbbls.  This is on the heels of record-level production levels of 2.897mmbbls and a soft weekly export level of just 1.231mmbbls/day (against a maximum of 2.335mmbbls/day).   This, in turn, is likely the result the reshuffling that came about on the news of tariffs, which when announced gave cause for a host of lifters to swap from 4:0 parcels to 2;2 cargoes in their attempts to deliver to non-Chinese destinations.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It’s starting to feel very Summery in this market, although perhaps we can lay some of the blame at the feet of Nor Shipping, which has lured a number of chartering protagonists into Oslo this week. Whatever the reason, there’s been a noticeable reduction in spot market activity, and this has in turn seen us reduce rates in the East for both 2-Strokes and TFDEs (we won’t comment on Steam ship rates…). With a growing number of disponent owners now marketing their July availability, one assumes that the next done in the Pacific will be hotly contested, especially when factoring in the independently controlled tonnage that’s currently idling within the basin. In the Atlantic, and on term, we’ve decided to keep everything on hold and whilst this does leave one-year 2-Stroke rates trading at a ~25% premium to spot, there’s no sign of any MEGI/MEGA/XDF owners discounting their tonnage for 12 months of coverage just yet. This is partly explained by the low base we’re starting from (there’s little incentive for portfolios to release their best ships at these levels) but it’s also the case that there are a number of term requirements for owners to choose from (we count ~15 for delivery in 2025 and at least the same again basis delivery from 2026). Given this smorgasbord of charterers, periods and trades on offer, it’s little wonder that Owners are ignoring current spot rate levels and placing their hopes in the various suppliers of jam for tomorrow. Of course, not all ships are created equally so whilst it’s been difficult to close the bid-ask spread for the newest 2-strokes, those charterers who are able to make use of TFDEs for their trade have been shown some competitive offers and this is likely where the best value sits for now.   Turning to the Newbuild market, there’s been no new conventional orders placed these past seven days, but there has been further growth in the SSLNG fleet with United Bunkers confirming a second 20k LNGBV order from CIMC SOE at the end of last week.

x: US Sellers heavily outnumber buyers in the US FOB market.  Offers of all varieties litter the market, both in June and into July, and are priced accordingly.  Most sellers have reduced their asking prices to the low 5cpg range, but the last known transaction was accomplished for a late-Jun 4:0 at 4.75cpg, nearer to the calculated netback level, and setting a new bar.    Freight rates are playing a crucial role in the matter and seem to have the upper hand at the moment as a rise in spot shipping levels results in a corresponding decline in terminal fees.  Some market participants had this week sidelined themselves after the holiday on Monday but were eagerly awaiting the data revealed today by the EIA.  A large propane inventory build was both hoped and anticipated as a higher build would likely allow Mont Belvieu c3 values to relax and thus open the arb and improve netbacks.  However, despite exceedingly robust production levels, exports were also strong and the EIA reported a 2.00mmbbl propane inventory increase to an overall total of 55.1mmbbls.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: If last week could be characterised by rates drifting away slightly due to a lack of firm interest, the market has woken back up this week with nearly ten spot requirements being worked worldwide at the time of writing. The bulk of activity in the West is centred around July laycans, though there are still one or two end June requirements to be covered. Any relatively prompt cargoes would likely see a lot of competition in the Atlantic and thus lower rates, but further out the balance appears to shift and levels are looking like creeping back upwards. Flexibility for deliveries into Asia and thus through the remainder of Summer continue to command a slight premium. The Middle East and Pacific regions also burst back to life with post-WGC activity and rise are firming, although competition is likely to keep a lid on rates. The collective exposure to the spot market is unrivalled compared with recent years and despite some corners of the market expecting weaker tonne mile demand due to European LNG pricing in Winter, there are still few players willing to release tonnage beyond the shoulder months as of now.   No sooner does one industry gathering end and another is on the horizon: Nor shipping returns next week and much like WGC, a healthy turnout is expected. For those joining us in Oslo, we wish you safe travels.

x: US The global LPG market is softening on all fronts and is led by the declines being seen in the US domestic market where propane, having rallied earlier in the month, seems to be succumbing under the weight of the latest EIA report. For the week ending 16 May total US primary stock levels rose by 2.7mmbbls to an overall total of 53.10mmbbls, or about 83% of last year’s total in mid May.  As anticipated, the EIA data showed production levels at 2.833mmbbls/day (against a high of 2.852mmbbls/day and a 5yr average of 2.440mmbbls/day).  Likewise, however, the export number revealed a decline which on its own was not surprising.  Total exports were listed at 1.690mmbbls/day, which is still above the 5yr average, but well off the 2.335mmbbl/day overall high-water mark.  This is thought to be the result of a host of parties switching export cargo ratios from full propane to 50:50 lots.  That, in turn, is because of the US-led tariffs. Meanwhile, terminal fees on the Gulf Coast have been hovering just over cancellation economics as the arb from Asia remains depressed and netbacks – in consideration of robust, healthy freight levels – have been held down.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As many market participants gather for the World Gas Conference in Beijing this week, one may be forgiven for expecting market activity to come to a halt as in previous years, but the LNG shipping spot market is a different beast in 2025. We have perhaps seen a downturn in fresh requirements building over the past week in the Atlantic; however, fixing activity remains quite brisk for June cargoes, although increased competition among owner and sub-letters has erased some of the gains seen over the past couple of months. East of Suez, several prompt positions have found employment though there remains an overhang of modern tonnage likely to reposition to the Atlantic, and a further decline in rates has been observed for June dates. Overall though, this past week has felt more like a drift downwards rather than a serious fall.   Rates for multimonth periods covering the coming Winter remain higher than prompt spot levels, and with interest for such periods building there is some consensus of late-Summer or Winter uptick. Longer tenures through 2026 are largely flat though, and the following Winter is still proving tricky to price for owners and charterers.    Whilst unconfirmed, there is growing noise around further large-scale Newbuilding orders for deliveries before the end of the decade. There have been very few new orders this year and prices have eased, but Shipyards sit comfortably with long forward orderbooks and this latest news may alleviate downward pressure on prices.

Current calculations, which are based on 5yr average weekly builds/draws, project that propane inventories will peak in late October in the 87-88mmbbl range – or just below the 90mmbbl average level for the 49th Week of the year.  Aside from potential weather-related production disruptions over the pending summer there is little impeding the lofty production rates in the U.S., which at more than 2.83mmbbls/day as of this week’s EIA report continues to push up against the 2.85mmbbl/day maximum.  Export volumes, meanwhile, are presently departing at 2.2mmbbls/day (against a maximum recorded rate of 2.335mmbbls/day).  Spot FOB USGC terminal fees are pretty squarely established at 6cpg, as a small handful of activity has been recorded at just above and below that level for June.  The tariff relief – temporary though it may be – brought freight back to life which is thus keeping a lid on spot terminal rates.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The wheels keep turning in the LNG shipping spot market as fresh requirements flow in steadily and plenty of fixtures placed on subjects in the last week. Rate levels have softened somewhat in the Atlantic, although this seems to be driven more by well-matched cargo dates and motivated sub-letters with very tight vessel availability than by a generally weaker trading environment. As such candidate vessels are fixed out the market, rates are likely to stabilise again especially as fresh requirements are emerging for the second half of June. The Middle East and the Pacific basins are also softening slightly, with some tentative requirements to work but little firm business for owners to get their teeth into.   There remains plenty of interest on longer periods through 2025-26, with a slight uptick in sentiment also observed in small part due to improved spot conditions but underpinned by the widely anticipated fundamental tightening in years to come. With a couple of recent fixtures being reported, there may be a little momentum building in this segment and owners and charterers will be considering their next steps quite carefully.  There were no newbuildings ordered in the past week, but with further positive news on US project developments and some softening in the rhetoric and implementation of tariffs, it has broadly been a “good news” week for LNG shipping.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: US Tariff-related market uncertainty continues, and very little is being accomplished unless necessary since no one wants to lock in a trade which might later prove to be unwise.  As such, while there was a rash of activity on the announcement of the tariffs – mostly attempts to secure 2:2 volumes (in place of 4:0 cargoes and/or fix pre-tariff deadline laycans) – the June market is now littered with both buyers and sellers.  There exists a divide, however, and where buyers are more apt to place value in the 4cpg range, sellers are reluctant to break below 6cpg.  Netback calculations presently show value at 5cpg.    The EIA this week reported a 1.0mmbbl propane inventory increase which brought stocks to a total of 48.20mmbbls, or ~81% of last year’s total, and just ~78% of two years ago.  The modest build was on the lower end of expectations but overall considered a step in the right direction.  It is anticipated by some that the recent switching from 4:0 cargoes to 2;2 cargoes could have an impact on stock levels, though terminal owners have indicated that in some other cases they’re seeing maximum propane volumes being nominated.  This speculation is largely related to the expectation that propane stocks may not rise to sufficient levels.  That, in turn, is a price-driver, and that, in part, determines the arb.  Armed with the ongoing uncertainty of whether or not trade deals will be achieved, the market naturally remains in limbo.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: There has been no shortage of chartering activity in the LNG shipping market this year, and the action didn’t let up last week. There hasn’t been a huge increase in rates over the record lows seen in the first quarter, but the recovery has been fairly well-sustained by emerging enquiries and a relative lack of modern tonnage. Lower landed LNG prices in Europe have encouraged interest from Asian importers and the subsequent tonne mile boost coincides with strong U.S. production, which is supporting charter rates through the summer months. Amidst all the uncertainty within and around the U.S. economic proposals, there has been good news on projects, with Woodside announcing FID on Louisiana LNG and the potential advancement in the delayed commissioning of Golden Pass LNG. With ongoing debates about the timing and extent of the anticipated tighter market towards the end of the decade, these developments present a positive outlook for LNG freight in the medium term. We remain cautious for the near term given the weak fundamentals on paper, though demand for the most modern ship types is certainly driving some of the recovery and this segment is leading the way in edging rates higher. TFDEs are continuing to find a role in the market with several fixtures recently, although the differential to 2-strokes is wide and likely to grow over time, while steam turbines are struggling with few attractive requirements and most focus being on Sale and Purchase transactions. Much of this has been expected, although uncertainty remains as to how quickly this rebalancing will take place and whether the recent uptick will be sustained considering the fleet growth still to be seen this year.

x: US Market conditions have by now deteriorated to the point where US cargo cancellations are being considered.  The nearly nonexistent arb and poor netbacks have pushed term lifters to the brink and it is being predicted that cancellations might occur as soon as this week.  All of this comes as a result of the trade tariffs which have disrupted global LPG market trade.  When, if, and how things might be resolved is a topic of ongoing debate, but in the meanwhile most regular market participants have adopted a ‘shelter-in-place’ approach so as to minimize potential exposure.  Those that can have already swapped as many 4:0 cargoes to 3:1 or – better – 2:2 parcels in order that non-Chinese destinations can be availed, though despite the best efforts the tariff-related barriers are proving most difficult.  On the domestic front, the EIA this week posted a weak build of just 600,000bbls, bringing overall US primary propane stock levels to 47.20mmbbls, or about 83% of the same time last year.  This is despite another record-level production figure provided by the EIA of 2.852mmbbls/day.  Mont Belvieu propane pricing on 1st April were 92cts/gal but by 1st May have fallen to 77cts/gal, a 16% decline over the month-long period.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Another active week in the spot market on LNG shipping where the crunch on tonnage for end May dates in the USG remains the topic of conversation since our last report. Charter rates have appreciated more quickly than has been seen at any point this year with 2-strokes in the Atlantic around the $40,000 pd mark on certain date ranges. Requirements continue to crop up on the back of cargo diversions away from Europe. Several lifters of U.S. volumes are strategically short whilst portfolios are also redelivering ships and replacing on a weak spot market, the resulting rush for tonnage highlights the potential for pockets of tightness to appear in the right trading environment, despite the overarching weaker fundamentals. The Pacific is yet to make up the widening gap in charter rates due to a lack of firm requirements of late, though with several ships sure to ballast back to the Atlantic we may see some rebalancing further forward.  On the period side, further interest in multiyear charters is being worked in the market this week although the story remains that whilst there are plenty of willing sellers for 2026, offers for longer period are more limited and priced accordingly.

x: US The market seems to be settling – for the moment – but uncertainty still reigns with regards to the implementation of trade tariffs.  There does exist hope that the US and China can come to some kind of agreement on both ethane and LPGs since those commodities have become so crucial for both parties; in 2024 LPG was the second-largest value commodity shipped from the US to China and it is presently being anticipated that the issues at hand may be ironed out sooner than later.  Meanwhile, the EIA recorded a very welcomed propane inventory build  of 2.2mmbbls, where a more modest increase of ~.500mmbbls was generally anticipated.  This brought overall stocks to 46.60mmbbls, or 82% of last year.  Based on 5-yr average weekly build rates, it is calculated that US propane stocks will peak at below 90mmbbls at the end of October.  This is based on domestic production levels (which should likely remain robust, save for a nosedive in crude values), and export levels (which are poised to rise in the next 60 days or so as Energy Transfer’s expansion is enabled).  As for Terminal Fees, the market now for May 4:0 cargoes is likely on either side of 6cpg, with June perhaps just a bit higher.  Very little is occurring, though, as participants seem content to wait as they seek greater clarity on the tariff(s) issue.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market continues to offer a safe haven for those of us looking for logic to underpin market movements, in a world where rhyme seems to bear more weight than reason in influencing financial markets. A marginal opening of the arbitrage has seen additional demand arise in the Atlantic just at a time when open tonnage lists have been squeezed especially for relatively prompt requirements. It hasn’t been an easy year for tri-fuel vessels but a couple of fixtures last week were the first to nudge the market up, and since then 2-strokes have taken up the baton to push levels higher still. By contrast, pressure is growing in the Pacific where very few cargoes have been worked and there remains a large oversupply of relatively modern tonnage on the prompt.   The stark difference in expectations for rates spanning into 2027 and beyond continues to hold up liquidity on longer term charters, and the sweet spot remains periods of 1-to-2 years. We are seeing an increasing number of vessels in lay-up and for sale as expected in current market conditions, which does lend support to the possibility of an earlier than expected recovery. Perhaps with the continued ramp up of new projects through 2025 we could see this impact continue to grow, where a strong preference for larger size and more modern technology of tonnage creates a considerably tighter supply outlook on the shipping side.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: US Uncertainty rules and predictable mayhem has ensued as a result of the ongoing tariff-related actions by the US government.  The markets are uncertain as to how to proceed as there is no known clear path at this point.  FOB USGC buyers almost instantaneously opted for as much butane as possible (per their respective contracts) and date-swaps have been common.  Meanwhile, though – and despite it all – MB propane values reacted by rising and thus squeezing arbs, thereby placing pressure on netbacks, which have declined and resulted in the lowest terminal fee levels since late 2023.  As if that were insufficient, the EIA data this week was a surprise to most participants, many of whom were calling for a .500-1.00mmbbl inventory gain but were met with a 1.3mmbbl reduction to an overall US stock position of 44.40mmbbls, or about 80% of the same time last year.  This is believed to be the result of higher exports (1.966mmbbls/day, up from 1.739mmbbls/day) and mildly lower production of 2.744mmbbls/day (versus 2.752mmbbls/day the week prior).  There is some speculation, however, that the increased butane liftings (at the expense of propane) will next week result in lower propane exports, and thus a build – though at this point it is difficult to gauge the level that stocks might build.  Whether or not the tariffs that will (or won’t) be imposed will (or won’t) include NGLs or LPGs remains a very hot topic that is being discussed and bantered by all.  The only sure thing at this point is that nothing is certain.

n: LNG Market Report
x: While US tariffs were eating up all the headlines a week ago, the LNG freight market kept calm and quietly carried on. We’ve seen a little bit of a switch-around this week though, with a back-down in the full implementation of tariffs allowing some calm to return to the wider economy while here in LNG shipping, there are fresh challenges emerging. In the near-term, fewer requirements were already resulting in increased competition among owners and sub-letters and leading to softening rates. On top of this, reports of production issues in Asia will not be welcomed by those that are long shipping. The most modern tonnage does still remain well above the levels seen earlier in the year, but rather than the Atlantic market pushing up to match the “Pacific premium” we’ve seen in recent weeks it is the Pacific market that is coming down to meet Atlantic levels. There are also major developments announced or being considered by national and international bodies that will need careful review, such as the additional USTR port fees and the outcome of the MEPC 83 meeting, both of which would have a considerable impact on shipping. The latter in particular has provided some clarity on the anticipated implementation of GHG fuel intensity regulations, but it is a little too early to really understand the implications.  There have been no newbuildings announced this week.

However, the swap fee (swinging following the tariff) are too far to breach and yet to hear much origin swap happened. This being said, limited heavy propane grade available from AG etc increased the swap difficulties. We are expecting some petchem plants to cut rates, or advance or extend their turnaround after using up feedstock. x: US As a direct result of the implementation of tariffs WTI was seen in virtual freefall over the course of this week, only to surge again yesterday after tariffs were – at least temporarily – rescinded, in most part.  As of this writing front-month WTI is pegged at $60.57/bbl, off from the $71.20/bbl level seen at the front of April. Correspondingly, Mont Belvieu propane has seen an equivalent descent and closed Wednesday at $59.00cts/gal, off from $92.00cts/gal on 1st April.  The EIA yesterday reported an overall propane inventory build of 1.6mmbbls, which was generally expected, and brought stocks to ~88% of the levels achieved at the same time last year, but just 81% of two years ago.  As a percentage of crude, propane has fallen from over 50% of WTI to just over 41% at the close of business Wednesday.  Meanwhile, terminal fees have slid, as well, with 4:0 parcels being talked at around 5cts/gal and 2:2 parcels at just below 6cts/gal.  In response to the tariffs being placed on China there have been a number of attempts to opt for 2:2 cargoes (in place of 4:0 parcels) as India and Southeast Asia are ostensibly meant to be the next best alternatives to Chinese delivery.  China, meanwhile, is expected to see additional volumes from the Middle East – but it is fully expected that the next chapter to the story has yet to be written.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It’s bewildering how rapidly the world has changed in the past week, and while time will tell just how seismic the impacts of the Trump administration policies will be we can perhaps take some refuge in the relatively calm and composed LNG shipping market. The modest gains we’ve seen over the past month have eased, and rates for 2-strokes in both Atlantic and Pacific basins have slipped again this week. The natural flow of vessels redelivering from spot charters has refreshed the availability lists but although activity has slowed a little, it continues to tick along and this is giving some support to rates, ensuring a soft landing (for now). Levels are a little higher for periods through summer, although the bid/offer spread for periods through winter may limit the number of longer-term fixtures.   Stepping out into the storm that has been unleashed through tariffs and other protectionist measures, how to predict what will happen in the LNG and LNG shipping markets? On the surface, none of this is good news: a global economic downturn will likely reduce LNG demand, and trade barriers between the largest LNG exporter and (almost) largest LNG importer may be particularly damaging given the long tonne-mile voyages involved. Yet very little US LNG has found its way to China recently anyway, with most Chinese off-take diverted into Europe, and the lower price environment could entice some price sensitive buyers back to market. Longer term, the mixed messaging behind the latest developments and the likely increased inflationary and tariff costs will not be helpful for project FIDs; however, the current US administration is committed to “energy dominance” and we still expect an under-supplied market by the end of the decade unless some of these projects move forwards.  There has been one new order, reported to be at $263m for a 180kcbm vessel from Hyundai-Samho.

x: US As if concerns about pending trade wars were insufficiently worrying, the full-scale enactment of (nearly) global tariffs by the U.S. instantly forced the markets into a tailspin, with WTI having declined immediately by over $4/bbl and – correspondingly – the MB propane markets by around a nickel since the start of trading.  The anticipated declines in propane market values which existed as a result of the surprising (and welcomed) inventory gains yesterday have now been not only exaggerated, but effectively rendered useless as the new trade policies have simultaneously impacted global markets, as well, and thus disallowed the arb from widening and fostering greater levels of trade.  Meanwhile, as for terminal fees, the market is dependent upon timing and ratio, since April trading is effectively concluded and butane product values have risen to exceed propane, thus giving cause for higher butane demand.  Thus, a 2:2 how commands a higher premium than a 4:0, though most have commented that this will likely be a short-lived phenomenon.

n: LNG Market Report
x: As many market participants return from Eid holiday celebrations, the LNG shipping market is experiencing a shift in rate sentiment in the Atlantic, whilst limited new activity in the Pacific and Middle East has kept rates relatively stable in these regions. Following a comparatively tighter second half of April and a period of rising rates in the west, the focus has now shifted to May laycans, where softening rate sentiment is emerging. Several recent fixtures have been concluded at lower levels than those reported last week, which can be partly attributed to a clearer picture of vessel availability as see ships gradually redeliver from existing charters, and partly due to a slowdown in the number of firm spot requirements. With an uncertain arbitrage and tonne-mile demand currently impacted by more to intra-basin trade, this trend may persist. We have seen how quickly the market can turn though, and considering the current geo-political environment caution is the name of the game for both owners and charterers. On the multimonth side, despite ongoing interest from Charterers looking to secure coverage across the summer and winter periods, the bid-offer gap remains, thereby stalling fixture activity for these periods. Meanwhile, the newbuilding market remains quiet, with no reported new orders this week.

x: US In between the nearly rampant discussions of the potential implications of the various tariffs that have been proposed, the market is meanwhile discussing the reasons behind the ongoing and robust nature of the price of propane at Mont Belvieu.  Inventories have drawn essentially as much as they’re going to this year, and the build season is commencing at present as weather-related demand has by now subsided.  Nonetheless, MB propane continues to outperform, and is at present ~52% of WTI, which should theoretically indicate that the market is poised for decline, but as yet this is not the case.  At just over 43mmbbls, overall US propane stock levels are below the 5yr average of 48.5mmbbls for this time of year, and while this is surely one of the reasons the pricing structure is so vigorous, it is the combination of low secondary and tertiary inventory levels which are being touted as supporting reasons – all while the influx of ‘outsider’ paper investment is bolstering market values.  As for the US propane inventory forecast, there are emerging doubts that stock levels will reach the 5yr average of 91mmbbls by end October, and that sentiment is also a driver.  A recent (and admittedly un-scientific) poll has estimates for 31 Oct stock levels clustered around the mid 80mmbbl level, which includes healthy production levels but also the anticipated gains that are expected in the overwater export sector that stem from the first (of several) announced marine expansions.

n: LNG Market Report
x: LNG freight rates remain steady across all basins, but under the surface, the market has a slightly softer feel. It was inevitable that chartering activity would slow compared to the flurry seen earlier in March, but looking further ahead spot requirements in both basins are thinning out. There is an ongoing debate as to whether this will herald a fall in rates, with the counter-argument that multi-month fixtures remain at a premium to spot levels and some portfolios are choosing to hold on to tonnage for FOB cargoes rather than subletting. Term interest continues to build especially for 2026–2027 coverage, but the bid/offer spread is a little wide; charterers are reluctant to commit while spot rates are below term levels, and with rate volatility and mixed macro signals, decisions are difficult to make. In summary, the LNG shipping market looks tight on paper but feels soft in practice.  On the production side, the recent lightning strike that disrupted pipeline flows to Freeport LNG caused only a brief hiccup and pipeline flows have resumed, yet it serves as a reminder of infrastructure fragility and the potential impact on the freight market.  There are been no new orders placed this week.

Crude, meanwhile, rose only 20cts/bbl on the day – but at the conclusion of winter it might have been anticipated that propane values would be softening by now. The EIA data for this week, however, showed a slightly higher-than-expected draw (of 2mmbbls, versus 1.0-1.5mmbbls anticipated), which then gave cause for the 2ct/gal gain on the day. Exports, too, were strong, and at 2.194mmbbls/day are a bit more than 300,000bbls/day above the YTD average of 1.865mmbbls/day.  As to the market itself, the draw recorded yesterday was one component, but rising freight rates are having an impact, as well. Recent fixtures at $105, $106 and (most recently) $110 for the Hou/Chi route have caused terminalling fees to suffer, and where the market earlier this week was on either side of 11cts/gal, a deal was fixed on Wednesday at 10cts/gal but at present bids are in the 8 (plus) cpg range, indicating that perhaps a 9cpg deal might be on the horizon.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market continues on a more positive footing this week amidst healthy levels of activity worldwide. Several short positions in the Pacific have led to a fresh flurry of fixtures East of Suez with rates firming to close the gap on the gains saw in the Atlantic last week. The crush on mid-April tonnage in the U.S. has been eased somewhat with several FOB sales, suggesting there are ships being held back that can relieve the pressure on freight, albeit pushing the squeeze onto the cargo side. There aren’t many signs of the upward pressure easing in the coming weeks, although the number of FOB sales does suggest a soft ceiling to rate levels for now, at least.  Multimonth availabilities with flex through the remainder of the year are beginning to look a little thinner, with several period enquiries being worked for up to 12 months with signs of tightening. Markets have also been made for longer term periods through to 2030, although the difficulty for term charterers covering forward positions lies in the sharp increase in rates and sentiment for the final three years of the decade. For mid-term periods, during what appear to be the weaker years fundamentally, the bid/offer spread for most parties remains wide so most mid-term interest reaches out to 2026 or 2027 to capture the lower rates seen during those prompt periods. There has also been plenty of activity in the FSRU market with Egypt, Iraq and Jordan looking for near-term (2025) start-up. Limited supply is keeping rate elevated and a niche-relet market suggests we may see deals at firm levels over the coming weeks.  Finally, projects news has also been overwhelmingly positive this week with news of further loan support for Mozambique LNG as well as the reinstatement of FERC approvals for Rio Grande LNG and Texas LNG.

With the recent uptick in freight, however, this may be short-lived as buyers are now pointing to the growing vessel availability on the Gulf Coast. The EIA data also revealed a 2.697mmbbl/day propane production level, just off the high-water mark of 2.823mmbbls seen in April 2024.  Exports suffered a bit due to lingering, persistent fog on the Gulf Coast over the past week (or so), and at 1.718mmbbls/day was a decline from the previous week’s export level of 2.248mmbbls/day.  For perspective, the highest export levels were achieved in Apr 2024 when the EIA reported export volumes at 2.335mmbbls/day.

x: After a very busy but soft start to the year, the LNG shipping market is gaining momentum and rates are rising across the basins. There isn't one single game-changing event that one can point to, but rather an accumulation of several factors that in themselves may not be decisive but combined, are creating a lot of headaches for traders and schedulers. These include the commencement of commercial cargoes from Calcasieu Pass, the potential arbitrage opening through summer, accelerated ramp up from Plaquemines and positive developments in the Ukrainian ceasefire talks. The strengthening prompt market is looking like hitting a very tight pinch-point in mid-April, and there are several cargoes uncovered. Against this bullish sentiment though, there remains a lot of geopolitical and economic uncertainty ahead and the fundamental oversupply of tonnage remains, so it's unclear how the markets will look in a few weeks' time let alone a few months.  There have been no newbuild orders placed this week.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The spot market has continued to firm across all basins this week thanks to sustained pressure from several short-term requirements against more limited supply, particularly in the Atlantic where Venture Global off-takers are no longer able to give the flexibility sought by charterers beyond April. A small number of March lifters have had to stomach significant jumps relative to last week in order to cover some prompt loadings, but rates are still depressed as compared with previous years. The spot fixing window is growing wider with charterers trying to cover more forward dates, but uncertain fleet schedules are not making this easy. As such, offers continue to show slight increases on last done and momentum is currently with owners, although the underlying fundamentals remain challenging and with a number of ships redelivering from spot business it remains to be seen whether the recent gains will be maintained.  Several mid-term requirements have also emerged for vessels delivering even further forward and into 2026, with optional structures remaining a key target for charterers. Interest in the same has been highly dependent on the length of the firm period, as owners are naturally reticent to lock in redelivering vessels at significant discounts from prevailing long-term rates. Nevertheless, we expect plenty of interesting discussions soon, and the emergence of term charterers is generally a sign that players are anticipating a market revival.  Newbuilding activity remains subdued when compared with recent years, there have been no new LNGC orders to report this week.

The arb / netback, though, doesn’t necessarily seem to support those levels but sentiment seems to have overtaken. On a Days of Supply basis there are 34 days of inventory, where at the same time last year there were 40 days, and in 2023 there were 44 Days of Supply.  This may be – in part – contributing to the relative strength of propane values at Mont Belvieu.  At more than 88cpg propane is pegged at around 55% of crude, which has bounced around since the start of the year from a high of over $80/bbl to a current value at below $70/bbl.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Spot charter rates are showing signs of firming, particularly in the Atlantic where spot rates are reporting into double-digits again. There is still considerable sublet tonnage to cap significant rate movements, but for those showing length this is a welcome sign. The Pacific premium remains intact but under scrutiny, as an oversupplied fleet offsets any tightening effects from higher chartering activity.  In the LNG cargo market, the Atlantic Basin saw FOB prices decline, tracking losses in the European delivered market, while Asia-Pacific prices held largely stable amid waiting tenders. Demand from Northeast Asia remains muted, with buyers hesitant to commit at current levels, keeping spot price movement limited. The narrowing arbitrage between Atlantic and Pacific deliveries has led to cargo diversions, with several Pacific-loaded shipments switching course towards Asia as the European premium erodes.  Storage dynamics are adding another layer of complexity. Europe's gas storage levels have fallen close to 40% of capacity, driven by a colder winter, though EU officials maintain there is no immediate risk to supply security. In response, discussions are ongoing to relax refill targets and provide market flexibility. In contrast, Asia’s LNG imports have dropped to a 22-month low, as milder temperatures in North Asia and elevated spot prices have dampened demand. Buyers remain hesitant to engage in the spot market at current levels, reinforcing the bearish outlook.      Geopolitical developments remain a source of uncertainty, with the gas markets awaiting news of the Ukraine war and potential ceasefire negotiations, the resumptions of some limited LNG traffic through the Suez Canal and news that the U.S. is considering restrictions on Chinese-built ships and operators with such vessels in their fleets. It’s never a dull week.

x: The biggest news in LNG shipping over the past week has been Venture Global’s announcement of the commercial start-up of its long-term offtake from CP1, commencing mid-April. Those that have received their notices will be reviewing schedules and aligning tonnage, and this will inevitably pull ships out of the spot market and reduce the number of disponent owners. While this is a welcome sign for those who still have length, and should lead to higher rates, it's unlikely to spark a renaissance in the spot market as the plant has been producing well for some time now and there remains strong competition for March laycans. On top of this news, there has been a healthy level of spot activity in both basins and slight increases in charter rates have been seen in the Atlantic despite ample vessel supply. Meanwhile, a clear-out of tonnage for Middle East loading has prompted additional Pacific enquiries reaching through March, with rates at a premium versus the West but broadly steady.

x: US Volatility is the key word at the moment, though maybe “uncertainty” comes in as a close second.  Crude is bouncing around, the weather is having a say, and while the EIA data this week was not entirely surprising, MB propane continues to ride at higher-than-expected levels.  Fog has invaded the US Gulf Coast and, in the morning hours at least, been a factor for over a week while – simultaneously – the Northeast US has been cold and is presently downright bitter.  This has kept MB propane values elevated and waffling at (or just under) 90cpg since the start of Feb.    Meanwhile, the EIA this week released its findings which were felt to be in line with expectations.  Current overall stock levels of 58.90mmbbls is over 103% of last year (though around 89% of two years ago).  Production levels in the US this week were recorded at 2.609mmbbls/day, or just about average on a YTD basis.  However, calendar 2024 averaged 2.669mmbbls/day, so 2025 – mostly because of freeze-offs in the Permian – is off to a slower start.    Terminal fees, all the while, were felt to be rising and asking-levels rose to the low double-digits (though not quite the ‘teens’) but the last known propane transactions are thought to have occurred in the low 10cts/gal range.  Buyers at this point, faced with a bounty of choices for March FOBs have their ideas set in the upper single digits.

x: The Fearnley LNG team has gathered in Oslo for our annual strategy session, just as the market is serving up a smorgasbord of topics to address. For the bread and butter, a fresh surge in requirements has emerged, particularly in the West and the Middle East, and will keep the attention of a lot of owners and subletters. We have seen a slight uptick in spot charter rates for more prompt business, and although we may expect some downward pressure to return later in the month these fresh enquiries could support rates. Appetite to charter in modern tonnage in the Middle East also remains strong, leading to slight increases whilst activity in the Pacific Basin is more muted at present. The excess of modern tonnage has not led to many term charters on fixed rates yet, but there is now at least one ship marketed for multi-months in an otherwise illiquid market.  There are also growing rumours of vessels being considered for lay-up, and less formally there are now a sizeable number of ships idling (including older vessels nudged aside by charterers taking in more modern spot tonnage) - it now appears to be a question of how many ships will be laid up and for how long. For those further along their life cycle, there is fresh uncertainty on scrappage given news of a vessel being rejected by buyers. And going full-circle, news that Hanwha Ocean had committed two 2027 slots to their own shipping arm may point to a slight softening on prices in the near term although this could quickly reverse if certain requirements for large numbers of vessels firm up.  Finally, for those joining the seminar hosted by Fearnley LNG and Wartsila in London next Tuesday, we look forward to seeing you for an engaging afternoon!

x: US  As anticipated, Mont Belvieu market levels continue to taper now that the (formerly) raging winter storm has subsided.  This is because while at the same time demand is in decline, production from the Bakken, the Permian and the Eagle Ford have, at 2.59mmbbls/day  resumed (as of the week ending 31 Jan) their approach towards the YTD 2025 average of 2.6mmbbls/day.  Meanwhile, and also as expected, export volumes have improved as the EIA report a 2.137mmbbl volume for the week ending 31 Jan which compares to the YTD average of 1.861mmbbls/day – so around 275,000bbls/day greater than average.  With fog in/around Houston this week the export number for next week may well decline.  Terminal fees these past couple of weeks have very slowly increased, having earlier dipped – notionally, at least – into the upper single digits, but as Mont Belvieu pricing softened and the arb fell a low 10’s/gal was seen fixed, and at present asking levels have moved up in to the low teens.  Very little is being accomplished, though, as the market has gone quiet with the now ongoing uncertainty surrounding the question of tariffs.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Spot charter rates remain subdued across the board despite a fair number of outstanding requirements both East and West of Suez. The Atlantic is where rates have been at their lowest due to Europe’s dominance as a destination of U.S. cargoes resulting in the bulk of 2-stroke length in the region. The premium in the Pacific is under close examination at the time of writing and whilst an increasing number of vessels with warm tanks is trimming availability to a certain extent, liquidity is likely not sufficient to create any tightness. Competition for any requirements remain strong. Few deliveries to India amid high LNG prices are limiting open tonnage for Middle East loading and rates are more resistant to the pressure observed elsewhere.   LNG has been making headlines once again across mainstream media this week as China responded to US’ tariffs on Chinese imports by announcing a 15% tariff on US LNG and coal, as well as 10% tariffs on oil and farm equipment. Short term, these tariffs will likely have limited impact as the Atlantic-Pacific arbitrage is largely shut and European storage targets throughout 2025 will continue to outshine Asian demand. The effect is likely a) more focus on FOB purchases from USA and b) a continuation of the increasing tendency for demand to be met by cargoes originating in the same basin, which is bearish ton-miles. Longer term implications are multifaceted, but it remains to be seen whether and to what extent this brewing trade war escalates before its impact is felt in the LNG space. No new LNG newbuild orders were placed last week, but yards remain busy with new containership enquiries.

x: US         Over the month of January 2025 U.S. Gulf Coast FOB terminal fees have declined from the mid teens to single digits, only to surge back to the low double-digits and then – as of this writing – land at just over 10cts/gal for March FOB propane cargoes.  The volatility within the Mont Belvieu propane market is not to be overlooked as the primary factor in this, as extreme cold weather pushed a generally soft market from the mid 80cts/gal range in early Jan to over 95cts/gal, only then to retreat to the upper 80s as of the close of the market this week.  Furthermore, the strength of the WTI market enhanced the volatility as crude values this month have moved from a starting point of ~$73/bbl to over $80/bbl and then back to its current level in the mid $72/bbl range.  During all of this time the market began looking towards U.S. stock level data for market direction, and for the week ending 24 Jan predictions generally ranged from a draw of 4 to 5mmbbls.  When the EIA reported a surprise decline of 7.9mmbbls, the market was again taken aback and MB levels rose by 2cts/gal on the day.  Volatility is key – but with the weather now beginning to subside, a softer MB market is anticipated, particularly since the C3/WTI ratio remains above 50%.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Fewer requirements have been seen in the market over the past week with holidays across most of Asia a contributing factor. On that note, we take this opportunity to wish readers a Happy Lunar New Year and hope it will be full of happiness and prosperity for all. The Year of the Snake is said to signify rebirth, and the LNG shipping market is in great need of shedding some of its older skin this year.   The removal of vintage vessels, which the market requires for rebalancing, will not occur at a rate to match the steady stream of newbuildings arriving in advance of delayed project start-ups. However, the charter rates observed on the most modern tonnage in today’s spot market are piling pressure on owners. Recycling is picking up and lay-up may be under consideration for some trifuels. If the Atlantic spot market continues to see 2-stroke tonnage fixing in the single digits and at implied negative earnings, this rebirth will surely be accelerated.   The market will also look to call upon the creativity and adaptability associated with this year in the Lunar calendar, as optional structures remain the most likely method of bridging the current gap on rate ideas for periods ranging from 1 to 3 years, prior to the longer term tightness forecast at the end of the decade.

x: The start of President Trump’s second term in the White House has dominated news this week, even eclipsing the promising developments out the Middle East. The reversal of a freeze on new U.S. LNG export applications is the key talking point for LNG shipping, although this has been widely expected and only likely to influence the market on a long term view. Elsewhere, the welcome agreement reached between Israel and Hamas for a temporary ceasefire and the resulting potential resumption of LNG traffic through the Red Sea could affect LNG tradeflows in the near term. However, weakening supply/demand shipping fundamentals have overshadowed the “closure” of the key chokepoint since transits came to a halt in 2024, hence a change of fortunes due to its reopening seems unlikely.   The current negative Arbitrage has exacerbated oversupply on the prompt driving rates in the Atlantic down further this week. The few fixtures recorded cleaned away most of the US Gulf requirements, and with few opportunities on the horizon those with tonnage scrambled to fix at levels considerably lower than previous weeks. The Pacific market also saw a concentration of activity around mid-February dates, although the market could easily drift lower again as a growing number of independent owners and portfolios show length through the first quarter.  Term discussions continue to be largely muted with the exception of index linked structures, which have proven a catalyst in an otherwise stagnant space. It has remained difficult to bridge the bid/ask spread for fixed rates, and many participants are increasingly comfortable working to indexed rates.

x: US It should come as no surprise at this time of year that the weather is playing a crucial role in the US propane market, and given both the current temperatures and the forecast over the next 7-10 days, there is little doubt that this is exactly the case.  “Freeze-Off” – the threat that sustained cold weather can negatively impact field production -  is the term of the day, and at present there is both sustained and cold weather in the Permian region of West Texas.  Simultaneously the robust crude oil market (which is being driven by the additional sanctions on Russia) is the combination that is driving the MB pricing structure.  Rising MB pricing against a more modestly behaved Far Eastern market has allowed the F/E arb to shrink to the $140s/mt range, and that is what has caused terminal fees to fall to single-digits on the buy side, and low double-digits on the offer side.  As for the domestic US propane inventories, stocks came in at the end of last week at 77.90mmbbls, a 4.7mmbbl decline from the week prior.   Still, though, current levels are ~102% of both last year and 2023, so there is little worry from that perspective – particularly since production levels – at 2.631mmbbls/day – remain satisfactory and exports have so far in 2025 averaged 1.790mmbbls/day (against a cal 2024 average of 1.757mmbbls/day).

n: LNG Market Report
x: Market participants could be forgiven for looking at the bigger picture on LNG shipping this week, with the spot market firmly in the doldrums and the widening supply-demand imbalance this year means there is broad consensus for the near-term outlook. The week saw plenty of spot activity but availabilities have been creeping upwards and putting pressure on levels in both basins, and current charter rates have dipped below the December averages. For the most part, multimonth charter ideas have found a floor for the timebeing, well in excess of spot rates and it seems this separation is likely to persist with both charterers and owners preferring to play spot rather than meeting the others’ ideas. On to that bigger picture, as the final week of the Biden administration plays out the seemingly ever-present threat of geopolitical influence on the LNG market is impossible to ignore. Whilst President Trump’s DoE takes shape, so too the optimism grows for future export projects pending FID and/or approval from the FERC to proceed. However, the nearer term impact of trade and sanctions policies are far less predictable, and yet will be wide-ranging in their implications. Europe further mulls its own sanctions of Russian LNG despite finding its current storage dwindling and the lack of an immediate replacement amidst sustained high prices. European refilling demand during the Summer will keep pricing into Europe relatively high, and whether Asia will compete for flexible volumes remains one key element of uncertainty which could provide the volatility needed to partially absorb excess shipping this year, but all this remains to be seen.  Several more vintage units have been marketed for sale, with cash buyers the likely suitors in most cases. There have been no recent newbuilding orders.
