x: Whilst many in the market return to their desks to start the New Year this week, we salute those who have kept their noses to the grindstone to fix over the festive period. While some of these fixtures are being closed out now, a further handful of short term fixtures have already been concluded and levels in the Atlantic are a little higher than they were before the break. Things remain a little sluggish East of Suez, with most activity focussed on the Middle East, and rates have been fairly flat as a result. With the arrival of additional tonnage and reduced risk of being short shipping, we expect a continued increase in spot activity this year. We are beginning to see date sensitive volatility within the Atlantic spot market where requirements stack up on a similar window, although the range within which rates ebb and flow seems likely to be narrow. Looking ahead, the LNG market may present some challenges for inter-basin trade, as European supply concerns due to the end of Russian gas flows via Ukraine and increased drawdown of storages in the prevailing cold weather is pushing summer prices higher. This mismatch between robust LNG prices and historically low charter rates for modern tonnage may present a buying opportunity for producers and large portfolios, though. The increasing acceptance of index-linked rates as well as a convergence on fixed rates should encourage further charters for multimonth periods.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The strange year that was 2024 is behind us now and for some, that will be quite a relief. The relatively flat cargo market and excess freight were widely anticipated, but it has still been a bruising ride for those that have enjoyed the benefits of a strong trading environment in previous years; naturally, the flip side is true for the net charterers these past months, and they will hope for more of the same in 2025! That simple narrative ignores many of the quirks and challenges of the year that really kept everyone busy though, such as an open arbitrage in summer that caused an unseasonal spike, and a subsequent collapse that saw a strange winter trough. The regulatory environment was also a major topic for owners and charterers alike, as both EU and IMO regulations rippled through markets, economics and charterparties: the EU ETS scheme kicked in a year ago today, and also the IMO EEXI and CII schemes were having a tangible effect on certain vessels.       It is likely that 2025 will also be a challenging year, with the trading environment again looking tough and the entry into force of the complex FuelEU regulations likely to cause some headaches, but periods like this can be beneficial to the longer-term health of a market. We will see growth following the commissioning of some new trains late in 2024, with congratulations to Cheniere and Venture Global, and we will likely see at least some of the following: a shift to index-linked deals rather than traditional fixed charter rates; more SnP activity; increased recycling of vintage tonnage; renewed focus on technical improvements to ship design and retrofitting; more project FIDs; the return of some speculative newbuild ordering; new entrants as both commodity traders or end-users; consolidation, etc. Add in to the mix the range of geopolitical and economic issues on the horizon, and we can be sure that 2025 will be just as interesting as was 2024.   Wishing you all a very successful year ahead!

In the East of Suez, firm opportunities have been limited, with the majority of shipping requirements appearing out of the Atlantic basin for intra-AB trades with arbitrage opportunities remaining scarce. Meanwhile, multi-month and term charter discussions have taken more of a focus, with several deals being executed in the past week, as players look to capitalise on attractive rates that are becoming more achievable across market. With the next seven days expected to be relatively quiet as the market slowly returns from the holiday period, we will see if any end-of-year surprises emerge. No newbuilding orders for conventional LNG carriers have been reported this week, with newbuilding prices holding.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The flurry of activity in the Atlantic last week saw a modest increase in spot LNG charter rates, which has continued into this week as 2-stroke availability for December cargoes has all but disappeared. Portfolios keen to maintain or gain flexibility amidst uncertainty on optimal cargo destinations has tightened availability considerably and prompted several other requirements to emerge for later in January. It remains to be seen whether this tightness will lead to anything resembling a spike on freight or, as we are seeing for the moment, a slight uptick. Similarly, East of Suez sees a healthy amount of enquiries both from the Middle East and APAC with requirements still being worked at the time of writing. On the surface, the market remains oversupplied with TFDE’s but with independent owners holding most positions, Charterers who require vessels to reposition and seek flexibility on charter period have less bargaining power with rates already at relatively low levels. There is also a sense of convergence on multimonth and multiyear levels, although the delta is still a little wide for now. With owners and charterers travelling around for the festive period and possibly preparing for CWC, it’s likely we’ll see some progress on these medium term periods in the coming weeks.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: There has been little change to rates and sentiment in spot LNG shipping over the past week, with a handful of fixtures spread between the two basins at levels largely unchanged week-on-week. Although as a word of caution for those claiming winter has already passed us by, storage levels in Europe are being drawn down quickly and Korea is experiencing record snowfall for this time of year. Traction on multi-month and mid-term charters remains limited though we could see some moves for periods in the range 12-24 months before the end of the year.   There are more positive notes for long-term LNG growth as President Trump and his team continue to outline plans for their return to the White House. The rapid restart of new U.S. export permit approvals featured prominently in a broad energy package floated this week, which is likely to support new long-term offtake agreements next year.   There has also been some moves on the FSRU front, with reports that the Energos Eskimo is heading to Egypt for a 10yr charter to EGAS once she finishes up duty in Aqaba, Jordan in mid-2025. EGAS is also looking for another FSRU in the near-term to support a widening gap between domestic gas production and expected growth in power consumption.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: European gas prices surged at the end of last week on the back of renewed concerns around Russian supply disruption, making headlines in mainstream media with recent winters still fresh in the region’s memory. Coupled with a sharp decline in JKM, Europe has rubber stamped its position as the premium destination for U.S. LNG in the near term, and now cold weather will increase drawdown on storages. The reality for LNG shipping this winter is starkly different, as bolstered regasification capacity and phenomenal growth in vessel supply this year fail to alleviate the bearish tonne-mile scenario brought by heavily-favoured intra-basin trade. Combined with no contango to support tonne-time, there really hasn’t been much to alleviate this ongoing weak freight demand scenario. Competition for uncovered December shipping requirements in the Atlantic has hence been fierce, with the slight gains on freight of last week erased in a flash. The Pacific continues to see a steady flow of requirements with charter rates for modern tonnage aligning with those in the West. There are also certain requirements being worked with more vintage sizes although the surplus of early spec ST and TFDE tonnage is piling pressure on rates, with fixing levels forced below OPEX in some cases.  Naturally, at this point in the cycle there will be discussions on laying older ships up or scrappage. The announcement by a Korean Ship Owner of the scrapping of four 25-year old steamships is likely to be the start of a trickle of such deals rather than a surge, although the prospect of a prolonged lay-up and the evolving regulatory framework may accelerate these decisions.

x: AMERICAS After a resoundingly successful and very well attended OPIS seminar in Houston last week, just after which an 18.50cpg Dec transaction was recorded, this week started with a 19.50cpg Dec deal, which was followed then by a 20.00cpg Dec fixture, each for 4:0.  Offers for 2:2 parcels were attempting to achieve an average of 13.00cpg, but late yesterday this was not only accomplished, but exceeded.  Offers now are squarely in the mid teens for mixed-ratio cargoes.  Meanwhile, talk of slow run rates at Targa’s Gulf Coast LPG marine terminal has been directly squashed.  It is not true, and – in fact – record rates are being achieved.    As for propane inventories, the EIA today was expected to report a small draw of around 400,000bbls.  However, the market was taken aback when for the week ending 8th November the EIA recorded a 2.1mmbbl draw for an overall total stock level of 98.40mmbbls.  The market was puzzled.   NWE Weak downstream demand, the marginal propane naphtha spread (-$50’s), and a very mild start to winter have effectively narrowed the US/NWE arb over the last few weeks. As such, imports to the region that had regularly eclipsed half a million tons in recent months have been marked at 300,000 -350,000 tons (depending on the heading of a vessel currently loading at Marcus Hook) as of this writing.   The low CIF ARA c3 and c4 prices have allowed for North Sea producers to begin re-injecting liquids back into the natural gas stream when economically incentivized to do so. The significant backwardation, which extends all the way out the curve until June, could make it difficult to attract tons from the US, and with some cold weather forecasted in the coming weeks, it could make for an interesting dynamic as winter kicks off.

x: The LNG shipping market continues flush with activity in both basins, with the number of spot fixtures in the past seven days reaching double digits whilst several others look set to be concluded before the end of this week. Looking a little further out, both East and West regions are showing uncovered spot requirements spanning end-November to end-December, and plenty of Charterers seem relaxed enough to leave vessel shorts in their Winter program this year. With healthy vessel supply keeping a lid on rates thus far, such charterers have been in the driving seat; however, we could still see sentiment start to build again if more of the prompt length gets tied up.  One silver lining of the unfortunate and untimely downfall of LNG freight seems to be the arrival at a sweet spot where DES trades can rival FOB economics, the strength of which had previously been eating away at spot shipping requirements. Add to this the low levels encouraging some tentative speculative demand for term tonnage into 2025, and we may be seeing the early signs of the multi-month market re-emerging.   On the newbuilding front, Maran has recently ordered two firm 174,000 cbm MEGI carriers at Hanwha Ocean, with the option of two additional vessels. Both vessels are expected to be delivered in 2027.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: With the U.S. Election results coming in on report day, we would be remiss to not consider the impacts of each candidate’s victory on LNG Shipping. However, the harsh reality is that the current market, which is extremely depressed despite geopolitically driven disruption of tradeflows and inflation of product prices, is unlikely to react in any such way in the near term. The long-term implications centre around approval of new LNG export projects in the U.S. which in part underpins the prevailing bullish sentiment for 2027 onwards. However, the Republicans’ likely acceleration of such approvals may come at the cost of New Energy’s rapid growth story, with the Inflation Reduction Act firmly in their economists’ crosshairs. Trump’s foreign policy could pave the way for a whole host of other outcomes with direct impact on the LNG industry but those of us in the market will have to wait and see what is in store.   On the spot, a gradual thinning of first half December availabilities for Atlantic liftings has lifted sentiment somewhat with subletters now holding firm in the mid $20s on the offer, although Charterers are not feeling the squeeze with open vessels still outnumbering uncovered requirements and FOB structures remaining attractive. With the Arb shut, the majority of flexible cargoes continue to point to Europe but a few potential inter-basin requirements on the horizon should lend some support to freight as we cross into 2025. East of Suez, activity remains very limited with Charterers firmly in the driving seat. A multitude of vessels, including some open prompt, are competing for a multimonth requirement starting in the first half of January, which is being worked at the time of writing.   On the short-medium term period, the gap between bid and offer on fixed price basis remains too wide for the time being, with further talk of index linked structures coming to the fore in the last week. Reports of one or two newbuilding contracts are also emerging from Korea, with one confirmed at SHI thus far and perhaps another one or two to follow elsewhere shortly.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Where did October go? A handful of spot fixtures have been concluded since our last report, with a similar number of requirements on the horizon or being worked at the time of writing.   Charterers continue to pile pressure on headline rates on the prompt, although with sustained activity there has been some resistance from subletters and levels appear to have bottomed out in the high-teens for modern 2-strokes in the Atlantic, at least for the time being.  With sentiment at its weakest, the fixing window is moving right out to cover periods into January and throughout the first quarter 2025 in some cases. Whilst we would typically expect a healthy premium for forward fixing, particularly at this time of year, rate increments appear minimal despite requirements effectively locking away vessels for the remainder of the traditional Winter period. Competition for similar requirements is likely to remain strong.  Yearly highs on European LNG prices and minimal arbitrage opportunities continue to ensure the bulk of flexible volumes remain in the Atlantic, skewing already weakening fundamentals in favour of oversupply. That said, with freight at such depressed levels there are plenty of fixing opportunities on spot and an increase in 1-2 year charters may soon follow. Whilst most discussions thus far have been on index-linkage, a correction in fixed price charter rate ideas for 2025 onwards could spur additional demand for the safe haven of period coverage.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Little change in sentiment on LNG shipping this week. Spot requirements in both basins continue to be covered for prompt liftings at levels below last done, with charter rates for all conventional vessel types converging at historical seasonal lows. Weak downstream demand for LNG combined with tonnage oversupply has led portfolios to aggressively bid on FOB cargoes to keep their vessels moving, resulting in negative implied freight economics. Nonetheless there is a reasonable amount of spot activity, and we expect further fixing opportunities throughout the remainder of Q4 albeit amongst strong competition.   As the steady flow of newbuildings continues to add pressure on overall fleet utilisation in the near term, the multi-month space is likely to remain muted. However, discussions around a redistribution of next year’s length are ongoing, as a handful of players show appetite to take on tonnage for additional trading flexibility, although it may be some time before we reach alignment on hire rate and structure.  Newbuilding activity has been limited this week although Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) have announced the long term charter of their ordered newbuilding FSRU with storage capacity of 200,000m3 to Singapore LNG.

Looking structurally at the curve, it will be difficult for importers to purchase and store propane due to significant backwardation, especially juxtaposed with belvieus modest contango. The propane / naphhta spread, now marked at -$50/ton, is nearing the levels of theoretical demand destruction for propane, due to thin margins, however several PDH plants including the new 437,000 ton/year plant that opened this year on the coast of Poland, have shown little signs of slowing down yet. As we approach the season of increased heating demand, it will be interesting to see how regional buyers bolster inventories, faced with such significant backwardation.

x: AMERICAS Product availability remains limited from the US – particularly from the terminals themselves - and spot FOB terminal resale fees continue to be robust, with October having closed out at above 30cts/gal, and a more recent 4:0 transaction was just seen in the mid-20cpg for November.    One of the supporting factors has been the relatively soft freight market, which has disallowed vessel owners from grabbing a larger share of the arb, which on its own has retained the bulk of it strength.  Today the EIA reported that US propane inventory levels rose sharply as of 11th Oct – and above expectations – to 103.10mmbbls, a 3.3mmbbl week-over-week build, where estimates ranged from +1.8 to +2.6mmbbls. This should motivate buy-side interest as it will likely cause MB to soften.  NWE From the end of September until last week, large cargo propane pricing surged by $61/t to $627.25/mt CIF Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp as markets braced for a possible retaliation from Israel following a missile attack from Iran. The price for large cargos swung from -$10/mt discounts versus swaps to plus $13/mt premiums,  That quickly led to the narrowing of the propane naphtha spread at the beginning of October.  Large cargo butane values also shot up by $44/mt to $625/mt across over the same time frame, as seasonal blending demand leapt while US exports to the region feigned.   This week however, the market has come off some, closing yesterday at $583/metric ton, effectively widening the propane/naphtha spread to  -$46/mt, from an the 18 month low of  -$30pmt seen at the beginning of the October.   In the North Sea, LPG exports remain on hold as maintenance at fields at Karsto is reduced to 70% until  26 October.

x: Sustained liquidity has contributed to a further reduction in spot charter rates in both basins this week. Oversupply of tonnage is felt most heavily in the Atlantic despite numerous requirements within the first half November window.    We expect 2024 to be a record-breaking year for the number of spot fixtures; however, the active start of the year has tailed off and the number of spot fixtures continues to slide each month. In part, this is due to a soft LNG market that is seeing tendered cargoes hoovered up by those with length in their portfolios, resulting in few firm requirements. The opportunities that do emerge are fought over keenly, and this trend doesn’t look like easing in the near future: rumours of sub-fixtures below all-time-lows for 2-strokes circulate at the time of writing.   There has also been further correction in the Pacific where competition for spot employment remains fierce. One sub-fixture reported on modern tonnage sees levels tracking the decline observed in the West.    The short- to mid-term period space has remained quiet with limited transactions seen since August. Further delays to two projects that had been expected to deliver first cargoes to long-term off-takers by the start of 2025 has not helped to alleviate any of this pressure. In addition to independent Owners, there remain a good number of sub-let tonnage over the next 12 to 24 months before the market is expected to tighten through 2027 and beyond.

x: The LNG Shipping market has come to life this week led by a burst of predominantly Atlantic Basin activity which saw at least seven fresh requirements emerge in the past seven days.  A welcome sight for those with length although the wide window of uncovered dates spanning late October to end November dampens hopes of any immediate recovery in charter rates.  Nevertheless, a healthy amount of liquidity ensures good competition, and we see several other cargoes which should be covered in the coming days, with Charterers keen to lock in freight for laycans over 45 days ahead. A few requirements have also played out in the Pacific across November dates with Tri-Fuels and Steamers the preferred taste of Charterers. Most modern ships are preparing to ballast back to the Atlantic Basin to compete for longer utilization through Winter.  The short and mid-term space remains muted with limited interest to bring in additional vessels on the prompt as the market awaits to see whether any semblance of the “Winter” we have come to take for granted hits during Q4-24/Q1-25.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: A new month in a new quarter but a continuation of recent themes in LNG shipping this October 2024 as weak fundamentals weigh heavily on short to medium term sentiment. There remains a degree of activity in both basins on the spot side although availability lists have continued to grow more quickly than ships have found spot employment. The spot-fixing window is becoming more prompt, typical of a looser freight environment. Whilst a handful of prompt fixtures have been seen, this is more likely an indicator of Charterers’ confidence in vessel supply, rather than an uptick in demand.  In the Atlantic, several prompter positions have been cleared out with charter rates largely stable. However, interest in multi-month coverage into Q1-25 has evaporated, with the East/West Arb firmly shut since traders returned from Gastech. There is a long list of modern tonnage available for early November liftings against next to no firm enquiry at present.  The oversupply on the prompt is more apparent in the East where several vessels are redelivering from period charters. Spot rates have shown some decline in response to renewed activity for end October dates. Visibility on November positions is more limited although with several cargoes seemingly heading inter-basin despite the closed Arb, the list is likely to be repopulated in due course.  The biggest, in all senses, news in the newbuilding space this week is MOL’s order at Hanwha Ocean for an FSRU to be delivered by October 2027. The unit, which will be utilized in Singapore, was reportedly contracted for $413.7mn and will feature high spec low-emissions and fuel-efficiency elements.

x: AMERICAS The combination of domestic NGL production, (effectively) capped exports and corresponding inventory levels has had an impact on MB propane prices, which are off by more than 6cpg (or ~$33/mt) since the beginning of September.    However, the relationship to crude oil seems to show that propane has consistently aligned itself less on the fundamentals and more alongside WTI, the ratio of which continues to be maintained in the 41-43% range.  Meanwhile, as to the inventories, the market was taken aback yesterday as the EIA reported a 1.5mmbbl decline in stocks to an overall total of 97.60mmbbls, or 96% of last year, and 118% of two years ago.  The market had mostly been anticipating a small build more in line with the 5-yr historical build rate of ~475,000bbls.  Terminal fee offers continue to be robust, though buy side interest has rarely peaked above what seems to be the psychologically important 30ct/gal threshold.  NWE An array of competing factors makes it difficult to summarize the current NWE propane market or make clear of what’s to come.   As we approach the tail end of what looks to be a record setting month for imports into the region (680,000mt) the economic incentive to crack propane over naphtha sits at its lowest of the year. The propane/naphtha spread ended Tuesday for September at -$53/mt, all while the North Sea processing facilities - both on and offshore - grapples with unplanned delays as they come out of a period of maintenance.   Due to the delays in the North Sea upstart, it is expected that October will mandate yet another month of significant delivers from the US.

x: As players in the shipping industry resume their normal work pace following Gastech, the LNG shipping market continues to exhibit subdued activity, mirroring the trends of previous weeks. There are few transactions and ample vessel availability in both basins, alongside limited shipping demand. In the Atlantic, freight rates have remained flat, with no significant fluctuations observed and while several fixtures were reported last week, the arbitrage remains volatile. In contrast, the market East of Suez has experienced a more challenging week; activity has slowed due to a lack of firm requirements and owners competing for the various FOB cargo tenders, and so rates have softened.  The multi-month term charter market has also remained relatively stable for another week, although there is a noticeable softening in sentiment primarily due to the increasing likelihood of a fairly flat winter. While several candidate vessels are available, charterers aren’t showing much interest at this stage.  On the newbuilding front, Peninsula has signed an agreement with Hyundai Mipo to construct a new LNG bunkering vessel with a capacity of 18,000m3, expected to be delivered in 2027. Conversely, there have been no new orders for conventional LNGCs this week, despite indications of softening prices in the newbuilding market.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Q3 2024 has seen the MB non-TET propane price decline by 20cpg, while correspondingly a 21% drop in crude oil has been recorded over the same period.  The ratio of propane to WTI has remained neatly in line and continues at around 42-44%.  It might have been assumed that MB finally reacted to the weight of the propane inventory levels, but the evidence shows that propane is walking in lockstep with WTI values.  As for the EIA report itself, as of 30 Aug a weekly increase of 1.1mmbbls was recorded, where the market was anticipating an approximate 1.5mmbbl rise, so slightly disappointing but not altogether unsettling.  This puts US propane stocks on track to conclude the summer build season at ~102mmbbls.  Production levels, say the EIA, are 2.702mmbbls/day, or just above both the quarterly and YTD annual averages.  Export volumes, meanwhile, are also robust, and at 1.833mmbbls/day beat the YTD annual average of 1.728mmbbls by 105,000bbls/day, but most are of the opinion that exports are unlikely to trend higher until some of the capacity improvements commence.  With regards the terminal fees, the market remains robust.  Hot, in fact, as firm offers of 30cpg presently exist.  Buy-side ideas, however, are in the ~27cpg range – and while this might be viewed as a standoff, there is legitimate logic and rationale from both sides of the spectrum.  Freight is slowly waning; the arb is up and there is little product to be had other than via trading houses.  From the buy side, however, 30 cents is a tough psychological barrier.   NWE September is set to be the busiest month this year for imports into Europe, due largely to scheduled annual maintenance on the North Sea’s largest LPG export terminal, Kaarstoe which has sidelined the facility for last 3.5 weeks. In Q2 of this year, the facility exported just shy of 70,000mt/month, thus requiring added imports from the US to make up for lost volume.   Elsewhere after multiple weeks of unmet offerings, a major petchem finally sold what’s thought to be the last of the September ToT cargoes, marking the conclusion of a very slow month in Window activity, and a turn in attention to a typically busier October.   At present, October Pro/Nap is marked at $59 and CIF ARA is quoted at $530, up along with the rest of the market since Tuesday’s slide, but off $18 from MTD average.

Spot demand is generally limited to optimisations and cargo tenders, and the margins available for shipping are not very generous, especially with ample vessel supply. While a winter upturn is still expected, it’s unlikely to match the peaks of previous years. The approach of a major conference is often associated with a quieter spell in the spot market, and we will see whether the present lull persists through Gastech.  In contrast to the spot market, longer-term requirements are keeping owners occupied and it’s likely that discussions in Houston next week will see more enquiries emerge or firm up.   Six more QC-Max LNG carriers have been placed on order by QatarEnergy. And while prices remain stable, the heavy 2024 delivery schedule could face delays later in Q4.

x: AMERICAS The month of August 2024 has seen very little in the way of propane pricing changes, as on Aug 1 non-TET c3 at Mont Belvieu was posted at 76.875cts/gal and on Aug 30 values were marked at 76.0625, a net decline of a little more than three-quarters of a cent. n: LNG Market Report
x: As anticipated, the LNG spot market started this week relatively sluggishly, with persistently low demand leading to flat levels. While several spot requirements have emerged from ADP cargoes or FOB tenders, the number of developing requirements in both basins remains limited.  The pace of discussions on multi-month and short-term charters has also slowed. However, we anticipate movement as both charterers and owners work to bridge gaps in periods and rates. Some activity is evolving in the second-hand market for older steamers, and we anticipate there will a surge in this segment as more vessels come off long-term charters.   The LNG product market remains balanced, with production shortages offset by comfortable inventory levels in importing regions. Despite limited demand, spot cargo prices continue to fluctuate within double digits, potentially encouraging spot market activity and potentially more shipping activity in the near term.  Despite relatively strong newbuilding prices, shipyards have not seen many new transactions for some time now. A few long term tenders could, however, end up with new orders.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Volumes of LPG direct from the marine terminal owners remains limited, but this is not to imply that product is not available since offers for October are littered across the calendar.  Most talks for Oct are centered around the 21-23cpg range, depending on timing/location, etc.  Meanwhile, Nov talks are still thin but early days values are pegged right at about 20cpg.  Initial talks for Dec are in the upper teens, but nothing is yet known to have been accomplished.  With regards the US stock report of yesterday, the EIA revealed a 1.00mmbbl build to an overall total of 93.10mmbbls as of 23 Aug, or about 97.5% of last year.  The 5-yr historical average build for Week 34 was 2.8mmbbls, so from that angle the data was disappointing.  However,  a large number of market observers were calculating a build of a half-million barrels, so from perspective the data appeared to be more accurate than not.    In any case, on a Days of Supply basis, the EIA report a current level of 110.9 days, which compares to the 2024 YTD average of 73 days, the 2023 average of 85 days, the 2022 average of 61 days, and an average of 49 days in 2021.  In short, there is a sufficient volume of propane in tank, but further to the point, the current Quarterly average (for Q3 2024) is 107 days, which is the second-highest Quarterly average since 2020.    NWE LPG imports for august totaled 550,000mt, the majority of which has gone toward feeding petchem plants in the region. The strong imports are likely one of catalysts for the European propane market steep drop seen Wednesday- as large cargo values dropped to CIF ARA flat from +27 the day prior, following an unmet offer from a major regional petchem on Wednesday.    In the North Sea, Karsto’s gas processing will see output cut in half, starting today, before a full shutdown tomorrow (August 30th) for yearly maintenance that will extend until the 20th of September.   At time of writing, the August propane/ naphtha spread has come in from-100pmt to -50pmt, theoretically dissuading the further imports, but so far the LPG crackers have continued to operate at high rates.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Last week saw a good number of fixtures, although they were insufficient to support rates, which continue to be under pressure. This week commenced with a relatively quiet Monday due to the UK bank holiday. However, over the past few days, several spot enquiries emerged for both basins, with cargoes requiring ships for end September and October. There is an ample supply of ships available promptly and in the upcoming months, and we can anticipate fixtures going forward. Owners are generally holding out for longer-term charters of at least one year, rather than fixing only for the winter months, to avoid being idle during the “shoulder months” of March, April, and May.  Regarding multi-year charters, there are ongoing enquiries, of which owners would be eager to secure long-term charters for their modern and newbuilding vessels. Meanwhile, there are more steam turbine vessels being circulated for sale, coinciding with the end of their current long-term charters. There have been no newbuilding purchases this week, as prices have not softened despite having no orders of LNG vessels at the shipyards for some time now.

x: AMERICAS The EIA yesterday revealed a weekly build of 2.00mmbbls, bringing total US propane stocks to 92.10mmbbls, which is almost exactly the same as last year, but 135% of two years ago.  On a Days of Supply basis, there are 121 days of supply as of last Friday’s reckoning, which is vastly greater than the 73-day average for 2024.  At the risk of repetition, propane inventories in the U.S. are solidly sufficient and can easily accommodate all fashions of demand.  It is calculated that US stocks will reach to between 102-105mmbbls at the first week of October, which would be the highest level in 10 years.  The pricing shows Sep MB propane as presently trading at over 78cpg and at a ratio of 45% of WTI.  There is very little pricing subsidence through Q1 2025 as the forward curve doesn’t allow for anything less than 78cpg until Mar of next year.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, remain solidly robust – though there is a bit of fade into Q4.  It is reckoned that Sep is effectively complete, as a mid-Sep 2:2 was fixed at a reported 21cpg.  Oct avails are offered in the low/mid 20cpg range, while Nov is offered in the very upper teens for a 4:0.  NWE In the first half of August, Europe's LPG market experienced a significant downturn, with prices sliding approximately $20 from August 1st to 15th. This decline was primarily attributed to steady supply  from US exports and more consistent output from the  North Sea.   The East-West spread narrowed and While seasonal demand loomed on the horizon, the market remained in a lull, as almost half a million tons of LPG discharged at Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) ports for the period July 15- August 15.   However, as of mid week this week, the propane market in Northwest Europe has showed signs of stabilisation CIF ARA propane has risen to $572/metric ton, up by $6/mt. The large-cargo CIF ARA propane market maintained a steady assessment at +$21/mt to September quotes.   Looking ahead, the European LPG market though well-supplied, could occur if maintenance is required in the North Sea or if temperatures drop.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It’s counterintuitive to be dropping rates as we charge ahead into the Q4 fixing window, but the conservative world of LNG appears to be shaking off the shackles of conventional wisdom these days. The main focus this week has been down the curve, with a handful of Charterers looking for big ships with laycans in the second half of this decade. This has kept the smiles on the faces of the fortunate owners who have Newbuild tonnage (or slots) on offer, and helps distract from the paucity of demand in the short term market. The latter is completely justifiable when the fundamentals are examined, but we’ve become so used to sentiment calling the shots that it seems unfaithful to write the rest of 2024 off too quickly. What we do know is that volumes on the water always spike in Q4 and this means that shipping utilisation will also go up. Will it be enough to turn a five-figure market into a 200k per day bonanza? Maybe not. But this certainly looks to be a buying opportunity for modern tonnage and if too many savvy charterers pick up on this, anything is possible. No newbuilding orders this week, but this will need to change soon also.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS After having declined over most of July, Mont Belvieu non-TET propane values have – alongside a modest uptick in the crude arena – turned a corner and found a home at just below 80cts/gal, the current going rate.  The lock-step nature of propane to WTI has kept the ratio between the two in the low 40-percentile range.  The maintenance of the propane pricing structure continues to confound, particularly in view of the fundamental factors.  It is summertime, after all, and export volumes are effectively capped until the expansions begin to emerge late next year.  Furthermore, stock levels of propane are indeed robust, having on yesterday been reported at 90.10mmbbls for the week ending 9th August.  This is 99.5% of last year’s level and puts the US on a trajectory to reach ~103mmbbls at the first week of October, which is entirely sufficient for all varieties of demand which regularly occur.  Meanwhile, as to terminal fees, they remain strong as they continue to be supported by a healthy arb, unfettered passage to the East via Panama Canal, limited terminal avails and – for the moment, at least – generally cheap freight.  September transactions are largely concluded by now, and October volumes are being discussed in the low/mid 20cpg range.  It is presently anticipated the Nov and Dec will likely commence trade soon, and then probably in the upper teens, though nothing is known to have been concluded yet.  NWE The European LPG market got off to a strong start in August, crossing the $600/mt mark for the first time in over a year, with physical premiums extending $6/mt higher still. But It has come off sharply on the back of comfortable stocks, bolstered by US exports and growing Norwegian output- as North Sea exports have increased, along with production, up 18 percent on the year.   Furthermore, while propane remains the more competitive feedstock in relation to naphtha, it’s been observed that steam crackers, have turned toward Naphtha as of late despite the spread (-$89/mt), in efforts to minimize Ethylene length. As of yesterday, OPIS report that 460,000 metric tons of LPG have discharged in NWE on the month, a level that the market finds more than sufficient given storage levels and demand at present.

n: LNG Market Report
x: With limited requirements observed across both basins, the LNG shipping market has seen a quiet week, resulting in limited demand for spot charters. Few requirements are being worked, and these are predominantly East of Suez. The lack of activity has resulted in a softer sentiment for the upcoming winter. Vessel availability is slightly long against the requirements seen in the market and ships opening prompt may see a discount for a spot voyage against present rate levels.  It remains unclear if this trend will dampen sentiment further down the curve into Q4, although in contrast to last winter, there is limited interest in securing tonnage for multi months despite more ships being available. However, the premium to charter a larger modern vessel is still present and with spot cargo prices currently stable, it’s likely to incentivise charterers to prioritise such vessels ahead of the cheaper tonnage for the upcoming “peak season”. Newbuilding prices remain stable and no recent transactions have been recorded this week.

While there is speculation on whether this will push rates higher across the basins, the prompt availability list remains quite long especially for steamships in the East, so competition should keep rates in check, for now.  There have been no new orders this week. However, all eyes are peeled on rumours that a wave of large orders might be on the horizon.

x: US: Cargo transactions concluded in recent days include a purchase at 21.50cts/gal, another at 21.75cts/gal, another at 22.50cts/gal and – the highest (as yet) – 23.50cts/gal.  And while these lofty levels might seem extraordinary – and they are – they are supported by the arb to the East.  Freight rates and robust Far East market values are the primary causes, since it is relatively cheap to transport product to the high-priced Asian markets.  Freight, in turn, has softened as a result of the more readily available slots at the Panama Canal, though this is often referred to as a ‘wild card’ these days since it is uncertain if delays might again occur as they did last October.  In the domestic market propane continues to track almost exactly with crude, at least on a percentage basis, and 42% was the average ratio during July.  So, as crude prices fluctuate, so go MB propane values.  Mont Belvieu propane concluded July at 78.25cts/gal – about 8% lower than on the first of July, and that compares neatly to the 8% decline in WTI pricing during the same period.  Meanwhile, as to the propane inventory levels in the U.S., this week the EIA posted a 2.9mmbbl build, which caught most by surprise as expectations were well lower.  In any case, overall US stocks are recorded as of 26 July to be 87.40mmbbls, or nearly 99% of last year’s end-July figure.  Based on 5-yr average builds for August and September, it is calculated that US propane inventories will quite easily breach 100mmbbls, and likely stand at ~104mmbbls at the first week of October.  Again, it is repeated that this level will be entirely sufficient for both domestic and international requirements.  Perhaps too much, in fact.

x: As we move into a new month, the market has been busy firming up and working spot and multimonth requirements. The end of last week saw a number of clean fixtures or vessels get placed on subjects in both basins, with the Atlantic basin remaining at a premium to the Pacific, while this week the spot market has quietened down and attention has been more on the longer term opportunities, with several ongoing requirements seeing indicative offers due. Thus, LNG players will be eager to see where rate levels will settle for the winter months. On the availability front, the list of prompt Steam vessels continues to grow, presenting a challenge in finding suitable charter requirements for these vessels as they warm up and await opportunities. Additionally, a number of 2-stroke vessels are expected to become available in upcoming months in both basins. On the cargo side, Freeport has resumed operations at all three of its liquefaction trains and this will draw down some of the prompt tonnage.  Meanwhile, there have been no new orders this week.

x: AMERICAS While the recent storms and disruptions along the Texas Gulf Coast have (mostly) passed and things have begun to settle down, there remain lingering aftereffects which some of the Gulf Coast terminals continue to have to work around.  Delays of between just a few days and just over a week are reported, and in the case of the Freeport shipping channel, draft restrictions of 39 feet are expected to remain in place for a period.  Otherwise, with no Atlantic basin hurricanes forming, things should return to normal by around the end of July.    That said, August availability is tight.  Most of the available laycans are in the hands of resellers, each of whom is pointing to the robust US/FarEast arb and relatively relaxed freight market while offering product in the 22-23cpg range – which is where a series of transactions are known to have recently occurred.  Meanwhile, stock levels of propane in the US continue to climb.  Per the EIA report for the week ending 19 July, overall inventories now stand at 84.50mmbbls – or just about 99% of last year at the same time, and 137% of what was recorded in 2022.  And based on average build levels over the past 5 years, the latest calculations point to an overall total of ~103mmbbls at the first week of October, which (to be repetitive) is entirely sufficient given the demand from the export market, the petchem arena, and the remaining domestic US requirements.  Product values have not entirely succumbed to the pressures of the growing stock levels, though, and at around 77cts/gal, propane is still 40+ percent of WTI.

x: It has been a bit of a mixed bag when it comes the sentiment of this week’s LNG shipping market. There has been robust chartering activity with multiple new spot requirements in both basins, which coupled with the partial restart of Freeport would usually mean a “full-steam ahead” in our ship order telegraph. However, on the other hand we have seen a flurry of new vessels been shown as available for various periods, especially from Asian subletters, causing some to question whether shipping demand is going to hold firm through the winter. But as ever, no one has the crystal ball to see how things will play out, and like so many previous cycles we must brace ourselves for some rate volatility in the months to come. As we currently stand, the Pacific spot rates have almost caught-up with the Atlantic rates; however, the exception remains for inter-basin rates, since most subletters are reluctant to show tonnage with worldwide flexibility from the Atlantic. On the newbuilding front, it has been a quiet week with no new orders, but we are almost at the end the “holiday month” so expect to see more activity going forward.

x: AMERICAS With the passing of Hurricane Beryl last week, the US Gulf Coast LPG terminals – and the corresponding waterways – conducted assessments and soundings, which resulted in relatively modest overall delays of days (not weeks).  There are some lingering after-effects, and product remains tight, but no physical hardware damage is known to have occurred.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, have remained robust and transactions are known to have occurred at (and above) 20cpg.  Current offers are seen in the low 20cpg range for Aug and into September.   Given the general weakness in the freight arena, the arbitrage to the East supports these price levels, and until either product becomes more readily available or freight turns in a different direction, more of the same is expected.  Meanwhile, the EIA yesterday reported that overall US propane stock levels rose by 4.6mmbbls – well beyond the 5-yr historical average for Week 28 of +1.7mmbbls, but this is directly related to the power outages which came as a result of Hurricane Beryl.   It is presently calculated that US propane stocks will reach to between 101-104mmbbls as of the first week of October, the conclusion of the traditional US stock building period.  And this is considered an entirely ample supply, which might only be bolstered further if crude strength carries on and domestic production remains robust.  NWE Two unmet bids in yesterday's window echoed the sentiment of tightness across the European LPG market, as North Sea maintenance, reduced Russian LPG exports, and steep competition from high FEI netbacks, lifted CIF ARA premiums into the double digits.  The tightness has been cause for concern for some European buyers looking to bolster inventories in the build up to strong seasonal demand- but help is on the way. Following a slow start to July imports from the US, over 200,000 tons is expected to discharge in the region in the balance of July, bringing the total number close to 500,000 tons, up almost 100,000 tons compared to June.  Whether or not the increase in US imports will be sufficient- remains to be seen, but for now, strong premiums and a narrowing propane/ naphtha spread seem to paint a picture of tightness in the short term.

x: AMERICAS The biggest news in July has been the effects on the US Gulf Coast LPG terminals after Hurricane Beryl made landfall early Monday morning.  The eye of the storm hit just south of Freeport at Matagorda Island, but the counterclockwise rotation of the storm absolutely pummeled the City of Houston where more than 1m people remain without electricity or connectivity.  All of the terminals were shut down at some point, though Energy Transfer’s Nederland facility escaped the brunt of the high winds and rain.  Enterprise and Targa – whose terminals are positioned along the Houston Ship Channel – suffered power outages and were out of commission for a period which resulted in the declaration of Force Majeure.  While both facilities are now operational, delays of around 3 and 6 days (respectively) are being reported.  Meanwhile, the P66 terminal at Freeport, TX – which was nearest to Beryl’s landfall location – is indicating today (Thu) that power has been restored and the Port of Freeport is technically open but there remain draft and daylight restrictions.  Additional assessments are pending today.  As to the market itself, Mont Belvieu propane values remain in the low 40-percentile range against WTI, which is very near to the average established for 2024 but some 5% above the 2023 average of ~38%.  Flat prices today are in the low 81cpg range, so approximately a nickel below the start of July.  Therefore, there is a lingering sentiment that MB propane has potential downside – particularly as demand levels during the summer months are traditionally lower.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, have spiked hard.  There were transactions at the end of June in the low teens, but since then – and so far in July – offers have been recorded at the mid-teens, the upper teens, and as of this writing offers are known to exist at 20cpg (and even above).

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we close out Q2, charter rates have rallied in the Atlantic especially for 2-strokes, although Owners across all propulsion types are enjoying improved levels and interest. Yet this week, the market seems more divided as some question the longevity of this early summer rally. In recent years, this strength had led to numerous multi-month fixtures being concluded, yet so far we haven’t seen the same dynamic. At the time of writing, there appears to be a slight rebalancing, with a little less activity and some more potential tonnage emerging. The delta between the Atlantic and the Pacific is historically high and is encouraging 174,000m3 tonnage to ignore pacific requirements and head West without delay. Historically, in this instance vessels located in the Pacific become the focus of Atlantic requirements and there is a balancing effect, yet it is quite clear that currently without sufficient demand to head back to the Pacific region the economics don’t stack up, thus we continue to see a price disconnect between the two basins. How the rest of 2024 will play out is a very intriguing discussion. Cargo pricing suggests limited contango or arbitrage and although we can expect a busy few months, it is not straightforward to anticipate how high rates will go. With both canals essentially out of action, there is scope for volatility yet cargo demand appears to surface on a very prompt basis. Perhaps unsurprisingly given these uncertainties, the LNG freight market is unlikely to drop as fast or as far as some may predict, and perhaps we will see a broadly flat market; however, as winter nears this dynamic will be tested for sure.   Looking at asset values, newbuilding prices remain stable whilst second-hand interest remains very robust.

The market did seem to sigh in relief with the release of yesterday’s EIA data which showed a solid 2.1mmbbl build.  The market had been anticipating something like 1.75mmbbls, but in hindsight it is thought that perhaps this week’s data included corrections from weeks past, during which time lower-than-expected builds were recorded.  At present US propane inventories are listed at 73.5mmbbls, which is 92.5% of last year, and 136% of two-years ago.  Current estimates for the end of the 2024 ‘build’ season (which traditionally concludes the first week of Oct)  have total overall stocks pegged at a about 99mmbbls – which would be sufficient for the winter season and anticipated export volumes.  Meanwhile, the Mont Belvieu market continues to be priced at stubbornly high levels.  Non-TET MB propane today is marked at ~84cpg, or just over 43% of crude oil which – in its own right – continues to make upward strides

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNGC spot market continues to show a significant regional imbalance, bubbling over in the Atlantic while remaining a little flat in the Middle East and Pacific basins. The arbitrage driving Atlantic volume into Asia is modest but still present, and the resulting conveyor belt taking ships East is making the summer far more interesting than many would have expected (and also, more than some would have liked). Taken globally, the fleet is more than capable of handling current LNG production levels with quite some length to spare; however, trying to find certain vessels for specific dates out the US Gulf is now proving very difficult – hence the spike in rates. There are some signs that the Pacific may feel a modest knock-on impact as disponent owners price tonnage off Atlantic levels, but this is not likely to push levels much higher since competition remains strong.   The multi-month market up to periods of a year has continued to firm up, although there is a sense of “wait and see” from some players on winter tonnage, whether chartering in or out. For multiyear business, sentiment is softening slightly mainly due to anticipated delays in project start-ups. Yet as today’s spot activity shows, a surplus of global tonnage does not necessarily mean a dull market.  Looking to geopolitics, there was a fresh round of sanctions adopted against Russian reloads from European terminals, but there is a considerable phase-in period and the overall impact will likely be small. There were no newbuildings ordered this week.

x: The market continues to show a high level of activity, building on the record start to the year in terms of number of fixtures. In the Pacific spot market, things have been a little quieter and the open West-to-East arbitrage has delivered an increase in availability ahead, but there are now more firm requirements emerging towards 2H July and 1H August. Meanwhile, in the Atlantic, interest in tonnage remains strong and this has pushed rates higher, since the arbitrage has stretched some fleets a little too thinly. As we approach the middle of the year,  the number of spot fixtures has almost reached the total for all of 2023 already.  Prompt vessel availability has slightly decreased across all basins this week, and the imbalance due to the arbitrage will play out in the coming weeks. Those vessels needed back in the Atlantic will need to take the long way around, although notably, the first LNG carrier (a steam-turbine vessel) since mid-January has now embarked on the Red Sea-Suez route.  The term charter market remains highly active as charterers seek to secure tonnage in preparation for winter, with several requirements already firm and expected to be worked in the coming weeks. On the newbuilding front, prices have remained stable with no new orders reported this week.

x: AMERICAS Volatility is the key descriptor of the MB propane market this week.  Crude strength and exterior influences such as hedge funds and price-shavers (i.e., not fundamental factors) have conspired and lifted values to near 80cts/gal, and propane/WTI ratios have reverted up to the low 40-percentile range.    How long this will remain the case is as-yet undetermined, but the present situation was exacerbated by the data revealed by the EIA for the week ending 7th June which showed a rather paltry 1mmbbl week-over-week increase to a total of 69.80mmbbls, or 92.5% of last year.  The market had generally been anticipating something nearer to a 2.5mmbbl build.  Nonetheless, stock levels remain on track for an early-October total of right around 100mmbbls, which – based on current production and, separately, export levels – would be deemed sufficient.  Meanwhile, terminal fees remain buoyant.  10cts/gal was fixed at least a few times, 11cts/gal was seen done, as was 11.50 and 12.00cts/gal.  At present the remaining (and by now limited) avails are offered at 14cts/gal, presumably to close in the 13s.  NWE    European propane price realized gains this week following a reduction of imports from the North Sea due to gathering plant outages, increased steam cracking margins in the region and crude gains in the wake of OPEC’s meeting.   Buyers have actively bid the window during four consecutive sessions for both propane and butane and while 250,000mts of LPG has already arrived in Europe in June (so far), only 30-40,000 metric tons is scheduled for the second half of the month, thus the moderately bullish sentiment in the NWE LPG market for now.

The demand for both two-stroke tonnage and mid-sized vessels, combined with a tightening availability list, has increased pressure on charter rates in the Atlantic and strengthened market sentiment. Conversely, East of Suez, activity has slowed due to a limited number of firm requirements, with the focus so far this week being directed to FOB cargo tenders and the growing number of developing requirements for the second half of July and August loadings. x: AMERICAS After a strong, unexpected storm in Houston a couple of weeks ago caused power outages and modest export delays on the Gulf Coast, the EIA yesterday reported that stock levels rose by 2.5mmbbls – almost exactly as expected – to a 31 May overall total of 68.80mmbbls, or 95% of last year but 137% of two years ago.  Based on average build rates through the end of Sep, the first-week of October is calculated to see an overall total of between 99-102mmbbls – which is clearly sufficient for all varieties of domestic demand, as well as export volumes.  Meanwhile, as to the US spot export market, avails are tight, and while June is largely complete, July saw terminal fee values gradually moved up from 10cpg (the level at which at least 4 transactions were concluded), to 11cpg, to 11.50cpg, and – finally – current offers which approach 13cpg.  Aside from the tightness of the market itself, one of the primary concerns remains the Panama Canal, and the auction levels which are being recorded.  While auction rates have recently been in decline $585k was reportedly paid this week), there remains risk that at the time of booking canal slots might be tight, and an elevated auction fee might have to be paid.    At Mont Belvieu, propane prices are mirroring the ebbs and flows of crude oil, and on a percentage basis propane seems locked in at about 38-39% of WTI.  Sentimentally, there remains an expectation that the ratio might still decline with the official commencement of summer.  May propane values started at 74cpg but currently propane is in the 69cpg range.

x: AMERICAS MB propane market levels started the month of May at ~74cts/gal and will finish at about the same – but the period in between the 1st and 31st saw prices drift to ~68cts/gal at mid-month, only to rebound back to the low/mid 70cts/gal range at present.   Crude oil values might naturally have been targeted as the cause, but WTI has mostly been range-bound between $78 and $79/bbl during May.  A look at propane stocks shows that inventory levels are growing as anticipated, leaving most to conclude that Gulf Coast tightness is the culprit, and recently surging terminal fees offer support for the rationale.  Single-digit transactions are not possible at this point, as a series of 10cpg July deals were concluded, and then followed by an 11cpg July deal which set a new tone.  Limited availability from the terminals (for a variety of reasons, but including recent large-scale storms in/around  the Houston area) has left spot cargoes in the hands of re-sellers, which – when coupled with a strong Arb – has allowed rates to rise solidly in to the double-digits.  As for stock levels themselves, the EIA this week reported an increase of 2.1mmbbls for an overall total of 66.30mmbbls, or about 94% of the levels recorded at the same time last year – but also 134% of two years ago.  Barring any unforeseen events, and if average build rates are achieved through the balance of the summer, total US propane stock levels are now calculated to be on either side of 100mmbbls at the first week of October.  NWE As May comes to a close and the first official day of summer approaches, we will see a second consecutive decrease of total monthly LPG imports into NWE (430,000mts), and while the propane price has climbed slightly over this period, the market is generally seen as comfortably supplied for now.  This could however change if logistical constraints at the Panama Canal continue to unwind, it will be more difficult for Europe to attract tons versus the far east, which has shown some signs of strength in the past couple weeks. It’s for this reason that the forward curve has propane sharply gaining on naphtha in the coming months, and thus, disincentivizing additional buying for feedstock purposes. And while butane has risen sharply in the last month, propane seems stable for the time being.

x: AMERICAS A pricing standoff currently exists between FOB buyers and sellers, and both – it seems – are correct in their assessment of value.  Buyers are pointing to the Panama Canal risks (and costs) as well as rising freight rates and placing July terminal fee prices in the upper single digits.  Sellers, on the other hand, reference the arb and limited Middle East avails and are holding out at double-digits.    The Mont Belvieu market has seen declines through the month of May – until today, when a bit of a rally has brought propane prices up to the ~72.00cts/gal level, or about a penny increase from earlier in the week.  This is initially believed to be a result of recently relaxed Panama Canal fees and contracting arbs.  As for the inventories, the EIA this week reported overall stock levels at 64.20mmbbls, an increase of 2.2mmbbls over the previous week, and which brings current stocks to 96.25% of the levels recorded a year ago.  Those in the US market are generally comfortable with the rate of build, and most estimates bring inventory levels to around 100mmbbls by the first week of Oct, which is mostly accepted as being sufficient for the following winter and for ongoing overwater exports.

x: AMERICAS WTI values have become a bit range-bound, and since the start of May have remained in the $78-79/bbl range, while – simultaneously – MB propane have drifted from 74.00cts/gal on 1 May to current levels in the low 69.00cts/gal range.  This has resulted in a modestly declining c3/WTI ratio which has fallen from 39% to 36% currently.  There remains a lingering sentiment that MB propane prices can – and likely will – continue to soften, perhaps to the low 30-percentile range, but much will depend on the rate at which inventories grow.  To that, the EIA reported a 2.9mmbbl increase in overall domestic US propane stocks for the week ending 10 May which brought the total volume of primary stocks to 62mmbbls – or 97% of the same time last year.  The build was within the anticipated tolerances, but on the higher end of the expected range.  Meanwhile, the struggle between freight rates and terminal fees seems to have tilted in favor of shipowners.  US/FarEast freight rates are now ~$145/mt (up from the low $130’s/mt on 1 May), where – conversely – notional terminal fees have declined from asking-levels of as high as 13cts/gal to more modest (though still) double-digit levels.  Bidders are squarely in the single-digits as of this writing.  NWE Large cargo demand in Europe has re-emerged slightly as the widening LST/FEI arbitrage has attracted US LPG cargoes to the Far East versus Europe, but a decreasing propane naphtha spread (off $20/mt since the start of May) will likely keep demand at bay.   At present, it is predicted that Europe will have imported ~410,000mt of LPG in May, off 40kt from that of the month prior. However, some expect that import volumes will increase as Auction fees paid at the Panama Canal have shot up, thus incentivizing US cargoes back toward NWE.   So, the market is in a period of competing factors but overall NWE prices have gained some ground this week and the region remains well supplied and perhaps angled toward being long when accounting for logistical pain points related to the US / Far East trade.

x: The market should be in the doldrums right now, but it’s hard to see fixtures on modern tonnage concluding at levels much below where we are today. The fact that owners have been able to protect their Round Trip (RT) econs in two out of three basins, as well as the hire element of the Ballast Bonus (BB) in all of them, is impressive. This is partly due to the high percentage of vessels controlled by portfolios at the moment (there’s a floor, below which traders won’t let the ships go) but it’s also the result of the tangible pressure that the multitude of geopolitical events are placing on the LNG market in general. Rain this week may presage the return of the Panama Canal, but we still have no obvious resolution that will see the Suez return to LNG life. As we move into a Q3 front month tomorrow, the risk of a logistically constrained winter may start to play more heavily on sentiment. Have we found the bottom of the market? As ever this is hard to say. Is there more risk to the upside than downside? We believe so.  No newbuilds were ordered this week but for most, given the recent spate of Qatari headlines, this will be a relief.

x: Following Golden Week, the current working week has seen more public holidays around the world and thus it has been a relatively quiet start to the week in the LNG market. There has been an uptick in enquiries and there will be more fixing in the coming days. High inventory levels in certain regions have led to stagnant prices though, and with surplus prompt tonnage in all basins spot charter rates are expected to remain stable. In contrast, there has been more activity in multi-month periods as cargo players are looking for winter shipping security.   HHI's announcement of two new LNG carriers ordered at $266 million each sets a new benchmark, indicating a strong outlook for the shipbuilding industry.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane market values declined by a nickel over the second half of April, and by nearly a dime since the front of April.  Prices now are marked in the mid 70cpg range, but still a solid 39% of WTI (basis today’s $79.36/bbl value).  Most of the market seem to agree that the weight of the (sometimes slowly) growing inventory levels will push prices down over the summer, but it appears now that a legitimate trend is developing.  With regards the inventories, the EIA yesterday recorded what is perceived as a disappointing 200,000bbl build in overall stock levels (as of 26 Apr), where the market was anticipating something over/under 2mmbbls.  Higher export volumes combined with (still) strong production levels are the culprits.  With limited spot availability known to exist in June, the spot terminal fee market remains buoyant, with the last known deal done at just under 9cpg, but offers now seen at double-digits.  Buy-side interest exists in the upper single digits.  NWE  Northwest Europe, now in decline and off the double digits, was unexempt from the crude-driven sell off of global LPG prices.  Compounding the region’s downward pressure was the nearly 600,000 tons of LPG imported during April, and the return to service of Karstoe and Mongstad refineries in the North Sea.  That said, with US propane under the most pressure at present, the LST/NWE arbitrage is open again, which will no doubt attract more US East coast FOB volumes to already well supplied Western European terminals.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: This week began at a slower pace compared to the previous week, as many regions around the world observed holidays. Consequently, the LNG shipping market saw limited spot fixtures concluded.  Vessel availability remains slightly longer than the spot requirements seen this week and while spot charter rates have remained unchanged across all basins, there has been an increase in enquires and a slight upward trend in rates for multi-month and short-term charters. There are also some signs of the arbitrage opening again and although trading margins would be limited, the market is braced for some longer voyages. Thus, there are positive sentiments for spot and multi-month charters as both charterers and owners work towards bridging those gaps to align on period and rates.   Aside from the open arbitrage, the broader LNG product market remains stable, with supply more than able to meet current demand. Inventory levels in Japan and Korea are at comfortable levels, while European storage levels experienced a slight increase. There has been some suggestion of floating cargoes into July or August, given the anticipated slight weakness in June pricing, and this has the potential to improve shipping utilisation in the near term. With a well-supplied availability list, any rate rises would be modest.  In the LNG newbuilding segment, Qatar Energy has reportedly expanded its orders for 18 LNG Carriers of 271,000m3 with Chinese shipbuilder Hudong Zhonghua, at an estimated price of approximately US$310 million per vessel. Eight of these newbuilds are slated for delivery within 2028 and 2029, while the remaining ten vessels are scheduled for delivery between 2030 and 2031.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been a busy week in LNG shipping, with a handful of spot requirements, term requirements and cargo tenders being worked in the last few days. Spot rates have taken a slight dip in the Atlantic basin, due to some competitive sublet tonnage being offered at lower levels than a week ago, but in the Pacific, it has been a different story with charterers facing firmer rate levels especially for 2H May / 1H June cargoes. There are no drastic changes on the overall sentiment however, and we believe the spot market will remain rather stable for the weeks to come. There is some good news in Freeport ramping up production again, which could lead to some of the prompt tonnage disappearing in the US Gulf, although set against this is the news that Hammerfest has had another outage which may free up a few prompt vessels in Europe. The term market, or more specifically the 1-year TC market, has definitely been the focus for many this week and rates seem to be firming, as more charterers are looking to strengthen their portfolio over the winter, especially with modern 2-stroke tonnage. In the newbuilding market, although no new orders this week, yards are keeping busy with their existing building schedules.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The EIA reported a +1.00mmbbl build in overall US propane inventory levels, which is about half of what most in the industry had anticipated and which left total stocks at 56.70mmbbls as of 19 April.  This is roughly 97% of last year and 145% of two years ago.  Even so, many continue to predict that by the first week of October propane stocks will have reached the mid/upper 90mmbbl range, with some predictions reaching up to (and in some cases beyond) 100mmbbls as of that timeframe.  Meanwhile, MB propane prices closed up slightly yesterday, likely because US crude inventory draws of 6.3mmbbls gave cause for a bit of a runup in WTI values, though news of large-scale Russian crude production and export volumes tampered sentiments.  The terminal fee market on the Gulf Coast, however, remains robust.  A ~10cpg May deal was believed to have been fixed and as news that the terminals are expected to be tight in June made the rounds, asking levels for June moved upwards to nothing less than double-digits.  This is partially due to the fact that the shipping sector is well-balanced for the moment and therefore unable to grab a share of the slowly rising US/Far East arb.  NWE As of mid week, CIF ARA propane values are hanging around $505 /metric ton, with the large-cargo propane market  assessed at -$7/mt to May quotes, The propane/naphtha spread however, is assessed at -182pmt and continues to attract significant quantities of us LPG (an expected 520,000 tons for April) - well above the Q1 average of 430,000 tons, which has more than made up for reduced imports from the North Sea and Ust Luga, which remain hampered by maintenance and the enduring Russia and Ukrainian conflict, respectively.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Where inventory data expectations ranged widely from a build of around one million barrels to a high of as much as three million barrels, most of the market was clustered around the 2mmbbl build range.  The EIA yesterday, however, posted a build of 4mmbbls – well above most (if not all) expectations.    The initial shock soon gave way, however, to the generally accepted view that the large build likely included corrective data from weeks past, versus the idea that there might be a correction in the coming weeks.  In any case, stocks as of 13 April 2024 stand at 55.7mmbbls, which is almost exactly 100% of last year’s level – but still 150% of two years ago.    The MB pricing structure reacted immediately and sharply increased the rate of decline for non-TET propane values.  Currently MB c3 is pegged at the mid 78cpg range with the expectation that further price erosion is likely on the horizon.  In looking towards the end of the build season – typically the first week of Oct – most calculations put stock levels at around the 95mmbbl range, which is based on robust production levels, generally capped export volumes, flat(ish) chem consumption, warmer weather and (therefore) limited summertime res/com demand.  NWE At present,  Europe is projected to conclude  april having imported just shy of 500kt-  half of which  will discharge at Terneuzen. The regions resilient  demand comes on the back propane's  utilization versus  naphtha  at Europeans petrochemical plants- The East /west spread continues to widen, and econs are becoming less advantageous- but for now, cargoes especially from Marcus Hook, continue to sail toward NWE.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Following the relatively quiet spell last week, there has been a significant upturn in spot chartering enquiries issued across both basins for May and June cargoes. Spot rates are experiencing a slight increase in the Atlantic but remain unchanged in the East. While there is an abundance of vessels in the available tonnage list, finding the perfect match for specific requirements can pose a challenge, particularly with some of the older vessels warming up. Interest in multi-month charters is also picking up and with periods through the upcoming winter, there is increasing visibility on market sentiment for the traditionally stronger months of the year. All of these market developments are happening under the shadow of more geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East, and although this unlikely to have a direct impact on the LNG shipping market (since the Suez Canal is already a no-go area) the wider impact on energy markets remains a risk. This week saw no newbuilding orders, with prices holding steady.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Terminal fee levels for 2H April and 1H May are pretty firmly entrenched at the 7cpg level – the rate at which a series of transactions are known to have occurred within that timeframe.  The 2H May market ranges a bit more widely as buyers and sellers ideas diverge – but only by a half-cent, or so.  The EIA propane inventory data for the week ending 05 April 2024 was generally anticipated to reveal a build of a half-million or so barrels of propane – which would have brought overall stocks well in to the 52mmbbl range.  However, a draw of 100,000bbls was recorded and stock levels now stand at 51.7mmbbls.   Not only did the overall total raise a few eyebrows, but a secondary surprise was noted with a 600,000bbl build on the Gulf Coast in PADD III.  Exports have been extremely robust and so to see a build is noteworthy.  From the higher vantage point, US propane stocks at the first week of October have ranged anywhere from 90-102mmbbls as of the first week of October.  This year should see little difference, as current calculations put the first-week Oct inventory level at between 94-98mmbbls … “right down the fairway”, as it is said.  NWE Competing factors have left participants puzzled when trying to conceive direction in the European LPG market- Following a month of seemingly unworkable arbitrage econs (US /NWE) already 430,000 tons have pointed toward NWE  from various US export terminals, which, given warm weather and balanced stocks, would cover any and all demand. However, Propane remains the preferred feedstock to Naphta,  both of which are off around  $10 from their April high’s. Scheduled  maintenance  at Karsto (April 12-18) and Mongstad (April 5-17), further compounded by an unplanned outage in the run up, will likely cause a disruption of north sea supplied LPG supplied to NWE, all of which could theoretically leave NWE LPG tighter than appears.
