t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Domestic US propane inventory expectations for the week ending 29 March ranged from a draw of around a half-million barrels to as much as a build of over a million barrels.  On yesterday the EIA reported a 400,000bbl decline in stocks which brought the overall total to 51.80mmbbls.  This is 93% of last year, but 150% of two years ago.  One of the components to the Mont Belvieu pricing structure – and one of the several reasons that the MB complex has retained it strength – is the concern that robust exports would limit the ability of domestic stocks to reach suitable levels later in the Fall.  However, calculations are presently indicating that stock levels will – in the first week of October – range somewhere between 94-98mmbbls which is well within the comfort zone.  Nonetheless, MB propane has enjoyed the support from the crude arena, which from the front of March to now has increased by $5/bbl (and rising).   The fact that domestic US crude inventories rose by 3.2mmbbls last week has had little (or no) impact, as geopolitical concerns continue to apply upward pressure.  With regards the US terminal fees, a couple of transactions were noted for end-Apr and (separately) early-May, each at 7cpg.  A couple of other parcels are on offer in the first decade of May in the low 7cpg range, with buy-side interest beginning to collect in the upper 6cpg range.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Following recent softening, rates have stabilised in the spot and period markets as national holidays globally have limited levels of activity. The main source of requirements has arisen from market cargo tenders across all basins that seek vessels subject to award, yet most of these opportunities are being covered through portfolios with available tonnage to utilise.  A consequence is that prompt availability remains well stocked, yet owners are unwilling to lock in a large idle periods at current levels, and with most requirements a few weeks out, the misalignment is causing protracted negotiations.    From the yards, four newbuilding's confirmed this week with a JV between K Line and Hyundai Glovis being awarded part of the QE Phase 2 requirement. Delivery August 2027 and a price in the region of $230M USD. For unallocated slots, prices remain flat. The second-hand market also continues to be active with robust prices as further sales are reported this week, although the details of these sales consisting of two mid-size carriers is not yet fully known.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we approach the end of the first quarter, the market can reflect on a very busy few months in which players have adapted well to the changing dynamics. With both canals essentially out of action, with the implementation of the EU ETS scheme, with engine power limitation restricting some speeds and with LNG supply surges and disruptions, there has been a lot to deal with! Perhaps unsurprisingly given these uncertainties, the LNG freight market did not drop as fast or as far as some had predicted, and the past weeks had seen a broadly flat market with spot rates for 2-strokes staying above the $50k per day mark; however, ongoing LNG production issues and vessel over-supply are now weighing on rates, and this important benchmark has been breached. There continues to be enough demand to keep owners and sub-letters busy and there is life in the arbitrage for US Gulf cargoes to go East, although many of the emerging requirements are tenders or optimisations and the spot market is now softening. On multi-month and longer term charters, there has been a slight lull as owners and charterers are a little out of alignment on periods and rates right now, but this is temporary and activity will pick up again as we approach the summer months. There have been no new orders this week.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane values, which remain remarkably resilient, continue to be buoyed by gains being recorded in the crude arena, and which thus have allowed propane prices to continue on an upward trajectory.  This is despite reduced weather-related demand across North America, effectively flat petrochemical demand, as well as the relationship to crude (which presently stands at ~41%), and that stock levels are not only sufficient, but are presently calculated to rise to the mid 90mmbbl level by around the first week of October.  Indeed the weekly export volumes have been robust, but on balance – and over the coming inventory build season - there is not a tremendous amount of upside to existing capacity levels.  Of course the lifting of the daylight restrictions on the HSC has had a positive impact, but some of those efficiency gains are lost to the regular calling of larger and larger VLGCs.  Meanwhile, the EIA yesterday reported a nearly flat (+300k bbls) propane stock level for the week ending 15 March, bringing total overall primary inventories in the U.S. to 52.2mmbbls.  This is 89% of the total recorded a year ago, and 155% of the total seen two years ago.  If only average weekly gains are achieved over the course of the next 6+ months, a ~95mmbbl inventory level will have been achieved.  Despite periodic arguments to the contrary, all signs point to a normal build season.  As for the current spot market, the March program is effectively concluded though a handful of parcels remain on offer in April – mostly at around the 8cpg level.  May cargoes and demand levels are beginning to be revealed, but terminal fees are expected to be a penny or so lower.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we approach the end of Q1 2024, the LNG shipping market maintains a steady course, a typical scenario for this time of year characterized by lower demand and moderated LNG prices. There is some uncertainty on the cargo side, with traders keeping a close eye on supply concerns such from potential cyclone disruptions in Australia, unplanned maintenance of Norway’s Aasta gas field and some lower production out of Nigeria.   In spite of the above, there have been signs of a reviving freight market with several requirements firming up in both basins and firming rates for modern tonnage in the Atlantic. The first half of this week saw some anticipated spot requirements firm up in the East, accompanied by a couple of new opportunities for tonnage holders out of the Atlantic. With the high vessel competition in the east, owners and charterers will be keen to see how rates will move in the wake of this activity. Furthermore, although cargoes have been traded within their respective basins, there is a small arbitrage flickering to life and charterers are seeking flexibility to head East. As well as increased spot activity, multi month and term business continues to be discussed although the specific periods being sought by charterers or offered by owners are not always aligned.   There were no newbuilding orders reported this week; however, prices remain stable.

x: After a volatile February, the shipping market has shown signs of stabilization in recent weeks. Both the Atlantic and Asia regions are experiencing a slowdown in spot market activity, with rates holding steady. However, it's important to note that availability continues to increase during this time of year.  In terms of the cargo market, we've observed a softening in TTF prices, with European storage remaining well above the average for this time of year, while JKM prices have seen an increase relative to TTF.,  This has presented some limited opportunities for an inter-basin arbitrage and as a result, we have seen several cargoes heading east. Given the availability lists, this dynamic hasn’t stressed the freight market yet, but may help explain the steady charter rates.  Market activity continues to lean towards more multi-month requirements, although levels are remaining steady in this segment, too. There haven’t been any fresh newbuilding orders placed this week.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: After a brief pause in activity, the shipping market came back to life this week with a handful of spot and term fixtures reported. The spot activity has been evenly spread across the main production centres and whilst it hasn’t resulted in firmer rates (yet) the good news is that this tempo should persist right into winter. This is due to the growth in FOB cargoes on offer, stemming from the number of long-term buyers who have exercised DQT under their SPAs (spot is significantly cheaper than a traditional oil slope at present). For those taking term tonnage, it is - as ever - about paying over the market in summer in exchange for more competitively priced winter coverage. In our new LNG price environment, however, these ships can also be the difference between a portfolio winning and losing a cargo tender; in short, if the best alternative to buying the cargo is to sit idle, it’s difficult for sub-award Charterers (buyers) to compete. On this basis, we expect term activity to continue as it is the best hope for owners to gain employment at present.   Turning to Newbuilding activity, following the 4 x LNGCs inked last week, we add an FSRU to the list this week with HHI securing the impressive $364 million order.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market has experienced a sluggish week, with limited activity observed across both basins.  While some developing cargoes have emerged, the lack of firm requirements have result in the softening of spot rates. Prompt vessel availability remains high compared to the demand seen this week, and ships opening end March to 1H April 2024 may see a discount against the current spot rates. The premium between the spot and term markets continue to persist, but as period-flexible vessels move closer to the spot fixing window, the bid-offer spread is expected to narrow, and a new benchmark awaits. On product, the current low-price environment has spurred recent activity in China, driving demand for more cargoes ahead of the Labor Day Week. 1H April appears to be tighter, with buyers ready to transact at levels above the spot JKM price.  As a result, optimistically, we hope for an open west-east arbitrage, leading to an increase in spot shipping activity for April and May. In the LNG newbuilding segment, a Greek Owner has reportedly placed an order for four vessels with Korean shipbuilder Hyundai Samho Heavy Industries at approximately US$270 million per ship. x: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane market values have shown themselves to be resilient, as weather-related demand has waned while the crude markets continue to provide support. The YTD propane/WTI ratio stands at over 48%, where the 2023 average was calculated at 38%.  There are, nonetheless, a slowly growing number who point to inventory levels and who expect the pricing structure to weaken.  The EIA this week, however, reported a 3.4mmbbl decline in stocks which brought overall volumes to 51.2mmbbls, or 85% of last year, but which is almost exactly equal to the 5-year total inventory average for mid/late February.  Expectations were almost unanimously calling for a ~2mmbbl decline, leading some to speculate whether this week’s data may have included ‘corrected’ data from the previous week.  In any case, if the averages hold true, US propane stock levels should conclude February at just above 49mmbbls, slightly above the 5-yr average.  Meanwhile, terminal fees on the Gulf Coast are pegged at somewhere between 6 and 7cpg in what is described as a ‘thin’ market.  A couple of transactions have been concluded, and at this point March is all but concluded – but April is presently littered with sell-side interest and only modest representation from the buy-side.  Several cargo cancellations have been noted for March.  NWE Northwest Europe got off to a strong start in January of 2024, importing close to 500,000 tons of LPG, of US and North Sea origin. It is expected February imports will total approx 345,000 tons, with bulk of the decrease coming from a reduction in North Sea liftings. US exporters, however, continue to favor Europe as opposed to the far east when able, for the obvious freight savings, along with rising auction fees in the Panama canal.  Mild weather across Europe, along with comfortable inventory levels allowed for a softening in NWE values to start the week-however propane’s discount to naphtha,  along with an increase petrochemical run rates in the region, are expected to keep the buying active in the short term.

n: LNG Market Report
x: It is the first week after the Chinese New Year, and as expected we have seen more activity in the market, especially in the Middle-East & Pacific regions. The spot market has really kept everyone busy, and the amount of requirements in recent weeks have brought back some memories from a few years ago, when spot fixing was the dominant activity, before the crazy days of term fixing experienced in the last two years. Furthermore, with the recent fixtures done at distinctly firmer levels than two weeks ago (at least in the Pacific), the spot market may have “bottomed out” at least for now. However, the LNG cargo market has a very shoulder month-esque feeling, and prices continue to track down with muted demand both in Asia and Europe. This is despite the fact that this year’s “black swan” event at the Red Sea is keeping everyone with waterborne cargoes on their toes, and unfortunately, as every week goes by, there hasn’t been any added glimmer of hope of things getting better anytime soon. On the newbuilding front, it was a relative quiet week for LNG carriers, albeit the biggest headlines were definitely yet another extension of the Mozambique project’s newbuilding deal of 17 LNG carriers, this time pushing the deadline of confirmation until later July this year.

Activity has been muted, and rates are holding at similar levels to last done yet there are still cargoes out there to fix so this lull may be only a brief respite. Gas prices continue to soften, which is expected as we transition towards the latter part of winter, and demand in both regions is not expected to rebound significantly. French strikes at terminals are effecting scheduling but are unlikely to have an impact on pricing as inventory levels remain high, with the arb opening slightly we may see some of these cargoes head out East if there are takers. Although no newbuilding orders were placed this week, it was yet another significant week for the QatarEnergy project, firming up an additional 25 vessels with fellow compatriots, Nakilat.   For those who have celebrated or continue to do so, we wish you a healthy, happy, and prosperous Year of the Dragon! Gong Xi Fa Cai.

Whether it's summer term coverage or single voyage charterers, all three basins have been buzzing and despite a surplus of tonnage being shown for each LayCan, rates feel like they're firming. This has translated into higher term fixtures and, in a few instances, a decent spot premium too. As ever it's anyone's guess as to how long this will last but it's given the usual short-term protagonists sufficient cause to stop and reassess their next steps.  On the newbuilding side, SHI has secured a large order to build 15 LNG carriers for Qatar for $3.45 billion with an average price of about $230 million per LNG vessel.

Meanwhile, as the days and weeks progress in 2024 the prospects of a meaningfully significant winter season in the U.S. continue to erode, and at over 60mmbbls as of early Feb, stock levels and product availability are not an issue.  Various models have Feb concluding in the low/mid 50mmbbl range, which is entirely sufficient even in the event of a major weather event.     Furthermore, there is little unused or lingering export capacity at this point, but production is expected to simultaneously continue rising which should put additional downward pressure on pricing.  As such there are a rising number of market participants who are forecasting that MB propane values will decline.  The question, however, is when, and by how much?     As for terminal fees, the high-water market was set at 13cpg for early March, but since then a host of sellers have emerged and asking levels have declined by around half.  Buy-side interest is limited, though, as the pricing backwardation has pushed some players to the sidelines.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market has continued to soften, despite the gradual escalation in the Red Sea now reaching a critical point with Qatari vessels diverting around the Cape of Good Hope. There is still more activity East of Suez than West, although firm requirements are now few and far between in either basin and even tentative enquiries are further out in late-February and beyond. And while demand remains muted, the supply side of the equation hasn’t helped either, with the availability list growing for spot and term tonnage. In these circumstances, the few charterers that are in the market have been pressing for less-than-round-trip economics and in some cases, they have been successful. At this point in the annual cycle, headline rates can be misleading as “round-trip equivalent” rates can take (and are taking) a battering. There has not yet been a material impact on the spot market from the situation in the Red Sea, but if the Qatari fleet goes the long way around for a sustained period, this should absorb at least some excess tonnage and support freight rates. The multi-month market is also under serious pressure, and although there are some discussions on several vessels there hasn’t been a surge of charterers for such opportunities. There haven’t been any fresh newbuilding orders placed this week, but the Qatar expansion project has exercised a further 15 slots.

x: AMERICAS Generally speaking the domestic US market has seen a slow start to 2024 as market participants have returned to the desk but have so far been engaged in finalizing their respective 2023 books.    While there has lately been in North America some weather-related demand, and export volumes are at a respectably healthy 1.720mmbbls/day (off from 1.882mmbbls in the previous EIA report), overall US stock levels for the week ending 29 Dec were given at 82.6mmbbls, or 2.1mmbbls lower than the previous week’s reported data.  Market expectations varied widely, but in the end a pragmatic prediction of an approximate 2.5mmbbl decline was deemed reasonable, and thus the 2.1mmbbl drop was considered appropriate.  As such, Mont Belvieu propane prices for Jan have not reacted much and remain in the upper 60cpg range.  Terminal fees, though largely untested so far this year, are expected to have remained in the mid/single digit range of around 6cpg.  NWE The TOT window has been quite to start the year, the reduction of US exports transiting the region as they avoid the Suez Canal has reduced window offers. Also causing the East West spread to narrow from $165/MT yesterday to $158/MT today. An increase in petchem demand in the region from 340,000MT in November to 420,000MT in December is a welcome boost of demand as mild winter weather has kept seasonal demand low. An increase in North Sea LPG production, due to LPG’s premium to Natural Gas halted rejection, has accounted for part of this new petchem demand. Large cargo butane trades have been absent from the market leaving value assessed at 81.5% January Naphtha.  MED The mild temperatures for the most part this winter have kept stocks in the region at healthy levels. While the large volume US imports have been accounting for any new demand.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been a quiet start to the New Year in the West, with a lack of firm requirements in the basin and general muted market activity following the public holiday period. This is typically the period when rates come off, although the lull could be short lived following the harsh weather that is prevailing through North West Europe, which has been and is expected to continue disrupting schedules. Moreover, with the ongoing challenges in the Red Sea, it will be interesting to see how shipping activity in the Atlantic responds and whether we see a response over the coming days as players seek prompt tonnage to address interferences. Such circumstances have the potential to disrupt the current softening market rates, given the shortage of modern vessels available in the West, especially if Owners withdraw tonnage amidst prevailing uncertainties.   The picture in the East is quite different, as Owners finds themselves engaged with several firm requirements for tonnage across various sizes and specifications, whilst potential developing opportunities also draw attention. With vessel availability high East of Suez, there has been a corresponding lowering in charter rates. While the possibility of a slowing decline exists if the cold weather persists in North Asia and demand increases, the current trend is marked by heightened competition. On the term side, the past week has seen limited activity. However, as charter rates become more attractive to Charterers, we can expect to see increased interest in term vessel availability over the coming weeks. There were no reported LNG newbuilding orders this week, however, we note a USD 1.5 billion order for a FLNG unit at Samsung. LNG newbuild prices remain stable.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Whether it’s due to the holiday season or it’s simply the normal murkiness that pervades our market, things are especially opaque in LNG Shipping at present. This has led to some significant spreads between fixtures concluded over the last few weeks, and in turn it further complicates the picture for Charterers who are looking to take tonnage now. In the West, at least one party is seeking a vessel for 2H January but with a comparable last done concluding at under $100k pdpr (on a 2-Stroke) it’s hard to reconcile the mid $100k numbers being shown on similar dates. It might be that geopolitical risks are to blame here, and just as we see shipping stocks rise and fall on the news of “who is and who isn’t avoiding the Suez”, so too are Owners and Charterers fixing ideas affected. In the East, recent business has been steam ship centred, and this might explain the sizeable discount to the fixtures completed in the Atlantic, but with another Pacific charterer now looking to cover a beginning of February cargo on a bigger vessel, we should have a new price point with which to commence proceedings in 2024. As always, a number of moving parts in this business and we are constantly reminded that every requirement is unique!  Putting the market aside for now, we thank you all for your support during 2023 and we wish you a peaceful and prosperous 2024. Happy Fixing!

x: AMERICAS The resiliency of MB propane prices is remarkable given that in spite of this week’s EIA inventory data which revealed a 2.2mmbbbl draw, it brought overall US stock levels to 93.7mmbbls, or 107% of last year and 134% of two years ago.  This is without mentioning that the weather outlook for North America through the balance of December is calling for generally un-winter-like temperatures and for only limited levels of precipitation.  MB non-TET propane is today valued at ~67cpg, having dipped to around 65cpg in mid-Dec.  Crude values are providing support, but WTI prices are effectively unchanged over the balance of December, and propane export volumes are recorded this week at 1.812mmbbls/day – which is up from last week, but off from the more than 2mmbbls/day reported earlier in the month, and overall volumes are not expected to see a surge of any kind through the end of ’23.  Meanwhile, terminal fees were seen at 7.50cpg for end-Dec – and while 1H Jan has seen little (or no) activity, 2H Jan values are off just a bit, with offers presumably in the 7cpg range, and lower for a mixed-ratio parcel.  Otherwise, the ongoing issues at the Panama Canal and, more recently, in the Red Sea, have conspired to force overwater volumes to the longer, more expensive Cape of Good Hope route, which – when paired with a generally weak Asian market - has made for a difficult trading period and forced some participants to the sidelines.  NWE  Few VLGCs will go East via Suez due to the risk of attack reducing the number of large cargo offers into the region, by traders hoping to get their vessels back promptly. Import volume for December is expected to be around 370,000 MT, low for the time of year, with January import volumes projected to be similar. Though TOT bid for a mid-Jan delivery is supporting the market somewhat, the physical tons remain discounted, assessed at January CIF ARA -$2/MT. A  repeated large cargo butane offer in the window has pushed values down from 92.5% balance December Naphtha to 82.5% today.   MED  Higher than average temperatures in the region are keeping demand in check. The reduction of VLGCs transiting the region due to the risk of attack in Suez will see less transitory offers.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The winter spot market this year has proven to be notably subdued when compared to recent years, lacking any significant spikes.  Sentiments have softened again, marked by spot fixtures concluded at levels lower than the preceding week. The current lack of demand and limited arbitrage opportunities has contributed to an increase in vessel availability, exerting downward pressure on spot rates. Subletters with shipping capacity are actively pursuing opportunities and vying for cargoes. LNG prices have also decreased, primarily attributed to ample inventories despite declining temperatures in the North Asia region.  In contrast, the escalating daily situation in the Red Sea has encouraged an increasing number of companies to redirect their vessels away from the Suez Canal and sail via the Cape of Good Hope. This heightened risk of further attacks may result in a temporary surge in tonne/miles and might create additional demand for shipping. With a weaker spot market, rate projections for multi-month and up to one-year term periods have also softened. As the year draws to a close, market participants remain on the sidelines, anticipating decisions for the upcoming year. No new orders were reported this week, however newbuilding prices remained stable.  In closing, for those celebrating Christmas, wishing you a celebration filled with joy and happiness.

x: AMERICAS The EIA this week reported an overall propane inventory total of 95.9mmbbls, revealing a 1.1mmbbl decline from the previous week.  The market had generally been anticipating around a 2mmbbl draw, but while export volumes were off (1.7mmbbls/day from 2.0mmbbbls/day), domestic demand requirements increased and thus only the modest drop.  The reduced export rate may also be related to overland deliveries to Mexico, which – due to lower production there – has recently given cause for additional rail/truck/pipe deliveries.   At the same time last year US propane stock levels were 90.3mmbbls.  In spite of many market expectations, the weight of the inventory levels has not (yet) caused Mont Belvieu propane values to commensurately decline as crude continues to mill about on either side of $70/bbl and weather-related demand is simultaneously providing domestic support.   Meanwhile, terminal fees were notionally bobbing along in the mid-single-digit range until a late Dec fixture confirmed the level.  Very little has been accomplished for 1H Jan, but a mid/2H Jan fixture was reported in the upper single-digits, prompting offers to be significantly increased amid a late-breaking demand flurry.  NWE No bids or offer were shown in the TOT window this week, leaving the physical market assessed at December CIF ARA minus $5/MT. December import volumes are expected to be low, around 260,000MT due to the mild winter so far and low petchem demand. For comparison 475,000MT of LPG were imported in November while 550,000MT were imported in October. While imports are low the physical TOT discount shows demand is being covered and reflects the low demand environment. The arb from the US is open, and we expect to see a larger volume of imports in January. Butane demand remains firm with levels at 92.5% December Naphtha.     MED US VLGC imports to the East Med have been rising with 3 VLGCs set to arrive in Dortyol in the last decade of December. The West of the region has been relatively quiet, the mild start to winter reducing demand

n: LNG Market Report
x: Global high inventory levels, coupled with a significant decrease in freight and gas prices, raise the question of whether winter has already passed. The widening delta between the Pacific and Atlantic persists. The possibility of more tonnage shifting westward from the Pacific could be contemplated given there seems more enquiry there, but the challenge lies in the time lag associated with redirecting vessels to the Atlantic, especially when both the Panama and Suez Canals routes are unpredictable. While rates have decreased with most fixtures in the East, it's worth noting that some prompter requirements have encountered difficulties in securing shipping particularly in the West. Despite the time available for a potential recovery before holidays commence in most countries, the prospect of a significant surge in activity seems highly unlikely at the moment. Although no newbuild orders have been placed at the yards this week, prices remain robust.

x: AMERICAS  At the cusp of Nov and Dec the prompt MB propane market took a sharp step upwards, having risen from the mid 60cpg range to over 71cpg in just a couple of days.  This is attributed to a couple of things, but most prominently to investor short positions which were in need of being covered.  By now the market has begun to subside and has retreated back to the 67-68cpg range after those positions were covered.   Meanwhile, though, LPG market sentiment continues to feel cautious, and many regular participants remain in retreat on the sidelines.  Ongoing delays (and costs) associated with the lack of rain in Panama persist and do not appear to be abating soon.  Crude oil values have seen losses of more than $20/bbl since the start of Q4 which, when coupled with the recently rising propane values have given cause for the propane/WTI spread to rise to above 40%.   Looking at the Jan cargo roster, there are presently believed to have been two cancellations, with two more which are pending decision.  Terminal fees have softened and for 2H Jan are notionally in the 5-6cpg range  NWE The TOT window was not bid for the first time on over a month, reducing the assessed premium for TOT deliveries from a $6/MT to a $3/MT premium to December CIF ARA. VLGC have been transiting the Panama Canal with more ease in December so far compared with previous months, bringing the January East West spread down to +$154/MT. Butane has risen to 95.5% to December Naphtha through strong buyside interest, and remains attractive after the large drop in crude oil and naphtha values seen Wednesday. The butane rise coupled with fewer aggressive offers from transiting VLGCs has seen European netback values improve. With US Gulf FOB cargo values assessed between 5-6cpg the arb to Europe is open for both propane and butane. On paper the European market is an attractive home for US tons, though the low petchem demand and slow rise in winter demand continues to make it a challenge to place tons in the region.  MED Crude oil price volatility saw trade discussions take a back seat. Fewer forecast LPG transits through the Suez Canal helped support values in the region while seasonal demand is beginning to support values in the region.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we enter the final weeks of the year, there is no doubt that the bulls are a little quieter than the bears right now. A couple of softer spot fixtures particular in Asia have dampened hopes of a stronger winter, and with the recent cold spells having barely any impact on LNG prices there aren’t many signs of a turnaround. It was natural then, that one of the main topics of conversations at last week’s CWC gathering in Athens and at the festive parties this week has been where the market will go from here (even taking airtime away from emissions clauses and the impact of ETS!). Some will be looking back exactly a year to the crash in the LNG spot market from those record highs, while others may point to fixtures already done for January at levels similar to those seen for November and December. Either way, the discussions are around the pace of change rather than the direction. The same is true for multimonth and multiyear charters: sentiment is softening and there are several candidate vessels, yet charterers are a little reluctant to move at this stage. To finish on a more positive note, with 2023 seeing a drop in the number of fixtures versus 2022 (and 2022 in turn seeing fewer than 2021), a consistent view is emerging of an expected increase in liquidity next year. There should be plenty to keep us busy! At the yards, there were no newbuildings reported this week and prices remained stable.

x: AMERICAS Much of the domestic US LPG market has gone quiet as the wait for winter-related weather demand has commenced.  While there have been recent, large-scale storms, nothing sustained has occurred as yet.    Meanwhile, propane stocks in the US fell by a generally anticipated 600,000bbls as of the week ending 24 Nov, and now total 98.7mmbbls, or about 109% of last year and 136% of two years ago.  At this point stock levels are sufficient in the event of a long, cold winter – as well as export volumes, which were most recently reported by the EIA to be 1.594mmbblss/day, but which are down from last week’s 1.787mmbbls.   As for terminal fees, the high levels seen for Dec transactions have receded, but buy-side ideas have declined more sharply and at this point – for Jan – interest levels is tentatively in the mid single-digit levels while offers (thin as they are) remain hopeful for double-digits.   At the forefront of it all remain the issues at the Panama Canal, and transit auctions have commanded between $1m and (nearly) $4m in recent weeks, which has, in turn, given cause for Eastbound alternatives such as the Suez Canal and the Cape of Good Hope, thus adding ton-miles which, in turn, has kept freight rates resilient.  NWE The first wave of cold weather has arrived in Europe and with it disappeared the TOT window offers. Leaving only BP bidding for a Dec 20-24 delivery, pushing the physical premium up to December CIF ARA +$4.25/MT. The region still looks well supplied and with a large percentage of US LPG exports heading East likely to transit the region over the next few months due to Panama Canal restrictions, expected to be in place until April 2024. Butane values in the region have increased to 83% December Naphtha, though large cargo butane activity has been scarce.   MED The region continues to see tons offered on VLGCs in transit to the Suez Canal. So far there has been no uptick in weather related demand.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The spot LNG shipping market has been relatively subdued of late, with only a slow trickle of firm requirements and fixtures in the past week. Despite the reduced activity in the market and an abundance of available vessels, the sentiment regarding rates remains resilient. We are almost at the time of year when the market dropped in the last couple of years, yet there are no discernible signs of a market collapse this year. Disponent owners of available vessels have maintained offers at market levels when responding to the limited vessel requirements that have been issued, and numbers out to January suggest a healthier tale end to the winter than we've seen in recent years. The current week has seen a little more demand for ships, primarily driven by prompt deliveries and January loadings. This uptick in demand raises the possibility of a "double-peak" in rate levels for this winter season, or at least a steady plateau.   Simultaneously, there are no indications suggesting any softening in the shipbuilding market. Consequently, the rate expectations for a long-term charter remain robust among owners with vessels available. Given that shipyards are operating at near-full capacity for the foreseeable future, the industry is constrained to working with existing vessels or those already under order. Notably, there have been no new orders this week, as newbuilding prices continue to hold firm.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Chartering activity remains limited for yet another week. In the Atlantic, there is still demand for 2H December tonnage but there hasn’t been much fixing, due to the limited number of available vessels in the basin. With European natural gas prices correcting, a inter-basin arbitrage has opened offering some opportunities on the paper markets, but with physical demand yet to follow, any such exercises seem rather opportunistic at the moment. In the Pacific, there is also a lack of new firm requirements, and in the Middle East most activity is centered around FOB cargo sales. In short, there is still a lot of uncertainty over the winter months and portfolios seem to be reluctant to release any tonnage at present. The term market is a little more active, with vessels being reported fixed for Q2 2024 deliveries, however rates have started their downward trend reflecting the typical shoulder months. There have been no NewBuilding orders reported this week and NB prices have remained stable.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Although it is now raining in Panama, the declining water levels in Lake Gatun (which feeds the insatiable appetite of the Canal itself) have taken center stage and become an entirely global issue as the number of daily transits has been reduced (and is scheduled in the coming months to continue falling) SHARPLY.  That has led to competition for the remaining slots which are being auctioned and a much wider use of the alternative routes: the Suez Canal and the Cape of Good Hope.  In each case, prices and freight rates have increased wildly.  Auction payments of $2m, $3m, and as much as $4m are known to have been made, while a $100/mt premium is being placed over the standard Baltic Hou/Chi (via Panama) rate for the ~15-20 additional sailing days which are required for passage via Suez or Good Hope (respectively).  The combined impact of these issues has led to downward pressure on US spot terminal fees which have been halved over the course of November.  Previous offers were seen at around the 15cpg mark, but buyers have been reluctant to engage beyond the mid/single digits.  Meanwhile, the EIA reported this week – after a week’s hiatus - that domestic US propane inventories as of 10 Nov stand at 99.7mmbbls, or about 14% higher than mid-Nov last year.  Stock levels are clearly beyond the 5-year high levels and expected to be fully sufficient for both export volumes and winter-related requirements.  NWE The TOT window continues to be active, with both bids and offers being show. So far delivery dates have not lined up for a deal to get done, TOT cargoes valued at CIF ARA November flat. November imports split between petchem feedstock 270,000MT and retail 170,000MT. Increased winter retail demand has not started. The drop in Brent will narrow the propane naphtha spread though this is unlikely to affect the largely stable low petchem demand. Panama Canal issues will keep the East / West spread wide, December E/W $205/MT today, as traders continue to offer tons into the region en route East via Suez. The butane market has been very quiet and remains at 81% Novmeber naphtha.  MED LPG values in the region are likely to remain under pressure as VLGCs pass through the region to head East, offering their tons if values make sense as they go. For now low heating, Autogas and petrochemical demand in the region means most vessels will pass on through.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Plenty of chartering opportunities are coming to market yet the lack of available vessels has dampened freight activity this week. The result so far this week - only a handful of vessel are being fixed! The lack of availability, particularly on the prompt, likely means most potential requirements will pass without taking shipping, although those that do conclude will be at charter levels equalling 2023 previous highs.    A wide spectrum of news stories emerged this week; reports of a power outage at Freeport saw concerns rise on the supply side, whilst seasonal bad weather effected European ports and the ability for vessels to discharge on time, potentially providing needed respite to terminals that remain almost at full capacity. Despite glimpses of colder temperatures appearing for brief intervals, high storage levels mean Mediterranean terminals are offering attractive reload parcels which seek homes further down the curve or in the East; however, Pacific cargo demand still appears limited and opportunistic. So, all-in-all there is plenty of uncertainty and control of tonnage remains valuable and priced at a premium.   In the Atlantic, 170,000m3 plus vessels showing December availability could be viewed as  “Unicorns”, and charterers are now looking to open vessels in the East for Atlantic loads as US gulf FOB tenders are offered to market. Not an easy exercise as rates in the pacific remain on par with those in the Atlantic. The next week will be an intriguing one for the LNG spot shipping market! If that is the case US stock levels will have declined to below the 100mmbbl mark.   Meanwhile, all eyes are on the Panama Canal where reduced transits – which have come as a result of a drought in Panama – have forced shipping to seek alternatives, most of which are more time consuming and, therefore, expensive.  A couple of recent deviations (both North and Southbound) are evidence of the disruption, and perhaps a sign of things to come in 2024.   The abrupt changes, combined with what has been described as a chaotic Asian market and an overbought European market wherein winter-related demand has yet to commence, are allowing for a wider arb, but simultaneously high freight costs, which have resulted in pressure on the US terminal fee market.  Those values, from the sell-side perspective, are now pegged in the mid/low teens but -as of this writing – buy-side ideas are more in the upper single digits.  NWE The TOT window continues to be active the latest activity an end November offer equating to CIF ARA November -$10/MT vs an early December delivery bid equating to CIF ARA November -$8.5/MT. Cold weather has yet to increase demand while petchem run rates remain low. A slide in crude oil values the week added to the bearish sentiment in the region. As winter approaches and TTF Natural Gas values rise, we will start to see maximum LPG rejection into the natural gas stream, reducing local LPG production. Dutch TTF average $13.40/MMBtu while Propane $9.45/MMBtu and butane $10/MMBtu. The butane market continues to be very quiet and remains assessed at 81% November Naphtha.   MED Imports to the region in November are likely to set a 1 year record. Traders continue to look to place in the region due to the difficulties in transiting the Panama Canal. A slide in crude values has added bearish sentiment to the already oversupplied propane and butane markets.

n: LNG Market Report
x: After a few weeks of relative calm in the shipping market, things got pretty busy pretty quickly last week. Many of the leading indicators of a tight shipping market have been flickering to life recently, such as increasing ballast speed and more FOB/DES and swapping activity on the cargo market, so it’s not surprising that some sublets are being pulled and the availability list is shrinking. This hasn’t led to an increase in fixing levels yet, and it may not do at all while LNG storage levels are high and pricing remains subdued, but it has led to more shipping enquiries as participants look for opportunities in the spot market. Likewise for term charters, there are more enquiries as traders and portfolios look to take advantage of what has hitherto been considered a buying opportunity next year. That being said, Panama Canal disruption, geopolitical tensions, uncertainty around the future of steam ships and the start of the EU ETS are all theoretically bullish 2-Strokes. Conversely, the wave of redelivering tonnage from Q1 next year should provide commercial opportunities for those who are more agnostic when it comes to propulsion, size and vintage. All in all, it’s hard to do anything other than sit on the fence this week! There were no newbuilding orders placed within this reporting cycle.

x: AMERICAS At 102.4mmbbls the domestic US propane inventory has wholly eclipsed the 5-year high level for mid-October (the previous high-water marks were 98.3mmbbls in 2020 and 99.6mmbbls in 2016.  The EIA report for the week ending 20 Oct showed a modest 100,000bbl weekly increase, which was regarded by the market as rather low as expectations ranged from a build of 250,000bbls to as much as +1.4mmbbls.  This puts the Days of Supply at 113 days, and the YTD 2023 average Days of Supply at 85 days, which is well beyond the previous (2016) high of 76 Days.  Stocks are high.  That said, exports were recorded at 1.843mmbbls/day, which is just below the highest weekly export volume on EIA record, and which occurred just two weeks ago (2.129mmbbls/day on 6 Oct 2023).  This is despite the various and sundry terminal-related export issues which continue to plague the Gulf Coast.  Meanwhile, as there is now winter weather to contend with in North America, heating-related requirements will follow.  Simultaneously there is winter-related demand now being seen in Northwest Europe and – it is now being reported – previous length in Chinese inventories has been drawing down, so in each case demand for US-sourced product should continue to prop up terminal fees, which moved from 10cts/gal earlier in the month to 13cts/gal more recently, and then to 16cts/gal where a transaction is believed to have been concluded.  Asking levels are indeed even higher, with known offers at 20cts/gal for December volumes.  With Eastern arb levels in the $320s and $330s, these types of rates are (at least temporarily) rationally supported.  NWE  The 1st decade November TOT market in the region is very tight. Constant bidding by multiple parties has pushed premiums up to November CIF ARA +$21/MT, a level last seen in March. The prompt market looks tight, partly due to the reduced US export volumes due to terminal loading delays over the last few weeks. Another reason for the tightness in Europe was the tightness in the VLGC market, which led to a larger volume of imports on MGCs rather than VLGCs for October and early November imports. The propane naphtha spread narrowed to multi-month lows as crude oil coming off dragged naphtha down, while prompt propane remains bullish. If the petrochemical sector was receiving any more than the minimum required volume, they would be reselling physical tons at these premiums. Butane in Europe has been quiet in the physical window and values remain at 79% November Naphtha.   MED  The region continues to be in a low demand environment and cannot keep up with the strong premiums innorthwest Europe.

x: The LNG shipping market has been relatively quiet this week with few new firm requirements in either basin, although there are a fair number of cargo tenders. It was a similar story East of Suez, with a lack of demand from Asian buyers keeping the cargo market flat. Thus, without huge cargo revenues or a strong contango, tendered volumes are mostly going to those with excess shipping length. This leaves the shipping market at the mercy of weather conditions in both Asia and Europe for the weeks ahead, and perhaps this represents a return to normality! On the newbuilding front, it was reported that Celsius have declared two options for 180,000 cbm LNG carriers at China Merchants Heavy Industry Jiangsu with delivery of the vessels scheduled for Q1 and Q4 of 2027.

The 800k bbl increase was not terribly surprising and the market took it in stride since predictions were rather wildly all over the board.  Some were calling for a draw of as much as 800,000bbls, while others were looking for a 3mmbbl build.  In cases when the range of anticipation is so wide it effectively means that the market lacks true confidence, and in this case likely references the past couple of EIA reports which were deemed in need of correction.   Meanwhile, the trio of Force Majeure declarations at the Gulf Coast terminals continues to plague the market, though it is expected at this point that two of the three will shortly be rescinded (if they haven’t been already).  In any case, product availability remains largely limited to re-sellers, many of whom have already committed their volumes.  As such, and based on the current arb, terminal fees remain robust.  Presently the spot FOB terminal fee for propane is pegged at around 13cpg, and for butane at 10cpg. t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: This has been a big week for the short-term market with a number of fixtures confirming what much of us suspected: there are more bears than bulls in 2024. With competitive one and two-year fixtures on 2-strokes transpiring, the correction has reverberated through the TFDE and ST fleet as well. Paradoxically, the market looks to tighten again as we move out to the three and five year mark, and accordingly the discount that one might expect to see, for these longer periods, has disappeared as the market prices in an uptick in demand from 2026. On the spot side of the house, a rise in LNG prices has helped stem the decline in rates and we are in “wait and see” mode as we go to print today. With most Q4 availability still in the hands of portfolios and projects, current volatility in the product market makes releasing tonnage a risky (i.e., expensive) prospect and it means that closing the Bid-Ask spread into the New Year will remain the biggest challenge. In any event, we have seen a few charterers return to the market for November through to January/February coverage and this may be the precursor for the eventual tightening that we have all come to expect at this time of year. In reality, however, 18th October is way too early to make a call on Winter and the fear is that we remain in our “wait and see” mode indefinitely. To Newbuilds, another quiet week with nothing to report although a number of Majors are heard to be in discussions with the yards, so it may be only a matter of time before we get our next keenly awaited price point here.

x: Spot shipping rates have come off again, reflecting bearish sentiment during the week.   The softening of shipping rates are very much linked to a lack of firm requirement in the market. As vessel availability exceeds the demand, there would be significant discount for prompt ships. With the decline in the spot market, a potential opening arises for charterers to secure term tonnage. Several charterers are actively exploring opportunities for early next year, seeking short-to-medium-term coverage at levels below last done for such period. Thus, taking prompt action to charter for an extended term can prove beneficial at the current levels. Although the market looks quite different this year to last year, there is a cautionary tale in that the majority of vessels are currently under control of subletters, and they can withdraw rapidly if market conditions change. And unfortunately, global events are only adding to these risks and we have seen the LNG price strengthening in recent days.   On the newbuilding front, prices remain firm with reports this week that a far east buyer is linked to an order for one LNG carrier at around US$260M from Samsung Heavy Industries for delivery in September 2026.

However, this week has shown no signs of that, as headline rates are lower and ballast bonuses remain unchanged at round trip. European inventory levels are currently high, and TTF has fallen this week which may in turn further solidify decisions to redirect laden vessels towards the East. In the Atlantic, requirements that were previously lingering have been fixed at lower levels compared to previous deals. In the Pacific, many major players have been inactive due to holidays in China and Korea, coupled with high inventory levels in Japan. However, as the week progresses and requirements start to firm up, we anticipate increased activity in this region, which may stem the decline. While the signs point to a weaker freight market, it's noteworthy that Charterers are attempting to extend the fixing window into December. There haven't been any new build orders placed in the past week, however, QatarEnergy has taken steps to reserve 17 slots at HHI.

This has created some uncertainty with regards to what might happen to the LNG shipping rates, since LNG prices are still high enough to avoid any cargo cancellations keeping supply intact, but on the other hand, we might see fewer floating opportunities and more available tonnage, unless of course we start seeing congestion at various disports. Throw into the mix the constantly fluctuating arbitrage and we a have proper conundrum on our hands! On the prompt however, we are seeing a bit of softening on the spot rates in both basins, and with only limited prompt opportunities to be worked, some vessels might see some idling ahead. We are seeing some charter opportunities for November and even for December, but these laycans are still a bit far out, and proposed levels are staying relatively strong amidst this uncertainty. On the newbuilding market, we have not recorded any new orders in the past week, but yards are keeping busy finalising the paintjobs in order to deliver a legion of shiny newbuilds for Q4 2023 and Q1 2024.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane market levels are in retreat after the EIA inventory data for the week ending 15 Sep showed a 1.6mmbbl build which pushed overall stocks to 100.7mmbbls – which was entirely expected, but nonetheless is an important milestone, if only from a psychological perspective.   In any case, there are a couple of weeks remaining in the traditional propane inventory build season and it is pretty widely anticipated because of the high production levels and simultaneously reduced export levels that stocks will in the next couple of weeks broach the 105mmbbl level.  As such, the pricing structure – which has lately been aligned with the strength of the crude markets – has reversed course and is now back in the low/mid 71cts/gal range.   Terminal fees, meanwhile, appear to have crested (at least for the moment) as offers for 1H Nov are presently seen in the 11-12cpg range and buy-side interest exists in the 9-10cpg range.  Shipping remains the stumbling point, however, as delays (and therefore costs) associated with the Panama Canal have forced a number of shipowners to transit via the Cape of Good Hope and/or Suez Canal.  Those routes require additional sailing days which, thus, further exacerbates shipping avails.  NWE The TOT window has been quiet since a 9-13 October offer pushed assessed physical values to -$11/MT to October CIF ARA. US tons continue to head to the region even though petrochemical demand remains low, tipping the market to long. The October East/West spread $116/MT will continue to see US spot cargoes head East. Many spot VLGC fixtures not offering West options to lock in sky high freight rates on longer voyages. Which could make it difficult for European buyers to attract cargoes to the region if demand rises. Butane remains at 88% September Naphtha, though trading has been quiet as crude oil & naphtha price swings have made it difficult to pin down a northwest European butane value.   MED The region continues to import large volumes of LPG, with 110,000MT set to arrive in the region in early October. Turkish demand has stayed strong and mixed ratio VLGC demand continues.

x: While rates remained relatively stable last week, the dynamics have shifted significantly this week due to a surge in vessel requirements in both basins. Although there are vessels available, Charterers are showing a clear preference for larger vessels to lift the larger cargo parcels especially in the West, leading to a perceived scarcity of LNG vessels available for charter. In the East, there has still been a market for the smaller steam turbine vessels. As a result, charter rates have increased from last week's levels, and this upward trend is expected to continue throughout the week, as vessel requirements remain unfulfilled as of today. Floating storage taking advantage of the contango situation are still occupying shipping capacities.   There have been no reports of newbuilding orders this week, as ship prices show no signs of weakening and demand for shipbuilding slots continues to be robust.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Following the resounding success of the Gastech conference in Singapore, LNG shipping is riding a wave of renewed optimism. Industry players have returned to their offices around the world with fresh insights and a collaborative spirit, and are now directing their attention towards chartering in preparation for the impending winter season and supporting ADP processes for next year. We are at the time of year when floating cargoes may start to emerge, and there is a contango through to December and with storage levels high there is also operational storage on the table. Risks to the downside include geopolitical factors (or industrial strikes) that could disrupt supply chains and influence pricing, although as we saw last year in particular such factors can reduce volume but higher LNG prices can produce a frenzy to secure tonnage. As the LNG shipping landscape evolves, stakeholders are closely monitoring these dynamics to make informed decisions and seize opportunities in this dynamic sector.  This week saw no newbuilding orders, with the persistently limited availability of shipyard slots and the ongoing strength in newbuilding prices.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS In a rather classic case of the market becoming “overdone”, spot terminal fees for 1H October rocketed upwards in late August and early September, reaching heights not seen for some years as a couple of transactions were noted above 15cpg.  Asking levels went even higher but the headwinds that accumulated alongside such levels became too great – particularly in the face of rising freight costs and delays associated with the lack of rain at the Panama Canal.  As such terminal fees for 2H have declined into what is now deemed to be the low ‘teens’ range.  The timing of shipping (and availability), though, remains a concern.  Meanwhile, 1H Nov is presently offered at 11cpg and bid in the 10s – still rather high from a historical perspective, but generally supported by the Eastern arb.   All the while the EIA reported on Wed that propane stock levels as of 08 Sep increased by 3.1mmbbls to 99.1mmbbls – well above the 5-year high point of 97.380mmbbls, 127% of last year, and 140% of two years ago.  There exists at this point no reason to believe that overall US propane inventory levels won’t reach 105mmbbls by the end of the month, and well positioning the market for what is increasingly expected to be a colder-than-average winter.   Otherwise, the persistent high heat in the US South and Midwest regions may have finally begun to abate, but nonetheless the production and transportation systems across the nation continue to struggle, perhaps most notably a recent power outage which caused several days lifting delays at one of the terminals.  Current estimates are calling for a full roster within the month of September, though.  NWE A TOT window deal was done between BP and ENI as BP raised their 3-8 October buying idea to a fixed price of $588/MT where it was booked. 26-30 September TOT cargo continued to be offered by ENI which pushed end September physical premium down $0.50/MT to September CIF ARA +$4/MT. September Northwest European import volumes look set to be above 450,000MT. It is not yet know if petchem demand will rise in October as some plants are set to go on maintenance while others come back online. Butane demand is starting to see the seasonal demand increase and although values are stable at 83.5% Naphtha outright value has increased with rising naphtha and crude oil.   MED The full effects of the devastating earthquake in Morocco and floods in Libya are not yet known. Mediterranean imports have been steady at a large volume of over 400,000MT for the past 11months. Flat price gains continue in the region due to rising crude.

x: Gastech offered the industry plenty of opportunities for discussion this week in Singapore. As the week draws to a close, sentiment looks to have the edge with another charterer paying up to cover a Q4 cargo. A reminder to all that the fundamentals (an increasing of available prompt tonnage) and the sentiment don’t need to be aligned for rates to escalate. A key theme of the conference has of course been new business and this week was no different, many new players offered interesting new opportunities in the near term but also from 2027 and beyond. It is clear ambitions, for many, are grand in scope! No newbuilds again this week but let's see if any announcements are made on the back of the remaining meetings this week.

x: AMERICAS Terminal fees for full propane cargoes from the US continue in the mid teens and show little sign of abating in the face of a now $300/mt arb to the East.  Some have recently predicted that the arb will rise to as high as $315/mt, which only bolsters the notion that terminal fees might be maintained at current levels well in to Q4.  Mixed ratio cargoes are believed available at a modest discount to all-propane cargoes, but there is little demand at present for anything other than 4:0 VLs.  And while the arb is wholly robust, so are freight rates.  In fact, the Hou/Chi route has today been established by the Baltic Index at $220/mt.  Overall export volumes are generally steady, with 1.694mmbbls/day recorded by the EIA last week, and 1.547mmbbls in its most recent report, that for the week ending 01 Sep.  As for inventories, the EIA reported a 500,000bbl week-over-week inventory increase for a current overall total of 96mmbbls.  This is nearly 130% of the same time last year – week 35 – and nearly 137% over two years ago at the same time.  This took the market by surprise as most had calculated an estimated 2.3mmbbl increase.  That estimate was based on historical averages, current petrochemical consumption levels and export volumes over the past week.  Over the past 5 years the average build for week 35 was 2.394mmbbls.  NWE  The region is finding it hard to attract trans-Atlantic VLGCs as netback values stand 5cpg below the East. The low demand environment due to reduced petchem run rates, is making it possible for traders to fill European demand on smaller size vessels. The October Propane vs Naphtha spread of $103/MT keeps propane the favoured feedstock, a bounce back from below $100/MT earlier this week. A TOT bid for end September arrival continues to be shown, with assessed value at September CIF ARA +$2.5/MT. The butane market has been quiet this week, keeping assessed value 83.5% September Naphtha.   MED  Turkey imprted a record 418,000MT LPG in August. Another 400,000MT of LPG on VLGCs is aimed at the region in September already, although it is difficult to predict if the volume will stay in the region or head East. The Panama Canal delays and auction costs above $2million USD are pushing VLGCs through Suez on both laden and ballast legs.

x: AMERICAS MB propane market levels have improved alongside the gains seen in the crude arena, but the percentage of propane-to-WTI continues in the 34-35% range, giving some cause to believe that propane is undervalued – particularly going into the winter.  Prior to that, however, crop drying demand is not expected to reach average consumption levels due to the general lack of rain in the MidWest and the scorching heat which continues to plague most of North America.  Meanwhile, in consideration of the OPEC crude cuts which have limited LPG output in that region of the world, much of the focus is now on the US Gulf Coast as an alternative source of supply.  However, with limited marine terminal capacity and burgeoning demand – not to mention ongoing limitations related to shipping availability – terminal fees have ramped up solidly.  Transactions are known to have occurred at above 15cts/gal for 1H Oct spot FOB deals, with talk of any remaining volumes at still higher levels.  As for propane inventories, the EIA report for the week ending 25 Aug stocks built by a surprising 3.2mmbbls for an overall total of 95.5mmbbls – well beyond what was achieved last year in late August when stocks were recorded at 72.2mmbbls.  With yet another four weeks in the traditional build season, it is well within reason that propane stocks will easily exceed 100mmbbls prior to what is now expected (by some) to be a colder-than-normal winter period.  NWE The TOT window has been consistently offered with no bids corresponding bids for a 2H September propane cargo. Leaving the physical discount at September CIF ARA -$7.50/MT. Propane naphtha lost almost $10/MT as propane gained whilst naphtha came off. Now at -$106/MT for September propane remains the favoured feedstock. The current issue is the continued reduced run rates and maintenance at petchem plants, which is shrinking the size of the European market. The September East/West spread has widened to +$107/MT. Though with Panama Canal transit costs and waiting times some traders see Europe as a safe option keeping US tons flowing across the Atlantic. Butane values tracked naphtha down and are assessed at 89% September Naphtha quotes.  MED Sonatrach prices were posted at $530/$550 for propane and butane respectively. Split ratio VLGCs continue to head to the West Med from the US as Turkish demand remains high.

x: As the market gets ready to descend on Singapore for what is looking like being a very busy Gastech, the past week hasn’t seen the usual “pre-conference” surge in activity although there remains a number of enquiries to keep people occupied between meetings. Uncertainty still rules the market, with the Australian labour dispute edging closer and the potential impact of El Nino set against high storage levels in both basins and a relatively flat forward curve. As such and unsurprisingly, many enquiries have fallen or will fall away as optimisations and tenders and cargo swaps play out. So, what next? This uncertainty may have resulted in less activity but it hasn’t stopped fixing levels rising earlier this year than we have seen in recent years, and although few expect rates to spike as they did last year, we are now on the cusp of the floating window. Let’s hope there are enough breakout areas at Gastech, just in case… There were no newbuilding orders placed last week.

However, recent gains resulting from an improving cargo market have been retained for larger, more efficient vessels and some see this as "winter coning early". Competition between owners with older tonnage vying for business in Asia has led to a cooling for steamships in the region. In the Atlantic, we continue to see a sizeable bid ask spread between owners of modern tonnage and charterers, however, it’s only a matter of time before we see this gap shrink as availability tightens in the weeks ahead. This is likely to be exacerbated while the labour disruption endures in Australia. There are no newbuild orders to report this week and prices remaining unchanged.

x: AMERICAS After languishing in the mid single-digits earlier in the summer, spot FOB terminal fees on the Gulf Coast rapidly rose to the mid-teens after a well-noted transaction.  Some moderation has been noted, but at present 13-14cpg is likely the most representative range for October.  This is in part due to the somewhat reduced avails on the Gulf Coast (which comes as a result of the ongoing and sweltering heat as well as a couple of recent mechanical tie-ins), but is also representative of the delays at the Panama Canal which has kept freight aloft.  To that, a recent $2.41m Northbound Canal transit payment has given cause for speculation as to additional return voyages via the Cape of Good Hope which would be seen as bullishness in the freight arena.  The EIA Wednesday reported that stocks during the week ending 18 Aug rose by 1.7mmbbls to an overall total of 92.3mmbbls, which compares to the 5-yr average of 72.3mmbbls and is 135% of the same time last year.  It is likely – based on 5-yr averages – that by next week propane inventories will total ~95mmbbls, and – barring any unforeseen events - put Sep overall totals in a position to rather easily eclipse the 100mmbbl mark.  Meanwhile, the relationship between WTI and propane continues to hover in the low/mid 30% range – well below the 52% overall average recorded since Jan 2021.  The rolling YTD average in 2023 has been on a slow decline, having started the year at just above 42% but as of now is ~39% of WTI.  NWE A recurring TOT window offer this week has kept pressure mid-September arrival tons, now assessed at Sept CIF ARA -$2/MT, with no public buying interest shown. The European market continues to import large volumes from the US, but with the September East/West spread nearing $100/MT European buyers will have to up their ideas to continue to do so. With almost 600,000MT set to be imported in August the region has done well to draw tons this summer. Refiners are beginning their blend-up period in order to meet raised winter gasoline pressure requirement. Supporting butane levels at 89.5% balance August Naphtha.    MED  US and northwest European imports continue to supply Moroccan demand, which continues to rise. In the East Med further Algerian and Russian LPG has been heading to Turkey as Autogas demand continues to be strong. 440,000MT is set to be imported to Turkey in August, a record since 2016.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS  WTI values have seen a $2/bbl decline since the start of August, and propane values have also weakened over the same period – from 68cts/gal on the 1st to below 62cts/gal at present.  The ratio of WTI to propane values, though, has weakened from just over 35% to 32%, perhaps signaling that MB propane values have room to again advance in the near-term.   Terminal fees, meanwhile, have made remarkable gains this month and moved from somewhere in the 6cts/gal level to 8cts/gal, then to 10cts/gal, followed by a 12.5cts/gal deal and – finally – a 15+ cts/gal transaction that was recorded earlier this week.  Asking levels have correspondingly increased, but buy-side interest at this point remain in the lower end of the double-digit range.   As for inventory levels, the EIA reported this week that stock levels as of 11 Aug had built by 700k bbls to a total of 90.6mmbbls.  The week-over-week increase was well below the 2.2mmbbl 5-year average build for the 32nd week, but inventories are now 133% of the same time last year and 135% of two years ago. Many are now rightly anticipating that propane inventories in the US will handily eclipse the 100mmbbl level by the beginning of October.    As the excessive heat of the North American summer continues and ocean water temperatures continue to post at record levels the threat of tropical storms and/or hurricanes has now intensified.  NOAA forecasters have just recently increased their Atlantic hurricane season predictions to ‘above normal’.  NWE  The region saw a significant rise in imports month on month, from 425,000MT in July to 582,000MT expected in August. Surprising as the netback to Asia has been considerably stronger during this period. The August Propane / Naphtha spread rose $10/MT to $126/MT, and remains the preferred feedstock. Though with many petchem plants on maintenance, shutdown or running reduced rates due to weak olefins markets feedstock demand fluctuations do not represent a huge volume. The TOT window is assessed at a double digit discount to September CIF ARA, public bids and offers have been scarce. Butane continues to be strong now at 87% September Naphtha as refinery demand beings to increase to meet adequate vapor pressures before blending season.  MED  The East Med has been buoyed by the wide arb from the US. Morocco importing 115,000 MT in the first half of August already, 60% of US origin. In the West Med Turkey has been importing a large volumes of LPG, and continues to look for prompt tons. As the summer driving season is keeping autogas demand high.

x: AMERICAS Following the upwardly trending crude markets which are rising primarily due to pending production cutbacks in the Middle East, the Mont Belvieu propane market rose by more than 20cts/gal over the course of July with non-TET values presently pegged at around 73cts/gal.  The reduced LPG output in the other primary supply region is putting the spotlight on the US and, predictably, spot FOB terminal fees have also increased – particularly since freight rates have stalled.   Where just a short while ago September business was being talked in the mid single-digit range, notional terminal fee ideas rose quickly as an 8cpg transaction was quickly followed by a 10cpg deal, after which price ideas rose to as high as 12cpg – all for the mid/2H Sep market.  Buyers are now known to be assessing values in the low 10cpg range, but little product is believed to be on offer.  This is partially due to a pair of mechanical tie-ins which have recently been undertaken – one of which is related to PDH efforts, the other to a terminal capacity improvement project.    Meanwhile, stock levels this week were recorded by the EIA to have risen by 1.3mmbbls for an overall total of 89.9mmbbls as of the end of the first week of August.  The increase fell short of the market’s expectations, but nonetheless propelled stock levels nearer to eclipsing the 100mmbbl mark by the end of September.   Over the past 5 years propane inventory levels have gained an average of over 15mmbbls during Aug and Sep which, if applied to the current 89.9mmbbl stock total, would put total US stocks at over 105mmbbls as of the end of Sep.  NWE Approximately 150,000 mt of US Origin LPG are scheduled to arrive in NWE first half August on VLGC's,  along with 70,000 mt on LGCs, along with a handful of MGC's also. All that to say, NWE is seemingly well supplied at present however the market still saw a bid for a September cargo in yesterday's window. It went unmet. European butane steadied after a sharp rise over recent weeks which saw prices at a 6-month high, however the arbitrage is expected to come in as blending season arrives.  MED This month will see the highest ever US origin imports into the region, totaling nearly 550,000 tons, and thus nullifying the need for more product at present. The bulk of the demand has been driven predictably by Morocco and Turkey, while Spain will import 140,000 tons also, contributing to the record levels.

n: LNG Market Report
x: As Singapore celebrates its 58th birthday, it’s testament to the role the country now plays in the LNG market that things have been very quiet in the East today. Of course, this is naturally a quiet time in the market anyway, as the holiday season continues across the Northern Hemisphere, gas storage continues to fill up in Europe and LNG tanks remain near their tops in NE Asia. The upshot of this supply build-up is that the contango that had previously kept 2H 2023 2-Stroke term fixtures ticking over has now contracted, and we return to a very wide bid-ask spread between Owners and Charterers. Turning to the prompt, we’ve seen fixtures in both basins this week and the main take-away is that owners are expecting rates to double in October. With the fixing window now in September, this has proven a sticking point in spot negotiations – especially when the charter period strays into October. Consequently, a handful of October requirements remain uncovered because even though Charterers have been keen to fix before rates shoot up, Owners (primarily portfolio players) see no benefit in locking in a fixture now when the market could roof again when we hit Q4. In any event, we’re printing higher rates this week as we close in on Q4 and we wait with interest to see who gives first on the next October fixture – Owners or Charterers? Newbuild prices remain flat this week and we have no new orders to report.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Once again, the LNG spot shipping market has experienced a subdued week. While some developing cargoes have emerged, there are very few new firm requirements seen. Vessel availability remains steady at present; nevertheless, as the seasonal breeze carries us closer to winter, a subtle shift is anticipated. Vessels primarily controlled by subletters may be withdrawn, leaving the market tighter. The West-to-East Arbitrage and the winter contango are currently open, hinting at forthcoming trade opportunities which should improve shipping rates further going into the final months of the year. A handful of charterers are still actively seeking tonnage for this period; however, closing the Bid-Offer spread remains a challenge as the current lack of spot activity is not giving much scope to optimise any spot length as a result. On the longer-term side, there remains considerable attention driven increasingly by fleet renewals.  In the newbuilding market, Evalend Shipping was reported to have placed an order for two 174,000km3 LNG carriers with Korean Shipbuilder Hyundai Heavy Industries. The vessels are due for delivery in late 2027.  Another Japanese shipowner was also heard to have place an order for one LNG carrier with another Korean Shipbuilder, Hanwha Ocean. The newbuilding is due for delivery around February 2027.
