n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Expectations of crude oil production cuts in the Middle East has put pressure on the US supply system, and with August effectively sold out and September avails limited, terminal fees have been on the rise.  Where at the end of July the market was hovering around the 6cpg range for the remaining Aug volumes, an 8cpg Sep deal is known and 9cpg is being asked – and justifiably since the arb is supportive.  Talk of a 10cpg offer for Sep was heard but is not known to have been concluded.   Part of the reason that dock space is limited is due to a couple of domestic mechanical tie-ins; the first being Targa’s terminal capacity expansion by a pair of monthly 4:0 VLGCs, the second being Enterpise’s PDH start-up.  In all cases, however, the ongoing and rather dreadful heat wave which continues unabated is slowing the flow of product, which – at +40C ambient temps – is making it difficult to achieve -42C refrigeration levels.   As for the stock levels, is not the volume of available propane supplies that is in question, but the limited dock space – particularly for 4:0 cargoes.  The EIA this week again posted an inventory gain, this time a build of 2.9mmbbls for an overall US stock total of 88.6mmbbls – or nearly 140% of the total seen at the same time last year.  The build was well beyond most expectations, particularly as compared to the 5-year average build for week #30 of 1.7mmbbls.

x: AMERICAS  Despite a widening arb to the East little activity has been noted as August is mostly sold out, save for a couple of lingering parcels which are being offered either CFR or include butane.  Sep is presently subdued but talks have begun to surface as early winter-related demand requirements emerge.   US propane inventories were recorded by the EIA at 85.7mmbbls as of 21 Jul, an increase of 1mmbbls over the week prior.  The average build for the 29th week of the year is 1.716mmbbls, and expectations were calling for stocks to rise by some 1.9mmbbls.  The relatively weak stock build is likely due (in part) to tie-in’s at Targa (due to its expansion efforts) and Enterprise (due to its PDH-related efforts).  Furthermore, the ongoing and persistent heat wave in Texas has made it difficult to achieve -42c, the temperature at which fully refrigerated vessels load most efficiently.   Meanwhile, terminal fees continue to plod slowly upwards (and in a relatively quiet environment), with a reported fixture in Aug of 6.75cpg.  Talks for Sep start in the 7s and will work from there, but buy-side interest seems to remain in the 6s for the moment.    Latin American demand levels are muted, as Southern Hemisphere winter-related requirements are being satisfied by term contract deliveries.  NWE The TOT window continues to be well offered with two 1H August delivery parcels being shown. One of the offers was from the petrochemical sector, which lent a bearish feel to the mid-August European market. Strong crude oil has supported European LPG paper values and kept the trans-Atlantic Arb open. The European market remains in a low demand environment and though the arb is open cargoes are finding it difficult to find homes. Another factor has been the low natural gas price, which has pushed Dutch TTF below propane and butane. This will increase North Sea LPG production as LPG will no longer be spiked into the natural gas stream. Which is starting to be seen, North Sea exports are expected to be 335,000MT in July, up from an average of 255,000MT in Q1 2023. Butane values remain at 69% August Naphtha, though outright value has increased with stronger naphtha values.   MED Butane in the region has been strengthening this week, pulled up by crude and naphtha rises. There are areas of North African demand, although these are not being worked with any urgency.

n: LNG Market Report
x: We are now almost at the end of July, and it has in actual fact felt like a proper summer (holiday) week in the markets. Aside from the many industry players reading this week’s reports from their hammocks, the relatively quiet 7 days can be attributed to the general lull in the cargo market. The Southern Europe heatwave has caused some increases in European gas pricing, but this seems to have been relatively well controlled.  We have had a few spot requirements concluded in the Atlantic with levels indicating a “balanced” market, whereas the Pacific (where people, paradoxically, aren’t on holiday yet) has stayed very quiet. Surprisingly, we have seen a few short voyages out of the Middle East emerge, with some charterers looking to capitalise on summer sentiment for Q4 liftings in order to optimise freight. Term and multi-month discussions continue in the background, as the market tries to price the contango into winter. Vessel availability has also stayed more or less balanced in both basins whilst on the newbuilding side there are some discussions on new orders, which should be announced out of China soon. Furthermore, it was reported that NYK has found lengthy term charters on their recent orders.

x: AMERICAS North American propane fundamentals are largely unchanged, and – considering the time of year – rather expected from a seasonal perspective.  Growing inventories and limited demand are the norm.  But the propane-to-crude relationship, which dipped down to the very low 30% range has begun to show signs of life and now has found a bit of life at the mid-30 percentile range.  This is still historically low, however.  Stock levels were this week reported by the EIA to have risen by 900,000bbls for a total of 83.8mmbbls as of 14 July.  The expected increase had earlier been pegged at well over 2mmbbls.  The minimal build – and 600,000bbl draw in PADD III) can in part be attributed to the current heat wave that much of the US is experiencing, and which makes it difficult to achieve the low temps required to quickly load vessels.    Terminal fees for Aug have struggled to leave the 5cpg range, but talk for 1H Sep is in the 6s and negotiations for 2H Sep likely start at 7cpg.  Very little is being accomplished, though, as cargo avails are limited in Aug and presently appear likely remain so in Sep.    LatAm supply / demand is deemed balanced in that winter-related requirements thus far do not exceed previously termed volumes.  NWE The TOT propane window has been quiet all week. Butane on the other hand has seen consistent bidding by a French oil major, which has rapidly pushed value up to 76.5% July Naphtha values. Raising butane/naphtha values from -$243/MT a week ago to -$139/MT today. Petchem plants are being idled or going on maintenance throughout Europe as ethylene and propylene demand remains very low. Feedstock LPG intake in July will be 425,000MT up from 395,000MT in June down from a high 650,000MT in May. The arb to Europe from the US is very much open though still well below going East.   MED  The regoin will imports 430,000MT of LPG from the US in August, which will be the lowest monthly volume since last August.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been another week in the doldrums for the spot market, as both basins defied all efforts to stimulate business. The scarcity of requirements is the central theme and with the fixing window now reaching well into September (and beyond!) prompt rates remain at relatively soft levels. However, LNG prices in Asia moved up slightly off the back of competition with European buyers as temperatures across much of the Northern Hemisphere sit at significantly elevated levels. The Arb is open and there seems to be some improvement on the contango into the Winter months too. The culmination of these factors is likely to bolster interest and should increase activity levels in the short term; so whilst the current situation is challenging for the spot market, demand for multi-month and long-term remains steady, with charterers still seeking coverage into winter and longer. No newbuilding orders or ship sales have been reported this week.

x: AMERICAS  Few transactions are occurring despite the relatively robust arb.  While one potential end-Aug spot re-seller elected to lift on its own account, another fixture was noted for end Aug but this likely nears the end of spot terminal sales for Aug.  Price talk was in the 6cpg range.   With a limited number of available vessels (and correspondingly robust freight rates) there is little that is available direct from the terminals through August.  As such, terminal fees slope upwards as Q3 progresses.  Where earlier in the summer low single digits were the standard, mid/upper single digits are on the horizon.   The EIA reported Wednesday that propane stock levels in the US increased by the anticipated amount of 2.7mmbbls to an overall total of 83.8mmbbls, or 144% of the total achieved at the same time last year.  The 5-year average increase for Week 27 was 1.584mmbbls, so this week’s rise – though expected – was quite a bit higher than average.  At this point inventories are well above the high end of the 5-year averages and rising; not yet to the point where concerns of containment issues are being discussed, but nonetheless they are surely stout.  NWE Imports to the region continue but with the East vs West spread at $77 in July and reduced demand in Europe this has the majority of July imports arriving on LGCs and MGCs. The continual bidding at a small discount for an end July TOT cargo has not been filled. The physical premium continues to be assessed at a small premium, +$3.5/MT to July CIF ARA. The netback to Europe remains workable for US imports, the main concern has been reduced demand through the rapidly falling cracker run rates. CIF ARA butane has been stable for some time at 58% July Naphtha, and though it remains heavily discounted to Naphtha, and propane, demand for C4 remains low.  MED Bids for a fully flexible ratio mid-August VLGC FOB tender from Algeria were due today. Which makes sense in a July market which is set to import 500,000MT of LPG. 150,000/MT of this heading to Port Said and likely on through the Suez Canal. Leaving 350,000MT in the region, the lowest volume for over a year.

x: Summer and / or Vancouver is keeping the industry quiet on the prompt, but down the curve there’s enough happening on the time spreads to reinforce the value of a 2-Stroke going into Christmas. That we are at the mercy of the weather is always the case in LNG but interestingly, consensus this year seems to have shifted "peak winter" firmly into Q4. This could prove interesting if we have a repeat of 2021 (with January the peak fixing month for February’s peak demand) because many of the recent fixtures will be returning to their (disponent) owners at this exact time. Of course, the bigger news this week is the "yet to be announced" FIDs out of North America. Next Decade and Delfin are expected to hit the launch button imminently, and given recent SPA announcements, one assumes that Mexico Pacific is just around the corner too? Given the number of vessels we have delivering over the next few years, the promise of more volumes will be welcome news to both Buyers and Owners. No newbuilds to report this week.

x: AMERICAS With the July market all but concluded at this point (save for a mid-month FOB) most are eyeing the August market, in which there presently seems to be only modest interest.  With shipping now showing volatile gains and declines it may prove difficult for tons to move.  Furthermore, competing volumes from the Middle East continue to compete for Asian demand. In any event, overall stock levels are now well above the preceding 5 years, and fully 17mmbbls above the 5-year average for the 26th week of the year.  The immediate reaction in the MB propane market has (so far) been an uptick in values against yesterday’s close of 52.625cpg.   Terminal fees, all the while, remain rather muted and any potential increases have been absconded by the freight market, though a recent reversal to the downside may allow for limited growth.  Current Aug FOBs are pegged in the mid 5s cpg range, with Sep talked in the upper 6s and lower 7s.  NWE Recent propane weakness in the region narrowed the East/West spread $10/MT so far this week, the spread now +$81/MT. Netback values to the region have been improving, although no new US imports have been heard. Naphtha saw strength widening the August propane naphtha spread $9/MT to $125/MT as propane lost ground. The hope is that the improved spread will increase petchem run rates through the summer increasing demand, end product demand will have to improve for this to happen. t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: This week the LNG shipping market remained buoyant with a number of fixtures being concluded. In its wake, July cargoes across both basins have been covered and the market turns its attention to August and September. Whilst that might sound bearish for prompt demand, July has, so far, set the record in 2023 for fixtures by delivery month. Given this backdrop, perhaps it is not surprising that fixtures this week have focused on laycans in 2H August and 1H September, however, this is a marked change compared to last year when owners valued tonnage so dearly that they only looked to commit to prompt laycans rather than to offering freight further out (and thereby losing out on contango opportunities). This is perhaps the most important item to consider this week, particularly thinking about what it may imply for the rest of Q3. National holidays will affect demand (and reduce activity) for the rest of this week yet there remains apparent length in the Atlantic as intra-basin trade returns tonnage in time to service the next USG requirements. This may in turn see the freight market continue on a flat trajectory, at least for now, despite the expectation that rates will improve through the latter part of Q3 and into winter. The Pacific remains balanced and given the shorter voyage length, as well as the propensity for projects to keep their surplus tonnage within the region, charterers have a little more time to consider their options.   No new activity was witnessed in the newbuilding market this week, and whilst prices remain stable, we continue to experience more upward pressure than anything else.

x: AMERICAS MB propane prices began the month at just over 57.25cts/gal, and as of this writing are off by about a penny at 56.25cpg, which is generally in line with anticipation which called for prices to see a decline under the weight of the rapidly growing inventory levels.  Stock level growth over the summer should continue to put downward pressure on the pricing structure.    This week’s EIA data, however, did not help that effort as an expected build of some 3.2mmbbls turns out to have been a 1.5mmbbl increase for an overall total of 77mmbbls.  The 5-yr average build for week 24 is 2.44mmbbls.  Meanwhile, though, freight is the word of the day as Hou/Chi rates have risen by over $20/mt (from just over $156/mt at the start of June to current levels approaching $180/mt.   Terminal fees have not yet seen any reaction and remain in the mid 5cpg to perhaps 6cpg range for July, modestly higher in Aug and a bit higher, still, in Sep.  NWE  The East vs West spread has widened to $78/MT which will make it hard for the region to draw US tons. Additionally with the rapid rise in freight rates, freight offers favour going East from the US. The constant bidding for a 1H July TOT cargo finally drew out a corresponding offer, and although nothing was concluded, this left the TOT cargo premium at July CIF ARA +$6/MT. Petchem propane demand is down with the Propane / Naphtha spread at $124/MT due to reduced run rates and butane being the favoured feedstock as the Butane / Naphtha spread is $244/MT. Butane remains at 56% Bal June Naphtha.    MED  Imports to the region from the US have dried up, although the 490,000MT set to arrive in June is large. The region is well supplied and any demand is being rapidly filled.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: After so many weeks in the doldrums, it’s refreshing to see material movements in the LNG freight market; however, those that enjoy a steady, ordered existence may prefer to skip to the rates this week. The volatility in the LNG markets that led to a contango emerging and then softening, and to an arbitrage that opened and then closed, has now filtered through to shipping, and more specifically to how traders and portfolios will manage their fleets as we get closer to winter. The swing between theoretical lowest- and highest-case scenarios for ship utilisation during the second half of the year (considering voyage distances and any floating plays) can mean many LNG players are facing up to being overly-long or worryingly-short, or anything in-between. The result is a fascinating mix of strategies, with some vessels being withdrawn from the market and held internally, while at the same time other ships are being shown for winter and are generating interest. On the spot side, the market is firming off the back of more enquiries and the redistribution of some Atlantic vessels into the Pacific. There were no newbuilding orders reported this week.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS  Netbacks to the US have improved in recent days, having climbed (in the case of the European market) from the depths of less than a penny in early June to around a nickel at present.  The East, however, continues to be rather heavily favored, but the gap has narrowed this week.  This is in spite of the freight market which continues to confound and is related in part to the growing inventory levels in the US.   Overall propane stocks were reported by the EIA to have risen to 75.50mmbbls as of 9th June, an increase of 3.2mmbbls, which is the second-largest build for the 23rd week since 2018 (which grew by 3.82mmbbls).  Nonetheless, propane inventories are now 145% on a YOY basis, and 137% of two years ago.    Terminal fees for July are seen at between 5.00-6.00cpg, depending on timing/location, etc., but are more in the low 6cpg range for Aug, followed by mid/upper 6s for Sep and onwards to the 7cpg range for Oct.  Very little is being accomplished as yet, however, as the summer doldrums seem to be setting in.   Latin American demand is satisfied in the northern tier, and best described as “pending” in the southern tier.  There are potential requirements through the summer, but it is dependent upon weather-related demand in the lower latitudes.  NWE An early July full propane VLGC offered in the window was equivalent to a small discount to CIF ARA, and failed to garner any interest. The vessel’s AIS data continues to show South China as the destination, so the offer is testing European demand. A TOT bid in the window also for early July dates increased to July CIF ARA +$4.5 for the contract 19.4-21KT volume, failed to find a counterpart. The import volume for the region remains at 385,000MT in June, a long way off the 600,000MT received in May. Butane remains under pressure with a large cargo offer in the window failing to find a home at 57% bal June Naphtha. Butane has seen a rise in demand from petchem buyers as the deep discount has it replacing propane in the feedstock slate where possible.   MED The region has seen a large increase in import volume in June, 500,000MT will be imported, a four month high. This has the market taking a breather and looking for demand opportunities.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Summer has arrived, at least in London, and as we know with the coming of summer comes the anticipation and build-up for winter in LNG. This past week, the market in the East has remained muted while the West has been abuzz with a flurry of requirements, a few of which with the potential to go East. However, with the recent volatility in JKM-TTF pricing and the frequent “open-closing” of the arb, these requirements have been left in limbo or quashed altogether given the inability to sell East. Although the case, activity and rates in the West seem to have started building. On term and multi-month, we see a similar story of growing sentiment for winter and 1-year periods as the bid-offer spread starts to narrow and liquidity starts to pick up with a pair of multi-month fixtures concluded in the past week. With that, we surmise even further activity to develop in the coming weeks off the back of this increased activity prior to the summer holidays. On the newbuild front, Chevron has been reported to order 2x LNGC’s for delivery in February 2028 at circa $260M.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Netbacks to the US from Europe and Asia have been on a bumpy, but overall declining trend since the start of Q2.  Where at first April there was a ~9cpg netback from Asia and a mid-4cpg netback from Europe, now – two months later – the Asian netback has declined to the mid-4cpg range and European netbacks are hardly a penny.   The trading climate, therefore, has become increasingly difficult and little is known to be occurring as buy-side interest at the start of summer is limited.  Europe is well supplied and Asian stocks are robust due to a dearth of Middle Eastern-sourced deliveries.   Meanwhile, on the domestic US front, the MB market received no pricing assistance from the EIA which reported a 1.6mmbbl build in overall US primary stock levels, which the market reacted to in bullish fashion and thus further eroding the netbacks.  The market had anticipated a build of some 2.5mmbbls, and the 5-year average build for the 22nd week of the year is 2.4mmbbls.  At an overall total of 72.3mmbbls, propane stocks in the US well eclipse the 5-year average of 54.651mmbbls, and are now 144% of last year’s early June total.   If (and when) domestic production rises in earnest, Mont Belvieu propane values will – as predicted publicly by several of the largest midstream producers / terminal owners – relax in order that US-sourced product can remain globally competitive.  NWE European demand is low as Petchems have reduced their run rates even though July propane naphtha spread is a wide -$160/MT. This is due to the lack of derivatives demand as the economy in the region remains under pressure. That said an early July propane bid was shown in the TOT window, leaving values assessed at July CIF ARA -$1/MT. LPG imports to the region in June are showing below 400,000MT so far, this volume will increase slightly but will be well below the 600,000MT imported in May. The July East/West spread stands at -$74/MT even after the arb narrowed significantly to start the week, so spot cargoes will continue to head East. Butane values continue to slide as tons are offered in the large cargo window. The last offer valued was 57% June Naphtha and still could not find a counter.  MED Butane in the West Med looks well supplied, with an offer in the region unmet. Increased demand in North Africa was quickly filled and the region once again looks balanced to long.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market has awoken right in time for the bi-annual Nor-Shipping Conference in Oslo, following a period of slumber through the European and Singapore end-of-May holidays. Movement into the July pricing month and the emergence of an arbitrage has triggered a number of developing and firm spot requirements west of Suez, as offtakers seek shipping coverage especially in light of potentially longer voyages into Asia; as such, headline rates have begun to firm up in the West. It’s a different story in the East as activity is quite muted; however, there is a similar outcome as modern tonnage is difficult to source hence an uptick in levels. On the term side, a fresh 1-year requirement released this week confirms the lasting demand from players eager to mitigate risk of coming out short over the winter months. There are no reported orders in the newbuild market this week, however, levels remain firm. To those that are attending Nor-Shipping, enjoy the sun and we look forward to seeing you over the coming days, if we have not already.

x: AMERICAS Having commenced the month of May at ~70cts/gal, Mont Belvieu non-TET propane values drifted most of the month to ~62cts/gal when - until the last few days - a sudden, sharp decline occurred.  Current market values are in the 55cts/gal range, a 22% decline over the 30 day period.  This is due to a combination of weighty inventories and depressed crude prices – which themselves fell from $75.76/bbl at the front of May to $68.24/bbl as of this writing, or a 10% decline.   Crude itself is suffering from lofty inventories, lengthy on-the-water stocks and larger-than-expected production levels – particularly from Russia.  Adding to the mix is limited demand, which in no small part can be attributed to the lackluster economic development in China.   With regards to propane stock levels in the US, the EIA had been expected to rise from 66.70mmbbls (as of 19 May) by ~2.2mmbbls for a total of 68.90mmbbls (as of the 26th of May), but – in fact – a 4.00mmbbl increase was recorded, bringing total US stocks to 70.70mmbbls, equal to the 5-year high.     Meanwhile, as to terminal fees, market levels have not wavered much over Q2 and bid/ask levels primarily remain in the 5cpg range.  There is some improvement going in to Q3, but shipping rates – which are astonishingly high – are the limiting factor.  NWE Petchem demand has slowed due to reduced downstream demand. This has left a bearish sentiment in the region where petchem demand was expected to support the majority of summer buying. With $177/MT propane naphtha spread in June propane remains the favoured feedstock. The June import program will be greatly reduced from the 600,000MT of LPG which came in to the region in May. Whilst local North Sea production continues to ramp up as natural gas prices continue to come off. A Butane offer in the window was seen for this first time in a long time and pushed values down to 68.5% June Naphtha with no interest shown on the buyside.   MED As summer starts heating demand has disappeared. Low Sonatrach pricing of $405/MT for both propane and butane was set for June. This followed CP being set surprisingly low at $450 propane and $440 butane.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: LNG as a fuel is back in vogue this week. Those shippers fortunate enough to control DF cargo ships are inundating their bunker suppliers with fuel stem requests. As one established LNG bunker provider put it, “Christmas has come early this year”. It’s a stark reminder for those of us on conventional chartering (who have been bemoaning the collapsed Contango) that every cloud has a silver lining. Like the owners of LNG fuelled container ships, price sensitive buyers have switched back to sea gas in recent weeks, helping to repair some of the demand destruction our chosen commodity has suffered over the last few years. Even though this exacerbated buyers’ market is unlikely to survive the next winter, this current period of competitively priced restocking in both basins will go some way to restoring LNGs role in the fuel mix. So, whilst this may not be a great time for those who are long product and / or shipping, it is a fantastic market for those buyers who can purchase at current spot market levels. Given where those prices were in August last year, it seems only fair that the pendulum has now swung so far in this direction.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: NWE  TOT window saw some activity with a 1st decade June offer which equated to CIF ARA +$2.75/MT. Early June buying looked to be almost done in the region and the offer level was seen as more hopeful than actual market level. The main issue is that the petrochemical buyers are well supplied during that timeframe and retail buyers are adding minimal demand. The June propane naphtha spread is $175/MT, and continues to improve through propane’s weakness, so petchem buying will remain at a maximum. The East vs West spread of $85/MT is side so US spot cargoes will head East. Butane remains assessed at 75% naphtha with little buying interest.  MED  The region had seen a rise in butane buying interest early week due to naphtha’s strength propping up butane values. With crude oil values off today discussions are likely to stall until these settle.  US Mont Belvieu propane prices declined overnight on the weight of rapidly growing inventory levels, which the EIA yesterday reported to have reached 66.7mmbbls as of 19 May, 2023, or 144 and 151% more than the third-week of May 2022 and 2021, respectively.  The 3mmbbl build this week is the second largest since 2019 and well ahead of the 1.4mmbbl 5-year average.  In short, stock levels of propane are increasingly rapidly, which is then having a predictable impact on the pricing structure.  That said, the value of propane at Mont Belvieu has been – with a couple of notable exceptions - in decline since the start of 2022, loosely mirroring (but modestly outpacing) the softening crude oil market.  The propane-to-crude ratio has been descending all the while and has been hovering on either side of 37%, which is below the 2023 YTD average of 43%, and well off the 54% average established since Jan 2021.  In order to incentivize exports, propane prices will need to continue the existing downward trend, and thus the ratio to crude will continue to decline, perhaps to unprecedented levels.  With regards terminal fees, offers are on the table in June in the low 5cpg range, with July being offered in the mid-5cpg range.  August offers currently exist at between 5.50 to 6.00cpg

n: LNG Market Report
x: During the past week, a handful of vessels have been placed on subjects but support for rates has been minimal. For “Owners”, each successive fixture has been lower than the last, which is especially telling in a sublet-dominated market. In short, the floor, which some envisaged the portfolios would not breach, has opened; now, keeping vessels cold and moving is more important than securing better rates. Accordingly, and despite a slight decrease in vessel availability, spot rates are softer this week, affording Charterers the confidence of securing spot tonnage as required in both basins. On the term front, all eyes are on the contango into Q4 which, when open, exponentially increases the demand for 2H 2023 2-strokes but whilst closed, sees Charterers defer their winter procurement activities until absolutely necessary. The gulf between the spot and term markets persists, but as period-flexible tonnage hits the spot fixing window, the Bid-Ask spread closes and another term deal is generally concluded.  This keeps the premium for term fixtures alive as the availability – especially from independent owners – of tonnage that can cover all of this coming winter is limited at best. Given that there are more requirements still under discussion, one expects that Q3 delivering term fixtures will be concluded at a premium to those we’ve seen on the prompt. No newbuilding orders have been placed this week; however, prices remain elevated with some yards now booked out until 2028.

x: AMERICAS Domestic US propane inventory levels – as reported by the EIA – are at the forefront of many conversations, and many have been left with the impression that corrective data will again be required in order that a truer picture might be revealed.  In any case, stock levels this week were said to have risen by 2.3mmbbls this week where expectations of ~1.4-1.5mmbbls was anticipated.    Most notably, however, was the 700,000bbl decline in PADD I stocks when there has been little demand pressure.  Overall stocks are presently 143% of the totals achieved in 2022 and 2021, respectively, and the second highest since 2015.  This has led to questions regarding potential late-summer containment, and whether there is sufficient above-ground brine storage capacity.  Most agree, however, that the owners/operators of MB storage are monitoring the situation but at present see no cause for alarm.   As for market levels, MB propane is off by about 6cts/gal from the start of May and presently marked in the mid-64cts/gal range.  And while WTI crude oil values have also declined over the past couple of weeks, the relationship between the two has declined from around 40% to approximately 37%, against the YTD 2023 average which is in the 43-44% range.   Terminal fees remain at modest levels and most talk for June and July is in the mid/upper-5cpg, having risen from the upper 4s and low 5s, but through the summer levels are slowly improving to the 6cpg range.  NWE The region has not been competitive vs the East on a netback basis from the US for a sometime. This has not stopped large volumes of LPG being imported 650,000MT in April and 600,000MT in May. This pushed the May/June contango out to $6/MT and though CIF ARA values have been weak they did track crude oil values upwards Wednesday. This was surprising after consecutive larger than expected build in US inventories. Petrochemical continues to buy their maximum potential volume with the  propane naphtha spread at $160/MT in May. The TOT window has been quiet with discounts assessed at May CIF ARA minus $12/MT. Butane is valued at 75% May Naphtha which has butane at a higher outright of TTF Natural Gas for the first time this year, while propane remains below.   MED US imports have been filling the Moroccan butane demand. Turkey is set to received 300,000MT in May, down from 320,000MT in April.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG spot shipping market has seen subdued activity this week. The emergence of a small number of spot requirements has highlighted the lack of opportunities relative to the size of the availability lists; the majority of potential vessels provided offers, suggesting that the market is quiet across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. Despite the muted spot market, LNG industry participants are actively engaged in managing internal fleets, including optimizing their portfolios, strategic vessel repositioning, cargo swaps, or time charter extensions to address operational requirements. Looking ahead, the second half of 2023 is anticipated to bring about a tightening of the market. Rates for multi-month charters during the winter season and multi-year charters spanning multiple winters are expected to remain at elevated levels, indicating that market participants anticipate strong demand and potential supply constraints during this period.  In terms of newbuilding LNG vessels, prices have maintained their firmness in recent times. The limited availability of the newbuilding slots is anticipated to keep newbuilding prices at higher levels, consequently exerting upward pressure on corresponding long-term charter rates. Shipowners with existing modern LNG vessels, influenced by the expectation of high newbuilding rates, are likely to maintain their rate level expectations or demand rates close to those required by newbuilding vessels.

Netbacks from both the East and from NWEurope have remained relatively flat, as well (~7-9cpg to the East and ~2-4cpg to NWE), but the number of transactions has been limited – mostly due to the ever-tightening freight market, which continues to push buyers to the sidelines.  Northern tier LatAm demand seems satisfied, with contractual volumes having met the existing requirements.  Nonetheless, Southern tier winter-related demand is now on the horizon and will perhaps reveal spot requirements.  NWE The weight of imports are being felt in the region, pushing CIF ARA into a steepening contango, May/June at $5/MT. 500,000MT are on the water for arrival in May, and new deliveries continue to point to the region form the US. x: We have finally had a somewhat "normalised" week as Japan and China both returned from their lengthy holidays. However, any expected boost for LNG demand was short-lived, as buying remains muted and as a result, JKM prices continue to test new lows.   On the LNG shipping side, the spot market continued to soften despite some new activity and regular tender cargoes. We even witnessed a spot fixture going below "roundtrip econs", which until now has been a strong support level. The softening can be attributed to the ongoing slump in LNG prices (and constantly regenerating sublet availability). However, it's a completely different story in the term market, as demand remains very healthy and new requirements appear every week. Unfortunately, closing the Bid-Ask spread is now more challenging due to the wide gulf between spot and term rates. Looking ahead, we expect spot market activity to pick up once we get the contango back into play. As ever, it will be a volatile road up to winter!  Turning our attention to the yards and no fresh newbuilding orders were placed this week - which has provided the sector with a well deserved breather.

x: AMERICAS Three significant events have occurred over the course the past week:  First, crude oil values declined by $4/bbl, mostly on economic fears based on the recent large bank closures (and the ongoing fear of additional problems).  Second, propane prices at Mont Belvieu softened by up to 5cts/gal as a direct response to the crude oil weakness.  Third, terminal fees have weakened as buy-side interest has retreated.  Current June offers are seen at 5cpg but buyers remain agnostic, even when shown that there is plenty of room for negotiation.   Meanwhile in rather a surprising fashion, the EIA reported that propane stocks as of the week ending 28 April actually fell by 600,000bbls to 58.30mmbbls from 58.90mmbbls.  This leaves current stock levels at 143% of those recorded last year and 140% of end April 2021.  This week’s data release is widely viewed as a correction from the week prior when a 3.4mmbbl stock increase was published.   If – in fact – that is the case then presumably the traditional ‘build’ season should resume with next week’s report.  In any case, at this point stock levels of propane in the US are well above the 5-year average and remain closer to the 5-year high’s, which in some cases has become worrisome in the sense that brine containment issues later in the season are now becoming a consideration.  NWE Large import volumes continue, around 600KT in April and 350KT set to arrive in 1H May. Despite the drop in crude LPG values the propane naphtha spread remains at a healthy -$144/MT in May. The spread continues to keep petchem demand at high levels which is driving this spring market. Additionally production in the region is increasing, though re-injection into the natural gas stream continues. The butane market has been quiet over the last few weeks and continues to be valued at 76% May naphtha which has lost significant value this week in line with crude.   MED  The butane market has come off relative to naphtha with decreasing seasonal demand.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market has seen a quiet week resulting in low demand for spot charters. However, there is interest in securing tonnage for longer periods, as more Charterers are seeking to prepare for the upcoming winter season. While spot rates have remained unchanged in all basins, multi-month and multi-year period deals have been observed, with more expected to follow. This trend is likely to reduce term availability and increase sentiment for term charters. It is always a question of where winter spot rates will be, and this will eventually be factored into longer-term rates as Charterers look to compromise on longer periods at the right price to cover this winter. At present, many Independent Owners are reluctant to fix for short periods and are instead enticing Charterers with better rates for longer-term charters. However, for now, some are struggling to find a bridge between the spread, but it is expected that either parties will bite soon. Despite the current subdued state of the spot LNG shipping market, the increased interest in longer-term charters suggests a positive outlook in the coming months. On the newbuilding front, prices remain firm with reports this week that an Owner have secured two 200,000m3 LNG carriers at around US$277M a vessel from Hyundai Heavy Industries for delivery in late Q4 2027.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Domestic US propane demand has naturally tapered as the winter requirements have subsided, but export volumes are now regularly at record-level, whether overland (rail, truck and pipe) or – overwhelmingly - by oceangoing vessel.  In spite of that, however, propane inventory levels rose sharply over the week ending 21 April, having been recorded by the EIA at 58.9mmbbls, up from 55.5mmbbls the week prior.  A build of that size might lead to the expectation of a lower pricing structure, but non-TET propane at Mont Belvieu has so far hardly budged from its 77cpg perch.   With regards terminal fees, there was earlier in the month a flurry of activity but things have slowed considerably as freight costs have risen and – rather correspondingly – terminal fees have softened to near-cancellation levels.  Presently offers are seen in the 5cpg range, but bidders are increasingly scarce and priced at least a penny less.     Latin American demand should begin to see some improvements relatively soon as Southern Hemisphere winter demand is poised to increase in the coming weeks and months.  NWE  The region continues to receive a large volume of US imports arriving in the end April timeframe with some cargoes slipping into early May timeframe. This volume is additional to term deliveries and is keeping the region well supplied, with cargoes waiting to discharge into petchem importers. So even with the pro/nap at $153/MT for May we do not see any additional prompt demand. The is hope the larger than expected US stock build will improve the arb to Europe, and whilst the East vs West spread is at $77/MT in May the West will have to close that gap before attracting further spot tons. A large butane volume is set to be exported from Marcus Hook in May. Butane value in Europe is 76% April Naphtha, that said, large cargo lots have not been actively traded and few importers are looking for additional volume.   MED The region continues to see offers of trans-Atlantic tons. Which has kept open discussions quiet.

The term market has been busier but not exactly surging, though with limited independent owner availability and and expectation of growing sentiment in the coming months, we may start to see some more activity picking up towards the end of Q2. In the newbuilding market, prices keep firming. NYK was reported securing four vessels at Hyundai Heavy Industries delivering 2026-2027 for EnBW.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Having reached over 83cts/gal at mid-month, propane values at Mont Belvieu have receded to 80.50cpg as of this writing.  Recent crude declines from the mid-$82/bbl levels to the low $77/bbl levels now have not offered support, and – curiously - neither has the most recent EIA data which revealed a 700,000bbl reduction in stock levels.   As of 14 April US propane stock levels were recorded by the EIA at 55.50mmbbls, down from 56.20mmbbls after record-level export volumes were made known.  On that note, exports from the US were reported at 2.511mmbbls/day this week, up from 2.395mmbbls/day last week.  For reference, at the same time last year exports were listed at 2.428mmbbls/day.  Propane inventories are now 150% of the levels reported in mid-April last year, and 137% of two years ago at the same time.   Meanwhile, terminal fees on the Gulf Coast have relaxed and for a full propane cargo talk now is centered in the mid-single digits mark.  Mixed-ratio opportunities are available below that, but little is being accomplished.  Latin American demand is presently satisfied, with no known requirements as contractual volumes are considered sufficient and Southern Hemisphere winter-related demand has not yet begun to surface.  NWE  An early May TOT offer in the window at a small discount reflects the CIF ARA April/May contango. Adding weight to the discount is the import program for April, with 250,000MT concentrated in the last decade. Propane naphtha spread has come in slightly but at $154/MT petrochemical buying will continue to drive demand through the summer. With US exports at record levels importers in Europe are not concerned about supply this summer. With the arb open further down the curve, some looking to lock in tons at attractive levels and hedge. Butane remains long in the region, with values directly tracking April naphtha downward  at 78.5%.  MED  The butane lull is keeping activity low as US tons continue to be offered into the region. North west Europe is experiencing C4 length though strong frieght rates are keeping the product in the region. French refinery strikes continue to hamper operations at Lavera.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Despite national holidays being enjoyed around the globe, activity in the LNG cargo market and subsequently the shipping market has remained buoyant, with a combination of anticipated shorts and FOB tenders leading to a number of fixtures being registered this week. Activity in the Atlantic saw a marked improvement with a flurry of fixtures for 1H May being concluded and prompt vessels continue to see interest with ships being worked firm as we issue this weekly publication. Although the shoulder months still have some weeks to run, rates appear to have found a floor. Should activity continue in the same vein, we can expect rates to stabilise and tick upwards in the comings weeks, yet it is perhaps important to reiterate that there is a big discrepancy in the level of activity and interest between the desirable 174,000m3 tonnage and anything smaller. It is not to say that smaller tonnage is irrelevant, but its marketability needs careful consideration in the Atlantic whilst in the Pacific, owners are offered more relief due to a greater variance in parcel sizes.   The newbuilding price sees another small increase, yet no new buildings were reported this week.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane values have risen over the past couple of weeks from a low point of 70cts/gal to current market values which have well eclipsed 83cts/gal.  This is due to the combination of inventory drawdowns at MB and the recent surprise announcement that OPEC will cut production by up to one million bbls/day.  That news led to a $5/bbl increase in the WTI price which, in turn, gave lift to the MB pricing structure.  That buoyancy remains intact as propane closed most recently at 83.625cpg.  Going forward, domestic US liquids production is expected to outstrip demand (which – as evidenced by the half-million barrel inventory build yesterday - is clearly beyond the winter boundary by now), and inventory levels have now begun to build.  The strength and rate of stock growth, though, is contingent upon exports remaining true to the forecast that they will continue to be robust.  Terminal fees dropped from early March when values in the low teens were being seen, and bottomed out in the mid single-digit range before beginning to recover.  Current terminal fees for May are focused around the 6cts/gal level for a full propane cargo, while 2H 2023 values are pegged at/above 7cts/gal.  NWE April CIF ARA propane has continued to strengthen throughout the week with a late April TOT bid going unanswered. This prompt demand surprised the market as an 8 month high of 560,000MT will be imported in April. This strength has been largely due to maximum petrochemical demand with will continue as long at the propane naphtha spread remains wide, -$188/MT in April. Natural Gas prices remain low so we expect to see an increase in the region’s production which has been ramping up since March. Butane has been weak since the end of blending season with netbacks values for US C4 in around Mt Belvieu flat.  MED Little activity has been heard in the region, with the market quiet during Ramadan. Traders are looking to place large cargo buatne in the region as C4 remains weak in both northwest Europe and Asia, while the US arb is open.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: After a week in which much of the world enjoyed a long festive break, LNG players were “welcomed” back with muted market activity and some lacklustre macroeconomic news. The LNG sector itself remains flat, with delivered prices in both basins showing little sign of recovery through the rest of the quarter; nor is there even the hint of an arbitrage opening up in the near-term. The impact on prompt shipping has been predictable, and in fact the renewed competition among disponent owners East of Suez reduced the regional disparity in rates. It’s not all doom and gloom though: this week saw several term fixtures concluded at strong levels, implying a degree of confidence in the second half of the year and beyond. However, away from LNG the IMF has lowered their projections for global growth in 2023, especially for advanced economies, and this may impact demand for LNG. If we’re again looking for a silver lining, then slower growth across the globe may lead to a lowering of interest rates and thus an improvement in the financing terms for shipowners and project developers. Good timing, as we await another round of FIDs.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Signs of spring are appearing and seasonal national holidays creep nearer, yet the LNG and freight markets continue to trudge through a period of low activity. The spot market still suffers from an excess of availability and a lack of prompt cargoes, yet this week has seen a few requirements being worked and some very small revs of the engine. Although fixing levels have been dipping marginally lower than last done, some indications are holding firm or are at higher levels – perhaps this signals that the bottom of the shoulder months has been reached? A pause for the Easter holidays is unlikely to change the dial though, and the next few months could continue down a mildly-bumpy road without major risks to the upside or downside. In the term market, sentiment for prompt delivery was softening on the back of falling spot rates; however, new price points imply that levels remain supported by the slim list of modern tonnage available. As we inch towards a modest summer, there is clearly a view that another strong winter and beyond lies ahead.    On the newbuilding front, it is reported that K-Line have secured two SHI slots with delivery November 2026 at ~$258.5M a piece.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS  Export volumes of 1.8mmbbls/day are the primary cause of this week’s reported 2.5mmbbl propane inventory decline, well beyond the average 5-year end-March draw of 514,00bbls, but directionally anticipated and surprising only because of the volume.  Current stock levels of propane in the U.S. stand at 56.2mmbbls, or 3.2mmbbls under the 5-year high of 59.424mmbbls, and more than 23.5mmbbls above the 5-year low of 32.671mmbbls.   Despite this, however, Mont Belvieu propane prices have risen with crude oil gains and are presently marked at (or above) 80cpg, which represents the peak of a two-week bull cycle.  The relationship between WTI and propane remains effectively static, however, as prices of each have recently moved in tandem, averaging ~45% on a YTD basis and presently pegged at ~46%.   Terminal fees have been challenging to accurately assess due to the recent conference and seminar schedule – which resulted in an overall lack of activity - but for 2H April have been established in the low/mid 5cpg range.  May is notionally around the 6cpg level, with June mildly higher, still.  NWE The TOT window continues to be offered, with large cargo physical values at April CIF ARA +$1/MT. Europe is importing a large volume of US LPG with 7 VLGC scheduled to arrive in the first half of April. The wide April propane naphtha spread of minus $166/MT is keeping petchem demand high and with crude oil values increasing the spread will remain wide. The downward VLGC freight correction seen this week will take some time to have an effect on the European market as much of the supply is imported on TC vessels. Additionally a large proportion of Europe’s trades are supplied on MGCs and smaller vessels, these spot markets are tight and have more resilient freight rates. This freight resilience could see the East West spread, today at minus $60pmt narrow and see further US volumes imported to Europe. Butane in Europe continues to be weak with few signs of additional demand.   MED Refinery strikes in Fance continue to disrupt opertations at Lavera. March export volume was half of the 40,000MT exported in February which was down from 70,000MT in Janaury. Length in northwest Europe in March has picked up the slack in local supply.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG shipping market continues to soften this week as we slide further down the shoulder months of 2023. The lack of prompt requirements in both basins has resulted in an eerily quiet week across the market thus far and has been made more apparent when reviewing the Fearnley LNG Availability Report. The number of available vessels in the Atlantic remains high, with Owners of modern tonnage struggling to find the prompt employment while tonnage East of Suez also appears to be stacking up. Consequently, we have lowered our spot rate assessments to reflect the softening market sentiment and surplus of tonnage which corresponds to the backwardation seen on the LNG product side going forward. On the term side of equation, the current lull in spot rates has translated into reduced short-term rates of 1-3 years, however, we expect this to correct upwards and remain bullish as we inch towards winter. For now, heads turn to the fiercely contested EGAS spot tender for which bids are due by 30th March.   On the newbuilding front, prices remain firm with reports this week that Taiping & Sinopec Financial Leasing placed orders for two 175,000m3 LNG carriers with China’s Jiangnan Shipyard while Capital Gas were reported to be identified as Owner of two LNGCs ordered with Hyundai Samho Heavy Industries for delivery by March 2027.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Timing is everything, as they say, and there’s no escaping the fact that we’ve run headfirst into the shoulder months once again. And as usual, this has caused a pile-up of tonnage that begets a natural rate correction. What is significant, historically speaking, is the location of this fleet build-up, however. This year it’s in the West rather than the East, which of course explains the premium that Pacific vessels are earning over their Atlantic counterparts. The size of the East-West delta is also noteworthy ($30k pdpr for a TFDE as we go to print this week) owing to the magnifying effect of fewer ships in Asia leading to more Eastern spot requirements. Whilst this will provide some comfort to owners delivering and /or redelivering into JKTC, there is still a rate reduction along the curve and accordingly term rates (for prompt delivery) have softened also. Ultimately, this may all be short lived as two regularly recurring themes of the last few years have been volatility and uncertainty. Nonetheless, based on the current outlook, one would expect this to remain a charter’s market until the middle of the year when the contango into winter should firm up and then the pre-Christmas rush can begin in earnest.    Whilst we don’t have any Newbuild orders to mention this week, we can congratulate Sempra on a new FID (their Port Arthur project) and CoolCo on their New York Stock Exchange listing. At the other end of the spectrum, there has been a solitary vessel scrapping (Sinokor’s 127k ST, Grace Energy) which brings the total number of demolitions for this year to three.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Were it not for the fireworks following the weekly EIA data releases, the market would otherwise be mostly eventless.  A handful of seminars, conferences, meetings, travel and Spring Break have left many away from their desks and conspired to limit activity levels in what has become a generally dull market.  The EIA, however, posted a rather unexpected propane inventory build last week, followed this week by a surprisingly robust draw of 2.3mmbbls for the week ending 17 March.  That decline brought overall total US stock levels from 61mmbbls last week to current levels of 58.7mmbbls – though even so, present inventory levels are 174% of last year and 142% of two years ago.  In spite of the fact that stock levels are very near to 5-year high’s, the draw yesterday might lead one to anticipate that prices might increase – particularly as crude values have increased from below $67/bbl last week to over $71/bbl currently.  And it did.  Non-TET Mont Belvieu propane last week was marked at 69.75cpg where values last night concluded at 74.50cpg.  Terminal fees on the Gulf Coast are known to have been fixed for April at between mid-6 and low 8cpg.  May is at this point likely within a similar range but little talk has yet been heard for the forward market.  A series of Mexican tenders have been issued and awarded, with one West Coast requirement presently outstanding.  Likewise, pre-winter South American demand was recently covered on a spot basis as at least one – but perhaps two – spot cargoes were reported fixed for April lifting.  NWE The TOT window continues to see activity from petrochemical traders, and the general mood is that CIF ARA flat is fair value. Sellers have been popping up at premiums to April CIF ARA, buyers at discounts. Nothing has come together in the middle yet for April cargoes. CIF ARA propane values rose as crude saw a recovery. Over 340,000MT of US LPG is expected to find it’s way to Europe in March partly due to the arb opening in February and partly due to the huge export volumes form the US. Butane has dipped to below 80% March naphtha as a large cargo offer continues to be seen.  MED  France’s refinery strike continues to reduce demand with almost 60% of it’s 1.15 mn b/d of refining capacity offline. That has not stopped two US MGC cargoes heading to the region for early April arrival.

x: AMERICAS  The historically improbable propane inventory build of 900,000bbls recorded yesterday by the EIA puts overall stocks at 61mmbbls as of 10 March, surprising the majority of market participants.  Current stocks are 183% of last year, and 148% of two years ago and are now effectively equivalent to the highest second-week-of-March stock level since 2015.  Since then there have been only two occasions when U.S. propane inventories have built – the other being around half of yesterday’s increase.   Propane stocks for the period from 2015-2023, when plotted, reveal a high, a low and a 5-year average, and current stock levels are now on par with the highest part of the range.  With no support from falling crude oil prices – and the fact that winter-related demand has by now subsided – Mont Belvieu propane values have sharply declined from the 90cpg levels seen in early March to today’s 68cpg, which continues to decline.   As for terminal fees, a rather wide range was established this week for April cargoes, with a 6.50cpg deal being transacted, but also an 8.25cpg deal.  Latin American demand was covered via both spot purchase and tenders this week, one of which was recorded as a typical spot purchase, the others via tender, which were awarded both for a one-off parcel as well as a term contract.  NWE Credit Suisse needing a $54 billion dollar loan from the Swiss Central Bank shook the LPG market. As many LPG trader’s LCs are issued by the bank. With the prompt market well supplied traders in the region are happy to sit back and watch CIF ARA track crude oil values. Leaving the majority of US cargoes, even US East Coast VLGC exports, heading East. Further down the curve the arb looks healthy and workable, and many are questioning what the LPG and Gas markets in Europe will look like later this year? As the conflict in the Ukraine looks no closer to resolution. Imports to the region in January are expected to be around 650,000MT. The majority of this volume has come from the US where fog delays and a large draw and strong Eastern demand, are contributing to the strength in European values. Sustained cold weather is being felt in Europe, adding to demand. Butane is another story as a CIF ARA butane sits at 85% balance January Naphtha and few demand signals are being seen. There have been some recent delays to loadings in Algeria due to storms, causing minimal additional buying as the catch up is set to be quick.

That said, there is some potential upside for the spot market with the cold snap hitting Northern China and Europe that could lead to cargo requirements to supply both landmasses, as well as the prospect of a Freeport restart. In the meantime, though, requirements are typically optimisations and tenders and these are not sufficient to keep everyone busy, nor rates high.                                                                                                                                                                             On the Newbuilding front, it was reported that Hyundai Heavy Industries has awarded a contract to build three 200,000cbm LNGCs for delivery in 2026. n: LNG Market Report
x: It seems premature to declare that winter is over, so we definitely won’t do that. It is hard to ignore the traffic jam of tonnage that’s worked its way onto the availability list this past week, though. The net result is a sizeable correction on spot rates and given that sentiment drives all markets, there has been a softening in the term numbers too. Available Newbuilds remain stubbornly impervious to the warm European winter, however, with one Owner reportedly securing a brace of fixtures at record levels (on Subs) to an Atlantic project for mid-2024 delivery. Returning to the here and now, there’s a spate of tenders and bilateral discussions to keep the prompt market turning but with an increasing number of relets competing for each cargo, this is looking more like a Charterer’s market. At least for now. A cold snap (like the one forecast for late January in NE Asia) or a post “zero covid” demand surge in China or indeed any hint of European reinjections failing to keep pace with the level required, will change the mood again. In fact, this is likely the new normal that we contend with this year (and beyond?) - increased volatility borne out of a hypersensitive market that has re-learned the hard way that LNG is first and foremost about security of supply. This rings true for the ships as much as it does for the molecules. If you don’t have a vessel, you can’t get the product to where it needs to go and whilst the availability list currently provides charterers with some degree of comfort, in a relet dominated market it doesn’t take much of a nudge for portfolios to reabsorb this length.   No Newbuild orders to report this week but prices continue their ascent as demand remains strong.

The earlier detachment from crude seems to have reattached as WTI has seen a resurgence of late, having moved from  $76.93/bbl on the 3rd of Jan to $78.69/bbl at present.  Meanwhile, the relationship between propane and crude is effectively static at just over 42%. Terminal fees have seen some buoyancy this year and fixtures at 8cpg were noted on a couple of occasions.  Asking prices have risen, as well, and offers are seen now as high as 10cpg for Feb, where buy-side interest presently exceeds availability. As for the inventories, the EIA this week revealed another large draw but the data is largely believed to contain corrective data, if only because of the recent holidays.  As of 6th Jan total stocks declined by 2.1mmbbls to an overall 78.6mmbbls – which is 126% of last year and 119% of two years ago at the same time.  With North American weather now trending warmer, early expectations include the possibility of a build, since production has resumed after reductions which were due to the recent storms and subsequent cold weather.  NWE Propane has rebounded in the second of the week on the back of firmer stronger crude and a bullish sentiment looking out to 2023. The front month propane price in Northwest Europe rebounded, shooting up $25/ and now stands at around $560/pmt. Freight has continued to free fall, causing some of the early stage volatility seen throughout the European LPG market, however the volatility is also playing out in some more fundamental ways. Propane remains the more attractive feedstock, versus naphta, which theoretically would spur on European buying, however, petrochemical margins are still weak, temperatures remain mild, and Europe remains well supplied-as reflected in inventories. That said, its theorized that Europe’s ability to land US tons could be quelled by the thunderous reemergence of Chinese LPG buying, seen over the past week. A sentiment compounded by expected Middle East gulf maintenance

x: AMERICAS The Mont Belvieu propane market was in 2H 2022 detached from crude, the percentage to which fell to the upper 30 range. At the start of 2023 the relationship improved and presently equates to the low/mid 40% level. Propane inventories are a component of that as prices in the US have been reacting to the declines in stock levels. Today’s EIA data revealed an unexpectedly large 3.7mmbbl decline from 84.4mmbbls to a 30th Dec overall total inventory level of 80.70mmbbls. The market had been anticipating a decline of as much as 3.1mmmbbls, though the averages estimates were in the -2.8mmbbl range.   Meanwhile, terminal fees have improved significantly in 2023, having been heard/reported twice so far this year in the 8cpg range. This is very likely due to the precipitous declines in the freight arena, which have declined by 14% from the end of Dec, and 44% since mid-Dec. That market, in turn, is being affected by the improved rates of passage at the Panama Canal, which today stands at 2 days (North) and 2 days (South). Latin American demand has been seen improving as the recent winter weather system which enveloped the U.S. has made its way south, prompting higher propane consumption levels  NWE Considerable European imports from the US and North Sea have exceeded the unseasonably warm continent’s demand, positioning propane as the favorable choice for the European Crackers. In the first 15 days of the New Year alone, and estimated 360,000 tons of LPG is slated to discharge in Northwest Europe, a level but 10,000 metric tons below December total import volume. Spot freight on a Houston/ Flushing basis has been cut in half month on month, where it’s now being worked around $68.50/t (down from the low 130’s realized in December) allowing for more aggressive bids for US FOB propane cargos. The same cannot be said for butane, following an upswing in US Butane prices that effectively closed the arbitrage. Traders continue to bid for Handy and MGC cargos to take to NWE in January, However February large Cargos are now front of mind, with the expectation for more typically seen seasonal temperatures yet to come.

n: LNG Market Report
x: As the year draws to an end, we look back and reflect on another rollercoaster year for the spot market. 2022 has been a year of highs and lows; rate and commodity price records, geopolitics & diversification adding yet another layer of complexity and a newbuild market so active, the yards had to slow down order intake and take a breather.  Market dynamics are often unpredictable in LNG, but it has once again highlighted the importance of the commodity in the global energy mix, cementing its role as we continue moving towards a “greener” future. In shipping, we also have to consider new regulations coming into force from the IMO, and how these will affect our markets over the next 12 months. As expected, the short term market was mainly wrapped up in the lead up to the end of the year, so activity has been limited over the past days and rates remain at similar levels last seen for both spot and term. Activity will likely resume over the next few weeks as many return to desks, it’s still winter and pre-holiday conversations will re-ignite.  After a record-breaking year at the yards, another 2 newbuilds were added to the tally late December with Oman LNG securing slots at KSOE. We also saw ENI place an order at Wison Heavy Industries for a 2.4MTPA FLNG unit which is planned to be deployed in the Republic of the Congo. From all of us here at Fearnley LNG, thank you for all your support over the last 12 months and we look forward to another exciting year 2023.

x: With limited activities observed across both basins, the spot LNG shipping market is rather soft this week. There are a few requirements being worked, but predominately within the East of Suez and mostly are “optimization” deals.  The prompt vessel availability is slightly long against the requirements seen, and ships opening after 25 January – 1H February 2023 may see further discount against the current spot rates. However, the premium to charter a larger modern vessel is still present and with spot cargo prices currently stable and significantly higher against the term, it should incentivize charterers to pursue the larger ships and maybe for a longer time charter.    A small window of opportunity has emerged as the spread between TTF and JKM spot prices have reversed in recent days, with JKM now commanding a premium amidst TTF uncertainty in view of the new €180 price caps implemented by European Regulators. Furthermore, with Europe’s cold snap now behind us and with Asian heating demand forecasted to rise on an outlook of colder weather, we might just see this TTF-JKM reversal remain in place in the coming weeks, resulting in cargoes and maybe even Santa potentially diverting from the usual European destinations to the Far East?   On the newbuilding front, despite no new orders in the last weeks, year 2022 ends up as a record ordering year for LNGCs, reportedly valued at above US$35 billion for the year.  And lastly, we at Fearnley LNG wish you a joyous festive season!

x: AMERICAS Its been a week of mixed signals and uncertainty in the US LPG market. On Wednesday, the EIA reported another week of record production US (2.626 million b/d), along with a 3-million-barrel inventory draw that definitively exceeded the expectations of market participants. Unsurprisingly, the Mont Belvieu propane traded up an average of 4% across the locations, further hampering the sparse speculative trading at present. That said, most recent draw included, US propane stocks stand at approximately 87 million barrels- the highest mid-December levels seen in nearly seven years. Crude also saw a substantial uptick, maintaining propane’s weakness to WTI – which now stands at 36 percent- compared to the 5 year average of 52% of WTI. Each market participants Christmas list is slightly different. Panama delays have quelled some, and now stand at 5 and 10 days delay for north and south respectively- while remaining high on the radars of traders. Some are hoping for continued resurgence of Chinese demand with the sustained walk back of their zero covid policy- While others expect the ease of freight costs with the arrivals of newbuilds in the first quarter of 2023 coupled with the near perennially Q1 slump in rates.  NWE The TOT window has been active this week and bids have risen from January CIF ARA +$5.5/MT early this week to January CIF ARA +$10/MT. On top of the physical premiums,  January CIF ARA flat price jumped up $12 partly as a reaction to the larger than expected draw in US inventories and firming crude values. It is looking difficult for European importers to secure US volumes, more due to tight freight that the draw of the Eastern market. So far 90,000 MT are heading to the region from the US for 1H January arrival. A low volume when 480,000MT was imported in December and 520,000MT in November. Large cargo butane values are assessed at 92% December Naphtha though this should be taken with a pinch of salt due to the lack of recent activity.  MED The cold spell which passed through North-West-Europe never made it as far South as the Mediterranean. This has left term supplies accounting for the majority of the demand in North Africa. The East Med has taken a VLGC into Kalamata, Greece, in early January. While Turkey is also expected to receive a 1st half January VLGC from the US.

This has in turn killed the LNG arbitrage for now, but at least the contango is looking rather firm into Q1 2023. On the LNG shipping side, most of the subletters that have tonnage have been carefully assessing the situation during the last few days, and consequently the spot market looks rather balanced, although it is to be said that all the spot opportunities are now for loadings past the new year. On the other hand, the term market seems to be holding firm with further reports emerging on term fixtures concluded with deliveries as far as Q3 next year. On the newbuilding side, it was a quiet week with no new orders confirmed, but the yards report tender activity and continue to be comfortable with the current orderbooks and future outlook.

x: AMERICAS There exists at present contradictory factors in the domestic US market whereby rising crude values are having an upward impact on the pricing structure while simultaneously the weight of the now heightened inventory levels is having a downward effect.  At ~40% of crude (and barely that), propane prices should theoretically be poised to increase, but current stock levels weigh heavily, particularly since there has yet been little weather-related demand across North America.  The EIA on Wednesday released its findings for the week ending 25 Nov and showed a 1.6mmbbl increase from 89mmbbls in the week prior to current levels of 90.6mmbbls.  This puts current stocks at nearly 125% of last year and just under 100% of two years ago - and pushing well past the 5-year average of 80.30mmbls.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, saw a short-lived increase but have begun to relax again as a host of sellers have emerged.  Current FOB USGC offerings can be found in the low 5s, with room to improve.  Interest, however, is a bit muted – mostly due to the lack of weather-related demand and poor petchem economics.  NWE Many European traders discussed the state of the market heading into winter at a very well attended Christmas party in London last night. One of the major concerns were if US East Coast export volumes would be enough to substitute Russian LPG export volumes unavailable due to sanctions. For the time being US cargoes continue to be offered into the region as traders look to place their cargoes avoiding the Panama canal. Although with the December East / West spread at $100 most cargoes will continue heading East. The propane / Naphtha spread in the region was bolstered by a recovery in crude oil values. Which also strengthened butane which remains 91.5% December Naphtha. Demand in the region does not look set to jump just yet and is covered by term deliveries. The main concern is if demand jumps unexpectedly would European traders be able to find freight at the last minute to cover prompt shorts?  MED Sonatrach prices set at $580 for propane and $600 for butane a rise from November. Action in the region was quiet as traders assessed these posted prices before any cold weather-related demand has hit the region.

x: Last week we commented “It’s long been understood that what goes up must eventually come down, and the question for the spot LNG shipping market has been when and by how much”. Well, it has impacted with gusto this week as interruptions continue to occur at Freeport and  Calcasieu Pass LNG production facilities and storage in Europe remains high. Predicted colder weather is likely to bring to an end to the winter preparations as floating cargoes commence their discharges. There is an outside chance that the colder weather will significantly reduce gas reserves, yet this should be treated with some trepidation as the contango remains narrow despite the weather getting colder on the prompt. The result is tonnage is opening up for portfolio needs and reducing the demands of the large portfolio players that have been so active over the last few weeks and months. Again, as commented last week, without an arbitrage to pull cargoes East this will put downward pressure on spot rates and we don’t foresee this changing anytime  soon given the restrictions in China due to increased covid cases. The term market continues to invite interest and with CWC conference in Athens this week, we expect some renewed demand for freight to approach market in due course. In the newbuilding market we welcome the 14th Celsius vessel to the market with a 2026 delivery at levels close to last done, albeit for a 180,000m3 with top of the market spec.

x: It’s long been understood that what goes up must eventually come down, and the question for the spot LNG shipping market has been when and by how much. Well, as the World Cup kicks off and much of the wider world looks to Qatar with nervous excitement, those of us in the LNG world are looking at the floating situation in Europe with nervous…ness. As the contango narrows and the weather gets colder, floating vessels will start to head in for discharge and the resulting tonnage will either be cycled back into charterer’s schedules or else offered to the market. Either way, without an arbitrage to pull cargoes East this will put downward pressure on spot rates. In contrast, there are few signs of the term market slowing down: there are very few vessel coming open next year under independent owner’s control, and given relatively high LNG price forecasts and demand expectations shipping balances are being maintained with some additional length. There were also five further newbuilds reported this week: Seapeak are reported to have confirmed the 174,000cbm MEGA vessels for delivery in 2027.
