t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Upon us we have yet another stagnant week of spot activity, with rates dug-in and entrenched at record highs. With many requirements in the East & West still uncovered and portfolios still thirsting for any ship with a LNG tank on its back, it’s clear that rates aren’t going anywhere anytime soon with the ongoing lack of sublet availability and market liquidity. However, with Freeport facilities yesterday reporting continued delays in their anticipated start-up into early 2023, perhaps Off-takers might now be able to shed a smidge of shipping length to relieve some of this market pressure.   Shifting focus to the term market, availability from 2023 and beyond continues to get picked off week on week, further stoking term rates for all remaining vessel classes. With fewer 2-Strokes from Independent Owners than fingers on one hand, the focus for many term-takers at present are TFDE’s as headline rates for those few modern vessels maintain their hefty price tag premium. With that in mind, we marginally adjust our term shipping rates upward in view of continued demand while keeping spot rates constant. On the Newbuildings front this week, yard pricing remains robust as Minerva Gas has reportedly won contracts from ExxonMobil for two LNGC’s with anticipated delivery in 2026.

x: AMERICAS As of the first week of Nov US propane inventories had eclipsed the 5-year average by some 5mmbbls and reached an overall total of 87.7mmbbls.  Last week saw a modest 400,000bbl draw, but this week – which was anticipated to realize a draw of around a million barrels – saw a build of 100,000bbls.  In effect, the market is in the ‘shoulder’ period, late though it may be. In short, as of 11 Nov the US inventories stand at 87.8mmbbls, or 118% of last year and 94% of two years ago.  This propels the current stock level to around 5mmbbls above the 5-year average (82.6mmbbls).   The immediate explanation as to why stocks increased this week is that (for starters) winter is later to commence than usual, but also includes missed laycans due to shipping delays as well as reduced load rates over the past couple of weeks at one of the Gulf Coast terminals; the combined impact being the modest build.  Spot terminal fees now range rather widely, from the upper 5cpg level to over 7cpg, depending on timing / ratio / location, etc., but little is being accomplished due to shipping-related anomalies which stem from the fantastic delays presently being seen at the Panama Canal as well as the general lack of weather-related demand so far this season.  NWE The physical window has calmed down after early week excitement due to reported LPG production curbs at Kollsnes in the North Sea. Since the arb has not seen any marked change, though buying interest has come off. Attributed to the continued mild winter and unchanged petchem demand. The East / West spread remains near $110pmt for propane, so unsold US Gulf Coast loading in 2nd half November and 1st half December are not considering selling in the West. Butane demand remains strong primarily for blending and lies 94% naphtha.   MED The mild weather continues to keep demand in the region well supplied by term deliveries.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Normally when we talk about a market being “quiet”, it is synonymous with being in the doldrums – not so this market. A complete lack of liquidity has led to spot rate inertia but somewhat paradoxically, the levels seem paralysed at historical highs. Requirements remain uncovered due to an inability to find suitable tonnage, rather than any unbridgeable bid-ask spread. Past experience suggests that this situation can’t last but then again, past experience has oft proved irrelevant this year. Looking beyond this winter (odd to be writing this before thermostats have even marked its commencement) and the tightness in 2023 now seems to be written in ink. Charterers have been working their way through the term tonnage availability lists at such a rate that one wonders whether independent owners will have anything left to do next year? In summary, we see continuing demand for term shipping and no cause to moderate spot rates. And the sentiment has clearly flowed over to the Newbuild market; we raise our price estimates here once again on reports this week of a $252 Million order at DSME.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS An eventful week across the board as a number of market participants ascended on Miami as the year comes to a close, for a discussion on what to expect in the coming months. The answer. Uncertainty. While optimistic regarding recovering global demand, the timeline is very much up for debate. Freight too, has been the topic of uncertainty,  as traders try to find direction while weighing the near 50 new builds coming to market during 2023, with growing exports and operational delays, that cut into availability. In the spot market, December FEI/LST arbitrage traded as wide as $231.00/ton on Thursday,  but higher freight costs and Panama Canal delays have taken away the margins keeping speculative buying at bay. Presently, buyers' indications are in the mid 5cpg range, and a bit higher at Marcus Hook, while sellers are offering closer to 6.5cpg for December cargos.   In Panama, delays stand at 10 days for southbound travel, and 19 north, which coupled with sky high freight can prove exceptionally costly for traders.  On a Houston/ Chiba basis, freight was heard done as high as 192pmt earlier in the week but has since stabilized in mid to high 180's. On Wednesday, the EIA reported the first inventory draw of the season- showing stocks down approx. 300,000 barrels, where they now stand at 87 million barrels. The US Gulf accounted for the majority of the draw, 653,000 barrels, Conjoining with a draw of 404,000 barrels in the US East Coast (PADD1) . However, a large build in the midcontinent of 700,000 barrels mitigated a greater strain on stored barrels. The attitude around inventories is relaxed as the Gulf Coast levels are still 35 percent higher compared to this time last year. Exports were more or less flat week on week, totaling  1.4million barrels / day. While production saw a marginal decrease to about 2.5million barrels/ day. The draw, though surprising to the market, did little on the price of propane at Mt.Beliveu, which ended the session up only 0.25cpg on the day. That said, a forecast of Cold weather,  not yet seen, in coming weeks, could kick off the price activity more typically related with winter in the US.  NWE Multiple physical window bids and offers have been shown this week both on propane and butane. This pushed propane values to November CIF ARA +$6pmt, the strongest values since mid-July. Strong butane demand for blending is being seen in the region. With butane values at 94.25% November Naphtha, naphtha also being strong. The arb from the US has been improving, but with December East / West spread at +$97pmt all tons should go East. Although the potential of long waiting times at the Panama Canal or expensive auction fee to get through with reduced waiting has some traders looking to the West to stop their vessels being tied up for too long. The CFR market is active and will continue to be as freight is expensive and scarce making harder for traders to look FOB from the US and find freight.  MED Butane demand in the region is rising, though more to compete with demand from Northern Europe. As wintery weather is yet to be seen.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG freight market continues to hold firm this week as we see an uptick of activity from cargo owners seeking prompt shipping in both basins coupled with various term opportunities that have come to market, sustaining the demand for term tonnage both prompt and as far out as 2026. Despite fluctuating LNG prices and the continued absence of a West-to-East arbitrage, the appetite for spot shipping remains strong and there is still a lack of vessels being shown from subletters holding on to their winter tonnage. As such, when availability does appear rates remain high and command three-way economics. Such an environment has prompted the question amongst market participants of whether freight rates have reached a zenith? The answer is not yet clear, with the potential for floating plays to unwind on the one hand, set against the potential for colder weather or the emergence of an inter-basin arbitrage on the other hand. On the Newbuild front, there is continuing interest in ordering at both Chinese and Korean yards with at least 3 more orders placed since our last report.

x: AMERICAS Overall U.S. propane inventory levels reached 88.10mmbbls as of 28 October, having increased by 1.3mmbbls WoW, which is again viewed as a rather surprising high weekly build.  Current stocks exceed the end-Oct average of 84.478 by 3.62mmbbls. In looking closely at the data, most appears in line except for PADD I (the East Coast) where an increase of 600,000bbls was recorded by the EIA.  That level of build normally indicates the arrival of a seaborn import, but no imports occurred, which has now led to speculation that next week’s report may contain corrective data. Still, with robust production levels and very little weather-related demand in North America, it is quite possible that yet another build – though modest – will be reported next week. Terminal fees have meanwhile found life, and for Dec volumes now range on the buy-side in the 6cpg level to the sell-side of as much as 8cpg. Spiking freight rates and the East West spread, trading above $100pmt, had pushed CIF ARA up to fight with the East for winter tons. A strong large cargo butane bid was seen at 92.5% of Naphtha which has been strengthening in tandem with stronger Brent.     MED The lack of cold weather continues to keep the region subdued. Spiking freight rates and a wide arb from the US, usually factors which get the market moving, has had the opposite effect as no winter demand has been seen yet this year. That said Marcus Hook cargoes continue to find their ways to the West Med.

x: Although opportunities in the spot freight market are only trickling through, giving a sense of a slowing this week, this is driven more by the lack of availability rather than demand for vessels. This illiquidity, a persist characteristic of 2022, means vessels that do open for charter continue to set record highs: since our last weekly report, new watermarks for both spot and multi-year have been concluded on modern tonnage leading to almost zero 2-stroke vessels being available from independent Owners from now until 2024. 170,000m3 plus vessels with substantial availability remain a “Unicorn” these days, and we can almost say the same for TFDE vessels, leaving steam ships attracting lots of attention and successfully fixing. Open tenders for vessels continue to hit the market  for short and mid-term durations. With more Charterers looking for delivery beyond 2022, some are having to adapt their strategies to expediate the process. In previous years, it has been deemed slightly early to seek tonnage for next year during winter, yet the priority to secure shipping remains strong for many thus bringing forward many procurement needs. Yangzijiang Shipbuilding have made their debut in the large LNG newbuilding sector with two orders for 175,000 cbm vessels delivering between 2025 to 2026 and we kept LNG newbuilding prices stable this week despite shipyards continuously reporting good interest for LNG slots.

Above-normal temperatures are being forecast across the Eastern half of the US through mid-Nov, and production levels at/near record levels.   Further, and with respect to a modest hiccup in Gulf Coast export volumes, it stands to reason that additional low-impact inventory builds are being anticipated over the coming weeks. The weight of the additional inventories should further help the arb which has improved significantly over the course of October, though freight levels and canal delays will no doubt play a significant role. Terminal fees have all the while been seen improving and though the buy-sell range remains wide, buy-side interest starts in the low 5cpg range with selling interest – depending on timing/location – exists at or above the 6cpg range.  NWE The window continues to see both bids and offers, and is gaining value vs CIF ARA. This has pushed assessed window values to November CIF ARA plus a small premium for a TOT delivery. This accompanies CIF ARA’s rise in relative values vs Mt Belvieu, that arb increasing from high $110s to low $120s, a $5pmt improvement. Traders continue to look to place cargoes in the region due to the potential delays in the Panama Canal, and to optimize their vessels for future FOB loadings rather than having to consider spot freight. The the East/ West spread  for large cargo butane has been quiet and lack of activity means butane in the region has not tracked rising crude values, moving from 93.5% to 90.5% with no recent action.   MED The region is seeing imports from the US arriving to balance the market. The mild start to winter means term contract deliveries are satisfying demand.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Michael Schumacher said “records are there to be broken” and those words continue to describe the freight market week on week. As expected, the number of spot fixtures being concluded is less than usual going into winter, but the lack of tonnage available to those entering LNG’s busiest season short is warranting a huge premium. With force majeure declared at Bonny and Freeport still inactive, there is some theoretical potential to squeeze out some sublets; however, given the uncertainty within the markets and a contango in the LNG curve that is encouraging floating plays, in practice sublets are few and far between and in case are quite restricted in charter period. With such a tight tonnage situation in the foreseeable future, were now seeing discussions on both spot and term well into 2023 with prices remaining firm on both and all the signs of a high freight environment as we look ahead. No newbuild transactions have been recorded this week.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS  U.S. propane inventories are reported by the EIA to have risen by a half-million barrels during the week ending 14 Oct and are now pegged at an overall total of 86mmbbls, which is roughly 9mmbbls above earlier forecasts and 117% of last year’s total.  The data from yesterday shows that there was a draw in the Midwest (PADD II) of 300,000bbls and on the East Coast (PADD 1C), but that the Gulf Coast (PADD III) stocks increased by 400,000bbls.  Weather-related demand in the U.S. has been limited so far, though the draws described above point towards the beginnings of the winter season.  However, current forecasts are calling for a warming trend over the balance of October (per NOAA), and thus either small builds or small draws can be anticipated as the seasons shift. Terminal fees have recently begun showing signs of life and levels have moved up amid open arbs to present ideas ranging from the low 4cpg range to a high point of around the 6 cpg level.  NWE North Sea availabilities of propane and butane have fallen roughly 30% per month due to the re-injection of a portion of the LPG into the skyrocketing natural gas stream. However, a price spike and the need for additional tons has for now been mitigated, by the steady flow of US Origin VLGC's arriving in NWE.  The Propane price has gained ground in relation to Naphta- which fell more in parity with crude in the first few weeks of October.  But the focal point throughout the world of LPG this past week has been the emergence of some bullish indicators recognized throughout the market. Chinese run rates at cracking facilities have increased (and thus demand) on back of stronger margins, a curtailed Middle Eastern export program, and the theory that domestic retailers across the US will need to continue buying more product to cover for winter demand, as they elected not to do so earlier in the year due to sky high propane prices. The domino effect of the preceding could quickly matriculate into the European market,  making it difficult to attract tons from the US East Coast, where volumes- to-export perennially dwindle. The former, along with the unrealized probability of cold temperatures, has many market participants watching for a sharp increase in European LPG values on the horizon.  MED The large cargo market has been quiet as temperatures remain above average for the time of year. The butane arb from the US is closed. So, until the weather changes, term supply will be sufficient to maintain a balanced market.

x: AMERICAS U.S. propane inventory levels this week increased by 1.1mmbbls for an overall total of 85.50mmbbls as of 07 Oct and pushing stocks to nearly 120% of last year, per the EIA.  There are quite clearly sufficient volumes in tank to pose little threat to any domestic weather-related requirements this winter and to keep the exports rolling. Meanwhile, in the face of healthy freight rates terminal fees have seen an uplift and where before the bottom end of the range was in the 3cpg range, now the lower end of the range is in the 4cpg range.  Sellers, meanwhile, have adjusted their ideas from the low/mid 4s to the 5 cpg range. Through it all, activity levels are still subdued but sentiment seems to be improving despite only modest temperature declines and very little crop drying demand. A Chilean tender was released overnight which calls for a propane-only LGC or a VLGC to be delivered from 5-12 December, perhaps on a 2-disport basis.  Offers are due by 1pm CST on 13 Oct with the results anticipated by 10am CST Friday 14 Oct.  NWE A deal in the TOT window was booked Wednesday setting the end October and early November levels at CIF ARA minus $2pmt. This was the third TOT deal in as many weeks, and we do not expect the market to slow down. Netback values west are at parity with the East, and with the Panama canal delays lengthening to 10 North and 9 days Southbound the additional cost with going East has many traders looking to place their cargoes in the West. Importers have been waiting to see clear signs of additional European demand, or to be offered something which fits their needs. So the arb is wide open and the market looks tight, but counterintuitively, it is a buyers’ market. European naphtha has taken a hit which has pushed the Propane / Naphtha spread to $93pmt down from above $100pmt earlier in the week. Large cargo butane remains at a strong 93.5% of October Naphtha, though French refinery strikes are likely to weaken these levels.   MED French strikes have dampened the mood in the West Med. The effects of these on the waterborne LPG market are yet to be seen on the market, as a butane offer from Lavera was withdrawn and no other bids or offers have been seen. n: LNG Market Report
x: Whilst LNG prices have continued their correction this week, it appears that the only thing preventing rates firming further is a lack of available ships to be fixed. With a number of uncovered cargoes in the East, it’s not surprising to see projects selling their upside cargoes FOB. And herein lies the paradox of this market - there are ships that could lift all these cargoes, but for any number of reasons they aren’t being released. It’s a classic Prisoner Dilemma whereby portfolios are keeping their length in order to respond to Freeport’s potential restart or to capitalise on distressed cargo sales. No charterer wants to fix out in October for $500k pdpr if they have to give twice that amount back a month later to cover an unexpected short. Ultimately, it’s therefore no surprise that we now see Charterers in the market for 2023 tonnage because whilst current sentiment is keeping next year’s rates high, this year has taught us that the most expensive shipping is in fact no shipping.  On newbuilds, there’s been talk of one new order this week in Korea.

x: AMERICAS The U.S. propane market seems to have settled into a lull as we are presently between seasons and at a time when domestic inventories are well stocked but weather-related demand has yet to commence.   It is neither warm nor cold over most of the U.S., and things are presently calm.  Export volumes are anticipated to increase in Oct.  The EIA propane stock data was released and as of Sep 20 inventories reached an overall total of 84.4mmbbls, an increase of 1.6mmbbls over the previous week.  The latest intel puts U.S. propane stocks at 117% of last year and 81% of two years ago.  Nonetheless, as there is only limited demand at present there are likely to be additional – though modest – builds going forward, and as such even the current totals are considered sufficient to simultaneously accommodate both export requirements and weather-related demand.  US terminal fees remain generally depressed, with buy-side interest most often found in the upper 3cts/gal range, with sellers looking for anything above the 4cts/gal level.  In the meantime, very little is actually being accomplished and the market is in respite.   Going forward, one factor to keep in mind is OPEC cuts combined with higher Crude prices, should open the door for increased US production, leading to increased propane production and lower propane to WTI ratio.  NWE After an active start to the week in the European window propane discussions have quietened down. Leaving end October TOT cargoes values at October CIF ARA flat and 1H November cargoes valued November CIF ARA minus $2pmt. Although October propane naphtha spread in the region is -$109pmt, we are yet to see a rise in petchem demand. This low demand environment and, the lack of cold weather, is likely to have unsold November arrival cargoes look for a home in the East market instead of the West. The butane market remains active, with an open arb form the US. Though the one bid in the window at 89.5% October Naphtha for very early November arrival was well below the 98% bid seen earlier in the week.   MED The region has seen recent butane demand rise opening the arb from northwest Europe to Lavera. With northwest Europe also tight, US LPG is being imported to the region as the arb opens. The increase is the result of modestly reduced export volumes as well as stout production levels.  Inventory expectations earlier in the year were aimed at the mid/upper 70mmbbl level which while sufficient has been well eclipsed and has shifted the market to a lengthier – and perhaps more comfortable - position. t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The northern hemisphere summer may now be officially over: there’s a chill in the air, the rains falling and…LNGC spot rates are surging. There though, the similarity to previous cycles ends. Global gas and LNG markets are now front-page news on a weekly basis, yet despite the added scrutiny the various supply and demand levers are aligned in a completely novel way and are a direct challenge to those trying to predict what will happen next. What we can say with confidence is that gas storage levels in Europe are higher than anticipated, despite the low- and no-flow through Nord Stream 1, and forward curves look less intimidating for buyers. Much will now depend on the weather in the East and West as to how much demand there is for winter heating, but this is only one factor for the freight market. Perhaps of greater impact will be the behaviour of potential subletters in control of marginal shipping: the risks of missing a scheduled loading set against the returns of a neat sublet are skewed heavily against the latter. Without a seismic change in the LNG market, we may expect to see far fewer fixtures but record-breaking levels. As for today, most of the action remains east of Suez…given we’re in the middle of September, just another sign that this is anything but a typical year.  At the yards, Hudong have secured three newbuilds from MOL for delivery by 2028.

x: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane market levels began September at nearly $1.09/gal but have softened to current levels at around $1.03/gal.  Typically, this is the time of year when winter demand begins to reveal itself and prices historically have begun to rise. However, end August propane stocks concluded at 72.2mmbbls only to rise to current levels of 77.9mmbbls, or 5.7mmbbls, in the space of two weeks when the 5-year average build for 1H Sep is 1.42mmbbls per week.  2H Sep build rate averages are roughly half that at 707,000bbls per week, which from a starting point of 77.9mmbbls – and with three weeks remaining – should allow stock levels to easily eclipse the 80mmbbl mark.  Just a month ago this was not being widely forecast, and as such the propane inventory gains explain the weakness in the domestic pricing structure.  US propane stock levels are presently 10% higher than last year, and 77% of two years ago. Meanwhile, with big ship freight rates continuing to march upwards, terminal fees have correspondingly been undermined with buy-side interest limited and well below 4cpg.  Sell-side interest is presently at/above 4cpg depending on timing/location/grade, etc, and the number of cargoes being offered continues to rise. LatAm demand was punctuated this week with a CFR supply tender issued by a Chilean importer, while Mexican demand is anticipated to increase as Q4 nears, temperatures decline, and demand begins to improve.  NWE The anticipation of increased demand is starting to be seen as traders start to bid in the window. This has pushed the physical window to a +$3pmt premium to October CIF ARA. The transatlantic flow of VLGCs has been restricted to term commitments during the summer. Spot interest into the region is picking up since US inventories look set to be able to sustain exports this winter. CIF ARA propane has returned to a discount to naphtha which has been welcomed by pethcems, but at -$9pmt we are not about to see run-rates increase from the 70% capacity they were reduced to. The two factors keeping the run rates low are low demand for finished products and high energy costs to produce them, an unwelcome double whammy. As the weather cools and inland demand picks up, European traders are cautiously making plans to import more cargoes. Butane has remained firm at 95% September Naphtha, though no public trades have been seen recently.    MED Butane in the region is a buyers’ market, with both regional producers and US exporters looking to find a home for C4 in the region. Propane demand has increased as traders look to fill storages before winter. Not due to forecasts of cold weather, more due to supply uncertainties which could cause price spikes.

x: AMERICAS Poor economics continue to plague the US export market amid unattractive arbs.  As such, and alongside swelling freight rates, terminal fees remain depressed with buy-side interest in the 3cpg range and sellers offering at around 4cpg; hovering just at/above cancellation economics.  At least four cargoes are believed cancelled for Sep, with potentially more on the horizon due to persistently limited demand – particularly in Asia and Europe. t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we’ve watched LNG prices rise to previously unimaginable levels this week, someone reminded us that in April 2020, JKM was trading at US$1.83. Watching JKM breach the $55 mark this week serves as an expensive reminder of how much has changed in this period, but it’s worth noting that not everything is more expensive. In fact, shipping is relatively inexpensive at present. In April 2020, a spot cargo from Australia to JKTC would have cost about 25 cents in shipping which equated to approximately 13.5% of the total cargo cost. At present, and basis our rates this week, the Unit Freight Cost is $1.50 which means that shipping accounts for less than 3% of the total cargo price; a 500% decrease since April 2020 if you will. The purpose here isn’t to agitate for a rise in rates of course, rather it’s to point out the dilemma that the market faces in that almost all tonnage is controlled by Charterers yet their risk vs reward ratio for chartering out has never been less attractive. Freeport LNG’s announcement of a small delay to their restart should free up some October intra-basin tonnage, but with big ships proving harder to secure than a cargo slot into Europe, the question now is, how long until the bidding wars for the ST ships begin? No new orders again this week but then perhaps we will see a Gastech inspired flurry in a few weeks’ time.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: As we slowly make our way towards the end of the summer season, the market continues to apprehensively bubble and churn out a slew of spot and multi-month requirements, predominantly from the East, ahead of everyone’s return to desk. In tandem, this week a small but consistent arbitrage window has opened up off the back of a strengthening JKM (at mid-high $50’s) while a steepening discount to TTF (at high $60’s) prevails, further hinting at an anticipated pickup in activity in the coming weeks. With cool down slots still hard to come by and Charterers holding firm in their demands for cold ships, with the number of them relatively few and far between, we’ve come to a stand-off of sorts between Owners and Charterers. However, as LNG prices mount ever-higher, availability of cold vessels begin to deplete and perhaps even the prospect of a wider arb looms, the creeping pressure to fix might just have Charterers give way and take the best of what they can get while the gettings good. Otherwise, no newbuilding orders reported this week.

x: AMERICAS LPG market activity levels in the U.S. ground practically to a halt early this week with very little accomplished by a largely complacent and mostly disinterested trading community. The EIA data release on Wednesday appears to have spurred interest as a larger-than-expected build of 2.3mmbbls was reported and brought overall stocks to nearly 102% of last year at an overall total of 68 mmbbls.  Unless the newly released forecasts for a cold winter turn out to be incorrect, this should effectively set aside concerns that stocks might be insufficient as crop drying is likely going to be limited.  That, in turn, is due to poor crop yield and oppressively hot and dry growing conditions over the summer. Meanwhile, poor arb conditions, softening freight rates and limited end-user demand have kept pressure on terminal fees, which were this week quoted for 1H Sep at between 4cpg and  NWE The market continues to be well supplied with record US arrivals continuing and covering all demand. However, the market has begun to show signs of demand recovery with petchems and end users beginning to review their 4th quarter demand. Recent rains in Germany and Switzerland have given hope that Rhine levels will start to recover.   MED Lackluster market continues.  Algerian exports continuing to look East,  to take the place of Med demand,  until the market recovers.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: We observed last week that an unusual feature of this current market is the sheer number of prompt spot cargoes. Well, for better or for worse, this behaviour has now been normalised and so it is only natural that we released another August loading cargo requirement today. Of course, some traditional Asian Owners still adhere to the four to six week fixing window and accordingly they have stoked the fire in the September spot market with a brace of Australian cargoes loading on the same day (albeit from opposite ends of the country). Whilst this activity is welcome news for Owners, one noteworthy complication at present is the difficulty that off-takers are having securing cool down slots. The spread between warm and cold tonnage is unsurprisingly attractive at these LNG prices but with terminals holding firm to their presentation requirements (cold and ready to load) Charterers are faced with a limited pool of suitable vessels to pick from and in turn we have now comfortably moved into the 6-figure territory (Round Trip) for inter-basin cargoes. With a handful of term requirements still being pursued, sentiment has definitely turned bullish across the board and we are witnessing a narrowing of the delta between spot and term rates. No new orders to report this week; in fact, Q3 has been pretty lacklustre in this department, with a grand total of 4 new contracts inked to date. Notwithstanding this, Qatargas slot allocation is keeping concerned parties busy.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The domestic U.S. market has gone very quiet with activity levels almost nil.  Crude fluctuations have forced some to the sidelines, but the poor arb during the heat of the summer is the primary cause.  Buy side interest is also lacking. The EIA this week reported overall stocks at 65.7mmbbls, an increase of 2.1mmbbls which was slightly above the generally anticipated level, but which also brought current stocks to 100% of last year.  Barring any unforeseen events, propane inventories in the U.S. will likely conclude September at around the 75 (plus) mmbbl range; likely sufficient given not only the lack of crop drying but the lack of cancellations and cargo buybacks.  Both production and export volumes remain robust. Terminal fees are a bit subjective given the lack of activity, but ideas in the near term market remain in the mid 4s to mid 5s depending on location/ratio/timing, but move higher towards and in Q4.  NWE                                                 A window bid pushed the large cargo market into a premium to spot  CIF ARA price  (+$2.5/t) for the first time since July. The downward pressure in the recent weeks was a result of a handful of factors- notably, record imports from the US, compounded by very low water levels in the Rhine, not allowing for inland distribution and thus leaving the ARA hub considerably long. Macro discussions around the region have been centered around how LPG's will be utilize this winter amid the ongoing Russia/ Ukranian conflict. Some participants believe the gas shortage will induce a migration over to LPG, bolstering demand and subsequently bulling up price, while others remain convinced that the infrastructure to move from gas to LPG's in a meaningful way is not in place, and would take time and considerable investment. This is not to suggest European prices will not rise this winter,  but that they'd do so  inline with typical, seasonal-related patterns as opposed to the Russian gas supply shock.  MED The Med remains very much long in both the propane and butane markets, and saw a drop of 30/ton midweek. The levels have effectively snapped shut the arbitrage, and no US cargos are currently aimed at the region.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Arbs have suffered in recent weeks, primarily due to the influence on the LPG pricing structure by the declining crude market, and where at the start of July WTI was over $108/bbl it is now below $90/bbl and still volatile.  Propane values, meanwhile, have fallen from $1.21/gal to $1.09/gal over the same period. Relatively strong inventory gains have also been a factor in that propane stocks have risen to 63.6mmbbls as of end July, or 96% of last year’s level.  However, current stocks are notably just 71% of the 86.7mmbbl inventory level achieved two years ago.  Given the heat and dry climate across North America, crop drying should not be much of a factor which should then, in turn, allow stock levels to gain a bit more traction. With the inventory goal being somewhere near the 80mmbbl range, there is a 16.4mmbbl deficit at present, and to reach that target level a weekly build of 1.82mmbbls over the next 9 weeks will be required.  If the timeline is shifted to mid-Oct, then a 1.49mmbbl weekly build would suffice, and for an end-Oct deadline a 1.26mmbbl weekly increase would be needed. The August lifting roster is nearly complete with only a small number of potential cargo slots remaining.  Sep, however, is beginning to emerge and where the Aug terminal fee values are placed at/below 5cpg, Sep is perhaps at/above 5cts, at least for the first half of the month.  2H Sep is pegged in the mid 5s at present.  Q4 strips were talked in the 6cpg range. A full propane VL tender was issued last week for 2H Sep CFR Chile and was awarded at a price deemed to be ‘well below’ last year’s level.  NWE The TOT window in Europe has been quiet recently, without any bids or offers. August import volume is increasing, with term volumes starting to trickle in from the US. Netback values from the US for August are still in cancellation territory, and well below value to Asia. This is keeping August imports quiet in this period of low demand. Additionally export has resumed out of Mongstad and were around 70 KT in July, adding local supply. Baltic production exported from Ust-Luga continues to be STS-ed onto VLGC in the ARA region and head East. Until clear demand signs are seen traders in the region are happy to work on a more prompt basis, waiting for offers to be shown to them rather than going out searching for cargoes, in this well supplied low demand environment. Butane has continuously firmed up and is now 86% August Naphtha.   MED The summer market in the West of the region has ample supply from term contracts. The East Med is well offered, as traders with split ratio  US cargoes look for a home for their tons.

n: LNG Market Report
x: With TTF sitting comfortably above $60/MMBtu, it’s not surprising to see Charterers paying up for 2-Strokes. But with spot loadings fixing at a fraction of the Term rates, there’s a big spread to be bridged between now and Winter. Of course, geopolitical uncertainty is high and given the dollars at stake with every cargo, it’s arguably sound risk management to go into Q4 comfortably long. For those Owners who can monetise their length, however, recent reports of $200k pdpr deals in the 2-Stroke segment should provide the necessary incentive to optimise. Speaking of which, optimisation on the prompt is alive and well with an interesting development this past week being the emergence of very prompt cargoes in both basins. This has provided some excellent “keep cool” voyages for owners but also suggests that: i. projects are trying to squeeze out additional cargoes, and ii. portfolio players see real value in fine-tuning their schedules. If we see enough of these cargoes emerge, spot rates will firm again but for now, the only guaranteed strengthening comes from the yards, with Newbuild prices up again this week.

Consequently, spot rates continue to stagnate and there has not been a material shift in the number of available vessels in either basin as various subletters seek employment in the near term. With the divergence between spot and multi-month interest, there continues to be a disconnect between spot and terms rates, as has been the theme for much of this year. It was announced this week that two 174,000 m3 were ordered at DSME shipyard, as newbuild prices continue to firm up.

n: LNG Market Report
x: As the UK and Europe battle all that these current record temperatures are bringing, there’s no need to remind our Northern Hemisphere readers that we’re in the midst of Summer. Liquidity has dried up and the holiday season continues unabated. Nonetheless, there is definitely an undercurrent of repressed uncertainty about what might be in store when everyone gets back to their desk. NS1’s impending restart marks the first time many of us have read about the travel plans of a broken Turbine in the trade press but come tomorrow, all eyes will certainly be on East to West gas flows. Given that European volumes used for winter are currently being drawn down in some countries, the race to refill before the heating is turned on just got a little more intense. The Atlantic shipping market is displaying similar behaviours as protagonists weigh the weakness on the prompt with the need to ensure security of supply (i.e., tonnage) over winter. To this end, we see a massive disconnect between spot and term rates which makes life tricky for both Owners and Charterers at this exact time. In the East, we’ve seen a few requirements emerge this week which, as part of the usual churn of activity, sees the Pacific market retain its premium to the West. No Newbuildings to report this week (which is itself newsworthy) but as prices continue their ascent, there’s no sign of demand easing up in this segment yet.

x: AMERICAS Volatility in the crude arena has allowed WTI prices over the past week to range from $96.30/bbl to $104.22/bbl, only to trade presently at $95.87/bbl as of this writing.  That has translated to volatility in the domestic U.S. propane market where prices have ranged from over $1.14/gal down to just over $1.10/gal and now to current values just over $1.12/gal.  The less-than-robust EIA report this week has allowed propane to retain some of its value as the stock data this week revealed a build of just 1.4mmbbls where the market was anticipating something above 2.25mmbbls.  Current inventory levels are 94% of the same time last year, but just 70% of those recorded two years ago.  Sentiment is that inventories are veering towards being insufficient for the winter. Terminal fees have shown modest buoyancy and asking prices for Aug are in the upper 4s, perhaps 5cpg.  Buy-side interest, though, remains subdued.  2H 2022 is being talked in the 6cpg range. LatAm demand remains generally flat, though it is anticipated that modest volumes of spot demand may emerge for Sep.  NWE The run of record LPG import months look like they will come to an end in August. The region is well supplied and demand remains low as expected in summer. The buyers with large storages could be incentivised to buy if they have the capacity take more product, to take advantage of the CIF ARA contango. August/September CIF ARA at -$5pmt and September/October CIF ARA-$6pmt. The July East West spread is +$62pmt, so all spot cargoes should be heading East, although term volumes continue to flow to Europe. The butane market in the region has been very quiet since being well offered for end July and early August arrival. Butane value notionally 82% Naphtha, this value is firming up as the butane product overhang is being worked through.   MED The summer continues to progress in the region without much activity. x: AMERICAS Crude oil peaked in the first week June at just over $122/bbl but has softened rather dramatically over the last month and is presently trading in the ~$93/bbl range, though with quite a lot of inter-day volatility.  This is causing volatility in the LPG space, as well, with propane having declined from $1.24/gal the first week of June to $1.10/gal in robust trading sessions.  Butane length in the U.S. continues to play a role and RVP waivers are being sought to alleviate the surplus, though this was considered a bit of a long-shot. The EIA data on Wednesday showed a build of 2.9mmbbls to an overall total of 57.8mmbbls as of 8 July, or about 97% of last year but just ~68% of two years ago.  The market had been anticipating a build of between about 750,000bbls and 1.9mmbbls, and as such the healthy growth was welcome and well received. Terminal fees remain subdued, with buy-side interest at/below 4cpg, but sellers seem anxious to commence talks nearer to 5cpg.  Little is known to have been fixed, but at this point there seem to be more sellers than buyers.  2H 2022 values, however, are healthier and were seen worked at/above 6cpg.  NWE The European propane market sprung to life for end June/early July TOT cargoes, with two bids bringing assessed values up to a $2.75pmt premium to July CIF ARA. Surprising as July imports from the US are set to be 800,000MT smashing the previous monthly record of 700,000MT. The butane market in the region remains long and stocks high. The steepening contango could temp some traders to look at storing tons. The netback values form the US are not as attractive, the August East / West spread $59pmt, though many European traders have TC vessels and European systems, skewing spot cargo netbacks. The huge trans-Atlantic volume continues to flow!  MED Has been quiet as movements in other markets take front and centre in this low demand period of the year. The region remains long butane as Northwest European traders continue to try to place tons in the region.

x: AMERICAS Volatility has overtaken the crude oil markets which have been reeling from fears of a deepening global economic recession (not to mention a strengthening U.S. Dollar), the former causing governments to sharply raise interest rates in a bid to slow the economy.  As such, WTI saw highs of over $122/bbl in June, but new lows were posted this week at $98.53/bbl.   Correspondingly, the MB propane market has reacted, not only in terms of the flat price but as it relates to WTI on a percentage basis.  Propane at Mont Belvieu is currently valued at ~$1.14/gal, or about 48% of WTI, where at one point the relationship had dipped in to the low 40 percent range. The EIA today released its findings on US propane stocks which, for the first time in some weeks, was expected to reveal a more accurate set of data.  Most in the market were expecting a build but expectations ranged widely from under 1mmbbls to over 3mmbbls.  As of 01 July 2022, however, the Overall Total propane stock level in the US is 54.9mmbbls, or 95% of last year, but 70% of two years ago. Terminal fees were earlier in June seen fixed in the upper 5cpg range, but buyers retreated to the low 4s until recently when the market turned and two separate transactions are widely believed to have been fixed for August at 5cpg.  2H 2022 values are at/above 6cpg.  NWE Butane Storages in the region remains full and multiple cargoes are looking for homes with no luck so far. In the propane markets, Europe is on track to import close to 625,000 tons In July, (a new record  high) , prompting a handful of unmet window offers, and a decidedly weak market sentiment to begin the short week. That said, LPG Avails from the North Sea will likely tighten further still, as liquids continue to be re-injected into the Nat Gas stream.   MED Butane is long in the region as traders look to the region to release some of the North West European butane pressure. Propane in the med appears long for the time being, as demand has quelled per usual at this point in the year. Sonatrach postings for July of $700 propane and $650 butane, will have done little to spur demand in the region. Demand above term supplies is not being seen.

Importers from Europe and Asia keep battling for cargoes amidst the global natural gas supply shortage, but current record high seasonal prices have deterred some buyers. x: AMERICAS The EIA’s propane inventory report yesterday was viewed with skepticism, if only because of the technical-related hiatus the bureau took in the week prior.   For the week ending 25 Jun the 5-year average build has been 2.85mmbbls, where the two week span from the last EIA report to the most current showed a build from 51.8mmbbls on 10 June to 54mmbbls on 24 June, or a 2.2mmbbl increase.  In other words – on average – a 1.1mmbbl weekly build, which was viewed as weak, thus causing the market to resign itself to wait until next week’s data, which is hoped to provide a clearer view of stock levels. That said, at 54.00mmbbls as of 24 Jun 2022, propane stocks in the U.S. are 94% of last year, 72% of two years ago, 76% of three-years ago, 97% of four years ago, and 97% of five years ago. With regards current market rates, spot terminal fees were earlier fixed at as high as 6.50cpg, but have softened at present.  Spot FOB offers are presently seen at 6.00cpg, but depending on timing/ratio there is some room to the downside.  A recent four cargo tender to supply Mexico was awarded to a trader who will deliver 30,000mt propane parcels: Two in July and two in August, reportedly at 5cpg FOB. Brasil and Chile also remain active covering their winter demand.  NWE The butane bloodbath has been the main talking point in the region this week. Storages for butane in the region are full and multiple cargoes are looking for homes with no luck so far. Window offers for butane have fallen from 87% to 84% July Naphtha this week and are yet to find buying interest. The European propane market has taken a backseat and has been relatively quiet. It is clear that the market is not short propane, netbacks from the US for July and August are deep in cancellation territory. We are approaching the seasonal demand lows for the region at the same time as seeing some North Sea LPG production increases, and this increased supply and reduced demand has caused the market to go quiet.  MED Butane is long in the region as traders look to the region to release some of the North West European butane pressure. Sonatrach postings for July of $700 propane and $650 butane, will have done little to spur demand in the region. Demand above term supplies is not being seen.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Record temperatures in Tokyo has seen an increase in cooling demand in Japan and with it the emergence of long needed Eastern demand as LNG reserves at power stations has fallen over the past two weeks. It is reported that there is some resistance from some smaller Japanese utilities to purchase LNG as LNG prices remain close to record highs for the time of year as supply disruption continues to persist. Instead there is a push to curb demand but despite these efforts additional LNG cargoes will be required and it can be anticipated that more ton-time should help alleviate the oversupply of tonnage in the Atlantic through Q3 as vessels head East.    Fixing activity remains muted in the Atlantic with FOB cargo tenders being awarded to entities with their own tonnage. Yet in the Pacific, on the back of a couple of fixtures, rates have stabilised following a couple of consecutive weekly falls and sees owners returns in the Pacific usurp the Atlantic.     In the newbuilding market, Knutsen was awarded by Qatar Energy eight LNG carriers taking their total to ten LNGC in the Qatar Energy process. In addition, NYK was awarded seven LNGC by Qatar Energy, both the Knutsen and NYK vessels will be built at HHI.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The Jekyl and Hyde nature of the market in the wake of the Freeport outtage has continued this week. A jump in prompt availability has depressed spot rates in both basins; yet further out towards winter and beyond, levels remain strong with more risk to the upside. In fact, many signals such as reduced production and higher demand for LNG in Europe are bearish for shipping on paper but very bullish for LNG pricing. The old adage "cargo is king" may come to define the coming years, and access to reliable shipping  is clearly supporting multimonth and multiyear rates. That aside, the prompt months may be a challenge for those with excess tonnage.  There were two newbuildings ordered last week.

x: AMERICAS Fears of recession and US governmental fuel-tax relief ambitions have caused crude to tumble, though propane has yet to react at corresponding rates.  As such, the propane-to-crude ratio has increased from the low/mid 40-percentile range to 47% at present.  Current Mont Belvieu propane for July is pegged at 120.25cpg while WTI is off by $2.25/bbl at $103.80/bbl.  Wednesday’s WTI market closed at $106.19/bbl. Propane arbs, meanwhile, heavily favor the Asian markets, but buy-side interest does not appear to have fully materialized as Middle East export volumes appear to be satisfying demand levels there. The EIA propane inventory data was expected to have been released today (having been delayed due to the newly established “Juneteenth” holiday which was observed on Monday) but a systems issue has reportedly caused the EIA to postpone until next week at the usual Wednesday 9.30am CST time. Lastly, terminal fees crested earlier in the month in the low/mid 6s for July business but have receded for late-July / early August transactions to the mid 4cpg range.  NWE Record imports to the region has closed the trans-Atlantic arb. With butane storages full and looking long in the region. Propane is looking long, with early July being offered in the window with any bids being shown in reply. Retail demand for LPG is low as to be expected with much of Europe experiencing temperatures of over 30 degrees. The petchem sector looks well supplied through 1H July and opportunistic sellers hoping to place spot tons in the market are getting worried, as record imports coincide with seasonally lower demand.   MED The East Med is long due to Yanbu butane coming into the region. While the west Med has been well supplied from the US, during this period of low seasonal demand. Additionally weakness in physical naphtha is further reducing butane value.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: With the buzz of Posidonia behind us, we are rattled back to reality by the recent Freeport LNG explosion and a 40% cutback of LNG flows from NordStream 1, due to technical issues, further tightening an already stretched LNG market and releasing a flurry of prompt LNG vessels, many only until recently committed, back unto the market. In turn, while LNG prices across the forward curves of Asian and European indexes rise in the wake of these events, vessels’ spot rates across both basins plummet, bringing us back to levels not seen for some weeks. However, with a fair few requirements still out there in the Atlantic and Pacific, and in anticipation of increasing demand from the East as we inch towards winter, we can expect spot rates to maintain some level of support and buoyancy going forward. On the term side of the equation, a similar story can be told as 1-Year term rates soften off the back of current events. That said, this is driven by prompt availability discounting the coming weeks. Subject to Freeport start-up, the market remains structurally tight and the prompt discount vanishes for later deliveries.  On newbuildings, two new orders have been reported this week from a Greek Head Owner as vessel prices continue to tick upwards, and with the rise in US interest rates the impact on newbuild charter rates is likely to be significant.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The EIA report on Wednesday showed a modest build of just 1.6mmbbls for an overall propane stock total of 51.8mmbbls as of 10 June 2022, which is about 94% of last year’s total and 73% of the total achieved two years ago.  It’s also well below the average for the second week of June, which is +2.12mmbbls.  The market had been expecting something between 2.8-3.2mmbbls (with a couple of noteworthy outliers who were calling for a “flat” or “minimal” builds).   On the whole, propane values over the last week have declined from 124.50cts/gal to current levels around 118.00cts/gal.  All the while, netbacks were seen in decline as re-sale terminal fees have shrunk to ~4cts/gal.  However, by the close of business on Wednesday there appeared promise as the arb showed signs of improving – opening, even.  Furthermore, a series of offers appeared this week and supplies seem plentiful despite the three known July cancellations on the Gulf Coast. Meanwhile, demand in Latin America appears to have been satisfied via a spot sale and a tender award, though the re-opening of storage caverns near Pajaritos in Mexico may allow for some volumes to move in that direction.  Current consumer demand levels in Mexico are seasonally limited, however.  NWE  An end June propane bid continues to be show in the TOT window, supporting the market. The value was equal to July CIF ARA +$7.5pmt. With the increased Marcus Hook exports and the majority of these tons flowing to Europe, it was expected this bid would have been hit rapidly. The summer mood continues in region as storages begin to fill up. Butane in particular is long with storages full at all major demand centres. Term supply and European traders picking up Marcus Hook tons has blocked the hopes of Eastern placing some of their length in Europe. The July Propane Naphtha spread in Europe is at $98pmt and demand from petchems remains good. The East/West spread is $56pmt in July and it is likely that July USGC cargoes which were not cancelled will try to find homes in the East rather than looking to the West.   MED The region is quiet with the mood dominated by butane length and Eastern traders trying to find homes for US split ratio cargoes. Low demand and heatwaves make for a soporific market.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Propane market levels at Mont Belvieu continue to drift, though rather inconsistently, having peaked in the second week of March at 163.75cpg, and closing most recently at ~123.00cpg.  Conversely, WTI has been trending up since early December and overwater LPG exports remain robust – the combination of which might normally lead to a firm pricing structure.  The conclusion of winter demand and rising stock levels, though, have colluded and allowed values to decline.  Meanwhile, propane as a percentage of crude has been drifting, as well, as Q4 2021 levels were in the 80-percentile range but this week are flirting in the low 40% range. LatAm demand was revealed this week as a primary buyer issued a tender for 33-44,000mt for delivery from 3-9 August.  Offers are expected by 1pm on Thursday 9 June and are to remain valid until Noon EST on Friday 10 June. Terminal fees have reached a plateu of sorts, with buyers and sellers at/above 6cpg, though out-month 2022 transactions are known to have occurred at 6.00cpg, 6.25cpg and 6.50cpg. The EIA this week showed a 600,000bbl build to a total of 50.20mmbbls, or over 93% of last year’s total.  Expectations ranged from 2.75-3.25mmbbls, so the weak build was seen as disappointing – and at least mildly bullish on a short-term basis.  NWE The region looks well supplied with a large volume of trans-Atlantic cargoes arriving in the second half of June. Counter intuitively the TOT window premiums remain for 2H June delivery at June CIF ARA +$5pmt. A stronger premium than the June / July backwardation of $2pmt. Crude continuing to climb has kept the propane / Naphtha spread above $120pmt, supporting industrial propane demand in the region. The majority of US East Coast exports continue to come to Europe, and these exports are growing rapidly. Butane has been steady at 91% Naphtha, though this level has not been tested recently in a fairly stagnant Northwest European butane market.   MED The region is well supplied through term contracts and no additional demand has been seen. Although a fire at Fawley refinery in the UK is expected to tighten butane supply to the Med.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The EIA data for the week ending 27 May was revealed today and showed a 3.3mmbbl increase over the week prior.  Current overall stocks stand at 49.6mmbbls, which is nearly 103% of last year and just under 70% of two years ago.  Concerns as to stock levels at the conclusion of the summer are beginning to dissipate, though any forecast at this point would likely be premature. Meanwhile, propane values – as a result of the larger-than-anticipated inventory increase – are trending down, having peaked before the end of May at $1.25/gal and now posting at below $1.22/gal.  At present propane is 45% of WTI, having been in decline against crude almost consistently since Q4 2021. Terminal fees in the near-term have softened, with buyers clustered around the 5cpg level but sellers holding on for values nearer to 6cpg.  The second-half of 2022 has been more healthy, with a slew of transactions occurring at between 6.00 and 6.50cpg.  NWE The June CIF ARA propane price came off 11 dollars prior to the holiday closure, and presently sits at $744/t. A tug of war persists as North Sea product remains tight, however ample exports from the US have kept demand satisfied and the muted window activity illustrates the regions balance, and  it is unlikely many new spot purchases will be made to meet new spot demand. Looking farther down the calendar, the ongoing Ukrainian conflict has some participants concerned regarding supply shocks in the coming winter. Natural gas continues to trade at premiums to  LPG, incentivizing its utilization as an alternative fuel source when/ where logistically feasible- But for now, given that it is summer, exports from the US East Coast, coupled with sparce supply available from the North Sea are proving sufficient.    MED The region has been well supplied by US cargoes in the past month due to the open butane arb. Supply to the region has been satisfied through the end of the month, with the only bright spot for demand being Turkey due to the high LPG vs Gasoline spread for autogas.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Over the last few weeks, the LNG shipping market have seen consistent gains.  Firm sentiments and rate ideas were predominately driven by the West of Suez as more requirements were seen for delivery into Europe.  Lack of vessel availability for June to 1H July in the Atlantic have spurred spot rates to break the six-figure barrier for the larger vessel sizes, which are highly sought after.   The growing demand for modern tonnage is holding sturdy and anticipated to continue for the remaining of the year as US exports increases.   Charterers with limited flexibility on their requirement have seen fewer options and often with a significant premium attached.  Discussion on longer term charters are ever-present as offtake agreements especially from the US are being secured.  With the ongoing geopolitical issues and gas supply disruptions, FSRU/ FSU related LNG projects have also gain traction with more engagements than previous years as Utilities, National Oil companies and governments prioritize energy security.  There are no new orders reported this week, nevertheless, shipyard capacity continue to diminish as demand for Newbuilds from all other shipping sectors continue to push LNGC newbuild deliveries further into the backend of 2026.  One LNG vessel arrived for recycling this week, which is the first for the year 2022. In 2021, 7 units were recycled.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The spot market remains firm this week with a steady amount of fixtures concluded. Rates continue to hold at relatively ”healthy” levels for spot voyages, with a lack of prompt vessels both East and West of Suez. Availability further out in the Pacific remains high but the fixture window is extending closer to these vessels. This tonnage is unlikely to be open for long as the majority of sublets have a backstop and may be needed internally.  European LNG storage levels remain high and we may see more vessels head East if discharge slots can’t be secured in Europe. Along with an active spot market, the term shipping market also remains on the gas (excuse the pun) with plenty of interested parties still in or coming to seeking tonnage, and term rates are firming as a consequence. Tonnage from head owners for term requirements still remains elusive. Security of tonnage for the future, predominantly modern tonnage, remains at the forefront of term discussions. Newbuild activity remains high, 6 more orders placed this week and newbuild prices may continue to increase. The first larger LNG event since Covid restrictions were lifted is currently underway as the World Gas Conference in Korea kicked off this week, drawing in crowds from across the industry. For those attending the event in Daegu we hope it has been a great success.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS A week-over-week propane stock build of 1.8mmbbls was recorded by the EIA as of 20 May, which puts this year’s inventory levels at 105% of the same time last year – though they remain below 70% of May 2020.  The build was smaller than anticipated, but easily explained by the robust 1.6mmbbls/day export levels. Most are now anticipating that domestic US propane stock levels will reach “acceptable” levels by end Sep, and likely continue to build well into Oct.  The NOAA, however, just issued its 2022 Hurricane Season forecast and is calling for 21 named storms and up to six major hurricanes this season.  A typical year sees around 14 named storms and up to 3 major hurricanes.  Depending on how things ultimately develop, both domestic production levels and export volumes could potentially be impacted, which would then affect overall stock levels. Meanwhile, terminal fees now seem a bit more fragile than in 1H May when levels of up to the mid 6cpg range were achieved.  At present there have just emerged early signs of retreat, particularly from the buy-side, which was talking 5s for near-term business.  NWE As it stands, June CIF ARA propane sits at $722/t, marking a negligible uptick on the day on the back of upstream brent utilization for diesel. However, the region appears balanced, rather than tight, and it is unlikely many new spot purchases will be made to meet new demand. While natural gas' premium over LPG would suggest an incentive to source it as an alternative fuel , the unwinding of seasonal demand and adequate refinery runs, coupled with healthy liftings from Marcus Hook, make for an agnostic attitude for NWE LPG end users.   MED The region has been well supplied by US cargoes in the past month due to the open butane arb. Supply to the region has been satisfied through the end of the month, with the only bright spot for demand being Turkey due to the high LPG vs Gasoline spread for autogas.

n: LNG Market Report
x: This week has delivered on the premise that the shipping market is indeed strengthening, for which the signs were already starting to be visible a few weeks back. The latest levels for concluded spot fixtures have not only made us increase the headline rates across the board, but also required a notch-up on our Ballast Bonus sentiment, since charterers might now have to absorb more idle time to secure vessels unless one manages to find a perfect matching delivery/redelivery dates and location. Modern vessel availability also continues to slim down, although it is to be noted that many of the recent spot fixtures are for relatively short single voyages, meaning that the forward availability still have some length. Term markets have also been active, as new modern vessel positions are met with considerable interest, although term levels seem to be more stable, with slight upward pressure. Last but not least, the general newbuilding market remains red hot with ordering interest from several shipping segments. Newbuild prices remain firm and shipyards are receiving interest on their next available slots, even if it’s getting bit far out in time.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS A surprise EIA report this week showed an unexpected and very modest 300,000bbl build for the reporting period ending 13 May, dashing hopes that a larger build would compel the Mont Belvieu pricing structure to move lower and allow for a widening of the arb.  The market had been anticipating anywhere from a 1.0-3.0mmbbl improvement in stock levels (though most were clustered in the +1.9mmbbl range), but it would appear as though corrective data was utilized  this week as the accuracy of the previous week’s data was considered rather dubious. Ultimately crude oil softness did allow propane to weaken, closing the day at $1.20/gal, off by nearly 2cts/gal from the day prior.  At this point propane has fallen to 47% of WTI, having been sliding since Oct 2021. Terminal fees in the U.S. have been slowly rising, having been in the low 4cpg range only a couple of weeks ago and in the upper 4s/lower 5s range last week, only to eclipse the 6cpg level this week.  Asking levels are now at least 6.5cpg, with some priced even higher, still.  NWE The European prices lost ground after crude slid this week, this coupled with the less than inspiring US inventory build has narrowed the arb and hurt netbacks in this strong freight environment. That said in European summer the market tends to be driven by petchem demand. We continue to see crackers return from spring maintenance and fill demand from the US both FOB and CFR. With Pro/Nap at $149pmt petchem demand will continue to be at maximum. On the butane side not many tons have been openly traded which has left estimated values at 97% May Naphtha. This is seen by many as above true market value, and shows a wide open arb from the US which has many traders who would normally head East with 2+2 cargoes offering CFR in Europe. So far none of these trades have been heard done and without window deals the levels have not seen a correction. For the time being Europe is seeing good demand and though much of the prompt looks to be accounted for, we expect to see European petchems looking to buy CFR cargoes for June arrival.    MED There is a distinctly summer market feel in the region. With no new demand being shown the market is subdued although the arb is open. Much of the spot demand has been filled by US cargoes. LPG – Gasoline arb is making Autogas favorable in the East Med.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The market was taken aback by the large inventory build reported by the EIA on Wednesday, which showed a build of 3.4mmbbls on a week-over-week basis and which now stand at 44.2mmbbls, or just over 100% of last year.  Notably, however, current propane inventories are just 66% of two years ago. The market had been anticipating a build of between 1.25-2.25mmbbls, with most centered around the +1.75mmbbl level.  To then realize a build of nearly double was surprising, but that soon gave way to a sense of skepticism, mostly related to the PADD III build of 3.8mmbbls, which suggests that either production levels have grown dramatically, or waterborne exports have declined – or both.  But neither seems plausible and hence the doubt.  As such, observers and participants alike are now expecting a set of corrected numbers in the forthcoming data. Terminal fees remain under pressure, though very little has been accomplished this week.  The last known June transactions were fixed on either side of 5cpg, with 2H 2022 strip interest generally talked on either side of around the 6cpg level by both buyers and re-sellers.  NWE The end-May TOT buying interest in the window from BASF was hit by Vitol at 84.75% May Naphtha. Total, the other sellers disappeared. That deal was the last expected to be done for May. The European market is now focused on June and with crackers expected to come out of spring maintenance mid-May through mid-June and the market is showing strength in anticipation of this rise in demand. This weeks rise in Brent coupled with a large build in US inventories has propane at a slightly better than $160pmt discount to Naphtha and netback values form the US above 5cpg. Workable once again! Freight has continued to rise, taking a large chunk of the wider arb particularly to Europe as owners set a premium for US to Europe voyages in the hope of fixing longer voyages East at today’s high rates. Spot butane deals have not been seen in the market for some time and any new deal would set market levels.  CIF ARA Butane values have come off as US supply heads to the region. Charterers who were originally targeting cold 2-strokes are now more willing to accommodate older and warmer tonnage, as the list of available vessels to meet a growing number of laycans diminishes. This will be welcome news to “owners” of older tonnage who should be increasingly popular in this age of energy and shipping security. x: AMERICAS The EIA reported a 1.6mmbbl week-over-week increase in domestic US propane stocks for the reporting period ending 29 April.  This brings the overall total stock level to 40.8mmbbls, or 98% of last year’s total and 66% of the total achieved in 2020. In order for inventories to reach the desired 80mmbbl level by end Oct 2022, and with 26 weeks remaining in the traditional ‘build’ period, an average weekly improvement of 1.51mmbbls will be required.  For the past five years, and for the period from May through Oct, the weekly build rate has averaged 2.064mmbbls.  Therefore, the desired level of approximately 80mmbbls should be achieved with relative ease.  This is in spite of generally robust export volumes but because of the rising production levels. Meanwhile, current terminal fee market levels for June range from around 5cpg to 6cpg, depending on timing, grade(s) and level of desire (from both sides).  A number of offers – particularly 50/50 parcels - have recently populated the market, but buyers note the ongoing backwardation and remain cautious.  NWE The spot market in the region has been active, and is trading end May. The bid/offer level in the TOT window has been wide, with many bidders today seeing an inflated market value in the window. Today the bottom line is that the arb from the US is closed and that production in Europe remains 30-40% below usual. Some spring maintenance is being carried out by petchems reducing demand at the same time as mild weather in the region further reducing demand. Cargoes remain well bid and offered, and physical value we assess at a small premium to May CIF ARA. That said cargoes continue to flow to the region from the US and find homes at premiums to CIF ARA outside of the window. So it looks like netback values are not painting the whole picture. x: AMERICAS  Pricing volatility is the key factor in the domestic U.S. propane market, as Mont Belvieu values have declined over the course of April but seen vast pricing swings in the meanwhile.  The combination of reactive crude and natural gas prices - which are tightly linked to both the lingering Covid-related issues in the East and the war in Ukraine – has allowed April MB propane to conclude in the high $1.20’s/gal. According to the EIA, US propane inventory levels as of 22 April increased by 2.2mmbbls from the previous week, though some observers cast doubt on the accuracy of the data and are already anticipating a set of corrective data in the weeks to come.  The build was larger than expected but the market nonetheless gained a penny on the day, confounding many. Domestic production levels reached their highest levels ever, but robust exports in April (and going forward) have left the impression that a series of pushes and pulls – a ‘tug of war’, in essence - will be seen through the summer in a battle pitting production levels versus export volumes.  NWE May CIF ARA propane was last marked at $752/t (up by $4/t) as the European market looked to buy May propane and butane due to multi-dimensional supply constraints in the North Sea. The first due to lagging output in Norway due to maintenance at gas processing centers, in addition to notable decrease in exports availability pertaining to disruption in Russian product. OPIS reported a decrease nearing 35% in April exports compared to the same period last year. That said,  propane has continued its weakness in relation to naphtha- The spread has averaged -$136/t in April, compared to -$78/t same time last year, and presently sits at  -$138/t. For this reason, LPG cargos loading from US East Coast, continue to garner heavy interest as European buyers look to maintain equilibrium due to the aforementioned supply disruptions in the North Sea.  MED The Med continues to be tight, butane which has been hard to find in the region allowing the arb from the US to the Med to widen- acting as a valve to mitigate supply pressure -as vessels STS into coasters in the region. Continued maintenance on a pair of West-Med crackers has been extended slightly, however the news did little to exacerbate current tightness.

WTI as of this writing is up 2.5% at $104.63/bbl but largely dependent upon both the events related to the Russia/Ukraine war, but also Covid-related shutdowns, particularly in China. From the domestic US perspective, the EIA data released yesterday showed a build of 1.6mmbbls – just a bit more than anticipated – to an overall total of 37mmbbls, which is 91% of last year but 62% of two years ago.  Stocks built on the Gulf Coast (PADD III) but showed a decline in both the East Coast and Midwest regions (PADDs I and II). Due to the lack of cancellations and ‘buyback’ cargoes, ongoing and robust export volumes in April were expected to have limited the build in Gulf Coast stocks, but instead the decline in domestic demand is being cited as the explanation.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, range rather widely as buy-side ideas remain in the 4cpg area but sellers seem to content in the 6 cpg range.  Reduced arbs and higher freight rates are contributing factors, as well.  NWE The arb to the region has narrowed bringing trans-Atlantic netbacks into the high 3cpgs or low 4cpgs. The build in US inventories did not have an immediate bearish effect on MT Belvieu values and any moves were negated by strong freight. Houston-Flushing is now heard to be nearing $70pmts with no sign of coming off for May loadings. Propane vs Naphtha in the region continues to heavily favour propane with April, May and June Pro/Nap in the $140pmts. Though this figure has to be taken in context, with Natural Gas at $25mmBTU, making power expensive, and reduced demand for manufacturing due to supply chain issues clouding the picture. The spring weather in Europe has been very pleasant this year, so any additional inland demand has been due to larger geopolitical issues and crude oil price moves. Demand in the region remains and though urgent buying has not been seen since returning from Easter holidays.  MED The Med continues to be tight, butane in particular hard to find in the region. The arb from the US to the Med is open which will release some supply pressure as vessels STS into coasters in the region.
