x: AMERICAS  Since the end of March the Mont Belvieu propane market has seen intermittent declines which have been interrupted by small spurts of buoyancy, though all told the market has seen more softness than not.  This is owing to the combination of declines in winter-related demand and that crude oil has been coming off in recent days. Inventory levels in the U.S. have for two consecutive weeks risen, though rather modestly. Current stocks are posted by the EIA at 34.4mmbbls, or about 86% of last year and 57% of two years ago.  The market is beginning to think about how robust exports over the summer will match against slowly rising production levels, and calculating a required average build of 2mmbbls over the coming 5 or 6 months in order to reach ~80mmbbls by end-Sep / early Oct.  Convention wisdom is calling for a traditional tug of war between the two factors, and through the duration of the coming summer. Terminal fees on the Gulf Coast, meanwhile, are presently seen on offer at 6.00-6.50cpg, though a more enthusiastic seller was seen in the upper 5cpg range.  Buyers, however, have generally retreated to sub-5cpg levels unless a cargo is in need of being fixed immediately.    A spate of fixtures was reportedly accomplished over the past few days, and market intel indicates those parcels were concluded with a 6-handle.  NWE US crude oil inventories, rather than LPG publishing a big build caused a rapid drop in global crude oil values. This kept traders out of the TOT window and pushed outright CIF ARA values down over $30pmt. The transatlantic netbacks have been squeezed all week. Weakness in the European market has been partly attributed to the shift to the summer market and partly due to industrial demand expected to be reduced by planned maintenances. Production in the region has not increased as LPG continues to be spiked into the natural gas stream where possible. The continued question over whether European countries will put sanctions on Russian Energy, which would turn the market on it’s head. For the time being the crude moves and warmer temperatures coming in are keeping the market fairly quiet.  MED The Med remains tight, particularly propane, as strong winds hamper Algerian loadings. The commencement of Ramadan will keep the market quiet in the near future.

x: AMERICAS Having risen with crude, which was following the unfolding news of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the MB propane market reached a peak of $1.63/gal on 8th March, only to then sink to the low $1.20’s/gal by mid-month.  At that point the market turned again to the upside and was trading on an upwards trajectory towards $1.48/gal, only to reverse course today to current levels of $1.45/gal. In the background the EIA report for the week ending 18 March showed a modest build of 300,000bbls for an overall total of 33.6mmbbls (thus signaling the conclusion of winter), and which is 81% of the total achieved last year, and 56% of the total recorded two years ago.  The small rise in stock levels is attributed to three factors:  The decline of weather-related demand in North America, cargo buy-backs in March, and cargo cancellations in March (which when combined are reckoned at around a dozen or more cargoes). Domestic U.S. production, though healthy at 2.36mmbbls/day, is effectively flat on a week-over-week basis, but as well on a year-over-year basis. As to the trade, the steep backwardation continues well in to Q2.  While March is effectively concluded, April European netbacks are more than $20/mt below March, and May is at least $10/mt below that.  Thereon, the summertime netbacks flatten out, but as with all things LPG, crude is the ultimate driver and at this moment the headlines are the primary influence. Buy/sell terminal fee ideas, meanwhile, had at one point widened from the low/mid 5cpg range to as much as 12cpg during the height of the recent volatility, but have for now settled in a more modest range of 6-8cpg, generally speaking.  NWE April CIF ARA is showing strength as the March/April backwardation comes out of the market slightly. A bid in the TOT window also increased the physical premium assessed at April CIF ARA +$33pmt. Though this is for very early April arrival rather than whole month. The arb from the US remains open and if you take into account the physical premium Northwest Europe should be drawing tons from the US. A sever with the European market the worry is that multiple cargoes will head to the region and very quickly shift the tight market into an oversupplied one. The issue has been finding US cargoes in the second half of March for arrival in early April. These cargoes were worked well ahead of time and to draw them to the region now would need them to be redirected from heading East, not impossible with the East not showing much strength. April butane also remains valued at a high level at 92% April Naphtha, though this is approached with caution due to lack of April butane activity so far.   MED The expected ramp up of buying pre-Ramadan has not materialised. VLGCs have been stuck in Moroccan ports causing delays since early March. The Chinook is now discharging C4 having arrived at Mohammedia on February 27th. This is now starting to affect coaster discharges into Morocco and is keeping the butane market in the region subdued.

In all term charter markets, the story is more or less unchanged, as more modern (and lower boil-off rate) vessels command a hefty premium, due to a predicted strong LNG price environment for the foreseeable future, although on a week-to-week basis, the prices for LNG and oil have come down from their recent highs, mainly due to the increased concern of extended lockdowns in China caused by the reappearance of COVID-19, and potential return of Iranian oil to markets. However, the narrative is a bit more complicated in the spot market, as the wide array of spot requirements have shown that despite the fact that the current LNG prices – at least in theory - create a massive disparity between the various vessel types, in reality not all requirements are equal, and many of them have factors and/or limitations that could, for example, favor smaller vessels in this type of commodity price environment. This has in turn created quite a mixed bag of fixture levels seen in the spot market and thus finding a fitting rate for each vessel type really depends on the requirement itself. However, generally speaking, the spot market has stayed relatively flat, since added availability has been matched with new emerging spot requirements. With regards terminal fees, there remains but one large unsold cargo in March, which at one point commanded double-digits.  Because of the backwardation, though, April avails are priced more moderately at between 6 and 7cpg, depending on the timing and grade(s).  Talk for May is slow just yet, but initial asking levels start with a 7. The volatility seen earlier in the month has subsided and the netback levels have come in a bit but remain positive for the time being.  Crude values – $102.50 for WTI and $106..00 for Brent  – will have a deciding hand.  NWE The physical TOT window premiums stand at April CIF ARA +$25pmt. Showing the tightness of the April market. The arb from the US is open and although Mt Belvieu has again strengthened the European market is expected to draw imports. The problem for Europe is that US East Coast exports have been reduced by the hefty draws and cold weather seen this winter, so traders have to look for cargoes from the Gulf Coast and compete with the East market, a higher netbacks by $10pmt. Petrochemical buying should still be at maximum with high Crude oil and propane vs naphtha in April above $140pmt. A full propane VLGC offered in the window pm a naphtha related price is not drawing any interest, due to the naphtha price swings. These swings continue to keep the NWE butane market quiet, and butane remains valued at 92% March naphtha.                                           MED With Ramadan less than 3 weeks away buying activity was expected to pick up. So far this has not yet materialized and the market remains subdued. Vessels discharging in Western Morocco have been stranded in port due to bad weather, the VLGC Chinook in Mohammedia since the beginning of them month.

Energy supply concerns, along with uncertainty and a genuine lack of tonnage available for term, sent that particular part of the market into overdrive. Term rates increased across the market with a scramble to secure modern tonnage at the back end of last week and continuing through this one. With TTF pricing where they are and more cargoes headed into Europe, tonne miles will be reduced, but tonne time may increase. However, tonnage availability may increase around the Atlantic basin. This could soften the Atlantic regions spot market in the near future despite the upward trend we are currently seeing on term rates. That being said, ships that are being taken in for term have reduced availability for the remaining enquiries now being discussed. The newbuild market remains active with another 3 new vessels ordered for delivery in 2025 from Hyundai. These vessels will be fitted with the ME-GA engine with a cargo capacity of 200,00cbm. We may also welcome another yard to the list of LNG shipbuilders as it looks like Jiangnan in China are working towards their first large LNG vessel orders.

x: AMERICAS  Volatility has been the primary characteristic of the domestic energy markets this week, having been spurred on by events in eastern Europe, rising crude values, softening freight and widening arbs to both the East and the West.  The result is that propane prices at Mont Belvieu rose by more than 12cts/gal over just this week to $1.53/gal.  There remains, however, quite steep backwardation which extends well in to 2H 2022 and then in to the upper $1.20’s/gal. Meanwhile, terminal fees this week spiked hard and the few remaining March cargoes are known to have been fixed in the double-digits.  Motivated buyers, sensing stronger demand in Europe because of the Russian advancements into Ukraine, emerged for March and 1H Apr volumes.  It is anticipated that around 175,000mt per month of LPG formerly supplied by Russia requires replacement, and hence the enthusiasm. With regards the inventory levels of propane in the U.S., the EIA revealed an 800,000bbl overall weekly reduction which brought stock levels to 37.2mmbbls.  The market took that in stride and essentially shrugged off the large decline in PADD 2 but pointed to the week-over-week increase in PADD III, the Gulf Coast, which saw a build of 900,000bbls.  Cynics were prepared to wait for next week’s release for a ‘truer’ stock picture, as many believe there have been data errors in recent reports.  NWE As the European LPG market tries to come to grips with the effects of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, supply concerns have come to the fore in an already tight market. This led to a scramble from European traders to find US FOBs as transatlantic March imports were expected to be around 120,000MT far below the 460,000MT imported in February. With FOB US bids rising on European trader interest March cargoes surfaced and most believe these additional exports were only made possible by the lower than expected draw in US inventories. At least 3 additional VLGCs were purchased for the European market which will calm some traders for end March and 1H April. The prompt market is short with the TOT window premium valued at March CIF ARA +$18pmt. The butane market is valued at 97% March Naphtha which is a strong value in this market and only for March tons, as the end of the month ends the gasoline blending season. This week mixed ratio VLGC left the USGC bound for Turkey. Imports or high prices keeping bidders quiet.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Last week we noted considerable uncertainty and no reason to have a different view this week, geopolitical news needs to be under constant watch, not that this is particularly profound but now is a particularly sensitive time. On top of this backdrop, spot cargoes prices rose due to weather driven eastern demand amid colder weather in China and intensified competition with Europe for cargoes, something that could very easily continue unabated. This view could explain the rise in share prices of Asian shipbuilders and shipping firms which rallied, likely on the expectations that European countries may seek more seaborne energy sources on news that Russia’s Nord Stream 2 pipeline’s approval process has been halted.   On the prompt, tonnage remains abundant as a high percentage of vessels remain contained in their respective basin leading to persistent lower than average voyage distance and thus additional capacity remains plentiful. Multi-month activity remains active with several live tenders being worked and bidding interest in vessels remains. This week we increase the multi-year levels supported by a few fixtures yet despite this rise, the bid/ask spread oscillates depending on vessel type and delivery timings, plenty of nuances that need to be understood yet clarity should start to reduce these as we get closer to Q3 and charterer preferred delivery timings near.   In the new build market, one reported transaction this week with Hyundai Glovis booking a 2H2024 slot that is rumoured to be on the back of a charter. 2024 is all but sold out whilst 2025 follows suit with all slots reserved and as such the newbuilding price continues its ascent.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The market was taken aback by the surprisingly large inventory draw posted by the EIA, which reflected a 5.9mmbbl decline in weekly stock levels to 41.9mmbbls.  This compares to the overall total of 48.6mmbbls and 68.7mmbbls recorded over the last two years.  In other words, 1H Feb propane inventories in North America are 86% and 70% of the previous two years, respectively.  The market had generally anticipated an approximate 3mmbbl decline from the 4th to the 11th of February 2022. February price levels almost immediately spiked by over 5cts/gal, but March values were slower to respond, perhaps because the market is aware of around a half-dozen ‘buyback’ cargoes in March as well as the half-dozen (or so) cancellations which have been reported.  Furthermore, recently rising crude values are believed to have likely improved field production, all of which appear to have conspired to limit the immediate upside – at least for the moment. To that, the North American weather patterns will continue to play a role, as there remain a couple of forecasted storms over the next 10-14 days which are meant to allow temperatures (and snow) to drop once again.  That should likely, then, translate to additional demand pulls.   The general sentiment, however, is that this week’s EIA data likely included corrective data (from previous reports) but that this week’s report overreached, in which case next week’s data could quite likely also contain additional corrective figures.  NWE CIF ARA reacted strongly to the big draws in US inventories. The March price rose $27pmt on the day, most of that from when the draw was announced to close of European trading. Two bids were seen in the window with the high bid assessed a CIF ARA March +$10pmt. The European market is tight prompt all the way through 1H March, the February March backwardation widening to +$15pmt. The March East West spread has come in to +$54.5pmt and Eastern traders continue to look for homes for their cargoes in Europe. February Propane Naphtha spread is at $130pmt and continues to incentivise maximum petchem demand. Butane at 100% February naphtha with naphtha at 7-year highs. European traders are primarily interested 1H month US FOB cargoes, which can arrive in Europe in the same month as that of loading. For these they are the best FOB bidders in the market today.  MED Tight freight on larger pressurized vessels is hampering North South butane trade in the region. March trade discussions are yet to get going.

n: LNG Market Report
x: There is considerable uncertainty in the days and weeks ahead, but while the global LNG market and associated forward curves remain at historically high levels the freight market continues to bump along the seabed. Strong LNG prices particularly into Europe are providing profitable trading opportunities for those with flexible cargoes, but these routes are limiting the rates achievable by owners and subletters as the lower average voyage distance is dragging down tonne-mile demand and freeing up additional capacity. There are few signs of this dynamic changing in the near-future, although a flutter of life in the west-to-east arbitrage may be encouraging and the combination of political and economic stresses coupled with the balance of available vessels being under the control of portfolios and traders should be a warning against complacency. The multimonth market is a little more active, with several charterers interested in summer coverage, and beyond in some cases. Overall though, it does still appear to be a little bit “wait and see” from several market participants. On the newbuilding front, there were ten orders in the past week including four slots firmed up by Qatar Energies, four orders by H Line and two orders by Bono Energy.

x: AMERICAS  Mont Belvieu propane prices softened earlier this week and interest levels were renewed as both buyers and sellers emerged for Feb and Mar when netbacks improved significantly.  Prior to that the market seemed to have begun to resign itself to waiting for the conclusion of the Olympics, the Chinese New Year, and, perhaps, some encouraging news on the Covid front. With the renewed interest levels terminal fees were buoyed from the lows seen at the front of Feb to a current bid/ask range of around 6.00-6.50cpg, depending on timing and location, etc.  Meanwhile, the EIA report for the week ending 04 Feb shows the U.S. to have consumed a ‘net’ 2mmbbls from the previous week and putting the overall U.S. propane stock total at 47.8mmbbls, or about 93% of last year.  The market, however, based its expectations off of cold weather and heavy exports, and was predicting a draw of around 3.8-4.0mmbbls.   The difference has now given cause for speculation as to whether next week’s number will include corrective data.  NWE Crude rises again! With CIF ARA lagging leaving the propane naphtha spread at $117pmt in Feb and widening, heavily favouring propane as a petchem feedstock.  A physical propane deal was done for end Feb at February CIF ARA -$7pmt, seen as low by the market. The regions production continues to be reduced due to LPG spiking into the natural gas stream. Which has lead to a large, 430,000MT being imported to the region in February, and these large monthly import volumes are expected to continue. The strength of the European demand has been keeping the arb form the US open. Drawing US volume form the Gulf Coast. The reduced US East Coast supply due to the cold weather in the region, and the reduced February export volume from the USGC forced European traders to pay-up and buy FOB cargoes from US terminals direct this week. As the market flipped from heading for cancellation to 6-7cpg FOB, for cargoes which will be 1H March arrivals in NWE. Butane is at 99% naphtha and with naphtha strengthening in line with crude this has opened the butane arb from the US.   MED There has been some action in the Med this week with Cepsa offer 4KT butane FOB Huelva $931pmt. The market weakened in reaction to this offer, the North Sea Mediterranean butane arb lost $19pmt on the day. Morocco’s butane demand looks well supplied through February.

n: LNG Market Report
x: With the Lunar New Year upon us, activity across basins has remained limited this week, maintaining high levels of global vessel availability amongst Subletters and applying sustained downward pressure on spot rates. JKM & TTF LNG prices continue to be in flux however spreads between indexes have been diminishing towards parity in recent days. This has partly been a result of Lunar New Year but also due to milder European winter weather and increased gas flows from Russia, levelling off European gas prices to almost match those of Asia. That said, with geopolitical tensions remaining elevated in the region and Asia coming back online later this week, the window to opportunity remains ajar for now. Term shipping activity has similarly slowed however rates continue to be in markedly healthy condition and relatively unchanged in anticipation of business-as-usual later this week.   On the newbuilding front, TotalEnergies’ announcement to restart Mozambique LNG within 2022 has more or less mopped up any remaining LNG berth availability at shipyards through to 2027, further tightening an already tight LNG newbuilding market. Requests for earlier slots have been heard quoted at considerable premiums while anything thereafter, from 2027 onwards, have been marked up accordingly. No new orders have been reported this week.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS With the strength in the Mont Belvieu market the arbs to both the East and to Europe having declined so sharply in recent times that buybacks and cancellations are at the forefront of conversation.  As many as a half-dozen March cargoes are believed to have been ‘bought back’ by Enterprise, and a host of cancellations are known to have occurred, as well. The strength of the MB propane market, meanwhile, is based on generally robust crude values, but more so on the cold weather that has gripped the US over the past couple of weeks.  And though the immediate 10-day weather forecast is showing signs of a warming trend there are also signals emerging which indicate that another important winter storm might form towards the end of Feb or beginning of March. Meanwhile, the EIA revealed a rather expected set of propane inventory data for the week ending 28 Jan, culminating in an overall total propane stock level of 49.8mmbbls, a decline of 4.3mmbbls from the week prior.  This puts current inventories at 88-89% of the totals recorded last year, and 69-70% of two years ago. Terminal fees in the U.S. have weakened all the while, and an effective buy-side ‘floor’ has most recently been established by Enterprise (as well as an active trader) in the range of 4.50-4.75cpg.  There remain more sellers than buyers in the March timeframe, as again, the arbs remain poor.  NWE CIF ARA propane strengthened $3pmt as crude oil saw a downward correction Wednesday. Demand for propane in the region remains driven by the petchems, and will grow as Dow’s Terneuzen system gets back to full operating capacity. The February propane naphtha spread at -$83pmt continues to drive the petchem demand. European netbacks for US cargoes are looking good, although it is hard for traders who do not have assets in the region to find shorts into Europe. The region’s traders are waiting until the last minute to pick up the best values cargoes, as they see more offers on the horizon due to the reduced demand in the East. The TOT window saw the first offer of the week which equated to CIF ARA Feb +$4pmt, and with no window counter seen the market was assessed at around CIF ARA +$2pmt to CIF ARA flat. Marcus Hook export volumes have decreased due to the cold weather, leading to a larger volume of NWE imports being sourced from the USGC.  MED The weather in the region has been on the mild side, keeping residential demand low. Term deliveries are covering most of the Moroccan butane demand. 4KT butane was offered FOB Huelva, but the offer was well above the market and attracted no interest.

x: Muted chartering activity continued across both basins this week. The ever fluctuating LNG price seems to be doing little to bolster freight but levels being discussed remain firm rather than continuing to drop. Current vessel availability remains high globally, and this will probably keep rates under pressure short term as more subletters look to push out tonnage. With Lunar New Year approaching in Asia, activity within the Pacific is likely to continue waning - any short positions that needed covering are likely already concluded, and offices will start to empty for the holiday period. However, more activity was seen in the Atlantic. Both geopolitical tensions and gas prices competing with Asia are causing some unsettlement and could drum up activity for shipping. The term market remains strong with a steady stream of enquiries entering the market. Rates however soften slightly as some subletters willing to consider such periods are putting downward pressure on levels, albeit still healthy. The recent order boom on newbuilds takes a breather this week with no new orders being placed at yards, however newbuild prices remain robust.

The wind went out of the sails, on the theory of there not being enough product to support large exports and weather demand, due to increased production forecasts for 2022, but it will be interesting to see if this changes if the cold weather lasts into the second half of Feb. This week propane inventories registered a seasonal and expected draw of 4.6 million barrels and we are expecting a similar number next week. Europe remains well supplied for the balance of the January and into Feb as mild weather has done little to further demand. Chemical demand is moderate and propane's widening weakness in relation to naphtha could further insight the demand to the region for cracking. Further still, Dow plans to restart their ethylene cracker in Terneuzen by the end of the week. Struggles at the terminal began at the beginning of December, due to an issue with steam supply, but it is likely facility capable of absorbing 1.8 million tons / year should be back on line shortly. That said, weak ethylene margins could potentially act as a point of friction in the equation. As it stands, the propane naphtha spread sits at $100 pmt in the front month furthering the delta in favor of propane. Natural gas prices have softened, it has not been to a degree to absolve LPG from internal refineries where its being used as a cheaper alternative.    MED On paper, the appetite for LPG appears to be on the rise in the Med again, butane prices into Lavera saw double digit gains, along with an uptick in Moroccan demand, however no public cargos have changed hands yet.

x: AMERICAS US propane stocks are in generally better condition owing to robust domestic production and fewer ‘buybacks’, and despite healthy exports.  Expectations as to this week’s EIA report again ranged rather widely, this time from a draw of 1.5mmbbls to as much as 3.5mmbbls.  Ultimately a draw of 3.7mmbbls was recorded, but the larger-than-expected draw was met with a rather lackluster response and the numbers were rationalized and explained as having been generally in line with sentimental expectations.  Nonetheless, market values did begin to climb after the release of the EIA figures and were marked at $1.1875 before the lunch hour on Thursday.  Domestic US propane stocks have risen to within 2% of the level achieved last year and as of mid-Jan 2022 stand at 58.70mmbbls. Terminal fees have seen a bit of weakness, having started the year at / around 6cts but coming off of those levels to the 5.75cpg level more recently.  Traders were keen on 5.00 cpg for March ideas, but sellers thus far have resisted.  The terminals are priced well above.  NWE Demand in the region remains decent though slightly more bearish as 2 offers and a discounted bid emerged in the window. That said, the region seems equipped to absorb 400,000 MT that has or will be delivered into the region this month. Winter weather has been tepid, however forecasts are now predicting a dip back below seasonal average which could possibly stoke demand.  Chemical demand is moderate and propane's widening weakness in relation to naphtha could further insight the demand to the region for cracking. That said, weak Ethylene margins could potentially act as a point of friction in the equation . As it stands, the propane naphtha spread sits at -$94.25 pmt in the front month- or the widest its been since May. Natural gas prices have softened, it has not been to a degree to absolve LPG from internal refineries where its being used as a cheaper alternative.    MED The Med remains balanced, with muted activity. While the arbitrage for butane has widened on paper (US Butane has come off a bit following the drive-heavy holidays, along with some crude related CIF ARA gains) logistical constraints have hampered any opportunistic trade in the region.

n: LNG Market Report
x: Rather surprisingly, the second week of the year hasn't delivered much new activity to the market. The LNG spot shipping market has remained very quiet, with only a handful of ongoing requirements being worked, most of which are cargo tender related. Furthermore, availability for prompt tonnage is increasing in both basins, mainly due to lack of arbitrage opportunities that have led to many charterers being long on freight. We don’t see this situation changing anytime soon either, since it seems that especially Korea and Japan have sustained enough LNG inventories to cope through the remainder of the winter and thus the main Far East buying activity depends on China’s demand. This has led to a real hammering on the spot rates, as those looking for tonnage have seen a large number of vessels offered – mainly from subletters. The clear bright side for Owners is the healthy activity and gradually reducing availability in the term market, which has kept term rates steady especially for the more modern and larger LNGCs.  The newbuilding market also remains active as amongst others, Maran Gas Maritime added to the fresh tally for 2022 with a pair of LNGC newbuilds from DSME. Yard capacity is now quite limited for any new orders with delivery in 2025. In addition, market participants are eagerly waiting for the final decision from the European Union antitrust regulator with regards the DSME and HHI merger, which might get vetoed by the EU according to the latest rumours.

x: AMERICAS  The combination of colder temperatures across North America and healthy export volumes over the holiday period have given cause for a robust draw in propane inventories, which recorded a 3.3mmbbl decline for the week ending 7 Jan.  This weighs against the 66.00mmbbl level recorded one year ago, and puts current stocks at just under 95% of last year at the same time. Additional winter weather is on the near-term horizon, as well, and forecasters are calling for below-average temps and significant snowfall over the balance of January.  The EIA’s Days of Supply calculation as of 7 Jan stands at 39.9, versus 38.6 days one year ago.  The current supply rate compares to the 5 year average of 47.92 days for the first week of January. Meanwhile, recent terminal fee levels have been noted as trading within a very thin range, with full-propane deals recorded at 6cts and mixed-ratio parcels being fixed at around 5.75 within the last trading week.  More recently, though, offers to sell mixed-ratio cargoes are seen at 5cts/gal, and full-propane lots in mid/2H Feb are presently being marketed at the “high 5s”. Mont Belvieu prices have all the while been slowly climbing, and started Dec at $1.03/gal but as of this writing have reached over $1.18/gal, supported – in part – by both the weather, the healthy export volumes and the nearly endless gains in the crude sector.  WTI is off at present, but remains well above $82/bbl.  NWE Demand in the region remains strong and is sufficient enough to absorb the over 400,000 MT of LPG set to be imported to the region in January. Winter weather is not severe but still generating good demand. Whereas chemical demand is getting back to maximum as Terneuzen is now back online. The propane naphtha spread at -$36pmt in January favouring propane, as Naphtha strengthened with recent rise in crude oil. The large import volume in January has calmed the market which looks relatively balanced. That said a persistent bid in the TOT window for January 22-26 delivery window has yet to be taken out after being shown all week and improving values, now valued at Jan CIF ARA +$2.5pmt. The window will need to improve to tempt further US volume as the arb narrowed significantly since the large draw seen in US inventories. Traders are holding fire on February buying for the time being as they wait to see how much demand remains once the January import volume has been absorbed.   MED The West Med has yet to see increased winter demand, and remains well supplied by term volume. In the East Med, LPG is currently better priced than Gasoline in Turkey, leaving importers searching for tons for Autogas.

x: It is the first week of 2022 and the LNG market is slowly finding its pace after the Christmas break. Small developments so far, as market participants enjoy their last days of Holidays. For now, the West-to-East arbitrage is closed but should the volatility persist, we may see some more requirements emerging in the coming weeks. The term market, on the other hand, has continued to be active throughout the end of the year and we anticipate 2022 to be another year with focus on securing term coverage from the various portfolios. n: LNG Market Report
x: As we prepare to raise our glasses to the start of a New Year in LNG, it is only prudent to reflect on the year past. From baffling bouts of volatility giving way to landmark records across freight and LNG indices alike, to recent reversals in longstanding trade flows unexpectedly drawing us into uncharted territory, 2021 has been one heck of a year for our segment. Now, as we build off the momentum of this rollercoaster we can only look forward to another exciting 12 months.    What we can say in the leadup to this New Year is that the market finally seems to be catching a breather after an exhilaratingly tight and action-packed few months. With a number of portfolios and end-users closing out positions pre-holidays and limited activity across shipping and cargo markets since, we see a general softening of rates across the board. European gas remains at a premium to its Asian counterpart resulting in more and more ships diverting to Europe mid-voyage, setting the scene for an increase in tonnage in the West along with a decrease in tonne-miles for the LNG fleet given the pull from Europe persists into the New Year. However, even with this at the forefront our minds as we sink back into our sofas for Harry Potter marathons in reticent fashion, there is a general unspoken understanding among us LNG folk that nothing is for certain these days in LNG, one can only wait and see. Bring on 2022.   On the newbuilding front this week, prices remain firm while one order has been recorded at SHI.   Wishing all of our readers a very healthy, happy and prosperous New Year!

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Global LNG cargo prices continue to rise yet again, with energy hungry Europe leading the charge. Stockpiling in North Asia has currently left the region well supplied whilst European gas storage runs at around 60% capacity compared with a 5 year average of 76% for this time of year. In response, traders are re-directing cargoes West and with colder weather predicted in Europe ton-mile is likely to remain weak. Freight levels have taken a steep dive as multiple portfolio players foresee increased idle time and envisage strong competition in a market that is low on firm requirement. The problem could be exacerbated by the potentially very costly daily boil off when needing to keep vessels cold. Looking East, supply demand looks more balanced today but with the West-to-East conveyor belt drying up as vessels remain in the Atlantic or reposition West, freight levels may be forced higher especially if Asian demand starts to pick up again, as usual at this time of year.    This week saw an LOI signed between China Merchant Energy Shipping Co. and Dalian Shipyard for two vessels which would be the first LNGC built in Dalian. In other news, we eagerly awaiting the annual sighting of a very rare vessel (sleigh) built by K. Kringle & Elves, inc in the North Pole yard which probably performed its first voyage circa 24th December 343 A.D. It has interesting dimensions: length 75 cc (candy canes) / 150 lp (lollipops), Width 40 cc / 80 lp and height 55 cc / 110 lp (note: length, width and height are without reindeer). It’s ability to remain in service with emissions targets looming is difficult to assess as emissions remain classified, yet I’m sure all Children around the globe hope its top speed isn’t limited (currently faster than starlight).     We wish all our readers a very merry festive break!

At the time of writing, JKM pricing hadn’t responded to the same degree so the arbitrage is very firmly slammed shut. On a year-over-year basis this equates to approximately 3.63mmbbls of additional monthly production.   Weather-related demand in the U.S. has been negligible as yet, though a strong Arctic front is now being forecast for the Christmas/New Year’s timeframe.   Terminals fees are seen on the buy side in the upper 5cpg range, with sellers offering in the mid/upper 6cpg levels.

x: AMERICAS Contrary to expectations, the EIA propane inventory for the week ending 3 Dec revealed a 600,000bbl increase to an overall total of 73.3mmbbls, or nearly 84% of last year at the same time.  As such, it remains to be seen as to whether a corrected set of data might be released in the coming weeks. The market this week had been predicting a draw of ~1.25mmbbls, the difference thus leading to even closer scrutiny of the data.  Overall export volumes are off the high’s seen earlier in the summer, and the buyback scheme at Enterprise remains underway so the 900,000bbl build in PADD III (the Gulf Coast) can generally be rationalized once higher production levels are additionally considered. Meanwhile, the pricing structure appears – for the moment at least – to have settled at around the $1.00/gal level, having fallen rather steadily from the $1.52/gal seen during the first week of Oct.  Terminal fees have softened, as well, and now range from a low just under 5cts/gal to a high of just over 7cts/gal for spot business. As it remains generally warm across North America, the market seems increasingly dependent upon two factors:  Weather (or the lack thereof) and petrochemical consumption rates – both in the US and abroad.  NWE The TOT window continues to be assessed at a small discount to December, with late December and early January looking well supplied. Through the recent global price swings the arb to Europe has remained robust. The only weakness in the market was caused by disrupted operations at Terneuzen, which continues to undergo maintenance to try to fix the issue. With December pro/nap now -$63pmt petchem demand will remain high and we expect the Terneuzen cracker to come back online as quickly as possible. Weather related demand has been rising and cold temperatures across much of the region are keep railcar demand high, as well as retail sector demand. The arb to Europe has been competitive with the East market for a month now, though FEI strengthening is causing traders wait and see if CIF ARA strengthens in line and continues to draw US imports.   MED The market looks balanced and winter demand has not exceeded tons already programmed to arrive in the region. Colder than average seasonal temperatures are yet to spread further south, and prompt demand lacking.

Optimization has surely been key to lucrative trading reported, with most sublets seen from portfolio players and traders dominating the vessel list. On term shipping, given a fair few vessel redeliveries to Head Owners are expected within Q1 of 2022, several multi-month and short term enquiries appear to be on hold with Owners and Charterers as they evaluate the market and consider their approach. That said, we still do see and expect continued activity on the term market as Charterers seek coverage through 2022, with some even issuing requirements earlier than expected.  On the newbuilding front, it was an active week with Qatari, Asian and Greek Owners all adding to their newbuilding orderbook in Korea.

x: AMERICAS The sky is probably NOT falling but it sure feels like it. Lack of weather across the US has caused propane prices to crash from a 1.41 per gallon a month ago to 97 cents per gallon today.  The inventory situation, which a month ago looked as though the US would not have enough product to cover first quarter export demand,  is no longer an issue. Talk of 10 percent production growth, the lack of weather and falling Asian demand,  have all contributed,  but the bottom line is, we are not running out of product. The weekly number showed a draw of 1 million barrels which had little effect on the market.  Terminal  fees have continued to fall with Jan cargos bid at 4.50 cpg and sellers at just under 6.  NWE  The European market seems to be the only one which knows what winter is! CIF ARA continues to show relative strength in the context of FEI losing over $50pmt today and Mt Belvieu propane dipping under the dollar mark for the first time in months. Europe is feeling winter weather already and is forecast to have coldest winter in 30 years. But that is not the whole story as PDHs started buying again in December and January, ramping up imports from the US. And local supply continues to be around 36% less than usual as LPG is spiked into the natural gas stream. The arb East coming in has the December East/West spread at +$32 and more US loading VLGCs looking to come to the region. A seen by today’s window offer of a full propane VLGC cargo for end December arrival at December CIF ARA flat. This offer was basis 1 port with EU qualifications for buyer and equivalent to an offer of CIF ARA +$5pmt for a TOT stem.   MED The market is calm in the region and it seems buyers are waiting to see offers before showing their hand. Cold weather is being felt and demand is increasing, although this is yet to translate to action in the market.

Expected tender news for demand in Asia will give more direction to the commodity market moving forward, but with availability of vessels currently light this is unlikely to have any effect on shipping rates in the spot market. The surfacing of more sublet availability probing for enquiry into January hasn’t put the dampeners on the market further out either, and as the fixing window stretches well into 2022, rates are maintained. The regional imbalance continues as rates in the Pacific remain at levels not yet achieved in the Atlantic. Though with so few ships in the basin, and the possibility for more volume to have to remain within the Atlantic, we could see this flip/reverse at any time. The potential for a prolonged Winter, Owners continue to ride the wave, with no signs of a change on the horizon.    Despite no newbuild orders being placed this week, prices remain firm and yards remain busy with plenty of enquiry and interest being recorded.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been a volatile week since our last report. In the East, stronger buying interest from end-users has prompted moderate gains while in the West, these gains have been outstripped on news of NS2 pipeline delays due to regulatory approvals, firmly slamming shut the window to any arbitrage opportunities. Although the ramifications of headline pipeline delays has yet to be uncovered fundamentally, the matter of fact is that the LNG shipping market continues to stay very tight. If last week appeared to be the calm before the storm, this week we may’ve just started to feel the breeze picking up. In recent days this has been made clear by an emergence of new requirements issued in advance from apprehensive end-users seeking coverage for their peak winter cargoes, aware that shipping availability over the coming period to be sparce. To this end, with many subletters holding tight onto their dear tonnage and most independent owners sold out, Charterers may have few other options than to pay up, and more often than not, also absorb hefty idle time costs in order to secure a vessel.  The newbuilding market also remains firm with another week of new and confirmed orders, this time by Maran Gas Maritime with DSME and Celsius Tankers with SHI for a pair of newbuilds each. Besides attending signing ceremonies, yards have their hands busy with multiple ongoing newbuilding enquiries.

x: AMERICAS Massive volatility has overwhelmed the market this week, both prior to and after the EIA inventory numbers were released on Wednesday.  Mont Belvieu propane closed Monday at $1.22/gal, saw massive inter-day price swings all day Tuesday and closed at $1.21/gal, then finally went a bit calm prior to the stock data Wednesday morning but then fell sharply in afternoon trade, only to rebound again and close at $1.19/gal.  By Thursday morning $1.10/gal was seen in early activity, but then rebounded to $1.14/gal as of this writing. As of 12 Nov 2021 overall US propane stock levels were listed at 74.6mmbbls by the EIA, down by 200,000bbls from the week prior.  This took some by surprise as a decline of some 1.0-1.5mmbbls was generally anticipated.  PADD I built by a half-million barrels while Gulf coast stocks fell by 400,000bbls – not altogether surprising since export volumes are believed to be back at robust levels.  Propane inventories in the US are now 80+% of last year and nearly 84% of two-years ago.   All the while, US terminal fees have seen their fair share of volatility, though there remains a multi-tiered structure where the terminals themselves have purposefully priced themselves out.  Re-sellers have been seen offering various ratio cargoes at between 7cts and 9cts/gal, though availability is becoming thinner through the balance of 2021.  NWE The bids in the TOT window are not being hit, even it is thought 4 VLGCs 2 LGCs and an MG are expected to arrive in the region between end of November and early December. The bids have been shown at a premium to Naphtha values or at fixed prices. This week’s price swings have led to caution form traders and a fixed price is seen as an easier risk to manage. It is possible that VLGCs could consider re-routing to Asia if the East/West spread continues to widen from December +$61pmt. This uncertainty is keeping the arb to the region wide and the netback competitive. The Propane Naphtha spread has come in this week leading some traders to expect PDH buying to pick up and dramatically increase the regions demand. A butane offer in the window for early December jolted the quiet market and has just pushed values down from 110% to 105% Naphtha today on the lack of buying interest.   MED A full propane VLGC loaded Houston is heading to the region. The Butane arb from the US is open though no new cargoes have been heard making this trade. Morocco is yet to show additional demand above their existing term contracts. Though the arb is wide milder weather is yet to kickstart the Mediterranean market.

n: LNG Market Report
x: The exponential increase in LNG charter rates seen in recent weeks, slowed down slightly this week. However, we are still on an uptrend where rate levels may not have peaked yet and we are barely into full-blown winter. The strong European gas demand is still keeping more Atlantic cargoes than usual within the basin. This may change in the near future if Asian LNG demand strengthens against European demand. Asian inter-basin cargo deliveries would only lead to further tightening of an already very limited open tonnage list which could put further pressure on the current high charter rates and voyage economics. The availability of modern vessels are almost a rarity in today’s spot & short term market as most are on charter and utilised for the charterers' scheduled trades.    The firm newbuilding prices are not deterring new LNG ship orders. Capital Gas has reportedly confirmed another three orders with one at Hyundai Samho Heavy Industries (HSHI) and two at Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI). Not to be outdone, QatarEnergy also secured their first set of Korean-built newbuildings of 174,000m3 LNG vessels with four at Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering (DSME) and two at Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI). Expect more to come in the near future from QatarEnergy.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Flat price Mt Belvieu propane has come off considerably this week and we are not entirely sure why. Have the traders given up on winter already, are trader’s being stopped out.  Time will clarify,  but for us it seems a bit early to be giving up on Winter.  Terminal fees in the U.S. remain buoyant, and simultaneously continue to be multi-tiered.  The terminals – if there is product and dock space remaining – are able to offer product from between the low 9cts/gal up to the low 10cts/gal range.  The ongoing differential between ethane and propane values is believed to still be much of the cause.   Re-sellers, meanwhile, are offering at levels just below that, but product is somewhat limited.  On the other hand, Enterprise continue in their efforts to buy back cargoes (at its own facility) and are expected to be able to bid in the mid 5cts/gal range. Yesterday’s EIA propane inventory report for the US showed a decline of 1.3mmbbls as of the week ending 05 November, to an overall total of 74.8mmbbls – or 79% of last year and 82% of the total from two years ago.  The breakdown shows that PADD I (the East Coast) drew down by 1.1mmbbls, primarily because of cooler temperatures in the region.  PADD III, however, built by 200,000bbls, confounding many because export volumes for the week were robust.  NWE The December window in Europe opened trading with a bang as a bid at +$21pmt to balance November CIF ARA quotes for 1-5 Dec. Showing that the physical market is tight and supporting the wide arb from the US. With the December East/West spread at +$72pmt it seems strong bids are needed to attract tons to the region. This could also tempt traders to look at selling in the region rather than risk waiting time at the Panama Canal. With propane/naphtha spread at +$73 it seems winter demand is beginning to drive the market. The butane market saw some action early in the week and remains tight and at 110% Naphtha.   MED Weather in the region has been mild and spot trading activity quiet. The market remains on the tight side and the arb from the US is wide open as well as from Northwest Europe. So far no spot cargoes are headed to the region. As the weather gets colder imports will be needed for the increased demand.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Stepping into the new month, brisk November weather in tandem with an absence of prompt tonnage in the Pacific has burgeoned rates further. Cargo market volatility continues to be present and this week the arb has narrowed as LNG prices retract from recent highs. Of late, Charterers have stretched their reach in an attempt to cover winter laycans ahead of seasonal rate increases, as a consequence we witness a lack of November laycans and the focus is concentrated on December and early January.  Activity remains strong with multiple fixtures occurring the past week with last done repeatedly being usurped. Vessel availability remains tight, particularly in the Pacific. In the Atlantic, the situation remains slightly muted as pockets of sublet availability offer refuge to a charterer with timely and specific needs. In addition, project tonnage continues to be offered to market and when combined with these pockets of availability, the rate levels remain below those being achieved in the Pacific. This could, however, alter very quickly as projects require the use of their fleet and/or more tonnage is directed East due to cargo demand.  In the newbuilding market no new orders since the signing of 4*174k vessels by JP Morgan at Samsung for 2024 delivery, although we do expect further announcements to filter through in the coming weeks/months, especially from Qatar. For those celebrating tomorrow, we wish you a happy Diwali.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The month of October – historically considered the conclusion of the inventory ‘build’ season and the simultaneous commencement of the winter consumption period – has seen a series of surprises.  Stocks are now 79% of the total achieved last year, and 79% of the total recorded two years ago.  Wednesday’s build of 400,000bbls is being viewed as sentimentally bullish, as the Gulf Coast drew by 600,00bbls on the back of Enterprise buybacks and reduced rates in October at Targa’s Galena Park facility (which have been solved by now but were related to onshore hydrate issues).  But reduced market values yesterday afternoon paint a different story as MB Non-TET propane values fell below $1.39/gal however most believe the drop was more related to ZWTIs fall than propane directly.  As for the near-term prospects, most of it will depend on the weather, and then where that weather occurs, and when.  For the moment forecasts are calling for a cold and wet Thanksgiving which should propel the market in a bullish direction.   Terminal fees on the Gulf Coast remain tiered and based on whether the seller is a terminal owner or a reseller.  Bids and offers are nonetheless occurring on a resale basis on either side of 6cts/gal for Dec.  NWE The region is tight prompt propane tons. ToT window bid for 14-18 November delivery has been pushing up window premiums. The bid is equivalent to November CIF ARA +$4.5pmt, and it seems sellers are testing how badly the cargo is needed with window offers some way off at +$8pmt for Novmeber 23-27 and +$11pmt for November 20-24. With netback values from the US supporting trans-Atlantic trade late November is seen as balanced in the region. The East / West spread in November is at +$50pmt but this does not tell the whole story. With Panama Canal delays at expensive freight rates traders are factoring in around $8pmt in waiting time. US imports to the region will undoubtedly be higher than in October. The question is how much volume can the market take before coming off?  MED Temperatures are falling in the region and heating demand is increasing. There are two VLGC heading to Gibraltar from the US keeping traders from showing bids before tons arrive in the market. Though the more likely explanation is that these vessels are headed to the Suez Canal to go East. Cutting out waiting time in Panama. That said if the price is right traders could decide to sell cargoes in the region.

On the vessel supply side, availability remains very tight with most independent tonnage being sold out and portfolio tonnage remains subject to uncertainties around scheduling or are restricted on period. Those willing to take the risk are seeking higher levels of compensation, thus pushing the market higher. The term market also remains busy with Charterers focusing on securing coverage for 2022 and beyond.  There are no official LNG newbuild orders recorded so far this week but the shipbuilding market remains firm.

x: AMERICAS The overall U.S. propane inventory build of 2.1mmbbls as reported by the EIA Wednesday for the week ending 22 Oct was welcome news and appears to have had the anticipated impact, at least sentimentally.    The increase pushes stock levels to 75.7mmbbls, or nearly 77% of the levels achieved last year.  The bulk of the build occurred in PADD III (Gulf Coast) where export volumes primarily occur.  A typical month generally sees approximately 90 liftings, but total Oct volumes are expected to be down to around 75 liftings due to a host of buybacks, fog, and perhaps a bit more butane liftings (versus full-propane liftings).  Meanwhile, as winter begins to approach, terminal fees have seen a bit of buoyancy as Nov and Dec resellers are seen at just above the 6cts/gal mark.   The terminals themselves are around a penny above that, while Enterprise continues with its buyback scheme into Nov and Dec.   Mont Belvieu propane values have steadily relaxed over the previous 10 days, having moved from  1.49/gal on 18 Oct to a current value of 1.36/gal today.  NWE The TOT window went quiet Wednesday. After another build in Mt Belvieu inventories signalled to traders that there will be enough product to supply the North West European market in November. The VLGC being offered in the window was also withdrawn. No surprise with the East / West spread at +$51pmt. CIF AFA tracked the drop in Brent crude, leaving the propane naphtha spread at +$38/mt for November. The pro/nap spread remains in positive territory for Q1 2022. This combined with expensive natural gas for petchem’s power generation has traders questioning when demand from the sector will pick up. The inland propane market is picking up with trades for railcars occurring at strong premiums. Winter weather in the region is yet to bear it’s teeth, and the builds in Mt Belvieu have had a calming effect on the European market.   MED The coaster market in November was busy this week strong buying interest. This did not affect butane values in the region which slid lower with crude and naphtha. Large cargo discussions have moved on to December arrivals.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG market remains at historically high levels while the freight market continues to climb in fits and starts, with a definite break now appearing between the higher levels seen in the Pacific basin and lower levels in the Atlantic. This is an unusual situation heading into winter, and may be the result of fewer ships travelling on the West-to-East conveyor belt when Europe fought for USG cargoes. There are relatively few firm requirements for this time of year and not many vessels being actively marketed, and combined with fewer clean fixtures there is some uncertainty as to where rate levels will go from here. On paper at least, charter rates and TCEs could top the record levels seen last winter; however, it only takes one sublet with just the right availability seeking to mitigate idle time and costly boil-off for those theoretical returns to take a big hit. On the longer term, several charterers are already making a move for 2022 tonnage. Again, this is unprecedented for this time of year and all points to a very tight market in the coming years. There have been no newbuilding orders this week, however yard slots are few and far between due to activity in other shipping segments.

x: AMERICAS A primary U.S. propane inventory increase of 1.9mmbbls was recorded by the EIA for the week ending 15 Oct, surprising most of the market which had been anticipating either a modest draw or a small build.  Total stocks have reached 73.6mmbbls, or 75% of both last year and two years ago.   On a Days of Supply basis, there continues to be a deficit against last year, and stocks on that basis are still below the range of the last 5 years, hence the ongoing concerned focus related to the winter demand period as it relates to the continuing robust export volumes.  Although there has begun to be cooler weather in North America, there have yet to be any real storm systems which might mark the true commencement of winter.   Cargo availability continues to be split, with offers being seen from the trading community, while still being limited from the terminals themselves.  Terminal fees reflect this and for Nov spot trade is presently focused at just under 6cts/gal.  NWE The well documented news that LPG is being spiked into the LNG stream by producers has rapidly improved CIFA ARA values. Though TOT window offers have been generating the most discussions. Dow and Vilma both offering in the window was seen as bearish. Dow is expected to receive term tons and is not running at 100% so are looking to make an achievable profit on tons they have in the region today. For traders the arb is wide open, netback values from the US are around 9cpg for November for US liftings arriving in North West Europe in the same month. Raising the question whether selling in the TOT window can make more sense than waiting in the Panama canal to sell at a discount in the East. The question is whether these offers will push the window into a discount, or if the European market with less locally produced tons, can absorb the offered tons and more heading into this winter market?   MED The quiet market and prevailing tight supply environment continues. Moroccan public holidays adding to the lack of trade discussions. No winter weather in the Mediterranean region aiding the wait and see trader attitude.

That said, it’s on a small trading volume and in such an illiquid market there is considerable uncertainty and volatility. x: AMERICAS Despite ongoing gains in the crude arena which have brought Brent to $84.06/bbl and WTI to $81.31/bbl, MB propane values earlier this week seemed relaxed to around $1.42/gal, only to rise again prior to the release of the EIA to current levels of $145.00/gal which was fixed just before the inventory data release.    Expectations for this week’s inventory report – which was delayed by a US holiday on Monday – again ranged widely (and revealing ongoing uncertainty), from a draw of around a million barrels to a build of over a million barrels.    Given the strong export volumes and pending winter demand season, the prospect of a draw seemed the more likely, and that turned out to be the case.  For the week ending 8 Oct 2021, the EIA reported overall propane stock levels in the U.S. at 71.7mmbbls, which represents a draw of 600,000bbls.  The components to that include a draw of 800,000bbls in PADD I and the build in PADD III of 300,000bbls.  As there is little in the cold weather and ongoing strength in the export market this was eyed with some level of surprise.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, though still generally range-bound, have inched up and offers for 2H November 4:0 cargoes are seen at 6cts/gal – December at the same.  Buy-side interest remains limited.  NWE The VLGC cargoes which were slated for the region have redirected East. Buying interest in the window did compete with the seller’s netback taking the cargo East. The window bid seen this week has pushed up physical propane value to November CIF ARA +$5. Although the European market is tight the news did not affect CIF ARA which fell this week in line with other commodities. Though inland demand has been picking up, cold temperatures are yet to hit the region. The volume of propane set to be exported in October and November from the US East Coast is down on September due to regional demand. These volumes usually find their way to the European market, further tightening the NWE outlook in Q4. Butane has been directly correlated to naphtha at 105% October.  MED The Tunisia supply tender for 2022 was reportedly won by Petroineos. Tunisia’s 628,000MT demand comes from it’s domestic heating and cooking markets. This less local refinery production 185,000MT in the country leaves a required estimated import volume of 443,000MT.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG spot shipping market has exceeded expectations this week. The lack of workable vessels available and a couple of uncovered requirements, predominately within the East of Suez have firmed up “Owners” sentiments going into winter.  The strong product prices driven by the lack of supply and competition for LNG cargoes between both basins have also given more room and margins for freight.   History have shown how illiquid and volatile the LNG shipping market is and although most Charterers have taken measures earlier this year to cover shipping, an open West-East Arbitrage, continuous rally of spot LNG prices and potential Panama canal delays can trigger more appetite for spot tonnage. With the current cargo prices, being long shipping may be a preferred position.   We recorded another 4+2 new building orders this week and the total tally for the year is now at 52 large LNG vessels.

x: AMERICAS  Volatility is the keyword in the Mont Belvieu LPG market this week.  Intra-day price swings of up to a nickel have been recorded, leaving many on the sidelines.  Crude and natural gas strength have led the way, pausing only for profit taking. Propane stock levels in the U.S. continue to be the primary focus, though there remains a steady eye on both export volumes and ‘buyback’ numbers at EPD, of which there have been a solid 7 (if not 8) for Oct. Total inventory levels as of Oct 1 2021 were recorded by the EIA at 72.3mmbbls, down by 600,000bbls from the previous week – and 71% of the total achieved in 2020.  Weather-related demand in North America will no doubt compete with export volumes over the Q4 ’21 and Q1 ’22. Spot terminal re-sale values are in the sub-6cts/gal range for full propane lots in 2H Nov.  Buy-side interest is hovering at above a nickel but uncertainty is so far keeping the two sides at odds.  NWE Two VLGCs set to arrive in the region have pushed the physical cargoes to a $4.5pmt discount to paper. The propane naphtha spread for September averaged +$45pmt. This lead petrochemical users taking in 325,000 MT, to the lowest monthly intake for 15 months. The October Pro/Nap spread stands at $119pmt today, and some petrochemical users are still taking tons. Due to it being more economical to run a minimal rates than fully shutting down. The draw in Mt Belvieu inventories will keep the arb to Europe closed and with the East/West spread at $51pmt for October and rising further down the curve we do not expect to see many more tons imported from the US in the near future. Butane in the region continues to be assessed at 105% October Naphtha, though this translated to a $15.5pmt drop in value as naphtha crashed.  MED The regions is nervous about winter supply. With production issues in Algeria reducing propane output and the arb to the US closed, traders are wondering where they will find supply this winter. For the time being the market is on the tight side and traders are being cautious not to get caught in short supply if demand picks up.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: LNG prices continue to firm as competition for cargoes globally is driving the price per MMBtu delivered into Asia above $32’s. After the recent lack of activity, business now being concluded is showing all signs of firmness, with rates increasing across most sectors. As we see the fixing window move out into November, Charterers are seeing freight for winter now being priced into these discussions. There is also a lack of visibility on winter tonnage, adding to the firmer outlook. We may see gains in rates over the next few weeks as the prompt sublet tonnage retreats back into schedules and interest for spot cargoes for late November/December mature, however Golden week in China next week might put the brakes on a little.  No newbuild orders have been recorded placed at yards this week, but market talk is around the expected Qatar orders and for how many vessels they will do in this round.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane values have rocketed upwards, but appear – for the moment – to be resting at just above the $1.40/gal level, though earlier in the week trades as high as $1.47/gal were reported.  The strength in the crude market amid fears of an energy shortage are the immediate driving forces, but the entire LPG complex is being underpinned by concerns related to the domestic inventory position.   This week the EIA released its findings for the week ending 24 Sep which revealed a rather surprising 2.6mmbbl improvement in overall stock levels to 72.9mmbbls, or about 72% of the same time last year, and 73% of two years ago.   The ongoing worry is that US propane stocks will be insufficient to accommodate both winter-related domestic demand as well as the ongoing strength of the export market.  However, a bit of downtime at the Galena Park terminal combined with continuing ‘buybacks’ in Houston will likely allow total export volumes to relax in September, and perhaps increase to more comfortable levels.    This remains to be seen, however, since natural gas prices around the world have shot up, giving cause for discussions about fuel-switching in the direction of LPG.  Fuel rationing and an (at least temporary) shift to coal, however, could potentially limit demand levels from that angle.  NWE Propane market is tight, with continued buying interest in the window. The renewed 7 year value highs in CIF ARA have not been able to open the Arb from the US. With regional supply reduced due to refineries using LPG they produce instead of Natural Gas where possible. Local supply is unable to cover demand. So far that has been the only effect of the high natural gas prices in Europe on the LPG supply/demand balance. Though with natural gas in the region set to remain expensive for some time we could see LPG finding it’s way into new markets. Butane was bid at $755/t CIF Antwerp by Vitol and was booked by Equinor for 7,000t of normal butane. Whereafter Equinor offered a further 12,000t of butane at October CIF ARA +$7pmt. Equivalent to 109% of October Naphtha.  MED Sonatrach contract prices for October were set at $808pmt propane and $742pmt butane. The butane market remains tight, and the Sonatrach C4 to C3 discount was a surprise. Some traders were expecting the tons changing hands in NWE window at $755 might find their way to the Mediterranean at a premium. The worry is that a spell of cold weather will send prices, butane in particular, soaring in this tight market.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been yet another week of surging gas prices both in Europe and in Asia, causing a lot of speculations around how long this gas shortage can last and what will be the ultimate ramifications out of it. Naturally, this has been the hot topic this week in Gastech, as it is the first time in a very long time since we have seen a large (physical) industry gathering! Regardless of the striking headlines that the LNG cargo market has been causing lately, it has not reflected into more LNG shipping activity. On the contrary, it has been another lackluster week in the spot market, with only a handful of fresh requirements. We can perhaps partly blame the Gastech or multiple public holidays in the Asia region for this week's quietness, but the fact is that the surprisingly high gas prices in Europe have led trade-flows to be more intra-Atlantic heavy than anticipated causing majority of industry players to have sufficient length in their current LNGC fleet. However, looking past the relative weakness of the prompt shipping market, the view of the winter market still remains tight or at least extremely volatile, with no certainty on how availability might look like during the peak winter. On the newbuilding side, market is still keeping active and shipyards have their hands full with various ongoing discussions.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: NWE A quiet market was exacerbated by the draw in US inventories. Traders expecting a strengthening price reaction. This did not materialise immediately as the strength already priced in to the market. What this means for North West Europe is that it will be very difficult to attract imports to the region. The East West spread from the US at +$53pmt for October and widening for later months not tempting traders with the freight diff at $40pmt. Propane Naphtha spread at +$63pmt for October is keeping petchem demand at rock bottom for the time being. With weather in the region above seasonal averages it’s a gamble when weather related demand might shift the market to require imported tons. A butane deal done in the window set the C4 market at 101.75% October Naphtha.  MED The mood in the region is that the market is tight and it will only get tighter. Right now questions regarding available cargoes are being asked though firm price discussions are still lacking. The market is yet to see any winter demand though the general strength is keeping everyone on their toes.  AMERICAS The EIA this week reported that US propane stocks fell by 500,000bbls over the one-week period ending 17th September.  This compares to the 97.9 and 95.4mmbbl totals recorded during the same week last year and in 2019.  Inventories are now 71% and 74% of the levels achieved in each of the two previous years.   As regards terminal fees, there are multiple tiers which depend on the composition of a particular cargo, and whether that cargo is sourced from a re-seller or direct from one of the terminals.  The terminals themselves are offering full propane lots, but at rather steep levels: 7cts/gal in the highest case, but this underscores the ongoing issue of the Ethane/Propane pricing differential (among other factors), as well as the perceived expectation that terminal fees are being more closely managed.  Split ratio parcels are offered at progressively lower rates, some under 6cts/gal – and perhaps with some room for negotiation thereafter.    Resellers, meanwhile, do not have the same E/P pricing considerations (as they relate to the production of LEP from HD5) and can let full propane lots go at around 5cts/gal, depending on timing/location.  Buy side ideas, meanwhile, reside at (or, more likely, just under) the 4cts/gal level, but interest levels have generally been pretty sparse, particularly from end users.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: While cargo prices strengthened and remained strong this week, the high LNG prices have so far not translated to any strengthening of the spot charter rates - hence, the correlation between cargo price movements and charter rates is yet to be seen. However, a vast majority of the available LNG vessels for spot charters are controlled by portfolio players and traders. As sellers’ cargoes are offered with the requirement to procure spot shipping, they are more often than not, lifted by buyers with available vessels for further trading and filling up short positions given the ideal LNG trading market conditions. The market is also not flushed with a long selection of vessels as the availability list is relatively short.  Meanwhile, the term charter rates for 1 year period remain steady. Charterers’ interest in security over vessel availability for a term period continue to be a priority for various players.    Newbuilding prices continue to climb as Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) confirmed the orders for upto four (4) LNG vessels at Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering (DSME) on the back of charters with Novatek Gas & Power Asia. The 174,000m3 LNG vessels, fitted with ME-GA engines for propulsion, along with a shaft generator and an onboard reliquefaction unit, are expected to be delivered in 2024.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: NWE  Rising crude is dragging CIF ARA up to seven year highs. Though CIF ARA remains in the shadows of Mt Belvieu’s strength. This keeping the arb closed, though not by much, and the trans-Atlantic trade to a bare minimum. A trading house continues to bid the window, at a small premium, failing to attract interest so far this week. Petchems in the region are cracking naphtha where possible with September pro/nap spread at +$48pmt. Natural Gas prices in the region remain high and it will be interesting to see if this pushes propane into any new markets. Refineries using propane as fuel has yet to push up the volume of imports to the region. Butane 104.5% Naphtha rising to 106.8% in November.   MED The main import countries continue to look for product. Tightness in the East Med looks less severe in October than September, with sufficient volume heading for Turkey. West Med demand is present though not urgent, with Morocco looking for small volumes of butane.  AMERICAS Propane supply is now of concern to most parties, since the EIA inventory data revealed a bullishly paltry 700,000bbl build for the week ending 10 Sep, and which brought overall total stock levels to 70.8mmbbls, or 73.6% of last year.  Naturally, the pricing structure at Mont Belvieu is responding and has moved up to over $1.30/gal.  Inventory draws were recorded in both PADD I and PADD III, indicating that export volumes – despite the recent hurricane which landed near Houston and a bit of mid-month terminal downtime – remain robust.  To further illustrate the point, Gulf Coast inventories are 33.2mmbbls, down from 54.9mmbbls last year – a nearly 40% reduction over twelve months.  The ‘bright’ side is limited to the lack of crop drying in North America, but with a La Nina climate forecast on the horizon, winter – and any corresponding demand that comes alongside– looms.  Terminal fees in the US remain tiered, with spot buy-side interest at sub-4cts/gal levels, and spot re-sellers at/below a nickel.  The terminals themselves - depending on the ratio - have a stair-stepped system ranging from the low 5ct range up to more than 6.5cts/gal.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been pleasing to see that spot market activity picked up this week with FOB tenders appearing alongside firm requirements. Commodity prices remain strong yet perhaps surprisingly given cargo strength and increased freight activity, freight rates struggle to interrupt the depressed trend that currently overwhelms the market. The lack of prompt cargoes sees a sizable relet fleet open and interested in short localised business. As laycans drift into Q4, late October and November in particular, rates for long-haul voyages do rise significantly and we can expect the delta between BLNG2 and BLNG3 to widen in the coming weeks as winter gets priced in. Moving East, the thirst for vessels has improved yet insufficiently to absorb all open tonnage. Modern tonnage is likely to move West on their own accord in hope for Atlantic business. Those who remain East for spot Pacific requirements still have to compete with sublet vessels with pockets of availability which are dampening freight levels. LNG shipping availability may however tighten as we look ahead with the current future arbitrage opportunities. Yard prices hold firm, yet no new newbuilding transactions have been recorded.
