t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: NWE Surging Natural Gas prices have been dominating the headlines. In NWE this has led to refineries using more propane as fuel, reducing local production. CIF ARA propane and butane both reached seven year highs, the strength largely driven by CIF ARA following Mt Belvieu. The price strength has not been enough to keep trans-Atlantic cargoes flowing. With less than 100KT of imports from the US in August, the lowest volume in over a year. Propane is at an $8 premium to naphtha in September increasing to $30 in December. This is set to reduce already low petchem run rates to a minimum this winter. The low demand environment in this Autumn shoulder period is the reason a North Sea loading propane VLGC is set to be exported, a sign the supply floor has been reached. Cold weather will be the remedy to jolt the subdued NWE market into action!  MED The region remains tight in the East Med, with Turkey looking for volume and the lack of imports form the US are causing concern. The West Med has been quiet though traders are worried about buying for winter. With cold weather around the corner how expensive will the product needed for winter become.  AMERICAS The release by the EIA of propane stock levels in the US was delayed due to the American Labor Day holiday on Monday, but was eagerly awaited today as the domestic market continues to precariously hinge on inventory levels.  Prior expectations varied widely, with speculation from one perspective calling for a modest draw and from another a build of up to 2mmbbls.  Ultimately the EIA reported that an overall build of 800,000 barrels, though a draw of 100,000 draw was noted in PADD III, the Gulf Coast.  Stocks are – as of 3 Sep – 72% of the total achieved in 2020.  Ultimately the stats are considered generally bullish. Meanwhile, the pricing structure continues at elevated levels, but with winter-demand looming and propane at 71% of WTI the number of those predicting even higher levels seems to be growing.  This is based on the expectation that stock levels – such as they are – can not sustain both a cold winter and heavy export volumes.  That has led to concern as to where the low point of stocks will be next Spring, and where prices will reside at that point. Terminal fees, all the while, have been sagging and for October are now seen ranging from sub-4ct bids to the mid/upper 4s on offer.  Very little is being accomplished.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been another week of relatively low spot activity in the LNG shipping market. Portfolio sublet positions keep “flooding” the market at both basins, where the ones looking at securing tonnage can find some seasonal bargains at very competitive levels; yet period flexibility and promptness of available tonnage doesn’t always necessarily allow for these deals to get concluded. Looking at the cargo market, LNG prices keep climbing due to continuous supply disruptions and uncertainties, having JKM and TTF at a constant battle.  Charterers looking for tonnage for winter opportunities seem to struggle to get much traction from the few Independent Owners with available tonnage or from subleters managing their future schedules. As a result, we are witnessing a halt in near term charter activity, but with cargo market being volatile, this could quickly turn either way. NB prices continue their ascending trend, however no new large LNG orders have been recorded this week.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: NWE The lower than anticipated US inventory build pushed up Mt Belvieu propane and as a consequence CIF ARA propane prices. This has pushed propane/naphtha in NWE from -$2pmt Tuesday to Wednesday’s close of +$20pmt. Some petchem buying interest is said to remain due to traders hedging pro/nap at a a favorable spread. That said crackers are not running at capacity at the moment. CIF ARA butane has remained steady at 106% naphtha, the market is tight but quiet. The market has not followed the usual seasonal trends, LPG has been expensive throughout the summer. Soon weather related and gasoline blending demand will start to be seen. So the question for many European traders is when to start buying for winter?   MED Maintenance at Mohammedia storage which has taken out 80KT of it’s 200KT capacity has not had an effect on VLGC imports to the region. It is yet to be seen if discharge times will increase, or if stocks can be managed effectively. The rest of the region remains tight though there is very little interest in bringing in from the US as Mt Belvieu butane saw a $50pmt increase post US inventories being posted Wednesday.  AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane values continue to tick up on a daily basis, primarily on the back of concerns that inventory levels in the U.S. will be insufficient for the combined demand that is anticipated from the petchem sector, the winter period and – above all – overwater exports.  Current valuations for non-LST Sep propane are in the $1.17/gal range.  October bids were most recently seen at $1.20/gal.   The EIA this week reported a 600,000bbl build in overall stock levels, but a draw of the same volume occurred in PADD III, the Gulf Coast – where the bulk of the exports occur.  The overall total as of late Aug is ~73% of last year, and whether or not stock totals can make it to the desired levels is an openly discussed concern.    There remain between 4-6 weeks in the traditional ‘build’ season and so much will be determined over the next month.    Terminal fees remain tiered, with re-sellers offering at (or perhaps just below) a nickel and buyers – considering current economics – at levels well below that.  The terminal owners/operators themselves are generally at yet another, higher level – particularly for full propane cargoes.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS:  Strong US overwater export volumes in July will very likely be overshadowed by record-level volumes in Aug – despite the buyback scheme embarked upon by Enterprise earlier in the summer.  The September roster appears solid, as well, with only two cargo cancellations known.   The robust outbound volumes are the primary reason that domestic US propane stocks have been unable to rise to desired levels.  This week the EIA reported overall stock levels to be 68.7mmbbls – up by 1.9mmbbls week-over-week.  Still, this is just 75% of both last year and 2019 as domestic production simply cannot hold pace.  In 2019 production averaged 1.148mmbbls/day.  By 2020 it had risen to 1.179mmbbls/day, and on a YTD basis 2021 has so far improved to 1.235mmbbls/day – but still, exports reign and will likely continue to disallow stocks from satisfactorily improving. Crop drying expectations for this Fall, however, call for minimal demand as a lasting, dry and “scorching” Midwest heat has allowed crops to “wither” in the fields.  This should allow stock levels to build at a mildly better rate, but the hope of reaching 80+ mmbbls is fading, or perhaps already dissipated. Spot terminal fees in the US in September, while sentimentally up, remain on either side of the 5ct range for Sep, though little is being accomplished.  2022 contract terminal fee values, depending on the ratio, frequency, volume, etc., range from the upper 4cts/gal level to well over 6cts/gal.  North West Europe:  The physical market in the region is tight, window premiums assessed at September CIF ARA +$4.5pmt. Propane has once again switched back to a discount to naphtha. Though at a mere -$6pmt in September it is not nearing the -$30pmt needed to switch back to cracking propane instead of naphtha. The build in US inventories is hoped to widen the arb to NWE though, in this low demand environment it is unlikely a significant volume of US tons will find their way to the region. CIF ARA butane is at 104% naphtha showing uncharacteristic strength for the time of year.   MED: A quiet week though trends are the same. The region remains tight all grades. Butane particularly with values slightly above those in NWE at 106% naphtha.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: We pass another week with relatively few spot fixtures, and the running total for the year has now fallen some way behind the high watermark of 2020. Will the second half of the year generate enough spot activity to catch up? It’s unlikely, and in fact current trends suggest the fixture count may even slip below the 2019 tally. However, with very few ships under independent owners’ control and with the cargo market remaining buoyant, the rest of 2021 is set to be a fascinating game of chess, in which novel structures and creative deals on both cargo and freight will help charterers make the most of their tonnage - there is plenty of opportunity for win-win scenarios. The multi-month market is again more active, and the limited pool of independent owners and those charterers with enough length to sublet are being kept busy. There haven’t been any fresh newbuilding orders placed this week.

AMERICAS  U.S. propane inventory levels rose by 1.6mmbbls this week, bringing total levels to 66.761mmbbls as of 13th August.  Propane stocks are now 75% of last year, though as the weeks have progressed over this summer the level of concern has continued to grow.   The primary reason that stock build rates have been so limited is because export volumes have been so robust.  The month of August is no exception and is expected to see near record-level departures.  The buyback scheme initiated by Enterprise and the various cancellations which have been noted seem to be having little impact on the vessel tally.  Meanwhile, re-sale terminal fees have come off over the course of this week, with offers now seen at 4.25cts/gal and buy-side indications at sub-4cts/gal.  The near-term future of the domestic US propane market will be shaped by the outcome of the crop-drying season and the timing of the arrival and the ferocity of winter.  In the meantime, though, MB propane values have been on the slow, steady rise and are now marked at nearly $1.15/gal ($599/mt).

x: NWE  An offer was seen in the window which equated to September CIF ARA -$2.5pmt. This was the first bit of action seen in over a week. The offer changed the view that the market is leaning towards being balanced rather than tight. On the back of VLGCs loaded in the US heading to the region in early Sept. Butane saw a bid in the window and is at 95% September naphtha, though this is a moving target due to crude volatility. Petchem demand has come off significantly due to planned maintenances being carried out and importantly forward pro/nap values go from a meagre -$18pmt September moving to an unfavorable +$2pmt by December. The temperatures are cooler than seasonal averages though this is not expected to create enough demand to change the market outlook in the short term.  MED The region has been starved of tons with the arb from the US remaining closed. This has helped drive demand for locally sourced tons, FOB Lavera values particularly strong for summer. Both the East and West Mediterranean are tight of LPG Mix and butane.  AMERICAS  With many out of the office on holiday, the MB propane market continues to trudge along in the 1.08-1.09/gal range, though all the while the level of concern related to propane stock levels in the U.S. is increasing.   Wednesday’s EIA report showed a 1.5mmbbl build, putting overall total US propane inventories at an even 66mmbbls.   This includes, though, a 300,000bbl decline in PADD III (Gulf Coast) stocks and puts this year at 76% of the 86.7mmbbls recorded at the same time in 2020, and 81% of the 79.3mmbbls achieved in early August 2019.   There are around 10 weeks remaining in the traditional stock ‘build’ season, and to reach 80mmbbls another 14mmbbls of inventory growth is needed – or 1.4mmbbls (on average) per week.   The overarching question – and the source of the concern – is whether this will be a sufficient volume to accommodate domestic needs (crop drying + res/com + petrochemical) and overwater export requirements.   Meanwhile, terminal fees continue sitting between 5.00 and 5.25cpg, depending on location, timing, and ratio.  A host of mixed-ratio re-sellers have begun to emerge, and while there are full-propane cargoes available, the Ethane/Propane pricing differential issue continues to dissuade the terminals themselves from entering the fray at competitive price levels.

t: LNG Market Report

LNG prices continue to soar higher and higher amid surprisingly strong demand, keeping everyone discussing what to expect for the winter period. Nonetheless, some recently concluded shipping deals suggest a slight softening on the prompt spot rates compared to term levels, which indicates that those who have prompt vessel availability, are willing to compromise slightly on rates in order to bridge their next position closer to the winter months. It is however important to note that not all requirements are equal, and some charterers will get luckier with their laycan dates and requested period as many of the vessels in the availability list only have specific date ranges or basins they are willing to work. With overall vessel availability staying relatively tight, we are undeniably balancing on a razor’s edge trying to gauge the next market moves on a week-by-week basis. On the newbuilding front, activity remains high for many ship types, including LNG carriers but especially for container vessels, and yard prices continue to stay under pressure due to the recent hike in steel prices.

Meanwhile, rumors that Targa declared Force Majeure due to a fractionator going down are unfounded.  In fact, a minor mechanical issue occurred at the terminal itself, and though a F/M was declared, the problem was very quickly resolved and loading delays of no more than a day are expected, according to Targa.   As for terminal fees, the terminal operators remain priced out due to the E/P pricing differentials while the re-sale market remains approximately on either side of 5cts/gal.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Only a handful of spot LNG shipping fixtures concluded and placed on subjects last week and not enough to move the market, at least on the prompt basis. There were a few enquiries this week for possible charters subject to execution of LNG cargo trades, optimisation and tender awards. However, a relatively quiet week and not as intense as compared to the previous month. Despite July being the month of summer holidays traditionally with reduced LNG demand, fundamentally the cargo market is not weak, with firm support on LNG prices.  The list of available vessels is short with only eight open ships across the world with a few more coming open in August. Hence, the market can change in an instant, not just due to enquiries for charter-ins/outs in the upcoming weeks, but the timing of which these possible charter enquiries would be issued could be a strong catalyst. Assuming a few requirements or vessels are released at the same time (i.e. same day or a few days apart) and with similar vessel delivery terms, this could lead to a perception that the market is tighter/softer than it actually is. Charter rate levels may easily move quickly in these scenarios.   LNG vessel newbuilding prices continue the uptrend with commodity prices and currency exchange rates moving unfavourably for the shipyards. The continued high demand for newbuilding ships across all sectors add further pressure to the raising price for LNG vessel newbuilds.    We wish you a blessed Eid Al-Adha Mubarak!

x: NWE  The physical market in the region is assessed at a small discount to August CIF ARA. A bid and an offer were seen in the window, with the price difference to wide to bridge. The market is starting to settle back into a normal rhythm after the crude correction. Now that both Brent and WTI are trading above $70pmt propane/naphtha spread in August is at -$36pmt in the region. Keeping LPG demand from petrochemicals healthy. This being said the window offer was form a petchem company. The reasons for the resale is said to be receiving terminal congestion rather than demand reduction. For the time being the market remains tight with little volume set to be imported from the US in August.  MED Tightness prevails in the region. It seems like the buyers have outweighed sellers for the whole year so far. Mixed butane in the West Med is tight and at 96.6% Naphtha putting it at a premium to North West European coasters.  AMERICAS The nearly universal reaction to the news of this week’s EIA report, which showed a weekly build of 3.1mmbbls, was one of surprise.  Most had anticipated a more modest build of 1.6-1.8mmbbls.  But the Gulf Coast showed a build of 2.2mmbbls, putting the total US propane inventory level at 62.7mmbbls as of 16 July.  This compares to the 82.4mmbbls reported last year, and the 75mmbbls seen the year prior to that – and leaves current stock levels at 76% and 79% of the last two years, respectively.  The MB propane market did not immediately react to the EIA data with much enthusiasm in either direction.  Pre-EIA prices were flat at 106.00 cts/gal, and only a modest decline to 105.75cts/gal was noted in the hours after the data was released.  By Thursday morning, though, crude upticks had positively influenced the market and the prices were again above 107.00 cts/gal.  Otherwise, the buyback scheme embarked upon by Enterprise continues.  It is believed that Enterprise has bought back 5 (or maybe 6) cargoes in Aug and remain a buyer for Sep, as well.  Whether or not those same cargoes are then re-sold will then (somewhat) dictate the EIA’s inventory build rate, which will then have an impact on the pricing structure.  Terminal fee ideas from the buy-side are in the 4.50-5.00 cts/gal range, while resale market expectations are in the 5.00-5.50cts/gal range.  The terminal owners themselves, still under pressure from the E/P spread issues, have priced themselves at higher levels.

x: The market continues to see action in the multi-month-plus timeframe, and this is making up for a lack of activity in the spot market. The latest term discussions have piqued the interest of several owners and charterers, but we do see a growing reluctance from both sides to work terms that are too far away from their initial expectations. All this activity does mean the balance of availability this winter will be held by sublets rather than independent owners, and those curious to see how the peak season could play out may have been granted a glimpse in the past week: a recent spot requirement in Asia saw a number of sublets being offered and these clearly weighed on the levels achievable. Will this be the pattern for the rest of the year? Perhaps the opposite; with stronger cargo economics and longer voyages in winter, we may well see the same volatility but in entirely the opposite direction. There have been no new LNG orders to report this week as we end first half 2021. However, yard prices are firming

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: NWE  The market remains tight with strong petrochemical cracking demand dominating buying. July trading has been picking up though not many cargoes are being traded in the window as they are being snapped up before making it to the market. Butane is at 92.5% of July Naphtha, very strong for the time of year particularly as naphtha and crude are strong. Mt Belvieu strength is keeping the trans Atlantic arb firmly closed for the time being. Many traders expect this to change due to the continued strong petchem demand.   MED Sonatrach posted it’s July prices at $595pmt & $605pmt for C3 & C4 respectively, surprisingly strong, but then so was CP. This was a bit of a shock in the region, though it did not dampen trade discussions as the market remains tight. With crude rising today and butane trading at 90% of Naphtha the high SH postings will be taken in the market’s stride.  AMERICAS Non-TET market values for propane have risen from 92cts/gal at the beginning of June to 114 cts/gal as of this writing – a 24% increase.  But the last 5 trading days have seen the sharpest gains, having moved up by over a dime during that time. This is because of inventory-related fears in the U.S. market, which were compounded by this week’s EIA report that revealed a one-week build of just 1.239mmbbls and brought the total overall US propane stock level to 57.479mmbbls as of 25 June.  This compares to the Year Ago level of 74.599mmbbls. The ongoing concern – both from domestic and international market participants - is that propane inventories will be insufficient to simultaneously accommodate domestic demand (including potential crop-drying requirements), petrochemical feedstock demand, and export demand.  Indeed, the Days of Supply were recorded at 66.5 on 25 June, where at the same time last year there were 80 Days of Supply in stocks.  Meanwhile, cargo cancellations for August are being talked with additional vigor, and as of today we have seen at least 4. However please keep in mind we are not quite sure how to calculate the Enterprise buybacks and will they be traded on or simply put back into the inventory.  Export cargo terminal fees, meanwhile, have crept up slowly and quietly, having now loosely congregated at around the 4.50 - 5.0cts/gal range for the US Gulf.

x: Although the maintenance and drydocking season is well underway it doesn’t appear to affect the shipping market much. Spot rates continue to build on the previous weeks’ gains, supported by term discussions and a strong product market due in part to warm weather across Europe and some problems with European pipeline supply. There are available vessels particularly in the east, but it must be noted that most of those offering today are subletters and the tonnage could quickly be withdrawn if the cargo market strengthens further or the East/West arbitrage increases. We’ve seen two orders for multiple newbuildings this week: one from COSCO and PCI firming up three options at Hudong-Zhonghua, and one from Capital Gas at HHI. The Cosco tonnage is due for delivery at the end of 2024 and early 2025, whiles the Capital Gas tonnage is due for delivery by the end of 2023.

AMERICAS                                                                                                                                                                                Market values for July propane at Mont Belvieu have risen to $102.75/gal (as of this writing), riding the combined wave of support from both the crude oil sector as well as the most recent propane inventory data released by the EIA. In that report the government revealed a 1.046mmbbl increase in primary propane stocks in the U.S., bringing the overall total to 56.240mmbbls, which compares to last year’s total figure of 71.331mmbbls, or a 15.091mmbbl deficit YOY. WTI, meanwhile, was marked at $73.08/bbl for August, having been spurred by U.S. gasoline futures which – in turn – were being pushed by a bullish inventory drawdown. Terminal fees in the U.S. are presently in the 4.50-5.00cts/gal range, with offers seen on the higher end of the range and bids at the lower end, and more than a penny lower on the East Coast. Meanwhile, in an interesting turn of events not seen in well over a decade, Enterprise this week marked itself as a buyer of August Enterprise cargoes (any dates, any ratio) and is now known to have purchased a cargo from a term customer.  Additional purchases of similar variety are anticipated.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: LNG shipping rates, especially for term, continue to firm up with week-on-week gains across both basins.  While the Pacific is fairly quiet on the spot market, demand for shipping remains high in the West with several requirements to work on.  Owners with vessel availability are still very focused on either 1-2 spot laden legs or term period very close to 1 year + but nothing in between.  Charterers, on the other hand, prefer to secure vessels up till end Q1 – early Q2 next year.   Hence, it remains challenging to bridge that gap between Charterers preference to cover winter and Owners preference to secure longer period.   Furthermore, the current spot cargo prices have also fueled strong demand for ships which in part explains Owners stance at the moment. So the question remains on everyone’s mind: To fix at the current rates and duration or take “the wait-and-see approach”?   There are no new orders reported this week and newbuilding prices remain stable, with a firm undertone.

TOT window has been quiet this week, though still assessed at a premium, with many traders waiting for the dust to settle after crudes moves.   MED Butane in the Med has been tracking naphtha, showing strength. Prompt strength remains for 1H July with June trading all but done. Delivered buying interest is being seen both in the East and West Med for July arrival.  AMERICAS A weekly EIA propane stock build of 1.544mmbbls was met with trepidation as the previous few weeks have been riddled with corrected data.  And while there remains the expectation that this week’s data contains yet more of the same, it was perceived as directionally accurate. There remain concerns as to the ability of US stocks to build to sufficient levels, but to move from present totals of 55mmbbls to a desired level of 75mmbbls over the space of the next 16 weeks requires a weekly average build of just 1.25mmbbls, which (from a historical perspective) is entirely achievable.   With just one exception, the mid-Jun to mid-Oct average build rate has increased each year over the past 5 years, moving up from 1.3mmbbls in 2016 to an average weekly build of nearly 1.7mmbbls last year.  Therefore, it is well within reason that US stocks will rise to sufficiently comfortable levels.   The pricing structure, meanwhile, reacted to the EIA data in a bullish manner, moving from ~95cts/gal to over 96cts/gal.  By Thursday morning the market had realized additional gains and was traded at 96.5c/gal. Terminal fees have been waffling in the low/mid single-digits, with East Coast transactions occurring just under 4 cpg , and a recent Gulf Coast deal was reported at the “low 4’s” per gallon.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Activity in the spot market remained fairly muted this week. With firm commodity prices & freight rates, discussions around ship positions, cargo trades and optimisation of both were taking place, but few deals were concluded. However, the Far East thirst for 3Q deliveries are now dragging vessels from the Pacific into the Atlantic for US-sourced cargoes back to Asia. Spot Pacific requirements, offering owners shorter charter durations, would normally warrant a premium in these circumstances, but sublet vessels with pockets of availability have dampened this effect. LNG shipping availability may however tighten as we look ahead. With the current arbitrage opportunities, there is a clear risk for more and longer voyages West to East. Scheduling may then become challenging with potential waiting time in Panama versus taking the long route via Cape.  With yard prices firming across shipping segments, the newbuild market saw 2 interesting orders being concluded. JOVO place an order for a rare mid-sized 79,800cbm vessel at Jiangnan. Over at KSOE (HHI) 4x 200,000cbm LNGC were ordered and these vessels are apparently to be fitted with the new ME-GA two-stroke engines.

t: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: AMERICAS The EIA posted a weekly propane build of 5.5mmbbl as of the week ending 04 May, bringing overall US stocks from 48.151mmbbls to a current level of 53.650mmbbls.  The market was very surprised, having anticipated a build of not more than about 2mmbbls – on the high side. Prices reacted almost immediately to the unexpected build and declined from the low 95cts/gal level in to the mid 93ct range, though a slow resurgence was noted in the early afternoon hours.  24 hours later the market was bid at 95cts again.  This, however, may have been because buyers stepped in during the moment of pricing weakness as well as the strong crude oil markets.   While there remains quite a lot of skepticism as to the validity of the EIA data, it is generally believed that higher-than-anticipated butane exports, previously canceled cargoes, the reclassification of Gulf Coast propane inventory and healthy production levels are the reasons behind the increase. Terminal fees, having been in the low single digit levels, have this week seen a resurgence and are now seen in the 4cts/gal range.    In South America, continued buying demand from Brasil continues to provide a floor for the FOB markets, with Petrobras buying one to two spot cargos per month.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: It has been another slightly quieter week from LNG shipping perspective, which is somewhat surprising considering that the LNG cargo market continues to thrive as LNG prices done for deals into Europe and into the Far East elevate higher. Most of the ongoing shipping activity is now focused on July deliveries and we have witnessed a modest uptick on rates in the Atlantic basin, since some of the sublets have disappeared from the availability list. However, it has been a different story in the Pacific, as we continue to see further softening on rates, as prompt availability continues to build up and there hasn’t been enough requirements to significantly reduce this. Few of the independent Owners have noticed this as well, and have therefore decided to start ballasting their prompt tonnage towards the more promising Atlantic market. Evidently the spot market continues to stay volatile with its rather unpredictable movements from one week to another, but the big picture seems to be holding strong which is clearly illustrated by the term rates remaining firm. On the newbuilding front, it was a noticeably busier week, since amidst the strengthening yard prices, it was reported that SHI have secured an order for two modern 174,000cbm LNG carriers for an Oceanic shipowner and additionally it was also announced that DSME has signed a contract to build one 174,000cbm LNG carrier for Hyundai LNG Shipping which will go to Repsol under a long-term charter.

x: AMERICAS  The 4.1mmbbl build in propane stocks for the week ending 28 May was instantly met with both elation and contempt, and resulted in an almost immediate decline in Mont Belvieu propane values (to 89.75cts/gal for Jun), but also speculation as to whether next week’s data release would include corrected data. On the former point, and after some weeks of disappointing build levels, propane stocks in the U.S. were in rather desperate need of showing signs of improving.    In any case, at 48.2mmbbls as of the 28 May, domestic US propane stocks still pale in comparison to levels of a year ago when 67.3mmbbls were reported, a 19.1mmbbl deficit YOY.  The generally accepted comfort level for pre-winter propane stocks is in the 65-70 mmbls range, which will require an average weekly build over the next 21 weeks of sbout 1 million barrels per week which we believe is very achievable.  Meanwhile, terminal fees have been seen and reported in the 3.5-4.0 cpg range for June, with asking levels in July tentatively within the same range for the Gulf Coast and a penny cheaper for the USEC.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Sentiments for the spot market have certainly dropped as the recent spot fixtures were done at lower levels against the recent highs. More vessels are being shown as available to the market, following redeliveries from previous month’s string of fixtures. Players with spare tonnage capacities continue to seek opportunities for sublets in both basins, although these vessels have a limited available period of about one to three months. These sublets constitute of great proportion of the available tonnage list. Looking a little further out to July, and there are signs the current dip may be short-lived. There appear to be more requirements on the horizon especially out the US Gulf, and these may test how tight the market really is, with or without the sublets.    Despite the reduced sentiments in the spot market, the charter rate expectation for term employment, i.e. multi-months over the winter, one year and multi-year charters remain firm and intact, with little indication that rates for such a duration would soften based on the expectations from shipowners with the remaining available vessels for the period.   No orders reported this week, price indication for newbuilding LNG vessels are continuing its gradual upward trend.

x: NWE  CIF ARA values have been weaker than both the Mt Belvieu and FEI price quotes, leaving the June East/West spread at +$57pmt.  Houston / Flushing freight rates have stayed strong and just a bit below the Mt Belvieu / CIF ARA arb which is now -$47 for June. this not  leave buyers/traders much margin to look at US FOB cargoes and hence the FOB values continue to fall.  North Sea maintenance is progressing on schedule with production in the region is set to ramp up from June 3rd.  MED The butane market in the region continues to look long. May butane is well offered,  though 1H June shorts in the region are yet to be covered. Meanwhile with seasonal demand for propane non existent, it is very difficult to find buyers.  AMERICAS Most of the domestic US market players and observers were calling for a small propane inventory build this week; perhaps something under a million barrels, with most generally clustered around the 650-750,000bbl range. In fact, however, the EIA data revealed a decline of nearly 400,000 bbls from 44.4mmbbls last week to 44.1 mmbbls.  PADD I stocks fell from 3.9 to 3.7mmbbls, PADD II showed an improvement from 11.2 to 11.5mmbbls, while the Gulf Coast fell from 26.3mmbbls to 25.7mmbbls – all during a time when record-level exports are believed occurring. Propane stocks in the US are now squarely at minimum tolerances, with the Days-of-Supply tally running at 18.09 days, where the previous 5-year low (which occurred in 2018) was pegged at 19.83 days.    Prices reacted immediately, moving up within minutes from ~85cts/gal at Mont Belvieu to over 87cts/gal before lunchtime.  Netbacks, meanwhile, which were already suffering to the point of cancellations – seven of which are believed to have occurred for June – may be sent over the tipping point, though no additional cancellations were immediately revealed.  Terminal fees, presently offered at 3cts/gal, reflect the difficult arbs.

x: After the rally of chartering activity over the past couple of weeks, there are now becoming noticeable signs of softening emerging as we move into summer. Prompt interest has eased, save for optimisations or speculative opportunities. Looking a month out, ship availability is increasing, but most of the tonnage emerging is controlled by subletters. Generally, their length is too short or have limitations to accommodate fully flexible periods/trades, but they are impacting market sentiment. Term fixing activity is also slowing as Charterers pause to assess what vessels are left and how the market plays out; however, Owners stance remains unchanged - at least for now - as they weigh the cost (and potential benefit, in winter) of spot exposure versus fixing for term. On the newbuilding front, there have been no new orders recorded, however prices are steadily rising for delivery in 2024.

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: Firstly, to those celebrating Eid – Eid Mubarak. National holidays have been plentiful recently and these “interruptions” could be seen to affect the rhythm of the market, yet LNG prices continue to rise throughout the curve and point to continued improvement in the underlying market. It’s impact on freight is very noticeable, owners remaining bullish with this bullishness being built on the evidence of persistent multi-month enquiries. As mentioned last week the activity in the multi-month market is likely to reduce due to the lack of supply, unless we see a step up in levels to encourage further sublets into the market as owners. Looking at availability generally, there appears to be a systemic shortage of availability within the independent owners fleets.  Although some vessel available is starting to appear in all basins from portfolio players, the prompt available remains stable with adequate yet not overbearing availability. Looking further out to June and Q3, availability is far improved and adds pressure to rate increases. Despite this the start of Q3 looks stronger than usual for LNG Prices and shipping activity.  In the newbuild market - no new orders have been seen this week yet the newbuild price continues its steady climb.

n: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
x: NWE CIF ARA propane was weaker than crude, pushing pro/nap higher into the $100-$110pmts. Large cargo butane value in the region was down now at 79.5% Naphtha. The region has been well covered for May demand mainly through imports from the US East Coast. Traders in the region are now monitoring the North Sea Maintenance and expect it to come back on time, June 3rd. With bank holidays in much of the region Thursday, many traders have bridged the long weekend and will reassess the market next week.  MED The butane market in the region is seen as under pressure. Due to split ratio US cargoes heading to the region to discharge their butane. The only offer seen in the window was an FOB meeting Moroccan spec which was withdrawn before the close. Both the propane and butane have lacked the strength.  AMERICAS If it’s not one thing it’s another. Asian and NWE CFR prices rose enough to what should have made cargos from the US workable, only to have freight go up further and faster, pushing the Arb back into cancellation economics.   The domestic propane inventory build of 2.5mmbbls allowed the market a sigh of relief as stocks moved up from 41.5mmbbls to 44.0mmbbls as of 7 May 2021.  The East Coast (PADD 1) saw a decline of 300,000bbls (from 3.8 to 3.5mmbbls) but given the volume of overwater exports that have been – and are still – occurring, this is not surprising.  PADD 3, however (the Gulf Coast) saw a build of 2mmbbls, from 24.8 to 26.8mmbbls.  Ostensibly this can be the result of either fantastic production levels, reduced export volumes or some combination thereof.  The EIA, however, reported that production in the first week of May declined to 635,000bbls/day, down from 1.353mmbbls/day – and neither figure seems believable, since the much-discussed cancellations did not occur in the first week of May, but are expected in 2H May. n: LNG Market Report
x: With much of the LNG world enjoying various holidays and some much needed time off over the past week, activity slowed down a little but the market has picked up right where it left off. The drive to take ships for winter coverage must surely ease up at some point, as owners with open tonnage are in no rush to fix and charterers weigh up the rising cost versus remaining uncovered. It’s a fascinating dynamic and one rarely seen ahead of summer. For those taking positions today, the lack of availability last winter and the LNG forward curve will be foremost in their minds and will justify taking on extra length. Those as-yet-uncovered may instead point to the tentative emergence of sublets as a sign that the market may yet soften, albeit such vessels are typically showing only quite narrow gaps in their schedules. Whatever happens in the coming months, we’re likely to enter winter with a lower proportion of vessels under control of head owners. It will be interesting to see how LNG shippers manage any excess length. On the newbuilding front, we note one LNGC order was reported last week. Finally, we note with sadness the re-emergence of coronavirus in some parts of the world, and as we all address the uncertainties ahead we hope all our readers and their families remain safe.

Overall US propane stocks as of 30 April are recorded at 41.471mmbbls, a deficit of 11.905mmbbls from the 59.376mmbbl total seen at the same time last year.  Stock levels will need to build at an average rate of 1.8mmbbls per week for the next 22 weeks – which is completely within reach- (but not with such a large export program) in order to achieve the generally established minimum of ~80mmbbls by the first week of October. The arb has narrowed due to the recent strength in the Mont Belvieu market, and to the point where the lengthy list of cargoes presently being offered is only growing as buyers remain scarce.   As for the EIA propane inventory levels, many now openly doubt that propane stocks will be able to rise to at least the 80mmbbl mark by early October – and that doubt is causing prices to increase.  The question is whether stocks at the conclusion of the ‘build’ season will be sufficient to accommodate both exports and winter-related demand simultaneously in the U.S.   Expectations for this week’s EIA propane inventory report was again a mixed bag of predictions.  Some were calling for a small draw of around a half-million barrels, others for a build of a million barrels.  The relatively lighter export volumes but improving petchem consumption rates were considerations, but there has also been strong production levels thus far in 2021.  The half-million barrel build that was ultimately reported is surely a step in the right direction, but hardly sufficient, and prices reacted by increasing. With this activity and LNG market setting, greatly reducing a charterers potential idle time over the next 12 months charter period, Charterers are able to justify to move quickly to secure tonnage. Available modern vessels are depleting fast in both basins as spot and term charters are being concluded.

x: AMERICAS US propane inventory levels continue to be of strong interest among both the domestic participants as well as the foreign players.  Ultimately the Mont Belvieu propane pricing structure is dependent upon availability, and as such stock levels are a focal point.   Using the current total US propane stock level of 41.2mmbbls as a starting point, and considering the 5-year average summer build of 43.5mmbbls, it can be calculated that an end-Sep/ely-Oct 2021 propane inventory level of ~84.8mmbbls should be achieved.  Except that this is no ordinary year.     If stocks build by 10% less than average (or 39.1mmbbls), a total of ~80mmbbls will be achieved.  Likewise, if the 5-year minimum summertime build of 37.9mmbbls is seen, a total of less than 80mmbbls would be seen, thus painting a rather bullish pricing picture.    Meanwhile, domestic production levels are mostly recovered after the storm in February, but the petchem sector continues at less than full operating rates, having fallen to the low 70% utilization range.  The domestic res/com sector will likely only realize averages this year, leaving export volumes as the deciding factor, which in Q1 2021 have been light.  The combination of sub-par chemical consumption and generally minimized exports should likely allow for some of the bullishness to be tempered.   As to the current terminal fee market, rates for Apr are seen bid at 4.5, with sellers offering around 5.50.  May values are tentatively pegged at just above that range, indicating that a bit of strength has emerged.  NWE Good cracker run rates continue in the region. Butane the most favorable feedstock, is at 91.5% Naphtha and on the tight side in the region. Split ratio large cargo volumes coming to the region have not hit the resale market. The TOT window remains high single digit premium. The market is still tight though a large volume of exports are arriving int he region due to planned maintenance at local gas fields reducing production. In ARA the switch to summer gasoline spec usually has a marked bearish effect on C4 prices. Though reduced gasoline demand this year has kept butane blending demand low throughout winter.   MED The logistics issues caused by the blockage of the Suez Canal have not had a marked affect on the LPG market in the region yet. VLGCs will be affected with at least four waiting to transit in the north and two at the Southern anchorage. No discussions to place tons in the region due the canal delays have been heard. Moroccan buyers are well covered dampening butane interest in the West Med.

x: AMERICAS  Though by now most of the problems related to the storm in February have been overcome, cargo loading issues persist on the Gulf Coast.  Delays and setbacks have beleaguered Gulf Coast terminals, with recent lifting rates having been exacerbated by fog-days – or at least fog-mornings.  Those days appear to have passed, however, as the weather along the upper Texas Gulf Coast is now clear, dry and cool.   The EIA yesterday reported that domestic US propane stocks fell by 170,000bbls as of the week ending 21 Mar, leaving an overall total of 41.029mmbbls of propane in primary storage.  This compares to the 61.379mmbbls recorded in mid-March 2020, a decline of 33%.    Notably, where stock declines were noted in both PADDs I and II, PADD III inventories rose from 25.464mmbbls to 25.920mmbbls.  This is likely due to a combination of curtailed exports and the slow return of the chemical sector.  US production figures, meanwhile, actually declined; from 1.894mmbbls/day on 5th Mar to 1.867mmbbls/day on 12 Mar.   March is all but done, but spot terminal fees for April remain the mid 5ct/gal range, with offers for May at 6cts/gal, or just below.  Corresponding bids are in the low 5cts/gal range for May.  Talk of June has yet to fully materialize, but notional rates were initially being talked at around 6cts/gal.  NWE Market has tracked crude down to some extent although this has not hampered buying interest. March Pro/Nap at -$53pmt is keeping the market supported by the petrochemical buyers. Rising imports from the US have all been snapped up and the market remains on the tight side. ToT Window premiums have come down to April CIF ARA +$5pmt. A bid for large cargo butane was seen in the region for early April delivery was seen. Lifting April  butane values to 90% Naphtha.   MED Has returned to it’s state of calm as demand in the region cools off. Increasing US tons finding their way to the Med has also helped. Moroccan demand has been off this year which has been attributed to persisting global travel restrictions depressing tourism in the country.

x: Spring is a time of renewal, and having endured a torrid few weeks we do see some encouraging signs for LNG shipping. After falling from record highs to unsustainable lows, rates appear to have bottomed out and if anything may be starting to firm again. The main drivers are on the demand side, as a flurry of spot and term enquiries hit the market this week with more to come. The cargo market is also encouraging, with forward pricing in both Europe and Asia considerably higher than last year. Back to the shipping market though, and the supply side remains challenging due to prompt availability and a number of sublets joining the fight for spot and term business. It’s too soon to report green shoots, but owners and charterers will be watching carefully in the coming weeks. There were no newbuilding orders placed this week.

The good news is that fog has played less of a role than expected in the days following the storm- and the forecast looks promising for the time being. x: AMERICAS Last week’s winter storm halted hydrocarbons production in the Permian Basin of West Texas.  Simultaneously, feedstock deliveries to the chemical sector were stopped as that system shut down, as at the same time millions of barrels of Raw Make production was lost.  All that while the Houston Ship Channel was closed. The weather has now abated and the various systems are being returned to service much more quickly than anticipated.  Most are indicating that the lost time will be caught up with by the end of the month (if not sooner).     The EIA on Wednesday reported that propane stocks in the US drew by a surprisingly high 5.2mmbbls as of the week ending 19 Feb.  The market had assumed a draw of between 3.0 and 5.0mmbbls.  The prospect of fog remains a possibility, and with that comes the potential impact on LPG vessel transits which could limit export volumes and, therefore, inventory draws.  Meanwhile, WTI strength should foster production levels and allow propane stocks to begin recovery in Q2. Terminal fees are on the Gulf Coast are bid at 3.5cts/gal, with offers at/above 4cts/gal.  Meanwhile, though, an East Coast March fixture is believed to have occurred at 5.25cts/gal.  NWE Strength in the front of the market remains although CIF ARA has not tracked the rapid rise in Mt Belvieu. The cold weather in the US affected East Coast exports leading to a lower than anticipated volume of LPG finding it’s way to NWE from 1H March Marcus Hook. This in turn has pushed up the CIF ARA window premiums which are assessed at CIF ARA March +$11.5pmt for a 1H March TOT stem. March Propane/Naphta spread in the region is now -$44pmt the widest spread so far in 2021. x: AMERICAS Its hard to stress the severity of the winter storm that has unfolded across Texas from both an energy and more importantly humanitarian standpoint. Millions of people were left without electricity and water for days on end - and as of Thursday morning, while electricity is being restored- due to infrastructure failures- water pressure has yet to return- and a boil order remains in effect. With regard to LPG, the big question is what will be impacted on a larger scale, exports or demand. The four major terminals on the US Gulf have all been impacted, all be it to different extremes. One believes that once they are operational again, they will be able to make up for lost exports in 5 days. Another hopes to be caught up by March 1st, and a third thought they would be up and running by the weekend at the earliest, and would not be fully caught up until march at the earliest, with no spot cargos until April. The last has declared a full force majeure and will have a better idea by Friday of the timeline to recovery. With regard to domestic demand, Severe winter weather has caused nearly every major chemical complex in Texas to board up the windows. Many shut over the weekend as feedstock, power, and natural gas supply has been interrupted at many locations.  All that said, cargo discussion has not been completely neglected. A couple of Marcus Hook cargos have been offered last decade march, just below 5 cents- the seller was commanding a premium to the Gulf coast FOB’s due to logistical simplicity (weather, fog, delays etc). In the US Gulf- an all-propane FOB was being discussed much closer to four cents earlier in the week. Though that has yet to change hands and now looks less likely due to the dwindling LST/FEI arbitrage. Due to the holiday weekend, the EIA’s much-anticipated inventory report came out a day late, showing an in line with expectations draw of 2.9 million barrels.

x: LNG shipping market continues to soften this week as the nearest fixing opportunities get pushed to March and beyond. There is no hiding from the fact that the recent build up in available tonnage has caused a deep dive on the daily rates in both Atlantic and Pacific basins, as owners compete with subletters for the limited spot requirements left in the market. Furthermore, with the Lunar New Year starting this week, we don’t expect any catalyst to the current market situation in the near term especially in the East, possibly adding to the injury for those who have available tonnage in the Pacific after the winter cargoes have been discharged. All things said, it is good to remember that this ongoing correction in charter rates was anticipated, and moreover, LNG shipping market has been epitomized by high volatility and seasonality during the last few years. Thus, it is no big surprise that we see a switch in focus from spot market opportunities to term market opportunities as market participants are already starting to gauge the next winter, however there still seems to be a bit of discrepancy in the rate ideas between charterers and owners. Finally, there are no LNG newbuilding orders to report this week, but it is noteworthy that earlier in the week Qatar Petroleum reached FID on its North Field Expansion project, which may indicate a greenlight for their LNGC newbuilding programme in due course.    Wishing all our readers a Happy and Healthy Lunar New Year – Gong Xi Fa Cai!

x: AMERICAS The current US propane inventory situation can be likened to travelling down the highway in a car with a flat tire, a fuel gauge nearing empty and a dirty wind screen:  Something will soon need to change. Speculation as to the US propane inventory data release this week was enthusiastic, but the matter has been settled (for now, at least) as a stock decline of 4.508mmbbls was reported by the EIA Wednesday morning and brought the total US propane inventory level to 51.545mmbbls as of 10 Feb 2021.  Last year at the same time there were 71.822mmbbls in stocks, or a 28% decline YOY.  Domestic production was off by 38,000bbls/day to 2.37mmbls/day while Res/Com demand grew by 714,000bbls/day to 2.204mmbbls/day.  It has been cold, after all, and weather forecasts over the next week or so are calling for extreme temperatures over much of the nation. Exports (both overland and waterborne) of ~1.1mmbbls/day were recorded and seem to have been negatively impacted by a recent spate of fog along the upper Texas Gulf Coast.  The weekly export average is around the 1.6mmbbl/day range. In turn, the Days of Supply has fallen by 4.5 days to 15.6 days.  This is encroaching on historical lows, where the highest level recorded was in the 60-day range.  PADD III (Gulf Coast) stock levels fell this week by 1.726mmbbls to 28.797mmbbls.  This is significant, and additional attention should be paid any time the 30mmbbl level is breached.  PADD III stocks have fallen this year by an average of 2mmbbls per week.  At that rate – and in consideration of the massively cold weather at present – it is easy to calculate that Gulf Coast inventories will in early March be at (or near) 5-year lows.  As of midday Wednesday, however, the Mont Belvieu market showed little, if any, reaction.  Belvieu yawned, in fact, making the situation uncertain and unclear. There is a balancing point ahead: utilisation should be relatively strong as end users seek to rebuild inventories that were depleted in this winter cycle, although vessel redeliveries and the uncommitted New Buildings coming to the market in the first half of 2021 are likely to keep some pressure on term rates moving forward. t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The record-breaking start to the year continues as both the LNG and shipping markets gain strength week-on-week. Availability remains tight, and our reported headline rates combined with full three-way voyage economics are pushing TCE levels above $300,000 per day for some routes. This seasonal cycle has several factors at play, from uncertainty in demand due to Covid-19 through to cold weather, but the full examination will follow in due course; for now, buyers, sellers, charterers and owners are focussed on their exposures or opportunities. There is perhaps a glance now away from “how high will it go?” towards “how long will it last and how hard will it fall?”, but while there is backwardation in the forward curve the commodity price sits materially higher through 2021 than it did just weeks ago. Rebuilding inventories and a more conservative approach to next winter should support a more stable market once the current dynamics have played out: we should see more utilisation and less volatility on the shipping side this year than last.

x: AMERICAS Expectations that the EIA would report on Wednesday morning a draw in US propane stocks was unanimous, though the anticipated rate of decline was contested.  Some were forecasting a 2mmbbl draw, while others were predicting as much as a 6mmbbl decline.  Historically, the largest single weekly draw occurred in Jan 2017 when stocks fell by 7.188mmbbls.     The EIA yesterday reported a 6.7mmbbl draw, surprising most and prompting discussions related to minimum comfort levels of propane inventories in the US.  As of last Friday there were 66mmbbls ‘in tank’, and there are another 9 weeks of winter-related demand (with winter ending mid-March).  History shows that stocks have declined on a weekly basis from between 1.1mmbbls/day to 2.4mmbbls/day.  At 1.1mmbls day a ~10mmbbl draw can be anticipated, at which point stocks will have fallen to 56mmbbls.  If, however, stocks decline at a rate of 2.4mmbbls/day, ~22mmbbls will be removed stocks and overall stocks will have fallen to 44mmbbls.   It is when stocks dip below around 30mmbbls that inventory difficulties are typically encountered, so unless an unusual series of events occurs it seems unlikely at this point that stocks will fall to jeopardized levels – particularly if crude oil prices are on the rise which should bolster domestic production levels.  Furthermore, according to the EIA,propane production rose by 83,000bbls/day to 2.34mmbbls/day as of last week.   The issue, however, is not necessarily the condition of the overall stock levels, but those on along the US Gulf Coast – in PADD III – which includes much of the production areas, but also most of the exporting sites.  There are, as of last week, 34.96mmbbls inn PADD III, down by a significant volume of 4.279mmbbls week-over-week.   Of course the price of the molecules themselves will ultimately have a say in the matter.  Mont Belvieu propane values very quickly (and rather predictably) rose after the release of the EIA data, climbing quickly to 90cts/gal for prompt barrels.  Perhaps the weather (or lack thereof) in the US will finally have a hand in the matter, too.

The Majors and LNG Traders doesn’t appear to be to dishearten by the current shipping rate levels as they themselves are trading the JKTC market at prices we haven’t seen since Feb 2014.

The recent record level of LPG exports has renewed fears of insufficient domestic inventory to see out the winter. If draws averaging 3 million barrels a week occur until build season (1st week of April, 12 weeks) we will be left with 37 million barrels in inventories. Tight! This fear pushed Mt Belvieu propane up to 70% WTI before Saudi Aramco announced they would cut oil production by 1 million barrels per day from Feb 1st. Lack of VLGC availability is set to leave US export tons unsold in January. A double whammy of reducing export volumes and building inventories. The question is will Mt Belvieu propane value strengthen so much as to destroy demand, or will US inventories remain manageable  and keep propane arbs open?

n: LNG Market Report
x: As we look back on the LNG shipping market throughout this year, it would be fair to say that most market participants were surprised, some very pleased by the rate levels seen in the last couple of months. Going back to the first half of 2020, sentiments were certainly softer for Q4 and the majority would not have envisaged fixtures being concluded at current levels. A colder winter with increasing demand for LNG in North East Asia particularly in China and the continual strength seen on the product prices are supporting an arbitrage for West to East trades, contributing to the solid demand for shipping. Challenges to secure slots through the Panama Canal have also resulted in longer waiting times, further tightening the market. As we edge closer to 2021, the lack of tonnage and clarity on vessel availability means there are still a couple of cargoes to be work for 1H February loading. Shipping remains tight for now and with JKM rising for the forward month and owners fueled by optimism, we are anticipating levels to remain buoyant.    On recent newbuildings, both HHI and SHI were reported to have secured a total of 17 LNG carriers with four shipowners, although with some conditions on the contracts. The newbuilds were reported to be allocated to the Mozambique LNG project. 2020 will end as a very good year for shipyards with a total close to 50 conventional LNG carriers.  From everyone at Fearnley LNG, wishing you a happy, healthy and prosperous new year !

n: LNG Market Report
x: Firm market conditions remain but with many expected to take some well-earned rest after a long year, we could see activity wane in the last two weeks of 2020. Bids continue to flood in for vessels with prompt availability and the drag from the Pacific into the Atlantic continues to be the preference for Owners. Those with Pacific requirement remain at battle against strong duration at high levels in the Atlantic. Tonnage opening in late January could be a cause of concern as current backwardation on the cargo side shortens opportunities for trade return at current freight levels. However, the prompt market is likely to continue to hold until we see the fixing window shift into play with increase of tonnage expected. Rates are likely to hover around current levels for now, but sublet availability could put a slight soft tone on rates towards end of winter period.  The newbuilding market remains active: at least four new 174,000cbm have been inked in this week, two will be built at Samsung Heavy, and two at HSHI. Despite a recent influx in orders, we are currently still down from the 19 orders placed in December last year.  For those who celebrate, a very merry Christmas from all of us here at Fearnley LNG.

x: AMERICAS As the US market begins it wind down to the end of 2020, a number of big questions remain. First and foremost being will propane production remain at 2.3 million barrels per day as it has for most of the 4th quarter. If so, despite the huge export numbers which have become the norm,  there should be enough propane to sustain the exports, the domestic petchem market,  and the retail demand. The second big question is will freight rates remain at these near-record levels, and to this, we can answer yes. We do not see any end in sight to the Panama canal delays, the US export levels, and the intensive drydock schedule.  And finally, the last big question is will the world continue to need US exports, even at a higher price, and once again the answer is yes. Thus with positive answers to all of the above, we expect the arb to stay open and record exports to continue. In South America Brasil continues to be a regular spot buyer taking at least one spot VLGC per month, while Mexico has yet to appear as a winter buyer as we expect they will..

t: LNG Market Report
n: LNG Market Report
x: The LNG market continues to stay boiling hot (ironically) as the Far East and the Middle-East delivered LNG prices hit new multiyear highs almost every day now, while short coverers and end-users are scrambling to find cargoes in the region. This in turn has caused the LNG shipping market to move from high-speed to hyperdrive, as every promptly available vessel gets taken in a heartbeat causing the global vessel availability to look very scarce indeed over the next month. Naturally, this tightness of available vessels have spiked up the charter rates, which have also reached levels that were last seen only during the peak winter of 2018. Furthermore, with new vessel requirements emerging this week to cover February liftings, we do expect this tightness to drag out a bit longer than we predicted just a few months back. That said, even if the first two months of 2021 look tight, we are still holding the view that vessel supply and demand will balance out before the end of Q1. On the newbuilding front, it was reported this week that Hyundai Heavy Industries have inked another four new LNG newbuilding contracts, two with Pan Ocean, one with Knutsen OAS and one with JP Morgan. All of these newbuilds are 174,000cbm and highly-equipped with XDF propulsion systems, and will be long-term chartered by Shell. With these new contracts, Shell’s total LNGC newbuilding tally stands at 18 modern XDF vessels, all being built by HHI.

x: The sense of market optimism radiates throughout the world as stock markets reach “all time high” and COVID-19 vaccines are issued out to citizens of various countries, contributing to the sense of hope to get back to normal times. In parallel, the buoyancy amongst the LNG players are increasingly evident as cargo prices continues to escalate, leading to trading opportunities for LNG traders, producers and buyers alike. LNG shipowners and sub-letters are currently enjoying the relatively firm charter rate levels in the markets which may be prolonged if the relatively strong demand for LNG continues. It is not implausible to expect the arbitrage to open, to pave way for more inter-basin spot trades where increased tonne-miles would maintain the tightening of the shipping market throughout this winter.   As the year is about to end, LNG buyers and producers are now close to complete their annual delivery programme. This could further reveal potential shipping requirements and/or availability for sub-let in gas year 2021. Despite a mere three weeks to the end of 2020, most certainly the intensity of LNG and shipping trades seems not to be tapering down short term.  No new LNG vessel orders were reported this week. However, one owner may have retired the 1981-built Pacific Energy and 1984-built Atlantic Energy as these vintage vessels were reported sold for demolition after being in lay-up for some years.

Activity and shipping requirements remain at high levels, but lack of available shipping, especially in Atlantic, combined with Panama delays, has turned charterers enquiring for Atlantic liftings to look East of Suez for tonnage. x: AMERICAS A relatively small – but nonetheless generally expected - decline of 844,000bbls in domestic US propane inventories left stock levels at 91.718mmbbls overall, which compares to the late-Nov 2019 total of 86.443mmbbls, a difference of more than 5mmbbls.  Overwater exports of propane during the period were reckoned to have improved to a robust level of around 1.5mmbbls/day while production was effectively flat at 2.291mmbbls/day, according to the DOE.    Most of the terminals are running well at this point, though a day or so of fog on both the Houston Ship Channel and in Freeport was recorded this week.  And while this has left a number of vessels waiting offshore, the terminals themselves report little disruption as they’ve become adept at managing their respective facilities during the (mostly) short-lived but periodic waterway closures.  The weather in North America has heretofore been relatively mild, but a healthy dose of Arctic air has by now descended and blanketed much of the Midwest and Northeast.  Still, however, NOAA are calling for a generally mild winter overall, with better-than-average chances for above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation.  If that prediction were to be realized, then reduced weather-related demand should likely allow the rate of decline of propane stock levels to slow, the weight of which should then cause MB values to soften and – in turn – support an open arb.  Exceedingly bullish freight rates, however, will likely play a role in the outcome, however.  Petrochemical consumption of propane is reported for November to have been upwards of 300,000bbls/day, where Dec is likely to decline towards the upper 200,000bbl/day range, though expectations of even lower rates were discussed for Dec.

Although there has been a short plateau in rates, requirements continue to surface as vessel positions firm up and ships are fixed with little idle time. Tight availability thus persists globally and is expected to remain light, as the wave of fixtures earlier this month will see ships employed through December and into the New Year. The regional imbalance continues with very few vessels in the Atlantic, and Panama Canal delays and longer voyages delivering into the colder winter in the East exacerbating the issue. There were reports of cancellations of January cargoes loading out the US Gulf, due in part to a lack of available shipping.  Views looking further into 2021 are more pessimistic, as reflected by the difference in spot and one year levels. Owners seeking utilisation over spot exposure may move to avoid competing with uncommitted new arrivals next year and the redelivery of existing tonnage. On the new building market it has been reported that Shell is adding to it’s tally of vessels by signing up shipowners to berths is has reserved in South Korea taking the total from 14 vessels up to 18.

x: The past week saw an open Arbitrage between the East and the West, which prompted several opportunistic traders to take on tonnage for US Gulf loadings. With the Atlantic basin so tight vessels had to be taken from the East, which locked in full utilisation at round-trip economics or more for these fixtures. Such longer charters are currently attractive to owners, with the knock-on effect being an uptick in headline rates and continuing three-way economics for shorter, intra-basin business. Both owners and charterers are looking at the fundamentals carefully for directional signs in the weeks ahead, and with low prompt availability, high feed gas into the US terminals and positive developments on the Covid-19 front we do expect the current conditions to last in the short term. Further out, a number of vessels redeliver from mid-December, but coming off the West-to-East convey belt the global availability will likely remain unbalanced.

x: AMERICAS Per the EIA report of this morning (which was delayed by a day), US propane inventories fell from 95.828mmbbls at end Oct to 94.889mmbbls as of 06 Nov, a decline of 939,000bbls.  A build of 812,000bbls was achieved in PADD I (US East Coast), and an increase of 305,000bbls was seen in PADD II (Midwest).  The Gulf Coast, however, saw a draw of 2.033mmbbls, on the basis of both stronger petrochemical demand and swelling overwater export volumes.   November marks the 6th straight month of improved propane consumption, having steadily climbed from 184,000bbls/day in May to 324,000bbls/day in Nov.  Overwater exports, meanwhile, continue to dominate – with more than 4m tons of LPG’s exported from the US in Nov (3.5m tons propane and nearly 700,000mt of butane).  At present there are no signs that the trend will abate, as the December rosters are largely complete. Buyers are eager to engage as the arb to the East is open, but sellers (most of whom appear to be re-sellers), are holding at robust terminalling fee rates.   Weather-related demand in the US came early, but for the moment seems to have left early, as well.  NOAA updated its prognosis for North America which (again) shows a propensity for a warmer-than-average temperature forecast over the Nov/Dec/Jan period, which doesn’t necessarily preclude the possibility of cold spells, but indicates the likelihood of a generally warmer winter which could, in turn, lead to softer domestic values.  That, however, may be decided – at least in part, and on a short term basis – by the petchem sector and, most importantly, exports. Finally , strong demand from Mexico and Brasil is continuing and looks like that will be the case through the first quarter of 2021.

x: Over the past few weeks, the LNG market have seen an upward trajectory on the spot shipping rates. The bullish sentiment resonated in the lack of availability for November loading which saw daily charter rates broke into the six figure barrier.  However, the current levels seem to be short-lived as activities and vessel requirements have decrease simultaneously in both basins.  The weaker performance of the product market, the decline in requirements for shipping and an increase in availability not just from Independent Owners but sublets shown by Portfolio players and Traders, have all contributed to the sentiment change. At the present moment, with so much uncertainty that could affect the overall shipping market, volatility is inevitable for the coming weeks.   From an analytical perspective, the area of concern is after Q1 2021 where many anticipate a slightly more challenging market. Utilization may be a priority versus rates and as we have already seen from recent fixtures, Owners were more willing to work requirements with longer periods to brace through the shouldering months ahead after this winter rather than working spot charters at current levels.   In the new building market, It was reported an Owner have secured two 174,000 cbm LNGC plus options for two additional vessels from Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI). The orders are at the back of time charter contracts concluded with PGNiG. The new building LNG carriers will be delivered in 2023 and is expected to lift volumes from Calcasieu Pass Terminal which PGNiG is procuring the LNG under long term contact.

x: The LNG shipping market slowed to catch its breath at the start of this week after the frantic finish of last. Many Charterers gave pause for thought as we saw the enquiry escalate as last week moved on, and this week Owners with availability kept the pressure up knowing there is a genuine lack of available tonnage ahead to match the current requirement. Owing to this, rates firmed into six figures in both basins. Tonnage Owners currently looking for employment continue to hold out in hope that the gains some have made are mirrored for the vessels they have opening. However, some of these marketed cargoes cannot support such high freight levels and as such, several Charterers looked at FOB options to move their product. Those with shipping in place, and the ability to purchase FOB, will be seeing strong gains as delivered prices in North East Asia jumped as end-users seek coverage for an anticipated cold winter. Despite the lack of activity early on this week, sentiment remains firm with Owners and backed with some robust fundamentals, especially within the Cargo market, this lull is likely to be short lived and activity is expected to ramp up again. In sale and purchase, no newbuilds have been reported this week and pressure on prices continue.

x: Winter for the year is establishing nicely for cargo owners and shipowners alike. Activities are ramping up as LNG prices are on the rise in the Far East, in anticipation of a relatively cold winter as compared to the previous years. Charter rates have risen substantially versus levels merely a month ago, and spot fixtures are concluded basis more than the standard round-trip. There have been a string of fixtures concluded and quite a few more being worked on this week, and remaining available vessels may not be open for long. We hear that the number of shipping enquiries received by players with available tonnage have heightened considerably and this is creating interesting opportunities for fleet optimization, cargo sales and freight trading. The winter market has only started and it remains to be seen where shipping rate levels could end up to in the weeks to come.  No newbuilding orders or ship sales have been reported this week.

Last year the mid-Oct stock levels were recorded at 95.282mmbbls.  This week’s decline in stocks and the simultaneous arrival of a cold front in the US Midwest appears to mark the commencement of the winter-demand season, but MB values have nonetheless drifted because of declines in the crude arena.  US exports remain robust, with Oct anticipated to see near-record level monthly lifting volume of 74 VLGC cargos.  Shipping delays at the Sabine River on the Gulf Coast are being overcome inasmuch as there were 6 VLGC’s awaiting transit yesterday, but 4 of those ships have resumed movement as of this morning.  Meanwhile, delays at the Panama Canal are presently reported at 8 days and are occurring primarily due to C19-related safety measures (specifically social distancing efforts and minimized crew numbers), but also to fog (10 days in Sep and 8 days – so far – in Oct) and the simultaneous occurrence of higher grain and LNG vessel passages.  Big ship freight rates from the US/Asia remain in the $103-105/mt range, while to Europe rates are pegged at $53/mt which is impacting the netback levels.

x: It has been another busy week in the LNG shipping market as the anticipated Q4 activity is really ramping up. LNG cargo prices are on a rapid rise in the Far East as buyers have started to secure their early winter cargoes in expectation of a colder winter. This has made disponent owners to think twice before subletting their vessels out since the risk of finding yourself short, or in the mercy of tighter shipping market, has gone up. Also, the possibility of arbitrage opening between the West and the East has increased, and capturing that potentially short period might only be available to those with enough length in their shipping portfolio. Aforementioned is also reflected in the current elevated spot shipping rates, with especially the East of Suez seeing highest demand for tonnage whereas the West of Suez is tightening up quickly, but still lacking slightly behind due to a few uncertainties, such as the latest hurricane aftermath to some of the USG liquefaction plants. During these times it is however good to remember that the final quarter has been historically the most volatile period within the calendar year, and this seems to be true even in this extraordinary year of 2020, and by the looks of it, we might have very interesting weeks ahead. In the newbuilding side, it was reported that DSME has signed firm contracts to build six Arc7- ice class LNG carriers for two separate European companies with delivery expected in 2H 2023.

Looking ahead, we see risk in potential sublet availability being withdrawn and with the expected restart of Hammerfest, US Gulf back to “normal”, we may see additional tightness in the Atlantic basin. As a consequence, Charterers may have to look at positioning tonnage from the East and coupled with a winter market approaching – it may result in further spot charter rate increases, which should not be a big surprise as it is seasonally “normal” this time of the year.
